Series Preface
Contemporary Food Engineering
Food engineering is the multidisciplinary field of applied physical sciences combined
with the knowledge of product properties. Food engineers provide the technological
knowledge transfer essential to the cost-effective production and commercialization
of food products and services. In particular, food engineers develop and design pro-
cesses and equipment in order to convert raw agricultural materials and ingredi-
ents into safe, convenient, and nutritious consumer food products. However, food
engineering topics are continuously undergoing changes to meet diverse consumer
demands, and the subject is being rapidly developed to reflect market needs.
In the development of food engineering, one of the many challenges is to employ
modern tools and knowledge, such as computational materials science and nano-
technology, to develop new products and processes. At the same time, improving
quality, safety, and security remain critical issues in food engineering study. New
packaging materials and techniques are being developed to provide more protec-
tion to foods, and novel preservation technologies are emerging to enhance food
security and defense. Additionally, process control and automation regularly appear
among the top priorities identified in food engineering. Advanced monitoring and
control systems are developed to facilitate automation and flexible food manufac-
turing. Furthermore, energy saving and minimization of environmental problems
continue to be important food engineering issues, and significant progress is being
made in waste management, efficient utilization of energy, and reduction of effluents
and emissions in food production.
Consisting of edited books, the Contemporary Food Engineering book series
attempts to address some of the recent developments in food engineering. Advances
in classical unit operations in engineering applied to food manufacturing are cov-
ered, as well as such topics as progress in the transport and storage of liquid and solid
```
foods; heating, chilling, and freezing of foods; mass transfer in foods; chemical and
```
```
biochemical aspects of food engineering and the use of kinetic analysis; dehydration,
```
thermal processing, nonthermal processing, extrusion, liquid food concentration,
```
membrane processes, and applications of membranes in food processing; shelf-life,
```
electronic indicators in inventory management, and sustainable technologies in food
```
processing; and packaging, cleaning, and sanitation. The books are aimed at profes-
```
sional food scientists, academics researching food engineering problems, and gradu-
ate level students.
The editors of the books are leading engineers and scientists from many parts
of the world. All the editors were asked to present their books in a manner that
will address the market need and pinpoint the cutting-edge technologies in food
x Series Preface
engineering. Furthermore, all contributions are written by internationally renowned
experts who have both academic and professional credentials. All authors have
attempted to provide critical, comprehensive, and readily accessible information on
the art and science of a relevant topic in each chapter, with reference lists to be used
by readers for further information. Therefore, each book can serve as an essential
reference source to students and researchers in universities and research institutions.

Preface
Vinegar is the acidic product produced by spontaneous or controlled mixed fermen-
tation by yeasts and acetic acid bacteria. It is known to humanity since antiquity as
an important condiment, food preservative, as well as an ingredient of traditional
remedies. It is currently produced worldwide using various raw materials, such as
fruit juices, grains/malt, sugarcane, honey, agricultural production surpluses, etc.,
while any material that contains fermentable sugars can be used for vinegar produc-
tion. Legislation in some countries defines as vinegars only those products obtained
from the fermentation of agricultural products, to distinguish them from dilute acetic
acid formulations. Depending on the raw materials as well as on the specific produc-
tion and ageing technologies used, there is a considerable variation in the quality of
vinegar products, reflected in a corresponding variation in pricing. The raw materi-
als vary greatly, ranging from side-streams of agricultural production to high-quality
substrates that can lead to unique and expensive products of protected origin, such as
some Italian and Spanish balsamic vinegars.
There are two main biochemical processes involved in vinegar production: the
```
alcoholic fermentation by yeasts and the acetous fermentation or acetification (etha-
```
```
nol oxidation) by acetic acid bacteria. The second is particularly sensitive to process
```
parameters, such as the fermentation temperature, type of starter cultures, substrate
composition, and oxygen supply, which critically affect the industrial production
efficiency, cost, and the overall product quality.
In industrial vinegar production, there are generally three main types of meth-
```
ods involved: the slow, handcrafted, traditional method (“Orléans” or “French”
```
```
method), the faster “generator” method, and the rapid “submerged” method. Despite
```
the plenitude of scientific knowledge that currently exists on vinegar production,
the industry mainly employs the traditional, batch, submerged fermentation method,
```
the centerpiece of which is the “acetator” (vinegar fermenter). Commercially avail-
```
able acetators are tanks usually equipped with temperature, aeration, and pressure
control units, alcohol and acidity measuring probes, defoamers, etc., and may differ
widely according to the seasonal production requirements or the different types of
```
raw materials and products. Solid-state fermentation (SSF) methods are also used in
```
some Asian countries to produce vinegar from grains. These methods include addi-
tional steps for starch liquefaction and saccharification.
The current trend is to fuse traditional techniques with state-of-the-art technolo-
gies, and a variety of approaches have been evaluated to increase vinegar fermen-
tation efficiency and reduce production cost and fermentation time. Most of these
efforts focus on ensuring a controlled environment regarding the process conditions
and also suggest that the use of carefully selected and cultured bacteria is essential.
The proposed acetification systems include recycling of the fermenting substrates,
application of successive discontinuous cycles, continuous operation, and use of
immobilized cell techniques. Engineering advances on acetators also aim to reduce
problems associated with scale-up oxygen diffusion.
xiv Preface
This book aims to report and discuss all the recent innovations and applica-
tions on vinegar production technologies, as well their advantages or disadvantages
compared to the traditional submerged fermentation systems. The new trends on
raw materials, substrate pre-treatment strategies, alcoholic fermentation, and ace-
tification systems are reviewed and discussed. Innovations on online monitoring of
processes, post-fermentation treatments, as well as chemical composition analysis,
metabolomics, modern techniques for classification, authentication, and fraud con-
trol of vinegar products, and life cycle assessment in the vinegar sector are also
highlighted and discussed.
The health benefits of vinegars are also presented and discussed, which, along
with the development of classification and authentication methods, constitute the
major part of the current scientific research on vinegar.
Most of the data used to compile this book derive from the current scientific lit-
erature, almost exclusively from the past decade, with special reference to previous
significant published works on vinegars. Information was also retrieved from the
```
World Wide Web (based on availability and accessibility, and randomly selected), on
```
products, techniques, and equipment available for the vinegar industry needs, includ-
```
ing specifications, intended uses, application instructions, and (claimed) advantages,
```
as offered by the respective commercial providers in the form of technical sheets.
Finally, a list of references and suggested readings is provided at the end of each
chapter to guide further study.

Editor Bio
Dr. Argyro Bekatorou, born in Greece in 1972, is an
academic and food science researcher at the Department of
```
Chemistry of the University of Patras (ChemUP) in Western
```
Greece. She obtained her Diploma in Chemistry in 1995
from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece,
and in 2001 she received her PhD in Food Science from
ChemUP. In 2001, she worked as a postdoctoral researcher in
the area of environmental microbiology and biotechnology
at the School of Biomedical Sciences of the University of
Ulster, in Northern Ireland, UK, and from 2002 to 2006 she
worked at ChemUP as a full-time researcher and part-time lecturer. In 2006, she was
appointed a full-time lecturer and since 2018 she has been an associate professor of
food chemistry and technology at ChemUP. She has supervised five PhD theses, par-
ticipated in many funded competitive research projects, is an active reviewer in more
than 25 scientific journals, and is co-author of 85 research papers in peer-reviewed
```
international scientific journals (based on Scopus, 2019), 15 book chapters, more
```
than 125 National/International Conference presentations, and 2 patents.
Her research interests lie in the area of the chemistry and technology of fermented
```
foods (alcoholic beverages, dairy products, probiotics, fermented cereal products,
```
```
etc.), the biotechnological exploitation of agri-food wastes and side-streams for the
```
```
production of novel foods, and products of added-value (ethanol, organic acids, sin-
```
```
gle cell protein and oil, etc.), and the application of immobilized cells technology in
```
food bioprocess development and scale-up.

1
History and Current
Issues of Vinegar
Seng Joe Lim, Chin Wai Ho, Azwan Mat Lazim,
and Shazrul Fazry
1.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar is a liquid product that consists of 4% or more acetic acid, which is com-
monly used and consumed, either directly or as an ingredient in food. Vinegar is
traditionally produced by two-stage fermentation systems, i.e., the alcoholic fermen-
tation of sugary substrates, and subsequently, the acetous fermentation of the ethanol
```
into acetic acid (Ho et al., 2017a). The commonly used raw materials or substrates of
```
```
the fermentation for vinegar production are fruit, such as apples and grapes (grape
```
```
must) (Plessi et al., 2006; Lea, 2012), and other plant sources, such as rice, malt, sug-
```
```
arcane, and other carbohydrate containing materials (Shimoji et al., 2002; Kocher et
```
```
al., 2006; Liu and Yang, 2006). In this chapter, the history, geography, definitions,
```
uses, market and statistics, legislation, authentication issues, health effects/func-
tional components, and current trends in vinegar production are briefly highlighted
and discussed. These issues of vinegar production and quality are discussed in more
detail in the subsequent chapters.

2 Advances in Vinegar Production
1.2 HISTORY AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF VINEGAR
The word “vinegar” came from the words “vin” and “aigre,” which literally means
```
“sour wine” in French. That in turn, came from the Latin term “vinum acre” (sour
```
```
wine) or “vinum acetum” (wine vinegar). In many cultures worldwide, vinegar has
```
been used as a seasoning or preservative agent in various food products as well as a
```
drink after dilution with water (Tesfaye et al., 2002). Thus, vinegar is intentionally
```
brewed for such purposes. However, it is interesting to note that in ancient times,
vinegar was seen as a food by-product made by the spoilage of wine due to contact
```
with air (Ho et al., 2017a). The history of vinegar dates back to 10,000 years ago
```
```
(Conner and Allgeier, 1976; Ho et al., 2017a), and its occurrence always coincided
```
```
with wine-making, during which the ancient civilizations (Persians, Egyptians, and
```
```
Mesopotamians) had observed that wines turn sour when exposed to air (Mazza and
```
```
Murooka, 2009).
```
Over the centuries, the use of vinegar was portrayed in both historical records and
```
popular literatures. Babylonian records (5000 bc) indicated that the fruit of the date
```
```
palm (instead of figs or grapes) were used as the main raw ingredient for wine and
```
vinegar making. Another interesting fact is that the Babylonians intentionally used
vinegars for pickling and food preservation. In the Mediterranean cultures circa the
```
12th century bc, vinegar became an extensively used and consumed product (Mazza
```
```
and Murooka, 2009).
```
```
In ancient Greece, Hippocrates (460–377 bc), a Greek physician often regarded as
```
the “Father of Medicine,” recommended the use of vinegar for cleaning ulcerations
```
and for the treatment of sores (Johnston and Gaas, 2006). Later, in the Roman empire
```
```
(58–50 bc), Julius Caesar wrote in his book, De Bello Gallico (his first-hand account
```
```
of the Gallic Wars), that vinegar was consumed by Roman soldiers as a beverage
```
mixed with water. The drink was described as highly refreshing and safer than water
alone, due to its antimicrobial activity in water of doubtful quality that was collected
```
in foreign lands (Mazza and Murooka, 2009).
```
During the 8th to 12th centuries in Japan, the Samurai warriors used to con-
```
sume vinegar as a tonic beverage for power and strength (Liu et al., 2014). In China,
```
```
Sung Tse (1186–1249), often regarded as the founding father of forensic science,
```
recommended the washing of hands with sulfur and vinegar to avoid infections dur-
```
ing autopsies (Chan et al., 1994). In the Middle Ages, during the outbreak of the
```
1348 plague, the famous Italian physician and Professor of Medicine, Tommaso Del
Garbo, suggested the washing of hands, face, and mouth with vinegar to protect the
```
public from infections (Mazza and Murooka, 2009). Later, the second president of
```
```
USA, John Adams (1735–1826), was known for drinking hard apple cider for break-
```
fast every day. The fact that he lived to 91 was considered a testimony that regular
```
apple cider vinegar consumption contributes to longevity (Liu et al., 2014).
```
In the 18th century, a French chemist named Durande made an important scien-
tific improvement by successfully concentrating dilute acetic acid from vinegar, to
obtain the product that was named “glacial acetic acid.”
Various important developments for industrial vinegar production took place from
the 14th century. Prior to that, vinegars were mainly produced as home-made products,
at inadequate amounts to cover the growing demands. On the 28th of October 1394,
3History and Current Issues of Vinegar
a corporation named Vinaigriers moutardiers sauciers distillateurs en eau-de-vie
et esprit-de-vin buffetiers was established in Orléans, France. This corporation,
believed to be the oldest in the world that specialized in vinegar making, developed
a vinegar production method, called the “Orléans process.” The Orléans process is
sometimes referred to as the “slow process,” due to the long time required for vin-
egar production, which could take up to several months to complete. Interestingly,
this process is still in use today, consisting of the addition of the “Mother of vin-
egar” in wine inside a barrel for the acetous fermentation to occur. When the desired
acidity and flavor is achieved, the vinegar is removed from the top, and then the
same volume of fresh wine is added for a successive fermentation batch. In this way
```
the production of vinegar is carried out repeatedly and continuously (Mazza and
```
```
Murooka, 2009).
```
As the demand for vinegar increased, newer and faster processes were invented.
Specifically, in Germany in 1823, Schutzenbach introduced the “generator” pro-
cess, which shortened the production of vinegar to 3–7 days. The centerpiece of the
generator process is the fermentation vessel called the “vinegar generator,” which
consists of a large container with two chambers separated by a screen. The largest
upper chamber, where the fermentation takes place, is packed with solid materials,
usually wood shavings, that carry the acetic acid bacteria. Air is blown through the
screen to the upper chamber for better oxygen diffusion, thus increasing the rate of
the acetous fermentation. The produced vinegar is filtered through the screen and
```
collected through the lower chamber of the generator (Ho et al., 2017a).
```
Another vinegar manufacturing method was also developed in Germany
by Hromatka in 1955, called the “submerged” acetification, which integrates
improved aeration and stirring methods to shorten the production time. Specifically,
high-speed motors are used to supply air and stir the suspension of acetic acid bac-
```
teria in the fermentation tank (the “acetator”), increasing the oxygen content and
```
thus accelerating the oxidation of alcohol to acetic acid. Three main phases are
distinguished in this method: the loading of raw materials and the inoculation of
starter culture, the fermentation process accommodated by strong aeration, and the
collection of the fermented product, the vinegar. Today, acetators with capacity of
```
10,000–40,000 liters are commonly available (Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
More details about the main acetification methods (Orléans, generator, and sub-
```
```
merged) are provided in Chapter 6 (Current Industrial Vinegar Production: Acetators,
```
```
Processes and Consumables).
```

1.4 USES OF VINEGAR
Historically, vinegar was considered a by-product of wine making, due to wine oxi-
dation that rendered it useless. However, through human observations and innovation
over the centuries, the usefulness of vinegar became apparent. As discussed in the
previous section, the Babylonians intentionally used vinegars for pickling and pre-
serving food, while other cultures used vinegars as disinfectants and for their health
promoting effects. Today, these uses of vinegars have somewhat remained the same.
As the composition of vinegars was unveiled through scientific studies, it was
found that besides acetic acid as a major component, vinegars also contain a wide
variety of phenolic compounds, vitamins, and other bioactive molecules, depending
on the raw materials used and the applied fermentation parameters. These com-
pounds were found to possess health promoting effects, and thus, vinegars are today
marketed as healthy beverages, which can be consumed directly or in diluted form.
Vinegars also serve as condiments, e.g., balsamic vinegar is perfectly combined with
olive oil to produce dips and salad dressings.
In addition to being consumed directly, vinegars are applied in various food prod-
ucts, such as in the formulation of condiments and sauces, including mustard, ketch-
ups, and mayonnaise. Vinegar is also a significant aid in cooking, as it provides an
interesting acidic taste and aroma to food. In a more trivial form, potato chips with salt
and vinegar flavor are marketed by major brands worldwide. In this case, the vinegar
is sprayed over a porous matrix, e.g., maltodextrin or modified starch, and the mixture
5History and Current Issues of Vinegar
is dried and powdered and used to flavor the chips. A mixture of sodium acetate and
vinegar in dry form can also be used. Some other acids, such as citric, malic, tartaric,
and lactic acid may be additionally used in such products to add flavor and texture.
Vinegar is also used for the pickling of a wide range of products, from fruits to
vegetables and meats. Pickling is a preservation method, where sensitive and fast
spoiling food is immersed in vinegar, sugar, and/or salt to prevent it from spoilage.
The high acidity of vinegar prevents microbial growth, making it ideal as a preserva-
tive agent. At the same time, vinegar adds flavor to the pickled products. Examples of
products suitable for pickling with vinegar are lettuce, cabbage, cucumber, beetroot,
carrots, olives, and other fruit and vegetables, as well as animal products such as
fish, meat, and sausages. Due to its acidity, vinegar is also commonly incorporated
in marinades to tenderize meat.
Moreover, vinegars have many non-food applications, such as the use as cleaning
and disinfectant agents, owing these properties to their high acidity level. One such
example is the use of vinegar to remove mineral deposits in kitchen and bathroom
faucets, appliances, and fixtures, since acetic acid can dissolve minerals and remove
them from the surface of these items. The ability of acetic acid to dissolve miner-
```
als and, to some extent, metals was reported in a study by Choi et al. (2012), which
```
concluded that wood vinegar can be used to extract chromium, copper, and arsenic
from chromated copper arsenate-treated wood, demonstrating its potential to replace
synthetic chemicals for metal elements removal from treated wood waste.
Another non-food application of vinegar is its use as disinfectant, which makes it
a good household cleaner. Wiping and spraying vinegar on wood panels is one of the
techniques used to prevent mold growth on furniture, which is a problem especially
```
evident in tropical climates. Baimark and Niamsa (2009) reported that the use of
```
wood vinegar as coagulating and antifungal agent for natural rubber sheets is effec-
tive, without compromising the natural rubber properties. The advantages of using
vinegar rather than synthetic chemicals are obvious, as vinegar is an inexpensive
product, functional for cleaning and disinfecting, and non-toxic.
1.5 DEFINITIONS AND LEGISLATION ON VINEGAR
```
According to Ho et al. (2017a) (adapted; copyright permission granted), the Codex
```
Alimentarius Commission defines vinegar as the liquid that is fit for human con-
sumption and that is exclusively produced from suitable products containing starch
or sugars or starch and sugars by a double fermentation process, i.e., alcoholic and
acetous fermentation. Vinegar shall not contain more than 0.5% alcohol, and stabi-
lizer is not permitted for use in fermented vinegars according to European law. The
```
vinegar itself shall not contain less than 50 grams per liter (w/v) of acetic acid (Codex
```
```
Alimentarius Commission, 1987; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mentions that vinegar is made by
```
the alcoholic and subsequent acetous fermentation of fruit juice and that there are no
standards of vinegar identity established under the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic
Act. However, the FDA considers that a satisfactory guideline for natural vinegars is
```
that they must contain an excess of 4 grams of acetic acid per 100 mL (FDA, 1977;
```
```
Ho et al., 2017a).
```
6 Advances in Vinegar Production
The European Union defines vinegar as a product produced by the double fer-
```
mentation (alcoholic and acetous) of substances of agricultural origin. Raw materials
```
such as wine, cider, malt, rice mash, whey, concentrated grape must, and various
```
kinds of spirits can be utilized (Erbe and Brückner, 1998; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
In France, vinegar is called “vinaigre,” which translates to “sour wine,” as also
mentioned above. The vinaigre can be made from almost any fermentable carbohy-
drate source, including but not limited to wines, molasses, dates, apples, pears, ber-
ries, beer, and honey. It should be fermented by yeast to convert the natural sugars to
alcohol, followed by conversion of the alcohol to acetic acid by acetic acid bacteria
```
(Acetobacter) (Johnston and Gaas, 2006; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
The Food Standards Australia New Zealand Code-Standard 2.10.1, which is the stan-
dard for vinegar and related products, defines vinegar as the sour liquid prepared by the
acetous fermentation with or without alcoholic fermentation of any suitable foodstuff and
includes blends and mixtures of vinegar. This vinegar must contain not less than 40 g/kg
```
of acetic acid (Food Standards Australia New Zealand Act, 1991; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
According to the Malaysian Food Act 1983 and Food Regulation 1985, vinegar is
defined as a liquid product prepared from the alcoholic fermentation and subsequent
acetous fermentation of any suitable food. The act also dictates that the vinegar itself
```
shall not contain less than 4% weight per volume (w/v) of acetic acid and shall not
```
contain any mineral acid. The vinegar may also contain permitted preservatives,
```
caramel as a coloring substance, and spices as permitted flavoring substances (Food
```
```
Regulations Malaysia, 1985; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (2012) states that vinegars
```
are products obtained by the alcoholic and acetic acid fermentation of any suitable
medium such as fruit, malt, or molasses, with or without the addition of caramel
and spices. They shall not be fortified with acetic acid. The acidity, calculated as the
```
acetic acid content, shall not be less than 3.75% (m/v), the total solids (m/v) shall not
```
```
be less than 1.5%, and the total ash content shall not be less than 0.18% (Food Safety
```
```
and Standards Authority of India, 2012; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
In Korea, the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) establishes food stan-
```
dards and specifications for vinegar production, according to which vinegar refers to
```
(1) brewed vinegar that is produced by fermenting grains, fruits, or alcoholic drinks,
```
or by mixing and ripening them with a grain-saccharified solution or fruit juice, or
```
(2) synthetic vinegar that is manufactured by diluting glacial acetic acid or acetic
```
acid with drinking water. The total acid content is quantified as the acetic acid con-
```
tent, which is in the range of 4.0–29.0% (w/v), and tar color should not be detected
```
```
(MFDS, 2014; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
Therefore, globally, the term “vinegar” is defined as a liquid product that is pro-
duced by the fermentation of carbohydrate sources and that must contain a minimum
```
of 3.75–5.0% (w/v) acetic acid (Ho et al., 2017a).
```
1.6 AUTHENTICATION OF VINEGAR
Due to the variations in sensory, nutritional, and economic value of vinegars, their
authentication is essential to ensure the protection of consumers and honest manu-
facturers. In general, any liquid with sufficient amount of acetic acid can be named
7History and Current Issues of Vinegar
vinegar, including synthetic vinegars, which are produced by diluting glacial acetic
acid to a certain percentage, depending on regional laws and regulations. The sale
of synthetic vinegar is allowed and regulated by laws. However, there are concerns
where premium vinegars are mixed with synthetic vinegar but not reported in the
labeling, thus victimizing the consumers and honest traders.
In brief, in order to prevent vinegar adulteration, there are many instrumental
methods available that can verify the authenticity of a vinegar sample. Each vin-
egar variety has its own distinctive compounds at a specific concentration range. For
example, traditional balsamic vinegar is made from grape must and requires a longer
```
time of production (up to 12 years for maturation), while apple cider vinegar is made
```
from apple juice in much shorter production times. The different raw materials and
maturation times lead to the production of specific compounds at different ratios.
Therefore, identification and quantitative analysis of these compounds can be used
to validate the authenticity of a specific vinegar.
Other technological advances for vinegar authentication, especially for high-value
premium vinegars, include the use of site-specific natural isotopic fractionation by
```
nuclear magnetic resonance (SNIF-NMR) (Consonni et al., 2008; Gregrova et al.,
```
```
2012; Hsieh et al., 2013) and gas chromatography equipped with isotope ratio mass
```
```
spectrometry (GC–IRMS) (Hattori et al., 2010; Gregrova et al., 2012). The isotope
```
ratio of a compound of a product from a different geographical origin differs, even
for the same product. Therefore, these methods can detect the isotope ratio of the
vinegar acetic acid to determine the authenticity of the vinegar.
More details on fraud and quality issues of vinegars, as well as methods for char-
acterization and authentication of vinegars are presented and discussed in Chapter 21
```
(Fraud, Quality and Methods for Characterization and Authentication of Vinegars).
```
1.7 GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATION OF VINEGAR
```
A Geographical Indication (GI) is a label granted to products of a specific geographi-
```
cal origin and with specific qualities or reputation that are correlated to that ori-
```
gin (WIPO, 2018). Under the European Union, there are three GI and traditional
```
```
specialties schemes, known as Protected Designation of Origin (PDO), Protected
```
```
Geographical Indication (PGI), and Traditional Specialties Guaranteed (TSG), to
```
```
promote and protect names of quality agricultural products and foodstuffs (European
```
```
Commission, 2018). The main difference between PDO and PGI is that for a product
```
```
to receive the PDO label, it must be traditionally and entirely manufactured (pre-
```
```
pared, processed, and produced) within the specific region and thus acquire unique
```
properties, while for PGI, the entire product must be traditionally and at least par-
```
tially manufactured (prepared, processed, or produced) within the specific region
```
and thus acquire unique properties.
Vinegars, as products with a rich history and diverse varieties, are commonly
protected by GIs. Specifically, the vinegars protected by GI under the European
Union are:
• Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena—Traditional Balsamic Vinegar
```
of Modena (Italy)—PDO
```
8 Advances in Vinegar Production
• Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Reggio Emilia—Traditional Balsamic
```
Vinegar of Reggio Emilia (Italy)—PDO
```
```
• Aceto Balsamico di Modena—Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (Italy)—PGI
```
```
• Vinagre de Jerez—Jerez Vinegar (Spain)—PDO
```
• Vinagre del Condado de Huelva—Vinegar of the County of Huelva
```
(Spain)—PDO
```
```
• Vinagre de Montilla-Moriles—Vinegar of Montilla-Moriles (Spain)—PDO
```
and in China:
```
• Zhenjiang Xiang Cu—Zhenjiang Aromatic Vinegar (China)—PGI (see
```
```
also Chapter 10: Vinegar Production in China)
```
The above list indicates that there are differences between Traditional Balsamic
```
Vinegar of Modena (TBVM) and Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (BVM). TBVM is
```
protected under PDO, meaning that it must be produced traditionally and entirely
in Modena, Italy, while BVM is protected under PGI, meaning that it can be par-
tially manufactured outside of Modena. The above protected GI products will have
a PDO or PGI logo on their labels, thus indicating the authenticity of the vinegar.
This functions as a means to protect consumers and ensure that the specific vinegars
are produced exclusively at the specific geographical locations based on the intended
quality.
1.8 FUNCTIONAL COMPONENTS AND
HEALTH BENEFITS OF VINEGAR
1.8.1 Volatile Compounds of Vinegar
```
As described by Ho et al. (2017a) (adapted; copyright permission granted), the unique
```
flavor and aroma of vinegar is mainly attributed to the acetous fermentation process.
The strong pungent aroma and sour flavor of vinegars are due to the presence of
acetic acid. However, besides acetic acid, other fermentation by-products are present
in vinegars, such as volatile organic acids, esters, ketones, and aldehydes, that also
```
contribute to their sensory properties (Ozturk et al., 2015). These compounds are
```
produced during the fermentation and ageing processes, in which acetic acid acts
```
as a major precursor for their formation (Yu et al., 2012). These volatile compounds
```
are also influenced by the initial raw material, the methods used for vinegar pro-
```
duction (alcoholic and acetous fermentation), and the duration of the acetification
```
```
(Pizarro et al., 2008).
```
```
In a study conducted by Ozturk et al. (2015), a total of 61 and 38 volatile com-
```
pounds were found in Turkish traditional and industrial vinegar samples, respectively.
```
Among the volatile compounds identified, α-terpineol (25%) and ethyl acetate (15%)
```
were the major volatile compounds in the traditional vinegars. Interestingly, ethyl
acetate was mainly found in the vinegars produced from grapes, while α-terpineol
was not observed in any of the grape vinegar samples. In the industrial samples,
```
octanoic acid (15.6%) and isoamyl acetate (18.6%) (banana odor) were found to
```
9History and Current Issues of Vinegar
be the major volatile compounds in grape and pomegranate vinegars, respectively
```
(Ozturk et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
Su and Chien (2010) reported that in vinegar produced using rabbiteye blueberry,
```
```
the major aroma-active compounds were: acetic acid (vinegar odor), 2/3-methyl-
```
```
butanoic acid (sweaty odor), phenethyl acetate (sweet, honey odor), 2-phenylethanol
```
```
(rosy, sweet odor), octanoic acid (sweaty odor), eugenol (clove odor), and phenylace-
```
```
tic acid (floral odor). Some compounds such as 2,3-butanedione (or diacetyl; buttery
```
```
odor), (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal (cucumber odor), ethyl butanoate (apple, fruity odor),
```
```
and linalool (floral, cut grass odor) had low concentrations or were not detected by
```
GC–MS but had some odor impact on the samples due to their low odor threshold
```
values (Su and Chien, 2010; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
Del Signore (2001) analyzed 56 samples of balsamic vinegars, traditional bal-
```
```
samic vinegars (aged; some for 25 years), and common vinegars from Modena and
```
Reggio Emilia, Italy. Their study showed that the common and balsamic vinegars
contained more esters and propionic acid than traditional balsamic vinegars, except
for 2,3-butanediol diacetate, which was present in larger concentrations in the tra-
ditional balsamic vinegars. Among aldehydes, diacetyl, hexanal, and heptanal were
found in larger quantities in the traditional balsamic vinegars compared to balsamic
```
vinegars (three-fold) and common vinegars (five-fold). Among alcohols, octanol was
```
present in larger concentrations in the traditional balsamic vinegar, while 1-propa-
nol, isobutyl alcohol, isoamyl alcohol, and 1-hexanol were found in higher quantities
in the balsamic vinegars. In the common vinegar, 2-propanol and ethanol were pres-
```
ent in higher quantities (Del Signore, 2001; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
Madrera et al. (2010) reported that some organic acids (lactic, acetic, and suc-
```
```
cinic) and volatile compounds (2-butanol, 2-propen-1-ol, 4-ethylguaiacol, and euge-
```
```
nol) in vinegars are significantly influenced by ageing. Specifically, it was found
```
that vinegars with higher levels of maturation contain higher amounts of these com-
```
pounds. According to Ubeda et al. (2011), the formation of esters during alcoholic
```
fermentation is very high when the fermentation is spontaneous compared to inocu-
lated fermentation, obviously due to the presence of different enzyme activities from
different yeast strains. In their study, persimmon vinegar presented higher levels
of volatile compounds compared to strawberry vinegar, except for acetaldehyde,
1-propanol, and isobutanol, while different alcoholic fermentation methods could
lead to different qualities of the produced vinegars. Overall, for persimmon vinegar,
inoculated alcoholic fermentation resulted in higher amounts of volatile compounds,
whereas for strawberry vinegar, the spontaneous alcoholic fermentation resulted in
```
higher amounts of volatile compounds (Ubeda et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
```
Yu et al. (2012) reported on the volatile compounds present in aromatic vine-
```
```
gar samples produced from cereals (sticky rice, wheat bran, and rice husks) from
```
```
Zhenjiang, China, using the headspace solid-phase microextraction (HS-SPME)
```
method to extract the compounds. The samples were found to contain alcohols,
acids, esters, aldehydes, ketones, and heterocyclic compounds. Among them, esters
were the major volatile compounds found, among which, ethyl acetate, acetic acid
```
2-phenylethyl ester, and dihydro-5-pentyl-2(3H)-furanone were responsible for the
```
fruity, peach, and intense coconut notes, respectively. 3-Methyl-butanoic acid was
also found in the samples, to which a strong, pungent cheesy or sweaty smell is
10 Advances in Vinegar Production
attributed. Among carbonyl compounds, diacetyl and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone were
detected, which are responsible for buttery flavor as well as caramel and fruity notes.
Alcohols that were responsible for the sweet and fruity aroma of the Zhenjiang aro-
matic vinegars were also found, namely, 3-methyl-1-butanol, 2,3-butanediol, etha-
nol, and phenyl ethyl alcohol. Finally, the presence of heterocyclic compounds was
also reported, among which alkylpyrazines, including 2,3,5-trimethylpyrazine,
2,3-dimethy-l-5-ethylpyrazine, tetramethylpyrazine, and 2,3,5-trimethyl-6-ethyl-
pyrazine, were the major compounds. These compounds provide nutty, roasty, and
```
toasty notes to vinegars (Yu et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2017a).
```
More details on the composition of vinegar aroma and its chemical or sensory
```
analysis are provided in Chapter 17 (Vinegar Aroma Profile and Analysis).
```
1.8.2 BioaCtiVe Compounds of Vinegars
Bioactive compounds are extra-nutritional constituents in foods, that can act as anti-
```
oxidants, enzyme inhibitors, and inhibitors of gene expression (Etherton et al., 2002,
```
```
2004). Specifically, antioxidants have been used to control oxidation and delay food
```
```
spoilage; however, many are used today because of their putative health benefits
```
```
(Finley et al., 2011). The antioxidative activities of vinegar are due to bioactive con-
```
stituents such as carotenoids and phytosterols, as well as due to phenolic compounds
```
and vitamins C and E (Charoenkiatkul et al., 2016).
```
The determination of the flavonoid and polyphenol contents in vinegars is very
important since these compounds play an important role in the antioxidant activity.
Polyphenols have antioxidant properties, as they contain aromatic phenolic rings that
```
can stabilize and delocalize the unpaired electrons within the aromatic ring (Qiu et
```
```
al., 2010). By comparing the data obtained from Qiu et al. (2010) and Verzelloni et al.
```
```
(2007), oat vinegar contained the highest amount of catechin (5.29 mg/mL), followed
```
```
by Zhenjiang vinegar (4.18 mg/mL) and traditional balsamic vinegar (3.72 mg/mL). In
```
```
addition, the flavonoid compounds in oat vinegar (2.04 mg/mL) were found at a much
```
```
higher concentration compared to those in Zhenjiang vinegar (1.10 mg/mL). Also, it
```
```
is worth mentioning that Ubeda et al. (2013) reported that strawberry vinegar has a
```
significantly higher amount of total phenolic contents at 1.61 ± 0.10 mg GAE/mL.
Anthocyanin breakdown is dependent on the pH value in the presence of oxygen
```
and is directly related to the level of pseudo-base (colorless) and inversely related to
```
```
the concentration of cations. A study carried out by Su and Chien (2007) indicated
```
that when the temperature increases, there will be an increase in the rate of antho-
cyanin monomer losses in the products. According to that study, the anthocyanin
content in wine vinegars is lower than in other products, because the breakdown
of anthocyanin is dependent on the pH and the availability of oxygen. In blueberry
```
wine vinegar production, the results showed that skin-contact (including the skin of
```
```
blueberry) vinegar fermentation results in higher antioxidant activity in the products
```
```
compared to non-skin-contact fermentation (Su and Chien, 2007). Blueberry wine
```
vinegar with the skin presented the highest amount of gallic acid, followed by blue-
berry vinegar and blueberry wine vinegar without the skin.
```
According to Jang et al. (2015), traditional vinegars, for example rural lacquer
```
vinegar and rural Korean black raspberry vinegar, contain high concentrations of
11History and Current Issues of Vinegar
```
total phenolic compounds and show high activities in the ABTS (or Trolox equiva-
```
```
lent antioxidant capacity assay) and DPPH (diphenyl-picrylhydrazyl radical scaveng-
```
```
ing activity) assays. Rural Korean black raspberry vinegar contains higher levels of
```
quercetin and cyanidin, which are metabolites associated with antioxidant activity,
and it thus showed the highest antioxidant activity among all samples used in the
study. Also, the saccharide contents in commercial vinegars are higher than those
in traditional vinegars, and this might be due to the addition of sugars during the
```
alcoholic fermentation processes (Jang et al., 2015).
```
```
Sakanaka and Ishihara (2008) reported that unpolished rice vinegar contains
```
higher total phenolic contents compared to polished rice vinegar because unpolished
rice contains the rice bran, which is rich in phenolics such as dihydroferulic acid,
dihydrosinapic acid, sinapic acid, vanillic acid, and p-hydroxycinnamic acid. In the
same study, apple cider vinegar was found to contain significantly lower contents of
total phenolics, probably due to the raw material used. A comparison of the results
```
obtained for unpolished rice vinegar and rice vinegar by Shimoji et al. (2002) also
```
indicated that unpolished rice vinegar contains more phenolic compounds compared
to rice vinegar. Moreover, traditional balsamic vinegar was found to contain higher
```
amounts of ferulic acid (Plessi et al., 2006) compared to unpolished rice vinegar and
```
```
rice vinegar (Shimoji et al., 2002).
```
```
Finally, Cerezo et al. (2008) studied the effects of different types of barrels (aca-
```
```
cia, cherry, chestnut, and oak) on the phenolic composition of red wine vinegar, find-
```
ing that catechin and resveratrol glycoside presented a significant decrease during
acetification, while gallic acid and gallic ethyl ester increased substantially for those
vinegars produced in chestnut wood barrels.
1.8.3 BioaCtiVities and HealtH Benefits of Vinegar
```
According to Etherton et al. (2004), bioactive compounds affect certain physiologi-
```
cal or cellular activities, resulting in beneficial health effects, and promote better and
more effective health benefits compared to nutrients. Many bioactive compounds
have been reported to be able to modify the risk of disease rather than to prevent
disease. In this respect, there is great interest in polyphenolic compounds as quality
determinants, which, in addition to their antioxidant activity, are also responsible for
```
the color and astringency of vinegar (Mas et al., 2014).
```
Several epidemiological studies have suggested that consuming natural antioxi-
dants, such as polyphenol-rich foods containing flavonoids, anthocyanins, and other
```
phenolic compounds, has a protective effect against specific diseases (Almeida et
```
```
al., 2011). For example, antioxidants can minimize the postprandial increase in lipid
```
hydroperoxides, which are generated during the digestion of food. Dietary antioxi-
dants help prevent the formation of peroxides and their assimilation in the digestive
```
tract (Verzelloni et al., 2007). Several studies have also shown that high oxidant
```
```
levels (such as reactive oxygen species, e.g., superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and the
```
```
hydroxyl radical) and low antioxidant levels in the human body could cause oxida-
```
tive stress, which leads to the acceleration of the ageing process and the develop-
```
ment of some chronic, inflammatory, and degenerative diseases (Maes et al., 2011;
```
```
Candido et al., 2015).
```
12 Advances in Vinegar Production
Vinegar is widely used as an acidic condiment, for the pickling of fruits and
vegetables, and in the preparation of mayonnaise, salad dressings, and other food
seasonings. Moreover, vinegars have been traditionally used as a food preservative
```
worldwide due to their ability to retard microbial growth (Tan, 2005; Pooja and
```
```
Soumitra, 2013). The various types of organic acids in vinegar, and in particular
```
acetic acid, can diffuse through the cell membranes of microorganisms, leading to
```
bacterial cell death (Booth and Kroll, 1989).
```
Vinegar has been reported to possess health promoting abilities, such as improve-
ment of the digestive system function, appetite stimulation, antioxidant properties,
exhaustion recovery effects, reduction of lipid levels, and regulation of blood pres-
```
sure (Fushimi et al., 2001; Qui et al., 2010). In addition, vinegar contains consider-
```
able amounts of polyphenols that have been shown to prevent lipid peroxidation,
```
hypertension, hyperlipidemia, inflammation, DNA damage, and cancer (Prior and
```
```
Cao, 2000; Osada et al., 2006; Pandey and Rizvi, 2009; Chou et al., 2015).
```
More specifically, vinegar has a high antioxidant activity, good antimicrobial
```
properties, antidiabetic effects, and therapeutic properties (Budak et al., 2014), which
```
could offset the development of the abovementioned diseases. For example, juice and
wine products derived from blueberry showed a high capacity for inhibiting linoleic
acid peroxidation in ferric thiocyanate assays. Blueberry wine vinegar fermented
with the skin presented the highest antioxidative activities compared to blueberry
wine vinegar without the skin and blueberry vinegar, in both beta-carotene bleach-
```
ing assays and ferric thiocyanate assays (Su and Chien, 2007).
```
Polyphenols such as chlorogenic acid, which is present in high levels in apple cider
```
vinegar, could inhibit the oxidation of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) and poten-
```
```
tially improve health by preventing cardiovascular diseases (Laranjinha et al., 1994).
```
```
According to Verzelloni et al. (2007), traditional balsamic vinegar has higher
```
catechin content compared to mass-produced balsamic vinegar and red wine vin-
egar. The values obtained in the peroxidase assay were lower than the values of total
phenolic compounds, since reducing sugars such as glucose and fructose react with
```
the total phenolic compounds but do not react in the peroxidase assay (Verzelloni
```
```
et al., 2007). Maillard reaction products (MRPs) react in a concentration-dependent
```
manner in the Folin–Ciocalteu assay, while the peroxidase assay will not involve
any reactions.
```
According to Nanda et al. (2004), the ethyl acetate extract of Kurosu vinegar, a
```
traditional Japanese vinegar made from unpolished rice that contains rice bran, can
```
inhibit the growth of human cancer cells (Nanda et al., 2004). In addition, according
```
```
to Lee et al. (2013), tomato vinegar presented powerful anti-visceral obesity proper-
```
ties in high-fat diet-induced obese rats. The intra-abdominal deposition of visceral
adipose tissue is known as a general type of obesity that is associated with conditions
such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and coronary heart
disease. They found that consuming tomato vinegar regularly can reduce the total
```
visceral fat and the epididymal adipocyte size (Lee et al., 2013).
```
```
According to Kondo et al. (2001), the residues of rice vinegar can inhibit angio-
```
```
tensin converting enzyme (ACE) activity and can reduce blood pressure in vitro. The
```
mechanism of blood pressure reduction by acetic acid could be mediated by a differ-
ent mechanism than that of the ACE inhibitory activity. In addition to reducing blood
13History and Current Issues of Vinegar
pressure, vinegar showed a decrease in rennin activity upon the ingestion of acetic
acid. Rennin plays an important role in the initial reaction of the rennin–angioten-
sin system, where the reduction of blood pressure could take place. Therefore, the
consumption of acetic acid could reduce plasma rennin activity as well as blood
pressure.
Vinegar may also improve the insulin sensitivity of humans contributing to anti-
```
diabetic effects, as shown in various studies (Salbe et al., 2009). In humans, the insu-
```
lin response curve is decreased by 20% after consuming sucrose co-administered
with vinegar. Several studies have also shown that the acetic acid in vinegar may
prevent the complete digestion of complex carbohydrates by increasing the uptake of
```
glucose by tissues, resulting in reduced blood glucose levels (Fushimi et al., 2001).
```
```
Fushimi et al. (2006) reported that consuming 0.3% of dietary acetic acid may
```
help reduce the serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Acetic acid has also been
reported to enhance lipid homeostasis and help lower the cholesterol level in vivo.
```
Fukami et al. (2010) reported that acetic acid bacteria produce alkali-stable lipids
```
```
(ASL), which have a significant effect in improving cognitive ability because they
```
contain highly pure free dihydroceramide, a precursor to various sphingolipids such
```
as gangliosides (Fukami et al., 2010). Gangliosides are composed of sialic acid- and
```
ceramide-conjugated oligosaccharides, which have been shown to be effective in
```
improving the symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease (Svennerholm, 1994).
```
Additionally, apple cider vinegar has been reported to have the ability to balance
```
pH levels in the body if administered regularly (Brown and Jaffe, 2000).
```
1.9 CURRENT TRENDS IN VINEGAR PRODUCTION
The large market and demand for vinegar has propelled the research and devel-
opment of various exotic types of vinegar, including vinegars from tropical fruits
```
(soursop and papaya) (Ho et al., 2017b; Kong et al., 2018). Since vinegars are low pH
```
foods, which are very stable in terms of safety, waste materials and highly perishable
fruits can be converted into vinegar to reduce economic losses. Such novel vinegar
```
products are presented in more detail in Chapter 14 (Innovative Vinegar Products).
```
Moreover, novel vinegar production methods have also been developed, includ-
ing the use of selected and mixed yeast and bacteria cultures, the introduction of
```
alternative cultures (e.g., fungi, mushrooms, kefir) (Mat Isham et al., 2019), the use
```
of immobilized cell systems, the use of new types of batch, semi-continuous, and
continuous processes, the use of advanced acetator designs and effective aeration
systems, etc. Many of these recent advances are presented and discussed in the fol-
lowing chapters.

2
Types of Vinegars
Azwan Mat Lazim, Seng Joe Lim,
Chin Wai Ho, and Shazrul Fazry
2.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid produced by a two-stage fermentation pro-
```
cess: one stage that involves the conversion of sugars to ethanol by yeast, usually
```
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and a second that involves the conversion of ethanol to
acetic acid bacteria, usually Acetobacter. Vinegar was possibly discovered acciden-
tally when wine was fermented for too long in the presence of air, and it was well
known several millennia ago to the ancient civilizations of Sumerians, Babylonians,
```
Egyptians, Mesopotamians, and Ancient Greeks (Solieri and Giudici, 2009). It is
```
today used worldwide, primarily to flavor and preserve foods, as well as an ingredi-
ent in a vast variety of condiments. Vinegar is also used as a cleaning, disinfecting,
and therapeutic agent as discussed in more detail in the following chapters.
There are numerous different types of vinegars produced worldwide based on the
raw material and the production method used. Normally, a vinegar takes its name
from the raw material. For instance, there are various types of malt, cider, and wine
vinegars produced in Europe and a variety of cereal vinegars produced in Asia.
Among all the vinegars available, the most common types of vinegar, which are
produced in different parts of the world and include some top-quality famous prod-
ucts, are “balsamic vinegar,” “cider vinegar,” “rice vinegar,” “Sherry vinegar,” and
“malt vinegar.” The different raw materials and the methods used for the produc-
tion of the different types of vinegars lead to a variety of products with distinctive
characteristics.

20 Advances in Vinegar Production
In Italy, for example, balsamic vinegar is the most popular type of vinegar pro-
```
duced. Traditionally, the complex ageing method used (called “Rincalzo”) involves
```
```
ageing in barrels of different capacities and made from different woods (chestnut,
```
```
cherry, juniper, mulberry, oak). In the USA, the most popular type of vinegar is apple
```
cider vinegar, produced in a similar way to other types of vinegar, with the extra
```
initial step of raw material preparation (apple juice extraction). Asia is famous for its
```
cereal vinegars, which are usually produced by various traditional techniques using
```
rice (and occasionally other cereals such as sorghum), yeast/fungi starters (such as
```
```
“Koji,” a fermented cereal starter containing molds, yeasts, and bacteria) for alco-
```
holic fermentation and saccharification, and acetic acid bacteria for the acetifica-
tion process. The famous Sherry vinegars in Spain are produced by two different
```
methods: the static (“Sistema de Añadas” process in one barrel) and the dynamic
```
```
method (similar to the Rincalzo process carried out in a pyramid of barrels known
```
```
as “criaderas y solera”). Overall, the general procedure of every vinegar produc-
```
```
tion method includes raw material preparation (chopping, pressing, crushing, juice
```
```
extraction, clarification, saccharification, etc.), fermentation process (alcoholic and
```
```
acetous), and ageing.
```
A wide variety of different vinegars are produced around the world. The differ-
ent types of vinegars are highlighted below and are presented in more detail in the
subsequent chapters.
2.2 TYPES OF VINEGARS
2.2.1 Wine Vinegars
Wine vinegar is the most commonly used vinegar in the Mediterranean countries
and Central Europe. It is produced by the conversion of grape must sugars into
ethanol by yeast and subsequent oxidation of the ethanol by acetic acid bacte-
```
ria (Ríos-Reina et al., 2017). There is a vast variety of wine vinegars available
```
in the market, made from different raw materials and different production pro-
```
cesses (traditional slow or fast industrial methods, with and without ageing), and
```
with a wide variety of market prices, as discussed in more detail in the follow-
ing chapters. Some wine vinegars are also linked to a certain geographical area
and are protected by a regional legal framework that provides the designation
```
of “Protected Designation of Origin” (PDO) (e.g., Council Regulation (EC) No
```
```
510/2006 and Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 in Europe), indicating that the spe-
```
cific PDO product is produced, processed, and prepared in a specific geographical
```
area and with a specific production process (Ríos-Reina et al., 2017). Depending
```
on the wine used, there are red wine vinegars, white wine vinegars, Champagne
```
vinegars (made from the same grapes used to make Champagne in France, i.e.,
```
```
Chardonnay or Pinot Noir varieties), raisin vinegars (made after extraction of
```
```
raisins with water, followed by vinification and acetification), balsamic vinegars,
```
```
etc. Among wine vinegars, balsamic vinegars (in Italy) and Sherry vinegars (in
```
```
Spain) include some high quality (and high price) representatives, with PDO des-
```
ignations, as described below.
21Types of Vinegars
2.2.2 sHerry Wine Vinegars
```
The production of wine vinegar in Spain is centered in Andalusia (Southern
```
```
Spain). Andalusia is a region traditionally associated with wine culture where
```
wine vinegars have been protected by three different PDOs because of their
unique characteristics. The first two PDOs are already well established and
```
widely commercialized Regulations (EU) No 984/2011 and No 985/2011), whereas
```
```
Vinagre Montilla-Moriles was granted a PDO designation in 2015 (Commission
```
```
Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/48 of 14 January 2015). Furthermore, within
```
each PDO, there are different categories according to ageing time and type of
wood barrels used:
• Vinagre de Jerez PDO, also known as “Sherry wine vinegar.” The residual
alcohol content must not exceed 3% in volume, and the total acetic acid
content must be at least 70 g/l. Vinagre de Jerez includes three categories
according to the ageing time in oak barrels by the dynamic system: Vinagre
de Jerez aged for at least 6 months, Vinagre de Jerez Reserva aged for
at least 2 years, and Vinagre de Jerez Gran Reserva aged for more than
```
10 years). In the case of the Gran Reserva vinegars, the total acetic content
```
must be at least 80 g/l.
In addition, depending on the variety of wine used, there are the following types
of sweet Vinagre de Jerez vinegars:
• Vinagre de Jerez al Pedro Ximénez, to which must of raisined grapes of the
Pedro Ximénez variety is added during the maturing process.
• Vinagre de Jerez al Moscatel, to which must of grapes or raisined grapes
of the Muscatel variety is added during the maturing process. The residual
alcohol content in these two vinegars must not exceed 3% in volume, the
total acetic acid content must be at least 60 g/l, and the reducing sugar con-
tent must be at least 70 g/l.
• Vinagre Condado de Huelva PDO, with the following categories: Vinagre
Condado de Huelva with no ageing, Vinagre Viejo Condado de Huelva
Solera aged for at least 6 months, Vinagre Viejo Condado de Huelva
```
Reserva aged for at least 2 years (all aged with the dynamic system), and
```
Vinagre Viejo Condado de Huelva Añada aged for at least 3 years with the
static ageing system.
• Vinagre Montilla-Moriles PDO, which is wine vinegar obtained by the ace-
tous fermentation of certified Montilla-Moriles PDO wine with/without the
addition of certified must of that wine, followed by ageing, and having the
following categories: Vinagre Montilla-Moriles Añada made by static age-
ing for 3 years or more, and the vinegars aged using the dynamic criaderas
y solera system, i.e., Vinagre Montilla-Moriles Crianza aged for at least
6 months, Vinagre Montilla-Moriles Reserva aged for at least 2 years, and
Vinagre Montilla-Moriles Gran Reserva aged for at least 10 years.
22 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
The high quality of these PDOs is the consequence of the raw material (grape
```
```
variety, origin), the wooden barrel used (e.g., American Oak), and the ageing method
```
applied. The dynamic ageing system is called “criaderas y “solera,” in which aged
and young vinegars are sequentially mixed in barrels called criaderas for the inter-
mediate ageing scales and solera for the final ageing scale. The static ageing system
```
(in a single barrel without mixing) is called “Sistema de Añadas” (Figure 2.1).
```
2.2.3 BalsamiC Vinegars
Balsamic vinegar is a famous type of vinegar produced originally in Italy, where
three types of protected balsamic vinegars can be found:
```
• “Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena” PDO (Traditional Balsamic
```
```
Vinegar of Modena; TBVM)
```
```
• “Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Reggio Emilia” PDO (Traditional
```
```
Balsamic Vinegar of Reggio Emilia; TBVRE)
```
```
• “Aceto Balsamico di Modena” PGI (Balsamic Vinegar of Modena; BVM)
```
```
• Also, condiments that use the term “balsamic” (“condimento balsamico”
```
```
in Italian) are available.
```
Generally, balsamic vinegars are dark brown in color, concentrated, and highly
aromatic vinegars, made from blends of grape must, cooked/concentrated grape
```
must, wine vinegar, aged vinegar, and (authorized) colorants. The first two types of
```
```
vinegars (TBVM, TBVRE), sometimes referred to as “true vinegars,” are produced
```
exclusively in the areas of Modena or Reggio Emilia, using mainly Lambrusco and
Trebbiano grapes, and must be aged for several years in wooden barrels. They are
both protected by the European PDO.
TBVRE vinegars are available in different aged types: aged for at least 12 years
```
(refined or “affinato” type), aged for at least 18 years, and aged for more than
```
```
25 years (extra old or “extravecchio” type). TBVM includes vinegars aged for
```
at least 12 years and vinegars aged for 25 years or more. BVM, with “Protected
FIGURE 2.1 A schematic representation of the traditional Sherry wine or vinegar ageing
systems.
23Types of Vinegars
```
Geographical Indication” (PGI), may contain a maximum 2% caramel and other
```
thickeners and must be aged for a minimum of 2 months in single wooden barrels, or
for at least 3 years in order to be labeled as aged. It is usually a lower price industrial
```
product (Corsini et al., 2019; Wikipedia, 2019a).
```
The traditional balsamic vinegars are produced through a complex, dynamic age-
```
ing process that involves barrels made from different types of wood (oak, chestnut,
```
```
mulberry, or juniper) at successively decreasing sizes (Corsini et al., 2019). In the
```
barrels, alcoholic and acetic acid fermentation take place simultaneously. A sche-
matic representation of the set of barrels used for the production and ageing of tradi-
tional balsamic vinegars is shown in Figure 2.2.
Balsamic vinegars labeled as “condimento balsamico,” “salsa balsamica,” or
“salsa di mosto cotto” are products made using both BVM and TBVM/TBVRE as
ingredients but have no PDO/PGI designations, nor are they allowed to use the geo-
```
graphical names of Modena or Reggio Emilia (these can only be mentioned for the
```
```
contained ingredients). The balsamic condiments are made in a similar way with the
```
vinegars, but by producers which can be located outside of the Modena and Reggio
Emilia areas.
2.2.4 Cider Vinegars
Cider vinegar or apple vinegar is made up of apple juice or concentrated apple juice.
The production process also involves double fermentation steps: alcoholic fermen-
tation by yeasts and acetic fermentation using acetic acid bacteria. The older and
modern methods are quite different, i.e., in the traditional method, both fermentation
steps occurred naturally inside a barrel, which was covered and placed in a damp and
warm place. The whole process took about 6 months to complete. The modern cider
vinegar production, on the other hand, involves three different steps: raw material
```
preparation (juice extraction, clarification, etc.), alcoholic fermentation of the apple
```
juice, and submerged acetous fermentation of the apple cider.
The apple cider vinegar market, although it has suffered an impact due to the
general global economic growth slowdown, it is expected to be expanded by 2021
FIGURE 2.2 A schematic representation of a set of barrels used for the production of tra-
ditional balsamic vinegar.
24 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
reaching 375 million US$ (Market Research Reports, 2019). The North America
```
and Europe apple cider vinegar market will be the dominant one over that forecast
period, followed by Asia Pacific. More details on apple cider vinegar, production,
and current research trends are presented in Chapter 12.
2.2.5 riCe /Cereal Vinegars
Rice vinegars are vinegars produced from fermented rice and are very com-
mon in Asian countries such as China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. According
```
to Kitamura et al. (2016), “rice vinegar” is defined as the cereal vinegar that is
```
produced using rice more than 40 g/l. Recently, “rice black vinegar” has been
differentiated from “rice vinegar” as it is made using rice more than 180 g/l
and has a dark brown or black color, which is developed during fermentation
and maturation. Rice vinegars are generally milder and sweeter than Western
vinegars.
Chinese rice vinegars are stronger than Japanese vinegars and vary in color from
clear to red and black. The stronger and higher quality types of Chinese vinegars
```
are the black vinegars (e.g., those produced in the Zhenjiang area), which are made
```
```
from black glutinous rice (sticky rice), although millet, sorghum peas, barley, bran,
```
```
and chaff may also be used for black vinegar production (e.g., in the Shanxi area).
```
Red rice vinegars owe their color and characteristic flavor to the red mold used for
```
their production (Monascus purpureus). Most Chinese vinegars are produced by
```
```
solid-state fermentation (SSF), as described in more detail in Chapter 8, or by com-
```
```
binations of SSF and submerged fermentation (SmF) processes. Famous Chinese
```
```
vinegars are (Chen et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2004):
```
```
• Zhenjiang aromatic vinegar (Southern China; made by SSF from sticky
```
```
rice and wheat Koji; involves a cooking method for ethanol production and
```
```
a fed-batch SSF acetification process)
```
```
• Shanxi aged vinegar (Northern China; made from sorghum and a very large
```
```
proportion of Koji; involves fuming, solarizing, and freezing/ice removal
```
```
steps during ageing)
```
```
• Jiangzhe rose vinegar (Chinese provinces Jiangsu and Zhejiang; made by
```
SSF/SmF by Monascus grown spontaneously on steamed rice, for sacchari-
fication and alcohol fermentation, followed by acetification by acetic acid
```
bacteria without further ageing)
```
```
• Sichuan bran vinegar (Southwest China; made by traditional SSF from a
```
special vinegar mother prepared from steamed rice, herb Koji including as
```
many as 108 medicinal herbs, and a liquid extract of a special smartweed;
```
```
wheat bran is used as culture carrier and substrate in the process; matured
```
```
for about 1 year)
```
```
• Fujian red monascus vinegar (made by combined SSF/SmF using steamed
```
sticky rice and red Koji dominated by Monascus, for SSF saccharification,
```
followed by repeated, fed-batch SmF acetification for 3 years)
```
```
• Shanghai rice vinegar (made by SSF adopting modern techniques using
```
```
amylase instead of Koji; maturation accelerated by infrared heating)
```
25Types of Vinegars
A review of Chinese vinegar production and current research trends is provided
in Chapters 8 and 10.
```
In Japan, rice vinegar (“Su” is vinegar in Japanese) is also mainly consumed
```
```
(Kitamura et al., 2016). The black Japanese rice vinegar, Kurozu, is considered a
```
healthy, functional food as shown by various scientific studies and discussed in
Chapter 18. The traditional method of preparing rice vinegar in Japan is similar to
Chinese vinegar. Rice vinegars are nowadays usually made from rice and Koji molds
```
(Aspergillus) cultured on steamed rice, with separate saccharification and alcoholic
```
```
fermentation steps. Production is carried out in stainless-steel or (rarely) wooden tanks
```
```
without mixing and aeration (Kitamura et al., 2016). On the other hand, traditional
```
types of rice black vinegar in Japan are produced by saccharification, alcohol fermen-
tation, and acetic acid fermentation in one pot. Some types of Japanese vinegars are:
• Komezu rice vinegar: a very mild vinegar, clear to pale yellow, made
```
from polished rice (Yonezu) or sake lees (Kasuzu). Seasoned rice vinegar
```
```
(Awasezu) is made by adding sake, salt, and sugar.
```
```
• Fukuyama pot vinegar (Kyushu, Kagoshima Prefecture, Southern Japan;
```
traditionally made from steamed rice, Aspergillus rice Koji, and water by
traditional saccharification, alcohol fermentation, and acetic acid fermen-
tation, which are conducted in loosely capped pots laid on the ground of
```
open-air fields; long-term ageing (Kitamura et al., 2016); Kagoshima no
```
Tsubozukuri Kurozu is a black, aged rice vinegar, made with Japanese
```
Geographical Identification (GI) since 2015. Kurosu is black and contains
```
more amino acids and vitamins than komesu and thus is used as a healthy
```
drink (Nanda et al., 2004). A general scheme of traditional pot black vin-
```
egar production is shown in Figure 2.3.
```
In Korea, rice vinegar (ssal sikcho) is made using either white or brown, glutinous
```
or non-glutinous rice, and the “Nuruk” fermentation starter, which is similar to Koji
```
(a mash of fermented, cooked, milled or whole grain, such as rice, wheat, or barley),
```
FIGURE 2.3 A schematic representation of traditional Asian vinegar production in pots
```
(e.g., Kurosu black rice vinegar production).
```
26 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
and water. Rice wine lees can also be used to produce rice wine vinegar (Makgeolli
```
```
sikcho). The species involved in the fermentation of Nuruk include lactic acid bac-
```
```
teria, yeasts (Saccharomyces and other species), and fungi (mainly Aspergillus and
```
```
Rhizopus species) (McKay et al., 2011; Wikipedia, 2019b).
```
2.2.6 malt Vinegars
```
Malt vinegar is made by fermentation of malted barley (produced in the same way as
```
```
in beer or whiskey production). It is, therefore, popular in beer or whiskey produc-
```
ing or consuming areas such as the United Kingdom, the USA, Canada, Australia,
Ireland, and other European countries. Chinese and Australian markets have domi-
nant positions in Asia Pacific, which has created a huge demand for the import of
```
malt ingredients (Mordor Intelligence, 2019).
```
There are several types of malt vinegars such as distilled, light, and dark malt
vinegars. Malt vinegar production involves alcoholic and acetous fermentation steps
```
using malted barley, with or without the addition of other “modified” (enzymati-
```
```
cally saccharified) cereals (Grierson, 2009). Depending on the malt production pro-
```
cess, the malt vinegar color ranges from pale yellow to dark brown, which may also
be attributed to the addition of barley extract or caramel. Distilled malt vinegar is
obtained by distillation under reduced pressure and is usually referred to as “white
vinegar.” It has about 0.2% lower acidity compared to the starting vinegar, since
```
the non-volatile malt acids do not distill (Grierson, 2009). The acetification process
```
for malt vinegar production may be carried out in “generators” packed with wood
```
material (e.g., wooden barrels packed with beech or birch shavings), or in modern
```
```
(stainless-steel) “acetators,” as described in the following chapters.
```
Surprisingly, there is little scientific research regarding malt vinegars. Most of the
available studies deal with the composition analysis or the health promoting proper-
```
ties of malt vinegars. According to Sáiz-Abajo et al. (2005), malt vinegars are bitter
```
vinegars with considerable amounts of lactic acid, higher than that of cider vinegars,
and with no L-tartaric and L or D-malic acids present. The use of malted rice for
vinegar production in Asia has also recently attracted attention. As in the case of bar-
ley, rice malt is a product of rice germinated under controlled conditions. It is highly
```
nutritious and contains many bioactive compounds (antioxidant phenolics, dietary
```
```
fiber, tocopherols, γ-oryzanol, thiamine, pyridoxine, and γ-aminobutyric acid), and
```
```
has low levels of antinutrients, such as phytic acid (Pawena and Yupakanit, 2015).
```
```
Recently, two Thai black rice cultivars, black waxy rice (Kam) and black non-waxy
```
```
rice (Homnin), were evaluated for malt vinegar production, and the results for the
```
Kam variety were very encouraging.
2.2.7 tropiCal fruit Vinegars
Due to the universality of the vinegar production process, various alternative types
of vinegars have been produced over the years, such as vinegars made using tropi-
```
cal fruits. For example, Ho et al. (2017) worked on the production of vinegar from
```
```
soursop fruit, while Kong et al. (2018) produced vinegar from papaya fruit. The
```
main reason for producing these vinegars was that these tropical fruits are highly
27Types of Vinegars
perishable, and thus the overripe fruits could be converted into vinegar to reduce
wastage. Interestingly, in the case of papaya juice conversion into vinegar, the total
phenolic contents and antioxidant activities increased throughout the process. This
showed that vinegar production not only can reduce fruit wastage but can also
increase its functional properties. More information on the production of alternative
types of vinegars produced by alternative raw materials, such as tropical fruit, veg-
etables, and generally surpluses of agricultural produce, are provided in Chapter 14.

3
The Biochemistry of
Vinegar Production
Chin Wai Ho, Shazrul Fazry,
Azwan Mat Lazim, and Seng Joe Lim
3.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegars are made by two-stage fermentation processes: alcoholic fermentation of
```
any type of fermentable sugar, followed by acetous fermentation (ethanol oxidation).
```
```
The alcoholic fermentation is carried out by yeasts (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
```
that convert the fermentable sugars in the medium into alcohol under anaerobic con-
ditions. Subsequently, the acetous fermentation occurs in the presence of oxygen to
convert the alcohol into acetic acid. Practically, there are two main types of tradi-
tional acetification methods for vinegar production: the surface oxidation and the
submerged acetification. The surface oxidation is a much slower process compared
to the submerged fermentation, which is rapid due to the higher contact surface with
```
oxygen (dissolved in the medium).
```
The two types of fermentation processes involved in vinegar production are
briefly described below.
3.2 ALCOHOLIC FERMENTATION
The alcoholic fermentation in vinegar production generally proceeds rapidly and
may usually deplete most available sugars in the first three weeks. The ferment-
able sugars are converted into ethanol by the action of yeasts, normally strains of
S. cerevisiae (Budak et al., 2014). Alcoholic fermentation is the natural process
