30 Advances in Vinegar Production
during which microorganisms consume organic compounds under anaerobic con-
```
ditions to produce cellular energy (adenosine triphosphate; ATP), carbon dioxide
```
```
(CO2) and alcohol (ethanol) (Bekatorou, 2016). It takes place through the Embden–
```
```
Meyerhof–Parnas (glycolytic) pathway, i.e., the metabolism of hexose sugars, such as
```
glucose, into two molecules of pyruvate and two ATP molecules per hexose molecule
```
(Figure 3.1). Wild-type S. cerevisiae strains can ferment glucose, mannose and fruc-
```
tose via the glycolytic pathway, while galactose is fermented via the combined Leloir
```
pathway and glycolysis (Maris et al., 2006).
```
The Leloir pathway promotes the conversion of beta-D-galactose into glucose-
1-phosphate, which can then be used in the glycolysis pathway. In most organisms,
including S. cerevisiae, five enzymes are required to catalyze this conversion: galac-
tose mutarotase, galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, uridine
```
diphosphate (UDP)-galactose-4-epimerase, and phosphoglucomutase (Sellick et
```
```
al., 2008). The initial step of the pathway is the conversion of beta-D-galactose into
```
alpha-D-galactose by a mutarotase enzyme. The galactose-1-phosphate, which is
then formed with the action of a galactokinase, exchanges the glucose group from
UDP-glucose to create UDP-galactose and release glucose-1-phosphate. An epim-
```
erase enzyme converts UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose (by changing the stereo-
```
```
chemistry of C-4). The glucose that is released in the form of glucose-1-phosphate
```
is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by the action of phosphoglucomutase and can
```
enter the glycolysis pathway (Sellick et al., 2008).
```
FIGURE 3.1 Synopsis of the hexose catabolism and alcoholic fermentation in Saccharomyces
```
cerevisiae [1: Galactokinase (GAL1; EC:2.7.1.6); 2: Galactose-1-phosphate uridylytransfer-
```
```
ase (GAL7; EC:2.7.7.12); 3: Phosphoglucomutase (GAL5 or PMG2; EC:5.4.2.2); 4: Glucose-
```
```
6-phosphate isomerase (PGI1; EC:5.3.1.9); 5,7: Hexokinase (HXK1/HXK2; EC:2.7.1.1); 6:
```
```
Mannose-6-phosphate isomerase (PMI40; EC:5.3.1.8); 8: Pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC1;
```
```
EC 4.1.1.1); 9: Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH1; EC:1.1.1.1)] (based on Bekatorou, 2016;
```
```
Maris et al., 2006).
```
31The Biochemistry of Vinegar Production
Mannose and fructose are two hexoses that can also be fermented by S. cerevi-
siae. After the phosphorylation catalyzed by hexokinase, mannose-6-phosphate is
isomerized to fructose-6-phosphate by mannose-6-phosphate isomerase as shown
in Figure 3.1. Under the anaerobic conditions of the alcoholic fermentation by
S. cerevisiae, the NADH that is formed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
```
is reoxidized to NAD+ by the combined action of pyruvate decarboxylase (PCD; non-
```
```
oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetaldehyde) and alcohol dehydrogenase
```
```
(ADH; an alcohol:NAD+ oxidoreductase) (Agarwal et al., 2013; Ho et al., 2017; Maris
```
```
et al., 2006). The overall chemical formula for alcoholic fermentation is:
```
C H O C H OH CO6 12 6 2 5 22 2→ +
with a theoretical yield of 0.51 g of ethanol and 0.49 g CO 2 from 1 g of sugar.
```
However, the actual yield of alcoholic fermentation is lower (commonly about 0.46 g
```
```
ethanol and 0.44 g CO2 in wine fermentations) (Bekatorou, 2016).
```
Vinegar can be produced from any raw material that contains directly ferment-
```
able sugars. Raw materials that contain starch or disaccharides (such as saccharose
```
```
and lactose) must be hydrolyzed before fermentation, as shown in Figure 3.2. Grapes,
```
apples and rice are the common primary starting materials used for vinegar produc-
tion, although malt vinegar, tropical fruit vinegars, cane vinegar and other types of
vinegar are also produced in some countries or have recently been researched and
developed, as described in the following chapters.
```
Saccharose is hydrolyzed into glucose and fructose by yeast invertase (EC 3.2.1.26;
```
```
beta-fructofuranosidase; S. cerevisiae gene: SUC2), which is an extracellular enzyme
```
```
widely distributed among plants and microorganisms (Sainz-Polo et al., 2013). Beta-
```
```
galactosidase (E.C.3.2.1.23; galactohydrolase; commonly referred to as lactase),
```
the enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, is not expressed
FIGURE 3.2 Schematic outline of vinegar fermentations.
32 Advances in Vinegar Production
in S. cerevisiae but is one of the predominantly occurring hydrolytic enzymes in
higher plants, animals and microorganisms, including bacteria, yeasts and fila-
mentous fungi such as Kluyveromyces, Bacillus, Bifidobacterium, Aspergillus and
```
Streptococcus spp. (Xavier et al., 2018). Therefore, the alcoholic fermentation of
```
lactose containing sources, such as cheese whey, requires prior hydrolysis by lactose
fermenting species.
3.2.1 tHe yeast SaccharomyceS cereviSiae
The yeast S. cerevisiae is the most widely used species for alcoholic fermentation
because it is tolerant to high sugar and ethanol concentrations, low pH values, low
```
temperatures, high pressures and sulfur dioxide (SO 2) (Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson,
```
```
2008). It can completely convert sugars under the conditions of common alcoholic
```
```
beverage fermentations (beer or wine), producing low amounts of undesirable com-
```
```
pounds (e.g., hydrogen sulfide, acetic acid and urea) and cell mass in the absence of
```
oxygen. Spontaneous fermentations, such as in traditional wine and vinegar making,
involve various yeast species that dominate depending on the substrate composition,
```
the process conditions and the process stage (Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2008).
```
In S. cerevisiae, glucose is transported via facilitated diffusion and, therefore,
glucose uptake requires a concentration gradient across the plasma membrane.
S. cerevisiae contains 32 members of the hexose transporter family (HXT) with
respect to transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulation, substrate specificity
```
(only specific substrates can react with the active site of the enzymes) and affinity for
```
```
glucose (Maris et al., 2006). Generally, for S. cerevisiae to ferment non-glucose car-
```
```
bohydrates (such as fructose, mannose and galactose), the fundamental requirements
```
are the presence of functional transporters in the plasma membrane, the presence of
enzymes able to couple the sugar metabolism with the glycolytic pathway and the
```
maintenance of a closed redox balance (Maris et al., 2006).
```
3.3 ACETIFICATION
```
Acetification in vinegar production is carried out by acetic acid bacteria (AAB),
```
which are obligately aerobic bacteria with the unique ability to incompletely oxi-
dize alcohols and sugars into organic acids. The incomplete oxidation is catalyzed
```
by membrane-bound pyrroloquinoline quinone-dependent dehydrogenases (PQQ-
```
```
dDs), which are connected to the respiratory chain by reduction of ubiquinone to ubi-
```
quinol. Reoxidation of ubiquinol is coupled to oxygen reduction by quinol oxidases.
Therefore, when alcohols and sugars are oxidized into organic acids in the periplasm
by PQQ-dDs, ATP is generated through oxidative phosphorylation. The organic
acids are in most cases stoichiometrically formed as dead-end metabolites that are
not further utilized as carbon sources. However, alcohols and sugars, such as ethanol
and glucose, may be sometimes simultaneously oxidized by the membrane-bound
PQQ-dDs in the periplasm and the soluble dehydrogenases in the cytoplasm, for both
```
energy generation and carbon assimilation (Arai et al., 2016; Sakurai et al., 2011).
```
Acetobacter and most Gluconacetobacter species grow on ethanol and accu-
```
mulate acetate by incomplete oxidation. However, when the substrate (ethanol) is
```
33The Biochemistry of Vinegar Production
consumed they may completely oxidize the accumulated acetate, a process that is
called acetate overoxidation caused by increased activity of the tricarboxylic acid
```
(TCA) cycle enzymes and acetyl-CoA synthetase (Acs) (Figure 3.3). The growth on
```
ethanol resulting in the accumulation of acetate takes place in the first exponential
growth phase, and acetate overoxidation takes place in the second exponential phase
```
(diauxic growth). This process is obviously unfavorable in vinegar production, and
```
the mechanisms that control the switching from incomplete/assimilatory oxidation
```
to energy and carbon metabolism in AAB are not fully understood (Arai et al., 2016;
```
```
Sakurai et al., 2011).
```
3.3.1 aCetiC aCid BaCteria
AAB are Gram-negative or Gram-variable, non-spore forming, ellipsoidal to rod-
shaped cells, occurring as single cells, pairs of cells or short chains of cells, and
may be motile through peritrichous or polar flagella. The catalase-positive and
oxidase-negative AAB are obligate aerobes, with oxygen as the terminal electron
acceptor. Their optimum growth pH is 5.0–6.5, but they can also grow at pH 3–4,
```
while the optimum growth temperature for most species is 28–30°C (Mamlouk
```
```
and Gullo, 2013). AAB are assigned to the order Rhodospirillales as part of the
```
Alphaproteobacteria, within the family Acetobacteraceae, and currently they
are represented by the following genera: Acetobacter, Acidomonas, Ameyamaea,
Asaia, Gluconacetobacter, Gluconobacter, Granulibacter, Kozakia, Neoasaia,
Neokomagataea, Saccharibacter, Swaminathania and Tanticharoenia. More dis-
tinctive characteristics of the various AAB genera and species are provided in a
```
review by Mamlouk and Gullo (2013), and the recent book of Matsushita et al. (2016).
```
AAB are found in substrates that contain sugars, ethanol and acids, such as
plants and fermented beverages. These sources are also widely used to isolate AAB.
FIGURE 3.3 Synopsis of the central carbon metabolic pathway of Acetobacter aceti pos-
```
sessing complete TCA cycle and glyoxylate pathway genes (based on Arai et al., 2016).
```
34 Advances in Vinegar Production
Most isolates can be maintained at 4°C for 1 month on suitable agar media, while
long-term preservation can be achieved by freeze-drying, storage in liquid nitrogen
or by cryoconservation at –80°C. To select AAB from a number of isolates, they
are usually tested for growth on glucose–ethanol–nitrogen media with pH 3.5. For
generic-level identification, the obtained AAB candidates are generally subjected
to 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis, especially to the construction of phylogenetic
trees. For specific-level identification, whole-genome DNA–DNA hybridization is
necessary and for strains that have already been identified or classified at the generic
```
level (Matsushita et al., 2016).
```
The oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid in vinegar production is mainly carried
out by Acetobacter, Gluconobacter, Gluconacetobacter and Komagataeibacter,
among the 17 members of the AAB genera. The genus Acetobacter is the oldest
in the classification of AAB and the type genus of the family Acetobacteraceae.
The genus is related phylogenetically to the genera Gluconobacter, Neokomagataea,
Swingsia and Saccharibacter. In the genus Acetobacter, there are two phylogenet-
ically different groups: A. aceti and A. pasteurianus groups. In A. aceti, acid is
produced from L-arabinose, D-xylose, D-glucose, D-galactose, D-mannose or etha-
```
nol (Matsushita et al., 2016).
```
As described in the previous section, under certain conditions, ethanol is oxi-
dized to acetate both in the periplasm, by membrane-bound PQQ-dependent ADH
```
(adhAB/adhS genes) and ALDH, and in the cytoplasm, by soluble NAD(P)+-
```
```
dependent ADH (adh1 and adh2 genes) and ALDH (Arai et al., 2016). In addition
```
to the genes adhAB/adhS, the adh1 and adh2 genes were also identified in the A.
aceti genome, sharing a high homology with the corresponding ADH I and ADH II
```
genes of A. pasteurianus (Arai et al., 2016). The membrane-bound ALDH (gene ald-
```
```
FGH) may be involved in the accumulation of acetate from the incomplete oxidation
```
```
of ethanol in the periplasm. Several genes encoding a putative soluble NAD(P)+-
```
dependent ALDH, which might be involved in the cytoplasmic formation of acetate,
```
were also identified in A. aceti (Arai et al., 2016). Before entering the TCA cycle
```
for complete oxidation, acetate is converted to acetyl-CoA via two pathways, one
```
catalyzed by Acs and the other by phosphotransacetylase (Pta) and acetate kinase
```
```
(Ack) (Arai et al., 2016). The generation of acetyl-CoA from acetate may also be
```
```
catalyzed by succinyl-CoA:acetate CoA transferase (SCACT) (gene aarC in AAB).
```
In A. aceti, the genes acs1 and acs2 have been identified but not the Pta and Ack
genes, indicating that the metabolism of acetate is initiated by the Acs pathway and
```
SCACT (Arai et al., 2016).
```
```
According to Arai et al. (2016), ethanol significantly represses the TCA cycle at
```
the transcriptional level in A. aceti, which may explain the accumulation of acetate.
Specifically, during the incomplete oxidation of ethanol by AAB, ethanol is utilized
as an energy source. When ethanol and glucose are both present in the substrate
of A. aceti, the overflow metabolism of glucose may occur due to the repression
of the TCA cycle genes by ethanol and the enhanced expression of the glycolytic
enzyme genes. The result is the cytoplasmic accumulation of acetate and acetyl-
CoA, which inhibit ethanol oxidation in the cytoplasm and lead to its incomplete
oxidation in the periplasm. A deficiency in the glyoxylate pathway, comprised of iso-
```
citrate lyase (aceA gene) and malate synthase (glcB gene), is desirable for industrial
```
35The Biochemistry of Vinegar Production
vinegar production from ethanol, since it promotes the glucose overflow metabolism
```
(Figure 3.3). The description of these metabolic features of A. aceti were based on
```
```
transcriptome profiles, and according to Arai et al. (2016) they should be confirmed
```
by biochemical and metabolomic analyses.
During the acetous fermentations, the Acetobacter species predominate at low
concentration of acetic acid. A. pasteurianus is the most commonly found species
in wine vinegars, while other Acetobacter sp., such as A. malorum, A. cerevisiae,
A. aceti, may also be found in fruit vinegars. When the concentration of acetic
acid in vinegar exceeds 5%, other species such as Komagataeibacter europaeus or
```
Gluconacetobacter intermedius may predominate (Gullo et al., 2009; Hidalgo et al.,
```
```
2010, 2012, 2013; Mas et al., 2014; Vegas et al., 2010). Gluconacetobacter europaeus
```
is the main species recovered from industrial vinegar, which is a species with high
ADH activity and stability allowing growth and metabolic activity at high acetic acid
```
concentrations. In other AAB species (e.g., A. pasteurianus and G. intermedius),
```
high acetic acid concentration causes cell stress due to faster decrease of the ADH
activity. A. aceti, during continuous industrial processes, evolves the ability to grow
at acetate concentrations higher than 5% producing a phenotype that is stable only
at specific pressure. In semi-continuous industrial vinegar processes, acid tolerance
as high as 11.5–12.0% has also been observed in strains able to adapt to the process
```
conditions (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Ho et al., 2017).
```
3.3.2 faCtors tHat affeCt tHe aCetous fermentation
3.3.2.1 Oxygen
Oxygen is a limiting factor in vinegar production due to its solubility which is signifi-
cantly affected by the bioreactor design, the aeration system used, the process tem-
perature and the substrate composition. To ensure an optimum acetification process
it is necessary to achieve and maintain a suitable level of dissolved oxygen, which
will influence the speed and yield of the fermentation, as well as the sensory quality
```
of the end-product (Ubeda et al., 2011).
```
In the traditional surface acetification methods, no forced oxygen solubilization
is applied. Oxygen transfer is done between the AAB film formed at the surface of
the fermenting vinegar and the air in the barrel headspace. Oxygen also penetrates
```
through the wood of the barrel at a rate of about 30 mg/L per year (Gullo and Giudici,
```
```
2008). In submerged industrial wine vinegar production on the other hand, the con-
```
centration of dissolved oxygen is crucial for bacterial growth, therefore air supply is
compulsory. However, excessive dissolved oxygen concentration may inhibit AAB
growth. The optimum dissolved oxygen concentration in semi-continuous processes
```
has been established to be 1–3 mg/kg (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Ho et al., 2017).
```
3.3.2.2 Temperature
AAB are mesophilic microorganisms, and their optimum growth temperature is
between 25 and 30°C. Above optimum temperature, the bacteria are deactivated
since essential enzymes are denatured, membranes are damaged causing loss of cel-
lular constituents, and the toxic effect of acetic acid is increased. The minimum
and maximum growth temperatures are difficult to define due to the variability of
36 Advances in Vinegar Production
the present species and the influence of the medium composition. Generally, in sys-
```
tems not equipped with temperature control (traditional processes), the AAB activity
```
is favored during spring and summer but stuck acetification may occur due to the
increase of temperature which may sometimes exceed 40°C in the vinegar producing
```
Mediterranean countries (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Ho et al., 2017).
```
In industrial submerged processes, the optimal working temperature is approx-
imately 30°C. The temperature increases during the process because the ace-
```
tic acid fermentation is a thermodynamically favorable aerobic process (around
```
```
8.4 MJ/L of ethanol oxidized), leading to irreversible reduction of the metabolic
```
```
function of AAB; therefore, temperature control is compulsory (Gullo et al., 2014;
```
```
Matsutani et al., 2013). Above upper temperature limits in industrial vinegar
```
production, several studies have shown the occurrence of thermotolerant AAB
```
strains, which were able to oxidize ethanol (up to 9%) in the range 38–40°C with-
```
out any appreciable lag time. For example, two screened strains of A. tropicalis
and A. pasteurianus, able to grow at 40 and 45°C, were proposed as suitable for
artisanal spirit vinegar production. Since the ethanol oxidation is an exothermic
reaction, thermotolerance is an advantageous AAB trait for industrial vinegar
```
production because it has the potential to reduce the cost of cooling (Gullo and
```
```
Giudici, 2008; Ho et al., 2017).
```
3.3.2.3 pH
```
The optimum pH value for AAB growth is in the range 5.0–6.5; however, some
```
species are also able to grow at lower pH values, as in the case of wine with pH
3.02–3.85 or in traditional balsamic vinegar production where bacterial activity
has been observed at pH values below 3. AAB strains have also been isolated
from acetate media with pH 2.0–2.3. The tolerance of AAB to low pH is strongly
```
dependent on various parameters, such as the ethanol and oxygen concentration;
```
```
specifically, it decreases at high ethanol and low oxygen contents (Gullo and
```
```
Giudici, 2008).
```

4.1 INTRODUCTION
The production of vinegar relies on the presence of the main actors that transform
the ethanol from any substrate into acetic acid. For this ability to produce acetic
acid, the bacterial species responsible for this transformation are known as acetic
```
acid bacteria (AAB). However, this denomination does not have any taxonomic
```
value, although it is useful for both the applied microbiology in industry as well
as for microbiologists who can group a bunch of species that share some common
characteristics. However, some species included in this group present a limited abil-
ity to transform ethanol into acetic acid, despite sharing the metabolic pathways to
perform these reactions. The analysis of this group of bacteria and their industrial
uses requires their isolation and identification. The isolation has been the first hurdle
```
for their study, because these bacteria develop in a hard medium (generally with
```
high ethanol or high acetic acid, two compounds that are normally used for their

```
antimicrobial activity), and their recovery has hardly mimicked the conditions of
```
these media. In fact, AAB are considered “fastidious” microorganisms due to their
poor recovery with classical microbiological methods such as plate cultures. The dif-
ferences between the enumerated microorganism population under microscopy and
on plates could easily be of three orders of magnitude or even without any recovery
```
on plates (Torija et al., 2010). This lack of culturability could be related to the use of
```
```
media that are not appropriate for AAB; there are also some other aspects that could
```
account for it. For instance, after microscope observation it is obvious that AAB tend
to form aggregates that after plating will form a single colony, although they could
contain more than one species. Despite these aspects of not appropriate and selective
media and cell aggregation, the main reason can be due to the status of “Viable But
```
Not Culturable” (VBNC). This status has been detected in extreme conditions such
```
```
as the ones present in wine (Millet and Lonvaud-Funel, 2000) or vinegar (Torija et
```
```
al., 2010). Culture-independent methods for the estimation of AAB populations in
```
```
both media (wine and vinegar) have been developed in our group for the last 15 years
```
```
(Andorrà et al., 2008, González et al., 2004, Ilabaca et al., 2008, Portillo and Mas,
```
```
2016, Torija et al., 2010, Valera et al., 2015). However, both methods (culture-depen-
```
```
dent and -independent) should be used together to provide an accurate description of
```
the real diversity present in wines or vinegars.
4.2 MICROBIAL DIVERSITY AND ISOLATION:
CLASSICAL AND MOLECULAR METHODS
The methods traditionally used for the detection and quantification of different
microorganisms are based on morphological descriptions under the microscope
```
(shape and size of the cells) or on plates (shape, structure and color of the colonies).
```
These descriptions have been accompanied by several physiological tests based on
the growth or changes in color of different media due to biochemical reactions per-
formed in the medium. Furthermore, the isolation is a requirement for the appropri-
ate identification and enumeration of microorganisms. Classification schemes have
been described in the successive versions of the Bergey’s Manual of Systematic
```
Bacteriology (last edition in which AAB were included, Sievers and Swings, 2005),
```
which have been a traditional reference for the identification of different bacterial
groups. However, it is necessary to conduct many tests for reliable identification
of most bacteria at species level, and polyphasic approaches have been proposed
```
(Cleenwerk and De Vos, 2008). Thus, this work is time-consuming, and the accurate
```
interpretation requires considerable expertise.
Gram stain and Catalase tests are routine analyses in bacteria, and in many com-
```
mon niches, it is appropriate to distinguish between Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) and
```
AAB. However, further differentiation to species level is very difficult, and physi-
ological tests are normally not enough. One of the first microbiological tests per-
formed is to examine the morphology of the microorganisms under a microscope
using phase-contrast microscopy. This examination will yield information related
to the shape, size and arrangements of the cells. This can lead to incorrect inter-
pretations, because the appearance of microorganisms depends on the age and the
41Advances in Enumeration and Identification
conditions of culture. Also, the morphology of the colonies grown in different spe-
```
cific media can be useful (De Ley et al., 1984).
```
The estimation of microbiological population density and diversity plays an
important role in any process where microorganisms play a relevant role, due to
their capacity to transform the substrates and, consequently, the populations that
develop on them. Population densities can be measured using many methods, but
the two mostly used are counts under the microscope and direct plating. Microscope
counting techniques are the quickest but require a minimal population. Alternatives
for lower populations are the concentration by filtration and direct plating methods.
The combination of both can be applied to those substrates suspected of having a low
viable population. Microscope counting consists in quantification, using a micro-
```
scope counting chamber (Neubauer or Thoma for instance). The main hurdle is the
```
```
limit of detection (large populations of cells are required) and the lack of discrimina-
```
tion between alive and dead cells.
Plate enumeration counts the colonies formed by different microorganisms on
selected media. There are non-selective media that allow the growth of all microor-
ganisms. However, in samples with mixed species, the more abundant species domi-
nate and will prevent the recovery of the species found in lower amounts. In these
cases, selective media are recommended, because these media can favor the growth
of some species, limiting the recovery of the most dominant microorganisms. In fact,
any culture media can be converted in selective media by the addition of antibiotics
that inhibit some microorganisms or by changes in the incubation conditions, such
as pH, temperature, presence or absence of oxygen, etc. Finally, media enriched in
different nutrients to facilitate the growth of different types of microorganisms are
also used. Often, a combination of the different conditions is used for a more efficient
enumeration.
However, isolation is not normally enough for the identification of microorgan-
isms. An important further step for the identification of microorganisms has been
the combination of isolation by plating and molecular methods, especially relevant in
ecological studies, where large amounts of samples are analyzed. Although several
molecular methods have been proposed, the most widely used are those based on
the nucleic acids, especially DNA. Ribosomal RNA coding regions have been the
prevalent targets for the identification of microorganisms. The genes coding for ribo-
somal RNA are organized in tandems that form transcription units repeated along
the genome. Each unit is formed by the ribosomal RNA coding genes and the inter-
```
nal and external transcribed spacers (ITS and ETS). The genes coding for ribosomal
```
RNA are highly conserved regions and their sequences can be considered species-
specific. Thus, these sequences can be aligned with those deposited in different data-
bases, which allows the classification of one microorganism as belonging to a given
species. On the opposite, the ITS sequences are less conserved and can be used to
differentiate further those microorganisms that cannot be differentiated by the genes
coding ribosomal RNA. This further differentiation can be applied for those species
that are closely related and have almost identical sequences in the ribosomal genes.
Phylogenetic trees can be generated with the known sequences from databases and
used for the identification of microorganisms.
42 Advances in Vinegar Production
Nevertheless, the main hurdle of identification after plating is that only the cells
that form colonies are considered. Thus, the population enumerated by plating is the
“culturable” population, measured as colony forming units, abbreviated as CFU or
cfu. This can be considered as an important handicap for the ecological studies of
AAB, especially if we focus on vinegar, where the differences between culturable
```
and total AAB populations are higher (Figure 4.1).
```
```
Furthermore, the time required to grow on plates (which could take up to
```
```
2–10 days) is an additional limitation. However, the main challenge of the studies
```
```
on the vinegar microbial ecology is the entrance of AAB into VBNC states (Millet
```
```
and Lonvaud-Funel, 2000). This VBNC state means that the microorganisms cannot
```
grow but still maintain their metabolic activity. Microorganisms undergo this state
when the environmental conditions are not the best for their development. Previously
it was assumed that the microorganisms in this state were dead, but they are alive.
One of the basic concepts of the VBNC state is that the microorganisms retain the
ability to grow again if they are placed in a medium that does not include the condi-
```
tions that have induced this state (Oliver, 2005). Their metabolism is reduced but they
```
```
can keep transforming the medium; it is only a matter of time. The basal metabolism
```
is maintained, the main cellular functions are active, and the genes are continu-
```
ously expressed (Lleò et al., 2000, 2001, Yaron and Mathews, 2002). Finally, VBNC
```
microorganisms modify their protein profiles and the composition of fatty acids in
```
the plasma membranes, maintaining the membrane potential (Day and Oliver, 2004,
```
```
Heim et al., 2002).
```
Thus, we can find easily a mixture of live cells, dead cells and several cells in
transient states from live to dead. The transient states could include old cells that
```
are able to grow in optimal conditions; old cells with limited ability to grow but
```
which are fully viable with metabolic activity and finally cells that start the lysis.
Nevertheless, the consolidated knowledge has been obtained from classical methods,
that is the analysis of the cultured microorganisms. The enumeration and identifica-
tion of microorganisms underwent a strong step forward when molecular biology
techniques were added to those methods. However, the last step was still to be done:
FIGURE 4.1 Differences in acetic acid bacteria quantification during vinegar produc-
```
tion. Total population: measured by microscopy; culturable population: recovered on GYC
```
medium.
43Advances in Enumeration and Identification
the use of those techniques directly from the substrates to be analyzed, without the
culturing steps. These “culture-independent” techniques have emerged after the 20th
century, and they have been applied for the quantification and enumeration of AAB
```
in wine or vinegar (Andorrà et al., 2008, González et al., 2006b, Torija et al., 2010).
```
The culture-independent techniques have also some limitations. As the main tar-
get of these techniques is DNA and its stability to allow its long-time permanence
in the medium, the DNA quantified can be from both live and dead cells. However,
there are some alternatives to solve this hurdle and quantify only live cells. Several
studies used RNA instead of DNA to quantify or detect the viable population, since
```
this molecule is rapidly degraded in the dead cells (Cocolin and Mills, 2003, Hierro
```
```
et al., 2006). Nevertheless, ribosomal RNA might be more stable than required, and
```
```
the use of this molecule could not be appropriate (Andorrà et al., 2011, Hierro et al.,
```
```
2006, Sunyer-Figueras et al., 2018). Other alternatives have used DNA binding dyes
```
that enter in dead cells or cells with damaged membranes blocking DNA amplifica-
```
tion (Nocker and Camper, 2006, Rudi et al., 2005). Ethidium monoazide bromide
```
```
(EMA; Nogva et al., 2003) and propidium monoazide bromide (PMA; Nocker et al.,
```
```
2006) have been used to detect viable bacteria. These chemicals do not enter live
```
cells, only cells that have their membrane integrity compromised. Thus, only the
DNA from live cells will be detected and quantified after the treatment with these
dyes.
4.3 AAB ISOLATION
```
The glucose, yeast extract and calcium carbonate (GYC) agar medium has been a
```
kind of universal medium for the isolation of AAB. This medium should also be
considered differential because AAB dissolve the calcium carbonate precipitates
```
(Figure 4.2). As a result, a halo is formed around the AAB colony, which is very
```
useful for a quick identification of the colonies.
FIGURE 4.2 Acetic acid bacteria growth on GYC medium.
44 Advances in Vinegar Production
However, the AAB origin produces physiological differences that allowed the
development of differential culture media for AAB isolation according to a selective
use of a carbon source such as glucose, mannitol, ethanol, etc. These media can incor-
porate calcium carbonate or other indicators such as bromocresol-green that respond
```
selectively to the production of acid (De Ley et al., 1984, Swings and De Ley, 1981). It
```
is also a common practice the supplementation with antibiotics, to prevent the growth
of microorganisms that are present in the same niches. For instance, pimaricin or
similar antibiotics are used to prevent the growth of yeasts and molds. On the other
```
hand, penicillin is used to eliminate the growth of LAB (Ruiz et al., 2000).
```
```
GYC [5% D-glucose, 1% yeast extract, 0.5% CaCO3 and 2% agar (w/v)] and YPM
```
```
[2.5% mannitol, 0.5% yeast extract, 0.3% peptone and 2% agar (w/v)] are the two
```
most broadly used media for isolation of AAB. The incubation of these plates at
28°C under aerobic conditions may take between 2 and 4 days to allow AAB growth.
```
These culture media have been used for wine samples (Bartowsky et al., 2003, Du
```
```
Toit and Lambrechts, 2002, González et al., 2005) or vinegar samples (González et
```
```
al., 2006a, Gullo et al., 2009, Hidalgo et al., 2012, Vegas et al., 2013).
```
However, AAB from some industrial samples, especially vinegar, are difficult to
```
recover on plates (Sokollek et al., 1998). The production of vinegar is developed in
```
very extreme conditions that produce high specialization of AAB cells. The intro-
```
duction of a double agar layer with different concentrations of agar (0.5% in the
```
```
lower and 1% agar in the upper layer) to media containing ethanol and acetic acid has
```
been partially successful. This is a simulation of the environment of the acetification
```
vessels (Entani et al., 1985). However, the recovery of AAB on plates is still a strong
```
limitation to studying them, and this is especially critical for ecological studies, as
it is based on the proper enumeration of all the individuals in a given environment.
Thus, culture-independent molecular techniques have been developed to solve this
problem.
4.4 AAB IDENTIFICATION
The quantification and identification of microorganisms in a given substrate or pro-
cess is based on the correlation between the target molecules and the biomass. This
is right for DNA, yet it is not always the case for RNA or proteins, as they change
with the different physiological states during the development and growth. In fact,
almost all the microorganisms that participate in wine or vinegar making undergo
life and growing cycles during the process. In bacteria, the main genes used for
identification are the ribosomal genes and especially the gene coding for the 16S
```
rRNA (Cole et al., 2005). However, sequencing for routine analysis of large number
```
of samples, as is required in ecological studies, has been very expensive and still
is. A cheaper practice frequently used for the analysis of large numbers of sam-
```
ples is the restriction analysis of genes coding for the ribosomal RNAs (polymerase
```
```
chain reaction-restriction fragment length polymorphism, PCR-RFLPs). This tech-
```
nique is based on the use of specific endonucleases producing fragments that could
be species-specific. When the region targeted is the 16S rRNA gene, it has been
```
denominated Amplified Ribosomal DNA Restriction Analysis (ARDRA). ARDRA
```
```
has been broadly used to identify AAB (González et al., 2006a, Gullo et al., 2006,
```
45Advances in Enumeration and Identification
```
Poblet et al., 2000, Ruiz et al., 2000, Vegas et al., 2010). However, in some cases the
```
species discrimination required the restriction analysis of the 16S–23S intergenic
```
spacer region (González et al., 2006a, Ruiz et al., 2000, Trček and Teuber, 2002).
```
Later sequencing of this region has been proposed as more reliable identification
```
protocol (González and Mas, 2011).
```
However, nowadays sequencing has become a more affordable technique.
Generally, sequencing, alignment with sequences in databases and elaboration of
genetic trees, is an acceptable criterion for the adscription of a given microorganism
to a microbial species. Nevertheless, in ecological studies that require processing of
a large number of samples, the association of the different isolates by RFLP of ribo-
somal genes or ITS can be considered an initial step. In this case we should presume
that all the isolates with the same banding pattern are the same species. Sequencing
at least two or three of such isolates as representatives for each group of isolates
should be required for a significant species ascription.
Besides the analysis of the nucleic acids as a tool for identification, other mol-
ecules could also be the target for identification. For instance, protein profiling
has been used, traditionally with electrophoresis, as a method for identification.
Nevertheless, new techniques such as matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization
```
time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) have become also alternatives
```
to DNA polymorphism. It has been used to differentiate AAB, at the level of genus,
```
species and even strains of the same species (Andrés-Barrao et al., 2013, Wieme et
```
```
al., 2014). The most interesting aspect is the absence of manipulation, because it
```
can be applied to intact bacteria or colonies. Furthermore, it might be suitable for
the analysis of a large number of samples, as required in routine ecological studies
```
(Trček and Barja, 2015).
```
Another relevant aspect when we try to analyze and identify AAB is that the
AAB taxonomy has undergone a thorough and dramatic change. Thus, the methods
for identification of AAB have had to adapt to the changes in classification. For many
years, the main consideration was the two genera: Gluconobacter and Acetobacter.
```
The 1984 Bergey’s edition (De Ley et al., 1984) incorporated molecular techniques
```
such as fatty acid composition, electrophoresis of cytosolic proteins, percentage of
G+C content and DNA–DNA hybridization. The DNA–DNA hybridization was the
most widely used technique for describing new species at the end of the 20th century.
This technique determines the similarity between genomes of different species. The
16S rDNA gene is a highly conserved region, and the small changes in its sequence
can be considered species-specific and, thus, used in most taxonomical studies of
bacteria. In some AAB species the differences in the 16S rDNA sequences are very
limited with differences in few nucleotide pairs. Finally, full genome sequencing can
be a definite tool for identification and for further studies on the industrial applica-
tion of some species or even strains. However, full genome sequencing is not possible
for routine analysis of large numbers of isolates.
The revision of the AAB group has changed from the two genera and five
```
species in 1984 into the current 19 genera and over 70 species (Guillamón and
```
```
Mas, 2017). Some AAB species of industrial interest have undergone consid-
```
erable changes in nomenclature, making it difficult to follow the literature
throughout different years. Two of the most valuable species, formerly identified
46 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
as Acetobacter xylinus and Acetobacter europaeus (De Ley et al., 1984), were
```
```
later reclassified under the Gluconacetobacter genus (Yamada et al., 1997)
```
and finally under Komagataeibacter, maintaining the specific names, that is
```
Komagataeibacter xylinus and Komagataeibacter europaeus (Komagata et al.,
```
```
2014, Yamada et al., 2012).
```
4.5 AAB TYPING
One of the important aspects of the isolation of AAB on plates is that it allows
```
the discrimination at strain level (typing). This is especially relevant for the appli-
```
cation at industrial level, as not all the strains perform with the same efficiency
the transformations sought. The molecular methods for genotyping use both higher
polymorphisms in some sequences as well as repeated sequences along the genome.
The initial technique applied for the identification of AAB strains was the random
```
amplification of genomic DNA (RAPD). This technique uses single arbitrary primer
```
sequences of nine or ten bases of length, resulting in amplicons different in size and
number for each strain. The band pattern visualized in gel electrophoresis should be
```
specific to a given strain. Trček et al. (1997) used this technique for the first time for
```
```
the typing of AAB from spirit vinegar, and Nanda et al. (2001) in rice vinegar. Later
```
```
on, it was used for the AAB typing in spoiled wines (Bartowsky et al., 2003) and in
```
```
sound grapes (Prieto et al., 2007).
```
Nevertheless, other techniques have been developed taking advantage of the
repetitive sequences in the genomes, designing the appropriate homologous prim-
ers to obtain a characteristic electrophoretic band pattern for each strain. For
```
instance, enterobacterial repetitive intergenic consensus-PCR (ERIC-PCR) or
```
```
repetitive extragenic palindromic-PCR (REP-PCR) are consensus sequences of
```
highly conserved palindromic repeat regions. Although initially described for
enteric bacteria, these sequences are widely distributed in the genomes of other
```
bacterial groups. Nanda et al. (2001) and Wu et al. (2012) used this technique
```
```
to genotype AAB from rice and cereal vinegars. González et al. (2004, 2005)
```
used these techniques to genotype AAB in wines and to follow their distribution
before and during alcoholic fermentation. For genomic fingerprinting microsatel-
lites have also been used. This technique amplifies genome fragments flanked by
these sequences, yielding amplicon patterns that are strain-specific. De Vuyst et
```
al. (2007) used (GTG)5 primer for the typification of AAB strains from the fer-
```
mentation of cocoa beans and this technique was later used in vinegar production
```
(Hidalgo et al., 2010, Vegas et al., 2010).
```
4.6 CULTURE-INDEPENDENT TECHNIQUES FOR THE
ENUMERATION AND IDENTIFICATION OF AAB
```
Although some of the previous techniques (for instance ARDRA) could be used
```
directly from the media, most of them cannot discriminate between more than two
species together and even often are not completely resolutive for a single species,
even when it is largely the main species. Thus, culture-independent techniques have
47Advances in Enumeration and Identification
been developed during the last number of years and some of them applied success-
fully to the study of AAB.
```
4.6.1 direCt epifluoresCenCe teCHnique (deft)
```
This technique is used for the direct enumeration of viable cells using specific dyes.
These dyes enter the cells and react with different intracellular molecules or are
incorporated into some organelles. The first dye to be used was acridine orange
```
(Froudière et al., 1990), although now there are some others available that use mix-
```
tures of different dyes that allow a more complete differentiation. For instance,
SYTO 9 green fluorescent stain is combined with propidium iodide, which is a red
fluorescent stain. SYTO 9 enters all the cells while propidium iodide penetrates in
cells with damaged membranes. Propidium iodide competes with SYTO 9 for the
same binding sites and, thus, reduces the staining of SYTO-9. When using this com-
bination, cells with green fluorescence staining are considered alive, whereas cells
```
with red fluorescence are considered dead (Figure 4.3).
```
Other combinations such as FUN 1 with Calcofluor White M2R are also used.
This is a rapid technique, and although it allows the differentiation between viable
and non-viable cells, it cannot be used for identification. This method has been the
```
reference for the evidence of non-culturable populations of bacteria in wine (Du Toit
```
```
et al., 2005, Millet and Lonvaud-Funel, 2000).
```
```
4.6.2 fluoresCenCe in Situ HyBridization (fisH)
```
Labeled probes can be designed for direct hybridization with some molecules of DNA
or RNA. This technique involves the fixation and permeabilization of cell membranes
to facilitate the entrance and hybridization of the probe into the cell. The hybridized
targets can be detected by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry. This technique
```
has been developed for AAB (Blasco et al., 2003), although the size of the bacteria
```
```
and the media where they develop (wine or vinegar) can limit their routine use. This
```
```
technique has been applied to detect Gluconacetobacter sacchari (Franke et al., 1999).
```
FIGURE 4.3 Observation of acetic acid bacteria under the microscope. A: Clear field in a
```
Thoma Chamber. B: Same picture after staining with LIVE/DEAD viability kit (bright spots
```
```
are LIVE whereas the dull spots are DEAD).
```
48 Advances in Vinegar Production
4.6.3 floW Cytometry
Flow cytometry can detect simultaneously several characteristics of single particles,
for instance size, internal complexity or fluorescence labeled cells, etc. A laser light
passes through the particles and the beam is scattered and registered as fluorescence.
This technique is normally coupled to DEFT or FISH to obtain both the identifica-
tion and viability. Although it has been used for enumeration and identification of
```
microorganisms in wine (Andorrà et al., 2011, Wang et al., 2014), its use for AAB is
```
difficult due to the media and the size of the microorganisms.
```
4.6.4 denaturing gradient gel eleCtropHoresis -pCr (dgge-pCr) and
```
```
temperature gradient gel eleCtropHoresis -pCr (tgge-pCr)
```
These methods are the most commonly used for the characterization of microbial
communities in different environmental niches. These techniques have been used
```
already for the analysis of the bacterial populations in wine (Andorrà et al., 2008,
```
```
Cocolin et al., 2000, Takahashi et al., 2014) and also vinegars (De Vero et al., 2006,
```
```
Gullo et al., 2009, Haruta et al., 2006, Yetiman and Kesmen, 2015). For bacterial
```
populations, the amplified fragments are from 16S or 23S ribosomal coding genes.
The individual electrophoretic bands can be excised for sequencing, and this delivers
the identification at species level of each band. However, the main limitation is the
bias introduced by PCR methodology, amplifying only the main species and over-
looking the minority species present in the studied population.
```
4.6.5 real time or quantitatiVe pCr (q-pCr)
```
This method monitors the PCR during the reaction, quantifying the fluorescence
```
generated during the PCR. Different binding agents (SYBR Green has been the most
```
```
common) or probes (for instance, TaqMan probes) can generate the fluorescence
```
```
that is released either when the PCR progresses (SYBR Green) or when the probe
```
is degraded by the Taq polymerase. In the case of the TaqMan probes, initially the
probe bounds the DNA and no fluorescence is detected because of the presence of a
quencher, but when the polymerase amplifies the DNA it degrades the probe releas-
ing the quencher and the fluorescence can be detected. This can be used to quantify
```
the DNA (or RNA after cDNA synthesis), which is also proportional to the quantity
```
of cells. Therefore, with this technique, it is possible to detect and quantify a targeted
species for which the primers or probes are designed. Thus, it serves to simultane-
ously identify and quantify a given population of targeted microorganisms. It can be
```
used to detect a group of microorganisms (for instance AAB). This technique has
```
been used extensively to detect and quantify different wine microorganisms, like
```
AAB (Andorrà et al., 2010, González et al., 2006b) or different species within the
```
```
group (González et al., 2006b, Torija et al., 2010, Valera et al., 2013).
```
4.6.6 massiVe sequenCing
Several names are in use for this technique based on the techniques of next gener-
```
ation sequencing (NGS). Thus, we can see these techniques mentioned as massive
```
49Advances in Enumeration and Identification
sequencing, metagenomics, high-throughput sequencing or pyrosequencing. This
technique derives from sequencing all the DNA amplicons that can be generated from
a sample. Thus, the organisms identified depend on the design of the primers: in theory
if the primers are universal, all the organisms can be amplified. The libraries are gen-
erally differentiated for prokaryotes and eukaryotes. However, there could be interfer-
ences in the determination, the most frequent being the presence of chloroplasts and
mitochondria in eukaryotes that are also amplified, as there were prokaryotes. Thus,
the origin of the sample is to be considered for the primer design and the protocol for
```
the analysis (Kiorouglou et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the large amount of sequences
```
generated for a single sample and the limited polymorphism of closely related species
```
makes it difficult to associate unambiguously a sequence to a taxon (genus or species).
```
```
Thus, the term operational taxonomic unit (OTU) is used to refer to closely related
```
```
sequences. It has been applied for the analyses of different microorganisms (among
```
```
them AAB) on grapes, wine and vinegar. In general, the grape microbiome has been
```
analyzed by NGS, and the observations have confirmed the predominant presence of
```
Gluconobacter (Bokulich et al., 2012, Portillo and Mas, 2016) and the development of
```
```
Gluconobacter, Acetobacter and Gluconacetobacter during wine making (Bokulich
```
```
et al., 2012, Campanaro et al., 2014, Pinto et al., 2015, Portillo and Mas, 2016). In vin-
```
egars NGS has been also used and made evident the presence of bacterial groups not
previously detected in such a harsh environment. However, the main AAB have been
```
detected in those vinegar processes (Trček et al., 2016, Valera et al., 2015).
```
4.7 CONCLUDING REMARKS
The enumeration and identification of AAB has enormously evolved during recent
years especially due to the development of molecular methods. This methodological
evolution has allowed the generalization of different ecological studies that previ-
ously were more limited because they were time-consuming, costly and with limited
discrimination capacity. Several culture-dependent and -independent techniques have
been developed and optimized for the study of AAB ecology and taxonomy. However,
all these techniques present some advantages and disadvantages. Culture-dependent
techniques are biased by the low recovery of these microorganisms on plates, espe-
cially when plated samples come from wines or vinegars. Instead, these techniques
provide pure strains to be characterized and allow their use in further applications.
On the other hand, culture-independent techniques allow the by-passing of the isola-
tion step, identifying the AAB species directly from the samples. However, these
techniques limit the identification to the major species, not being able to detect minor
species. Therefore, the better approach is to combine both types of techniques in order
to have a more complete vision of the AAB biodiversity in a given sample.
Nowadays, the development of different technologies to carry out massive
sequencing of all types of samples opens a new horizon to increase the available
knowledge about AAB biodiversity. However, the current identification in OTUs
```
limits this advance; thus, the challenge is to improve these technologies to achieve
```
better and more accurate identification. This improvement will surely allow us to
identify new AAB species never detected before, probably because they do not grow
well in laboratory culture media and they are not the main species in the sample.

Raw Materials and
Pretreatment Methods
for Vinegar Production
Sofia Maina, Aikaterini Papadaki,
Vasiliki Kachrimanidou, Effimia Eriotou,
and Nikolaos Kopsahelis
5.1 INTRODUCTION
As described in the previous chapters, vinegar can be produced by alcoholic fermen-
tation and subsequent acetous fermentation of any fermentable carbohydrate source.
It constitutes an important commercial product that is consumed either directly or
```
used in the preparation of various food products, including condiments (sauces, sea-
```
```
sonings, ketchups, mayonnaise, pickles, etc.), Asian foods such as sushi (Ho et al.,
```
```
2017), and others. Different types of vinegars are manufactured worldwide and are
```
classified based on the raw material, the starter cultures, and the fermentation pro-
cesses involved. Grapes, rice, apples, cereals, whey, honey, and a variety of fruit can
and have been used to produce vinegar. Balsamic vinegars account for the largest

56 Advances in Vinegar Production
share of the global market of vinegars, followed by red wine vinegar and cider vin-
```
egar (Solieri and Giudici, 2009).
```
The type and chemical composition of the raw material, the pretreatment process
applied on the raw material, and the vinegar production and ageing methods affect the
final quality of the vinegar products. Consequently, the sensory quality of vinegars
```
(aroma and taste) depends on the raw materials and the metabolically and chemically
```
formed constituents during fermentation, as well as those originating from the age-
```
ing process (Tesfaye et al., 2002; Raspor and Goranovič, 2008). The final aroma is
```
the result of the contribution of some hundreds of volatile compounds as discussed in
more detail in other chapters of this book and in several published scientific studies.
```
Furthermore, as discussed in Chapter 1 (History and Current Issues of Vinegar),
```
vinegar has been found to promote beneficial health effects due to various bio-
active constituents, including constituents with antimicrobial, antioxidant, and
```
anti-inflammatory activities (Samad et al., 2016). For example, vinegar consumption
```
has been associated with diabetes and obesity control, appetite regulation, and the
```
improvement of digestion (Li et al., 2015a; Samad et al., 2016). Red wine vinegar
```
has also been shown to reduce human blood pressure due to the action of phenolic
```
compounds (Honsho et al., 2005; Takahara et al., 2005; Li et al., 2015a).
```
The pretreatment of the raw materials and the subsequent fermentations are the
fundamental steps for efficient vinegar production. Pretreatments involve all the
necessary processes to extract the fermentable sugars from the raw material. As
depicted in Figure 5.1, these processes vary depending on the type of raw material
```
used. For example, grains require more pretreatment steps than fruit; however grains
```
are easier to post-harvest handle and store.
The second stage for vinegar production is the bioconversion of fermentable car-
bohydrates to ethanol followed by the bio-oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid. Process
FIGURE 5.1 Pretreatments of different raw materials for vinegar production.
57Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
```
parameters (temperature, pH, O2 supply, water activity) during vinegar production,
```
as well as the chemical composition of the raw material, affect the fermentation
processes and thus play a key role in the quality of the end-product. Therefore, diver-
sified pretreatments are employed in vinegar manufacture aiming to improve the
process and the quality of the product.
During the production of vinegar from fruit, dilution or concentration of sugars,
acids, and nutrients of the juice affects the fermentation process, the flavor, and the
final alcohol/acetic acid concentration. More specifically, the ethanol yield obtained
after the alcoholic fermentation depends on the initial sugar concentration of the
substrate, the acidity should be adjusted to pH 3.2–3.8 by the addition of water or
```
acid (citric acid, malic acid, or juice), whereas nutrients, like N-sources, may also be
```
```
essential for the metabolic activity of the cultures (Heikefelt, 2011).
```
```
Saccharification (conversion of polymeric non-fermentable carbohydrates into
```
```
fermentable sugars) is an essential pretreatment process for starch-containing raw
```
materials such as wheat, rice, barley, sorghum, ginger, and some fruit. Enzymatic
pretreatments, on the other hand, facilitate the efficient extraction of the juices.
Other enzymes are also used for the hydrolysis of specific substances of the raw
```
materials, such as pectins in pectin-rich fruit (e.g., apples), in order to facilitate the
```
extraction of clarified juice and avoid the production of undesirable compounds that
may affect the quality of the vinegar.
The effects that different raw materials impart on the vinegar production process
and on product quality, with respect to their composition and the required pretreat-
ments, are highlighted and discussed in this chapter.
5.2 TYPES OF RAW MATERIALS
5.2.1 Wine
Wine, either red or white, comprises one of the first onset material employed in the
production of vinegar, particularly in the Mediterranean countries, which are also
known as major wine manufacturing regions. Wine vinegar derives solely from the
acetous fermentation of wine and should not contain more than 1.5% v/v residual
```
ethanol (Solieri and Giudici, 2009). Balsamic vinegar, red wine vinegar, and white
```
wine vinegar account for a substantial share of the worldwide market among the
```
different types of vinegars (Sellmer-Wilsberg, 2009). Different processing and pro-
```
duction methods are employed resulting in diversified qualities of wine vinegars
```
(Callejon et al., 2009). Specifically, for wine vinegars, the implementation of special
```
types of wine as initial feedstocks and the maturation in wooden barrels entail the
```
production of higher quality vinegars (Cerezo et al., 2008; Hailu et al., 2012).
```
The French word for vinegar, vinaigre, means sour wine, indicating a product
that derives from the spoilage of wine that could be actually desirable and perfectly
pair with the warm climate of the Mediterranean countries that favors the growth
```
of acetic acid bacteria (De Ory et al., 1998; Callejon et al., 2009; Ho et al., 2017).
```
Indeed, Spain and Italy produce wine vinegars with Protected Designations of Origin
```
(PDO), i.e., the “Vinagre del Condado de Huelva,” “Vinagre de Jerez,” and “Aceto
```
Balsámico Tradizionale di Módena,” “Aceto Balsámico Tradizionale di Reggio
58 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
Emilia,” respectively (Alvarez-Caliz et al., 2014). The grape must that is used for
```
the wine fermentation process, in combination with ageing and the maturation of the
final vinegar product, constitute the principal differentiation between the traditional
```
balsamic vinegar and the balsamic vinegar of Modena (Bartocci et al., 2017), as also
```
discussed in other chapters. Traditional balsamic vinegar requires an ageing time
frame of at least 12 years, whereas the balsamic vinegar of Modena, deriving from
a mixture of vinegar and cooked must, is obtained after a minimum of 2 months up
to 3 years in order to be designated as product of Protected Geographical Indication
```
(PGI) (Solieri et al., 2006; Bartocci et al., 2017).
```
The composition of wine as raw material is associated with the sensory charac-
```
teristics (odor and taste) of the produced vinegar primarily by affecting the activity
```
of acetic acid bacteria that influence the final product. Therefore, the composition
```
of sugars, anthocyanins and polyphenols, alcohols (particularly ethanol), nitrogen,
```
and amino acids, along with sulfur compounds, comprise crucial factors during the
fermentation process. On top of that, given that acetification and ageing of wine
vinegars are carried out in wooden barrels, the type of wood employed during this
process affects the quality of the end-product by modifying the composition of vola-
tile and phenolic constituents.
Acetic acid is the dominant fermentation metabolite that affects the organolep-
```
tic character of wine vinegar; however, other organic acids, esters, ketones, and
```
aldehydes are also key elements of the final quality. These compounds derive from
the raw material or from the acetification and the subsequent maturation processes
```
(Ozturk et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2017).
```
Phenolic compounds in wine are due to their natural occurrence in grapes or are
derived from the ageing in wooden barrels. Identification of phenols can be used as
an indicator in quality control to assess the processing technology and the raw mate-
```
rial employed (Tesfaye et al., 2002). Specifically, red wine fermentation is conducted
```
in the presence of the grape skins, resulting in increased quantities of phenolics,
including gallic acid, epicatechin, catechin, tyrosol, benzoic acid, syringic acid, and
```
vanillin among others (Budak and Guzel-Seydim, 2010). It is therefore considered
```
that the use of red or white wine will have a corresponding impact on the organolep-
tic characteristics of the final vinegar product.
```
Cerezo et al. (2008) evaluated the change in the profile of phenolic components in
```
red wine vinegars during acetification in various kinds of wooden barrels, including
oak, chestnut, acacia, and cherry. It was presented that the acetification in chestnut
```
wood entailed an increase in gallic acid and gallic ethyl-ester, whereas (+)-catechin
```
```
and resveratrol demonstrated a decrease (Cerezo et al., 2008). A sensory analysis was
```
also conducted, in which oak and cherry wood barrels were assigned higher scores
for aroma and taste. Different wooden barrels and their effect on volatile compounds
```
during the acetification process were also studied by Callejon et al. (2009). A consid-
```
erable increase in total volatiles was found, whereas more specific was the increase
in ethyl furoate and ethyl benzoate during acetification in cherry wood barrels.
Surface cultures displayed a prominent effect in the profile of acetic esters due
```
to the prolonged fermentation and the indigenous microflora (Callejon et al., 2009).
```
```
According to Madrera et al. (2010) the maturation process acts upon the concentra-
```
tion of the ethyl esters of organic acids, i.e., lactic, acetic, and succinic, along with
59Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
```
the aromatic compounds generated by acetic acid bacteria. Ho et al. (2017) also
```
stated that grape vinegars presented a substantial amount of ethyl acetate, the ester
of acetic acid.
The anthocyanin profile in wine vinegars is regulated by the pH value and the
```
presence or absence of oxygen. Cerezo et al. (2010) studied the effect of anthocyanins
```
in red wine vinegars and the impact of acetification during submerged fermentation
to evaluate the effect on antioxidant activity. It was established that vitisin-type and
ethyl-linked compounds were induced, while monomeric anthocyanins and phenolic
acids were reduced. Overall, the identification of phenolic compounds displays a
binary significance, since along with the influence on the organoleptic character, it is
also involved in vinegar authenticity determination.
Amino acids and ammonium ions comprise the principal sources of nitrogen to
support the growth of bacteria, and regardless the fact that bacteria can synthesize
amino acids from ammonium ions, a minimum quantity is essential to trigger metab-
```
olite synthesis (Alvarez-Caliz et al., 2014). Vinegar is obtained from a two-step
```
process and, therefore, the substantial requirements for amino acids to maintain the
```
oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid might not be ensured (Alvarez-Caliz et al., 2012).
```
More specifically, when biologically aged wine is used in vinegar production, the
alcoholic fermentation of must by yeasts may result in the depletion of carbon and
```
nitrogen sources; therefore, supplementation with nutrients is essential to support the
```
growth of acetic acid bacteria.
```
Maestre et al. (2008) studied the changes in the free amino acids, ammonium
```
ion, and urea contents by the activity of acetic acid bacteria during acetification,
reporting the tendency of l-proline, l-methionine, l-leucine, and ammonium ion
```
consumption (68.1% of total nitrogen metabolism). During that study it was also
```
stated that l-glutamic acid, l-glutamine, l-proline, and l-histidine could enhance
the action of acetic acid bacteria. The concentration of l-proline in wine could be
attributed to its presence in the grape must along with the fact that it is not consumed
```
by yeast strains (Valero et al., 2005). On top of that, yeast metabolism during alco-
```
holic fermentation results in the production of l-leucine along with the production of
```
amino acids due to autoproteolysis (Maestre et al., 2008; Alvarez-Caliz et al., 2012).
```
Acetic acid bacteria belonging to Acetobacter species utilize ethanol whereas
```
oxygen is employed as the final electron acceptor (Mas et al., 2014). Therefore, the
```
yield of acetic acid is associated with the initial concentration of alcohol contained
```
in the raw material (i.e., wine), since ethanol might hinder the entry into the acetate
```
cycle. Acetic acid bacteria growth on ethanol is distinguished by diauxic conditions,
where the oxidation phase is followed by the initiation of a stationary phase, denot-
```
ing a decrease in bacterial cells (Maestre et al., 2008). Subsequently, the uptake of
```
acetic acid in the bioconversion medium leads to bacterial growth.
Growth is restrained when ethanol concentration exceeds 7% in the culture
```
medium, thus restraining the whole bioconversion process (Jo et al., 2015). Therefore,
```
carbon and nitrogen sources are supplemented to sustain microbial growth. Jo et al.
```
(2015) evaluated the effect of various starting alcohol concentrations on the qual-
```
ity of high acid strength wine vinegars without enhancing the fermentation with
supplements. They concluded that an initial alcohol concentration of 6% resulted in
a high acidity vinegar with improved properties. Consequently, in the case that the
60 Advances in Vinegar Production
concentration of ethanol in the starting wine is high, a dilution step is required to
```
avoid acetic acid bacteria inhibition (Raspor and Goranovič, 2008). Similarly, the
```
```
presence of sulfur dioxide (SO2) should be avoided. However, Du Toit et al. (2005)
```
studied the impact of free and bound forms of SO 2 and oxygen in wine, using spe-
cific Acetobacter and Brettanomyces strains isolated from wine, and among other
findings they reported the ability of both strains to grow under anaerobic conditions.
Current aspects of wine/raisin vinegar production and fields of improvement are
discussed in more detail in Chapter 11.
5.2.2 apples/Cider
```
Apple cider is the pressed, raw, or fermented apple juice made by ripe fruit (Oke
```
```
and Paliyath, 2006; Verdu et al., 2014). The apples, depending on their use, are clas-
```
```
sified as dessert apples and cider apples (Ho et al., 2017). Cider apple varieties are
```
generally bitter and astringent and are mostly used to produce apple cider beverages
```
or further treated (fermented) to produce apple cider vinegar, which is widely used
```
```
as table vinegar (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). The quality of the apple cider depends
```
on the composition of the fresh apples used and subsequently on the cultivar, the
production region, the harvesting season, and the level of maturity. For instance, the
utilization of ripe fruit is essential for the production of apple cider, since unripe fruit
results in juices with lower total soluble solids and higher content of starch and acids,
also affecting the product aroma and flavor. On the other hand, overly mature apples
```
have lower extraction yields and a flat sweeter flavor (Oke and Paliyath, 2006; Joshi
```
```
and Sharma, 2009).
```
The cider apple varieties in Europe have average total soluble solids of 9–11°Brix,
```
0.12–0.31% titratable acidity (expressed as malic acid), 37–233 mg/100 mL tannin
```
```
content, and 0.25–0.75% pectin content (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). Apple cider can be
```
classified as bittersweet, bittersharp, sharp, and sweet, based on the acid and tannin
content of the pressed juice. Specifically, the bittersweet and bittersharp ones have
>0.2% tannin content, and the sharp and sweet types are characterized by <0.2%
tannin content. The bittersweet and sweet apple ciders have <0.45% acid content,
```
while bittersharp and sharp types have >0.45% acid content (Miles et al., 2015).
```
The characteristic acidic and astringent flavor of the cider vinegar is also attrib-
```
uted to the origin of the apples (Raspor and Goranovič, 2008), due to the presence of
```
```
tannins and phenolic compounds (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). The successful produc-
```
tion of an apple cider requires the blending of different apple cider cultivars, in order
```
to achieve a balanced sugar, acid, and tannin composition in the final product (Lea
```
```
and Drilleau, 2003). A typical composition of an apple juice is presented in Table 5.1.
```
The principal characteristic of cider apples is the polyphenol content. Apple poly-
```
phenols contain mainly polyphenolic acid derivatives and other flavonoids (Budak
```
```
et al., 2011). The main classes of phenolic compounds found in apples are flavanols,
```
```
flavonols, hydroxycinnamic acids, dihydrochalcones, and anthocyanins (Tsao et al.,
```
```
2005). Their concentration in apples is affected by the growth conditions, the degree
```
```
of maturity, and the type of processing (Spanos and Wrolstad, 1992).
```
```
Budak et al. (2011) reported that the main phenolics found in apple cider vinegars
```
are gallic acid, catechin, epicatechin, caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, and p-coumaric
61Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
```
acid. Polyphenols influence the acidity, sharpness, color, and aroma of the vinegar;
```
therefore, the phenolic content of the apples is directly correlated with the quality
```
of apple cider vinegars (Joshi and Sharma, 2009; Verdu et al., 2014). Specifically,
```
the content of procyanidins, which belong to the group of flavanols, is related to
the characteristic sensory properties of cider, i.e., the bitterness and astringency
```
(Kahle et al., 2005).
```
The content of flavanols in apples used for cider vinegar is higher than in des-
sert apples, while the initial phenolic content of the raw material decreases after
the fermentation. This could be attributed to the yeast cell wall-binding of phenolic
```
compounds, the precipitation by bonding with proteins (Figure 5.2), or the oxidation
```
```
by enzymes naturally occurring in apples (e.g., polyphenol oxidase) (Nogueira el al.,
```
```
2008). Hence, the protein content and the activity of specific natural enzymes play
```
a key role in the initial phenolic content of the starting material for cider and cider
vinegar production.
The color of cider is also related to the composition of phenolic compounds and
their oxidation state. In particular, the enzymatic oxidation of specific phenolic
compounds that are present in apple cider, such as chlorogenic acid, procyanidins,
```
(+)-catechin, and phloridzin, contributes to the color of the end-product. Moreover,
```
hydrocinnamic acids, such as ferulic acid, are precursors of some characteristic cider
```
aroma compounds (Verdu et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2014).
```
Apples also contain high amounts of pectin, which account for about 42% of
```
the total polysaccharides (Voragen et al., 2009). Pectins are structural polysaccha-
```
rides consisting of polymers of galacturonic acid partially esterified with methanol.
```
Pectins are related to the body or viscosity of apple juice (Joshi and Sharma, 2009).
```
Consequently, the presence of natural pectinolytic enzymes in apples affects the
composition and quality of apple cider and cider vinegar. Specifically, pectin methy-
lesterase catalyzes the hydrolysis of the methoxy ester groups in pectins, resulting in
```
the release of methanol (Figure 5.3). Methanol is a toxic substance, which can cause
```
```
adverse effects on human health, when ingested in excess (Bourgeois et al., 2006).
```

62 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
The maximum permitted concentration of methanol in wine is 35 mg/100 mL (Silva
```
```
et al., 2007). The hydrolysis of pectin is common since commercial cider vinegar
```
is often made from unpasteurized cider, and therefore the enzymes remain active,
```
affecting the quality of the final product (Kahn et al., 1966). The hydrolysis of pectin
```
and the precipitation of phenolics result in losses of aroma, color, and body of the
```
cider vinegars (Casale et al., 2006).
```
The protein composition of the raw material is also associated with the quality
of vinegar. The amino acids composition can affect the microorganisms involved
in the vinegar fermentation by altering the metabolic regulation and physiologi-
```
cal activities (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Sainz et al., 2017). The acetic acid bac-
```
teria are aerobic microorganisms within the family Acetobacteraceae. They are
known for their ability to oxidize carbohydrates and release various metabo-
lites, such as aldehydes, ketones, and organic acids, providing thus the char-
```
acteristic aroma and flavor to the vinegars (Joshi and Sharma, 2009; Mamlouk
```
```
and Gullo, 2013), as discussed in more detail in other chapters of this book.
```
Specific examples of the effects of nitrogen compounds include the inhibitory
effects of valine on Gluconobacter oxydans, and threonine and homoserine on
Acetobacter aceti, or the stimulatory effects of glutamate, glutamine, proline,
```
and histidine (Drysdale and Fleet, 1988). The soluble nitrogen content of cider
```
apple juice mainly consists of asparagine, aspartic, and glutamic acids. Smaller
amounts of valine and traces of threonine and proline are usually present, among
```
other amino acids (Beech, 1972).
```
FIGURE 5.2 Polyphenol–protein haze formation in juice/wine/vinegar.
63Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
The volatile compounds formed during fermentation highly contribute to the
specific aroma of the vinegar. The major volatile constituents of cider vinegars
are acetaldehyde, ethyl formate, ethyl acetate, ethanol, isobutanol, 2-methylbu-
tanol, 2-butanol, isobutyl acetate, acetoin, isopentanol, and 2-phenylethanol.
Diethyl succinate, 2-phenethyl formate, and 2-phenethyl alcohol are considered
```
essential contributors to the cider vinegar flavor and aroma (Joshi and Sharma,
```
```
2009). However, the production of these compounds is highly correlated to the
```
chemical composition of the raw material. For instance, in the case of apple cider
vinegar, the formation of gluconic acid and acetoin arise from the oxidative ace-
```
tic acid bacteria catabolism of glucose and d,l-lactate, respectively (Joshi and
```
```
Sharma, 2009).
```
Another factor that influences the quality of cider vinegar, is the processing of
cores and peels during the apple juice extraction, which results in an increase of
non-sugar solids, including procyanidins. This further impedes the cider vinegar
```
production by haze and color development (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). Moreover,
```
when apple juice concentrate is used as raw material for apple cider, 5-hydroxymeth-
```
ylfurfural (HMF) may also be present in the cider. HMF is an aldehyde with char-
```
acteristic flavor produced by the heat treatment during the concentration of juices,
as a result of non-enzymatic browning reactions such as the thermal degradation of
```
sugars (caramelization) or the Maillard reactions between amino acids and reducing
```
```
sugars (Figure 5.4).
```
The concentration of HMF in a product strongly depends on pH, total acidity, heat
```
treatment temperature, sugar content (mainly fructose or glucose), water activity,
```
storage time and temperature, and the presence of divalent cations. Specifically, the
conditions during vinegar production are suitable for the formation of HMF due to
```
high sugar concentration (mainly hexoses), low pH, presence of organic acids, and low
```
```
water activity (Matić et al., 2009). Zhang et al. (2017) tested ten Chinese-style brewed
```
vinegars and found that HMF concentrations were in a range 0.42–115.43 mg/kg.
The nature of sugar also affects the HMF formation. Specifically, fructose is the
```
most reactive sugar compared to sucrose and glucose, under acidic conditions (Lee
```
```
and Nagy, 1990).
```
Traditional and current aspects of cider vinegar production are also discussed in
Chapter 12.
FIGURE 5.3 Pectin hydrolysis by pectin methylesterase.
64 Advances in Vinegar Production
5.2.3 otHer fruit
Fruit vinegar can be made from fruit juices as well as their residuals. Different raw
materials including banana, pineapple, mango, strawberry, orange, jabaticaba, and
```
coconut have been used for vinegar production (Ho et al., 2017). The chemical com-
```
position of fruits varies according to the botanical variety, the cultivation practices,
the degree of maturity, and the level of ripeness. Generally, fruits have high water
```
content (above 70%) and are rich in carbohydrates, whereas fat and protein contents
```
are relatively low. Commonly, the protein content is lower than 3.5%, and the fat con-
tent is around 0.5%. A typical fruit composition is presented in Table 5.2. Fruits are
also rich in amino acids, organic acids, vitamins, and minerals. These components
```
influence the flavor and aroma of fruit vinegar (Ho et al., 2017).
```
Fruit vinegars are rich sources of important nutrients such as carotenoids, pig-
ments, phenolic, and polyphenol compounds that could have beneficial health effects
on humans. Residues from fruit industries have also been valorized for fruit vinegar
production. For instance, pineapple residues are rich in sugars, minerals, vitamins,
and insoluble fiber-rich fraction consisting of cellulose, pectin, hemicellulose, and
```
lignin (Roda et al., 2014).
```
