65Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
During the production of fruit vinegars several parameters are important in
order to obtain a final product of high quality. The chemical composition of the raw
```
material is associated with the success of the vinegar fermentation process (Cejudo-
```
```
Bastante et al., 2016). In most cases, the raw materials contain enough nutrients for
```
```
the growth and metabolism of acetic acid bacteria; however the sugar content is
```
```
usually relatively low, thus affecting the final acetic acid production yield (Solieri
```
```
and Giudici, 2009). Juices with low sugar content are either supplemented with exog-
```
```
enous sugars or are concentrated by evaporation or reverse osmosis (Figure 5.5).
```
Also, the presence of fruit peel may affect the chemical composition of the vinegar.
The manufacture of fruit vinegar involves the preparation of fruit juice and the
subsequent alcohol and oxidative fermentations. The extraction of fruit juice is highly
dependent on the nature of the fruit. Various pretreatment processes have been con-
ducted in order to extract the juice, while retaining the highest level of nutritional and
sensory characteristics. The most well-established method is mechanical-pressing
extraction aided by enzymatic treatment. Novel juice extraction technologies include
```
ultrasound, microwave hydro-diffusion, and ohmic heat treatments (Mushtaq, 2017).
```
Fruit juices have also been utilized for Kombucha vinegar manufacture. Kombucha
is a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeasts with a wide diversity of strains. The fla-
vor of Kombucha is modified through the fermentation process resulting in a vinegar
```
broth (Figure 5.6). Recently Akbarirad et al. (2017) evaluated various fruit juices
```
for Kombucha vinegar production presenting the changes in acids, pH, and sugars
concentration. The juice of red grapes was also employed as feedstock for Kombucha
```
by Ayed et al. (2017), who reported on the antimicrobial activity and the sensory
```
properties of the product.
5.2.4 ginger
```
Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) rhizome is a widely used spice with distinct
```
aroma and is a source of oleoresin and essential oil. The main differences between
essential oil and oleoresin are the extraction method employed and the fact that the
essential oil is a hydrophobic liquid, rich in volatile aroma compounds, whereas
FIGURE 5.5 Fruit juice concentration by reverse osmosis.
66 Advances in Vinegar Production
oleoresin is a less volatile semi-solid extract, consisting of resin and essential and/
or fatty oil. Oleoresin and essential oil from ginger have presented remarkable anti-
oxidant and antimicrobial activity due to the presence of phenolic compounds, such
```
as eugenol, gingerdiols, and gingerols, among others (Pawar et al., 2011; Ding et al.,
```
```
2012). These may affect the activity of the microorganisms involved in the fermen-
```
```
tation process of vinegar (Leonel et al., 2015). In fact, hydrophobic constituents of
```
essential oils can cross the periplasm of Gram-negative bacteria, such as acetic acid
```
bacteria, through the outer membrane (Helander et al., 1998). On the other hand,
```
ginger rhizomes constitute a feedstock with high concentration of carbohydrates
that could be hydrolyzed into easily assimilated sugars for fermentation. Likewise,
```
Leonel et al. (2015) studied the effect of various parameters on the acetous fermen-
```
tation of ginger broth and on the profile of organic acids, suggesting an additional
outlet for ginger rhizome.
5.2.5 VegetaBles
New types of vinegars have been produced using vegetables like onions and toma-
```
toes. The composition of vegetables is characterized by high water content; nonethe-
```
less they contain carbohydrates that represent more than 90% of their dry matter.
```
They also consist of a low content of protein and fat (lower than 3.5% and 0.5%,
```
```
respectively). On the other hand, they constitute important sources of minerals and
```
vitamins that can be exploited for the production of functional foods.
For example, tomato is a rich source of lycopene, carotenoids, polyphenol com-
pounds, rutin, naringenin, and various trace elements and vitamins. Tomato has been
```
used for vinegar production, and the health effects (anti-obesity) of the vinegar have
```
FIGURE 5.6 Kombucha vinegar production.
67Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
been evaluated in both in vivo and in vitro experiments, demonstrating a decrease in
```
fat accumulation and in plasma LDL-cholesterol (Lee et al., 2013).
```
Onion vinegar is also rich in amino acids, organic acids, and minerals. The
quality of onion vinegar is dependent on the botanical variety, the cultivation prac-
tices, and the conditions of harvest. Generally, onions have high levels of pheno-
```
lic compounds (flavonoids like anthocyanins), organic acids, polysaccharides, and
```
sugars that contribute to the sensory profile of the onions. Organic acids and solu-
ble sugars influence the sweetness of onions, while sulfur compounds are respon-
```
sible for the distinctive onion odor and flavor (Liguori et al., 2017). Lee et al. (2017)
```
proposed the production of vinegar from onions, based on a semi-continuous pro-
```
cess. They also evaluated the chemical and functional properties (total flavonoids,
```
total polyphenols, antioxidant activity, reducing power, nitrite scavenging ability,
```
etc.) and the sensory properties of the product, showing better acceptability than
```
commercial onion vinegar. Finally, onion processing by-products and onions that
do not meet the consumers’ quality demands could also be processed for vinegar
production.
5.2.6 Cereals
Cereals are widely used as raw materials for vinegar production in Asian countries.
Different types of cereals, including wheat, millet, barley, rice, malt, and sorghum,
are used for cereal vinegar production. In East Asia, cereals and particularly rice and
sorghum are traditionally used to produce vinegars with different flavors. Traditional
Chinese vinegars are commonly called “cereal vinegars.” The most well-known
```
Chinese cereal vinegars are: Shanxi aged vinegar (sorghum, barley, bran, chaff, pea),
```
```
Sichuan vinegar (bran, wheat, rice, glutinous rice), Fujian Monascus vinegar (glu-
```
```
tinous rice, red yeast rice, sugar), Tianjin vinegar (sorghum, millet wheat, pea), and
```
```
Zhenjiiang vinegar (Giudici et al., 2017; Ho et al., 2017). Based on the acetification
```
method and the raw material, different flavors have been attained.
In Northeastern regions of Asia, vinegar is traditionally produced from rice. Rice
```
vinegars can be classified in three categories: amber (clear/pale amber), red, and
```
```
black. In Japan, rice vinegar is further classified into polished rice vinegar (Komesu),
```
```
unpolished rice vinegar (Kurosu), and sake-lee vinegar (Kasuzu) (Solieri and Giudici,
```
```
2009). Malt, on the other hand, has been widely used as a raw material for malt vin-
```
egar production in Europe, especially in England and Germany.
The chemical composition of cereals is characterized by high content of carbo-
hydrates and proteins, while non-starch carbohydrates, phytic acid, vitamins, and
minerals correspond to the minor components. Carbohydrates are the predominant
group of constituents in cereal grains, accounting for up to 75% of the solid matter.
```
The main carbohydrate is starch (56–80%) followed by minor amounts of non-starch
```
```
polysaccharides such as arabinoxylans (1.5–8%), β-glucans (0.5–7%), sugars (3%),
```
```
cellulose (2.5%), and glucofructans (1%) (Battcock and Azam-Alim, 1998).
```
Starch in cereals is found as insoluble granules packed in the endosperm
```
(57–74%) and in the bran (2–13%). Starch is a glucose polymer, consisting of two
```
types of polysaccharides: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is a linear mol-
ecule composed of α-d-glycosyl units linked by α-1,4-glucosidic bonds, whereas
68 Advances in Vinegar Production
amylopectin is a highly branched polysaccharide consisting of large α-d-glycosyl
```
chains linked with α-1,4-glycosidic bonds, with α-1,6-linked side chains (Koehler
```
```
and Wieser, 2013).
```
Non-starch polysaccharides are primarily constituents of the walls and the inner
layers of the grains accounting for 5–25% of total carbohydrates in oats, barley,
and rye. The pentosane fraction of cereals is a complex mixture of branched poly-
saccharides with an arabinoxylan backbone containing small amounts of glucose
```
and ferulic acid. Arabinoxylans are formed from a linear backbone of (1–4)-β-d-
```
xylopyranosyl-chains, which is mainly substituted at the O-2 and O-3 position with
α-l-arabinofuranosyl residues. Ferulic acid is a minor component of arabinoxylans,
which is bound to arabinose at the O-5 position. The highest contents of arabinox-
ylans are found in rye, while wheat contains 1.5–2%. β–Glucans are composed of
```
linear d-glucopyranosyl chains linked mostly by two to three consecutive β-(1,3)
```
```
and β-(1,4)-glucosidic linkages. β-Glucans are found in barley and oats up to 3–7%
```
```
and 3.5–5% respectively, whereas around 2% are present in other cereals (Xu et al.,
```
```
2016; Zhu, 2017).
```
Protein is the second major component of cereal grains exhibiting an average con-
tent of 8–11%. There are four types of proteins in cereals, namely albumins, globu-
lins, prolamins, and glutelins. The amino acid compositions and molecular weights
of proteins present in cereal grains display a vital role in the nutritional value and the
```
final flavor of vinegar (Battcock and Azam-Alim, 1998).
```
Due to the presence of polymeric carbohydrates in cereals, a pretreatment process
is necessary for cereal vinegar production to yield fermentable sugars. Chinese vin-
egars are fermented by solid-state fermentation or semi-solid-state fermentation by
```
four process steps: (1) starter culture preparation (namely Qu in Chinese or Koji in
```
```
Japanese), (2) raw material saccharification, (3) alcohol fermentation, and (4) oxida-
```
```
tion of ethanol to acetic acid (Chen et al., 2009).
```
```
Likewise, malt vinegar (as defined by the Codex Alimentarius) is produced by
```
```
double fermentation (alcoholic and acetous), without intermediate distillation, from
```
malted barley with or without the addition of cereal grains, the starch of which has
```
been converted to sugars solely by the indigenous amylolytic enzymes (diastase) of
```
the malted barley. Malted barley provides the required sugars for alcoholic fermenta-
tion, i.e., maltose and glucose, along with the nitrogen source necessary to support
yeast and acetic acid bacteria growth.
5.3 PRETREATMENT OF RAW MATERIALS
FOR VINEGAR PRODUCTION
5.3.1 direCt fermentation
Direct alcoholic fermentation is applied to raw materials that solely contain ferment-
able sugar, such as grape must and other fruit juices. The raw material in these cases
may be subjected to dilution with water, sugar addition, filtration, and pasteurization
treatments.
For example, wine vinegar is the final product of a two-step fermentation process:
the conversion of sugars to ethanol by the action of yeast strains belonging mainly to
69Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
the genus Saccharomyces, followed by the bioconversion of ethanol to acetic acid by
bacteria belonging to the species Acetobacter and Gluconacetobacter. The first step is
performed anaerobically, while the oxidation of ethanol is a result of the action of aero-
bic bacteria. The supplementation of oxygen during the latter step is strongly correlated
```
with the quality and the sensory characteristics of the final vinegar (Ho et al., 2017).
```
The fermentation temperature, the ethanol content, the yeast diversity, and the types
of acetic acid bacteria also constitute key factors in the formation of the end-product.
The modern production of vinegars from wines is mainly done by the fast, sub-
merged methods, where acetic acid bacteria are submerged, and oxygen is continu-
```
ously supplied to meet their respiratory requirements (Vegas et al., 2010; Ho et al.,
```
```
2017). Gullo et al. (2014) pointed out some of the prevailing features of the sub-
```
merged processes over solid-state fermentation and the traditional slow methods,
such as the higher yield and conversion rate of ethanol to acetic acid. As discussed in
other chapters of this book, high alcoholic strength wine requires dilution with water
before acetification, commonly to about 10% alcoholic degree.
Mature coconut water, which is a by-product of the coconut industry, is also used
```
for vinegar production by direct fermentation after addition of sugar (Othanman
```
```
et al., 2014). The coconut water is filtered, and refined sugar is added to adjust the
```
```
sugar concentration to about 162 g/L (Gonzalez and Vuyst, 2009), while pasteuriza-
```
```
tion at 90°C for 20 min is carried out prior to fermentation (Othanman et al., 2014).
```
Saccharomyces cerevisiae and A. acetii are used for the alcoholic and acetic fermen-
tations, respectively.
5.3.2 saCCHarifiCation
Saccharification is defined as the process during which a complex carbohydrate is
hydrolyzed to its monomers. Saccharification can be achieved by physical/chemi-
cal and enzymatic treatment. Frequently, prior to saccharification, a pretreatment
process is required in order to increase the permeability of the material for the sub-
sequent hydrolysis.
Starchy materials including wheat, rice, barley, and sorghum require a saccharifi-
cation process for the conversion of starch into simple fermentable sugars that will be
further used in the alcoholic and acetous fermentations. Prior to the saccharification
process, the grains are crushed to expand the area of contact and are homogenized
to ensure the effective utilization of the raw material. The insoluble starch granules
are dispersed in an aqueous medium, gelatinized by heat treatment, and liquefied
```
using thermostable α-amylases (α-1,4-glucan-glucanohydrolase, EC 3.2.1.1), which
```
are endoglucanases catalyzing the random hydrolysis of internal α-1,4-glycosidic
linkages points to produce different sizes of linear and branched oligosaccharides
```
(Souza, 2010).
```
Gelatinization is the swelling of the starch granules by heat treatment to eventu-
```
ally form an amorphous suspension (gel). Consequently, through the starch liquefac-
```
tion treatment the granular starch suspension is converted into a solution of soluble,
```
shorter-chain-length dextrins (Li et al., 2015b). The gelatinization and liquefaction
```
processes activate and accelerate the further enzymatic saccharification of starch
```
(Figure 5.7).
```
70 Advances in Vinegar Production
The above gelatinization and liquefaction steps are followed by the complete
hydrolysis of starch into fermentable sugar, which requires the action of various
```
hydrolytic enzymes including α-amylase, glucoamylase, and β-amylase (Lu et al.,
```
```
2018). Glucoamylase (or γ-amylase, or 1,4-α-d-glucan glucohydrolase glucan, or
```
```
exo-1,4-α-glucosidase, or amyloglucosidase, etc.; EC 3.2.1.3) is an exo-amylase,
```
```
which cleaves both α-1,4 (at the non-reducing end of amylose and amylopectin) and
```
```
α-1,6 glucosidic linkages to completely degrade dextrins into glucose (Saini et al.,
```
```
2017). β-Amylase (or 1,4-α-d-glucan maltohydrolase; saccharogen amylase, etc.;
```
```
EC 3.2.1.2) catalyzes the hydrolysis of the second α-1,4 glycosidic bond from the
```
```
non-reducing end of the starch chains, cleaving off maltose (Saini et al., 2017). Both
```
α-amylase and β-amylase are present in cereal grains, being the key enzymes for the
```
production of malt (Saini et al., 2017).
```
There is a vast variety of commercial amylolytic enzymes for food and bio-
technological applications, produced mainly by filamentous fungi and bacteria by
submerged or solid-state fermentation. For example, commercial α-amylases are
produced by Aspergillus niger and A. oryzae, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, B. sub-
tilis, B. licheniformis, and B. stearothermophilus, Microbacterium imperiale,
Streptomyces violaceoruber, Trichoderma reesei and T. longibrachiatum, and oth-
ers. These species may be natural or genetically modified to produce enzymes with
```
much better yield properties and purity (AMFEP, 2018). Donor species may include
```
FIGURE 5.7 Saccharification of cereal grains.
71Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
Thermoactinomyces sp., Aspergillus sp., and Bacillus sp. Commercial β-amylases
are produced by microbes such as Bacillus flexus or from barley, soybean, and
```
sweet potato (AMFEP, 2018). Available commercial glucoamylases are produced by
```
A. niger (without or with genetic donors including Aspergillus sp., Rhizomucor sp.,
```
or Talaromyces sp.), Rhizopus delemar and R. oryzae, and T. reesei and T. longibra-
```
```
chiatum (AMFEP, 2018).
```
In Asia, enzymes have been generated from solid-state fermentation processes for
```
the degradation of complex starchy cereals (Figure 5.8). Specifically, enzymes are
```
```
secreted from the growth of microorganisms (molds, bacteria, and yeasts) on cereals
```
such as rice, sorghum, wheat, and barley. These microorganisms can produce more
than 50 types of enzymes, including α-amylase, glucoamylase, protease, lipase,
and tanninase. The microbiological culture, known also as fermentation starter,
is applied for the breakdown of macromolecular substrates into smaller structures
like dextrin, glucose, peptides, and amino acids that provide the nutritional sources
```
for yeast during the subsequent ethanol fermentation (Wand and Yang, 2007; Chen
```
```
et al., 2009; Park et al., 2016).
```
In malt vinegar production, as abovementioned, starch is converted to fermentable
```
sugars by the action of the indigenous enzymes found in the grains (Figure 5.9). More
```
specifically, in malt vinegar production, the barley is initially malted. During malt-
ing, barley undergoes a natural germination process that involves activation of the
indigenous enzymes such as α-amylase, β-amylase, dextrinase, and α-glucosidase,
followed by a series of enzymatic degradations of the barley kernel endosperm by
these enzymes. The endosperm cell walls are degraded, and starch granules are
released from the matrix of the endosperm. During the subsequent mashing process,
barley is mixed with warm water in order to further convert the grain starches into
dextrin and fermentable sugars by the activated malt enzymes. Certain temperature
```
and pH values are needed for optimum malt enzyme activity. Blanco et al. (2014)
```
reported that α-amylase has an optimal temperature at 72°C, whereas proteases work
best at 52°C, β-amylase at 63°C, and β-glucanases at 45°C. The liquid extract from
the mashing step is known as “wort” and contains the sugars that are subsequently
```
used for the alcoholic fermentation by yeasts (Blanco et al., 2014).
```
FIGURE 5.8 Chinese vinegar production.
72 Advances in Vinegar Production
In the case of ginger, the starch saccharification step by the aid of amylases is also
```
essential before vinegar production. For example, Leonel et al. (2015) utilized the
```
commercial enzymes Termamyl 2X and amyloglucosidase AMG 300L to perform
the hydrolysis and the saccharification of ginger starch. Termamyl 2X is a heat-stable
endo-α-amylase and is used for the liquefaction of starch. The AMG 300L is an
exo-1,4-α-D-glucosidase, which hydrolyzes both 1,4-α and 1,6-α linkages in starch
removing glucose units from the non-reducing end of the substrate. The sugar pro-
file of the ginger hydrolysate consisted of glucose 85.6%, maltose 0.8%, maltotriose
0.6%, maltotetraose 0.4%, and dextrins 12.48%. Subsequently, the ginger hydroly-
sate was subjected to alcoholic fermentation.
The saccharification process is also implemented for the extraction of sugars from
fruit. At first a pretreatment of the raw material is necessary to improve the digest-
ibility of the raw material. For example, various physical pretreatment methods have
```
been investigated by Roda et al. (2016) for vinegar production from pineapple waste.
```
Microwave heating, boiling, cooking at high pressure, and autoclaving were used in
order to improve the sugar yield, prevent degradation of carbohydrates, and avoid the
production of inhibitory by-products for the hydrolysis and the subsequent fermen-
tation process. After the pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis was carried out using
hemicellulase, pectinase, and cellulase. The physical pretreatment of the pineapple
waste significantly increased the sugar yield, whereas the best results were obtained
```
by autoclaving (Roda et al., 2016).
```
Likewise, enzymatic treatment of strawberry puree was carried out for the release
of phenols and anthocyanin compounds. The extracted strawberry juice was used for
```
vinegar production with higher antioxidant properties and phenolic content (Ubeda
```
```
et al., 2013).
```
5.3.3 JuiCe extraCtion from fruits and VegetaBles
The extraction of fruit juice has been documented as one of the earliest agri-food
processes that could vary from a simple technique to a more complex process,
FIGURE 5.9 Malt vinegar production.
73Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
involving novel methods of extraction such as ultrafiltration and reverse osmosis.
The most traditional methods for juice extraction are pressing by traditional rack
```
and cloth press, screw press, and belt press (Sharma et al., 2017). Several processing
```
```
steps are also employed for fruit juice production, prior to the pressing (Lozano,
```
```
2006).
```
At first, a selection and thorough cleaning step is required to remove damaged
fruit and impurities. Peeling, trimming, and skin and seed removal steps follow, if
necessary, depending on the nature of the fruit. The next step of the process is the
crushing or milling in order to homogenize and facilitate the extraction of the liq-
uid contained in the fruit. Enzyme and heat treatments of the crushed fruit are also
```
applied in some cases (Rajauria and Tiwari, 2017). The enzymatic treatment is car-
```
ried out by addition of cellulases and pectinases aiming to enhance the breakdown
of cellular structures and facilitate the pressing, increase the juice recovery, and
improve the final product taste. Likewise, heating is an optional step that improves
```
pressing and color fixing (Sharma et al., 2017). The following step is the press-
```
ing operation which can be manual or mechanical. Mechanical pressing has been
applied in vinegar production from banana, mango, orange, strawberry, and jabati-
```
caba (Ubeda et al., 2013; Konate et al., 2015; Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2016; Dias et
```
```
al., 2016; Adebayo-Oyetoro et al., 2017). Different machines have been used for the
```
effective extraction of the juice. The texture and the size of the fruit are key factors
in designing and selecting the pressing equipment. The extracted liquid is composed
```
of water, sugars (sucrose, glucose, and fructose), organic acids, aroma and flavor
```
compounds, vitamins and minerals, pectic substrates, pigments, and small amounts
```
of proteins and fats (Lozano, 2006).
```
Clarification of the juice can be performed to avoid undesirable turbidity, haze,
```
and sediments in the final product (Pinelo et al., 2010). Juice clarification procedures
```
involve enzyme or non-enzyme treatments. Non-enzymatic clarification processes
heating, and addition of gelatin, casein, silica sol, and bentonite, among other clari-
fication agents. With respect to vinegar production, the most common clarification
method is heating. Finally, the clarified juice is either concentrated or supplied with
```
exogenous sugar solution to increase the sugar content (Nagar et al., 2012).
```
In the case of banana, mango, orange, and jabaticuba juice, due to the low sugar
content, the addition of sugar is a prerequisite for the alcoholic fermentation process.
5.3.4 fiBer and BioaCtiVe Compounds remoVal
The production of vinegar from fruit may require the extraction and recovery of
```
the essential oils from the skins (e.g., from oranges) prior to the crushing step for a
```
```
more efficient subsequent fermentation process (Cruess, 2013). Leonel et al. (2015)
```
reported that the yields during ginger vinegar making were affected by the phenolic
compounds present in the ginger essential oil. This may be attributed to the antimi-
crobial activity of these compounds.
The traditional methods used to isolate the essential oils from plant materials
```
are steam distillation, hydro-distillation, and hydro-diffusion (Tongnuanchan and
```
```
Benjakul, 2014). The recovery of the essential oil is also facilitated by solvent extrac-
```
```
tion; however, solvent residues could be retained in the final product (Tongnuanchan
```
74 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
and Benjakul, 2014). In the last number of years, green technologies have gained
```
great attention for the extraction of high added value compounds mainly due to the
disadvantages of conventional methods. These bottlenecks include the high water
and energy requirements, the low efficiency extraction, the losses of volatile com-
pounds, the long extraction times, the utilization of potentially toxic solvents, and
```
the degradation of sensitive compounds (e.g., unsaturated compounds or esters)
```
```
(Tongnuanchan and Benjakul, 2014; Chemat et al., 2017).
```
Currently, research has focused on green extraction methods involving the utili-
zation of supercritical fluids, microwave assisted extraction, and ultrasound assisted
extraction. CO 2 is an alternative and safe medium to extract the essential oil, as it
turns into liquid under high-pressure conditions. In this case, the isolated extract
is solvent-free since the liquid CO2 turns into its gas phase and evaporates under
```
normal atmospheric pressure and temperature (Tongnuanchan and Benjakul, 2014).
```
Microwave assisted extraction has been employed for green extraction of essential
```
oil in a solvent-free system at industrial scale (Filly et al., 2014). The solvent-free
```
microwave method performs the extraction under atmospheric pressure using a com-
bination of microwave heating and dry distillation. The advantageous characteristics
of this method are the high yield and selectivity as well as the short extraction time
```
(Tongnuanchan and Benjakul, 2014).
```
The ultrasound technology has also been developed to improve the hydro-distil-
lation extraction. The comparison of conventional hydro-distillation and ultrasound
assisted hydro-distillation extraction of essential oil from orange peels showed that
```
the second method can significantly reduce the extraction time (Pingret et al., 2014).
```
As depicted in Figure 5.10, the enzymatic pretreatment in the case of apple cider
vinegar with pectolytic enzymes is essential in order to break down the cellular
```
structure and increase the extraction yield of juice from apples (Joshi and Sharma,
```
```
2009). The efficient removal of pectin is essential, since its degradation by pectolytic
```
enzymes that naturally occur in fruits and unpasteurized juices leads to methanol
production, which is toxic and undesirable above certain limits for beverages, as
FIGURE 5.10 Pretreatment of apples and process flow diagram of apple cider vinegar
production.
75Raw Materials and Pretreatment Methods
```
mentioned before (Silva et al., 2007). The enzymatic treatment of raw materials with
```
high pectin content, e.g., apples and cashew juice, has been studied using pectino-
```
lytic enzymes, which included the primary types of pectinases from A. niger (pec-
```
```
tin methylesterase, polygalacturonase, pectin lyase, and pectin transeliminase) (Oke
```
```
and Paliyath, 2006). Another reason for the utilization of pectinases in apples and
```
```
other pectin-rich fruit processing is to facilitate the extraction of the juice (Oke and
```
```
Paliyath, 2006).
```
5.3.5 ConCentrate produCtion and dilution
Concentration is usually applied to fruit juices with the aim of increasing the sugar
content, concentrating at the same time the aroma and the taste. Many types of fruit
can be used to produce concentrated juices, such as oranges, mangos, cherries, and
bananas. In all cases, the fruit are mashed for juice extraction, heated for concentra-
tion until a sugar density of 28–40°Brix is obtained, and finally pasteurized before
```
the alcoholic fermentations (Coelho et al., 2015). After the alcoholic fermentation,
```
the alcoholic mash is centrifuged to remove the yeast and solids, it is diluted with
sterile water to obtain the desired alcoholic strength and is inoculated with acetic
```
acid bacteria to initiate the acetification process (Coelho et al., 2017).
```
Concentration is also applicable for cider vinegar production using concentrated
apple juice. The principal methods used for apple juice concentration include evapo-
```
ration, reverse osmosis, and freezing of the clarified apple juice (Joshi and Sharma,
```
```
2009). In the case of apple cider, vinegar dilution can be done either before the
```
alcoholic fermentation or before the acetous fermentation. The concentrated apple
juice has 60–72% total soluble solids. When it is destined for the production of cider
vinegar, it is diluted with water or apple juice in order to obtain 10–13% total soluble
solids content, before the alcoholic fermentation. Subsequently, if the resulting cider
has high alcohol strength, a second dilution with water is necessary to adjust the
ethanol content to about 7–8% v/v. Then, the diluted cider is mixed with cider vin-
egar from a previous cider acetification, as a means of inoculation with acetic acid
```
bacteria so as to avoid the growth of undesirable microorganisms (Joshi and Sharma,
```
```
2009).
```
In general, the utilization of concentrated fruit juices is desirable in alcoholic
fermentation, as higher sugar contents lead to increased ethanol production, whereas
the further acetification will result in a vinegar product with enhanced antioxidant
properties.
5.3.6 ClarifiCation
```
Clarification (or fining) is a necessary process either for the raw materials or for the
```
final vinegar product, aiming to eliminate the cloudy appearance of the product,
```
as discussed in more detail in Chapter 6 (Current Industrial Vinegar Production:
```
```
Acetators, Processes, and Consumables). The cloudy appearance of the juices is
```
mostly attributed to the presence of proteins, pectins, gums, and tannins among
```
other substances, as well as their interactions (e.g., protein–polyphenol haze forma-
```
```
tion). Clarification processes improve the appearance and stability of the product, by
```
76 Advances in Vinegar Production
removing particles, like plant debris, cells of yeasts and bacteria, and other smaller
```
compounds (e.g., proteins). Clarification/fining can be achieved by sedimentation,
```
```
simple filtration, activation of pectolytic enzymes, etc. (Heikefelt, 2011).
```
In the case of enzymatic clarification using pectinases, the viscosity of the juice
decreases through the degradation of pectin substances. The result is the formation
of flocculating particles, which are further removed by filtration. The fining methods
include the addition of specific compounds, like gelatin or bentonite, in order to bind
to the undesirable particles. The main disadvantage of fining is that polyphenols,
essential for the aroma and flavor of the final product, may also be removed. It should
be finally stressed that the enzymatic methods can restrain the fermentation rate, if
```
the apple juice is to be further utilized in cider manufacturing (Heikefelt, 2011).
```
```
Clarification treatments are also applied after the vinegar production (Chapter 6)
```
targeting the removal of bacteria and other solid particles. The traditional clarifi-
cation methods include decanting, diatomaceous earth filtration, paper filtration, or
utilization of polymer membranes. The current trend is cross-flow microfiltration,
```
which can perform clarification and sterilization simultaneously (Carneiro et al.,
```
```
2002), with many advantages regarding vinegar production, such as the elimination
```
```
of the pasteurization step and the improvement of the final product quality (López
```
```
et al., 2005).
```
5.4 CONCLUSIONS
Vinegar is the final product of a two-stage bioconversion process: the anaerobic
ethanolic fermentation performed by yeasts, followed by the aerobic acetous fer-
mentation, in which the ethanol is oxidized to acetic acid by bacteria. Several factors
affect the quality of the produced vinegar. These can be related to the fermentation
```
conditions (temperature, pH, indigenous microbiota) or with the composition of the
```
raw material used. In this chapter, the effect of the initial raw material composition
on the fermentation process and the final product quality are highlighted. Also, an
overview of the pretreatment methods to generate fermentable sugars, or facilitate
their extraction, as well as to treat the raw material in order to improve its qual-
ity characteristics, is presented, along with ongoing research on the development of
novel technologies.

84 Advances in Vinegar Production
6.1 INTRODUCTION
```
In industrial vinegar production, there are three main types of methods involved;
```
```
the slow, handcrafted, traditional method (“Orléans” or “French” method), and the
```
rapid submerged and generator methods. Despite the plenitude of scientific knowl-
edge that currently exists on vinegar production, the industry mainly employs the
traditional batch submerged fermentation method, the centerpiece of which is the
```
“acetator” (vinegar fermenter). Commercially available acetators are tanks usually
```
equipped with units for temperature, aeration, and pressure control, alcohol and
acidity measuring probes, defoamers, etc., and may differ widely according to the
seasonal production requirements or the different types of raw materials and prod-
```
ucts. Solid-state fermentation (SSF) methods are also used in some Asian countries
```
to produce vinegar from grains, including additional steps for starch liquefaction and
saccharification.
In this chapter the mainstream industrial vinegar production processes and aceta-
```
tors are highlighted and described, with special reference to the Frings (Heinrich
```
```
Frings GmbH & Co, Germany) (and other major vinegar technology providers) sub-
```
merged acetification systems.
Useful information for the manufacturers and the public is also provided on
```
currently commercially available consumables and auxiliary materials (fermenta-
```
```
tion nutrients, clarification, fining, and stabilization agents). This information was
```
```
mainly retrieved from the World Wide Web (based on availability and accessibility,
```
```
or randomly selected), and includes product specifications, intended uses, applica-
```
```
tion instructions, and (claimed) advantages, as offered by the respective commercial
```
providers in the form of technical sheets.
Finally, an example of a current industrial process for vinegar production from rai-
```
sins (or raisin finishing side-streams) is described, including raw material extraction,
```
alcoholic fermentation, submerged acetification, and post-fermentation treatments.

85Current Industrial Vinegar Production
6.2 CURRENT VINEGAR PRODUCTION
METHODS AND RESEARCH
```
6.2.1 tHe sloW (“orléans” or “frenCH”) metHods
```
```
The “Orléans” or “French” or “continuous” method (originally developed in France),
```
is one of the oldest methods for vinegar production that is still practiced today to
produce high-quality vinegars. It is a slow, continuous fermentation process carried
```
out in large wooden barrels (> 200 L) with a high diameter/height ratio, in which
```
```
the initial starter material (“mother of vinegar”) is a fermented mixture (for about
```
```
1 week) of high grade vinegar and wine (ratio around 4–5:1; for example 65–75 L of
```
```
vinegar and 15 L of wine), which is placed in the casks to fill about 1/2 to 2/3 of their
```
```
volume (Ho et al., 2017; Mazza and Murooka, 2009; Plessi, 2003).
```
The acetification proceeds at a very low rate only at the surface of the liquid
```
(surface oxidation), where there is enough dissolved oxygen that derives from the
```
```
air entering from holes on the cask above the surface of the liquid (Ho et al., 2017;
```
```
Rogers et al., 2013). After about 8–14 weeks (depending on the various process fac-
```
```
tors), an amount of 2/3 to 3/4 of the vinegar is removed and wine is added (weekly).
```
```
When the acidity and flavor of the produced vinegar is proper (after about 1 month),
```
the vinegar is removed, and an equal amount of wine is added. The remaining vin-
egar in the cask serves as the starter culture for the next acetification batch.
Historical facts and other information on the traditional Orléans methods can
```
be found in various sources (Ho et al., 2017; Mas et al., 2014; Mazza and Murooka,
```
```
2009; Murooka, 2016; Plessi, 2003; Rogers et al., 2013). The main problems associ-
```
ated with the slow vinegar production methods are the disturbance of the floating
```
bacterial biofilm (mat) during liquid removal or additions, the long production times,
```
and the large installation spaces required. Wood shavings can be added to provide
support to the bacterial mat, serving as cell immobilization carriers. In a more stan-
dardized version of the Orléans method, side holes are used to allow air circulation,
and an extended funnel allows wine addition at the bottom of the barrel, preventing
```
the disturbance of the bacterial mat (Mas et al., 2014) (Figure 6.1).
```
6.2.1.1 Current “Orléans” Style Vinegar Production and Research
Currently, vinegar companies use oak barrels and selected or indigenous bacteria
to produce vinegar by the Orléans method, and the process takes place at constant
```
temperature (21–30°C) and in complete darkness. Ageing of the vinegar is carried
```
out for a minimum of 12 months to several years in wooden barrels under con-
```
trolled conditions (e.g., in cellars). The barrels may contain ventilation holes that
```
```
allow fermentation by-products to escape, avoiding off-flavors (e.g., bitterness) that
```
are observed in some vinegars.
```
The vinegar flavor is a result of the raw material composition (wine), the met-
```
abolic by-products of acetic acid bacteria during and after acetification, the com-
pounds extracted from the wooden barrels during ageing, and the chemical and
```
physical transformations that take place during the ageing process (Mas et al., 2014).
```
Therefore, the vinegars produced by the slow traditional Orléans process are char-
```
acterized by flavor complexity (smooth and fruity) and are generally considered of
```
86 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
high quality (Mas et al., 2014). Moreover, the process involves no heating, which
```
may destroy the distinctive raw material aromas, and companies using this method
usually add no preservatives or do not pasteurize their vinegars, which are common
industrial practices known to deteriorate the delicate flavors of food and beverages.
The slow vinegar production method, followed by an extended maturation time,
is mainly used in balsamic vinegar production and other specialty vinegar products.
Pricing of the products depends on quality, maturation time, and rarity. High-quality
vinegars are made using good, balanced wines, matured for at least 12 years, and with
```
no addition of additives (such as caramel), which is common in the vinegar industry.
```
Some current vinegar producers worldwide produce good quality, slow fermented
```
vinegars containing carefully selected botanical infusions such as buchu (Agathosma),
```
```
honeybush (Cylopia), rose geranium (Pelargonium), wild olive (Olea), wild rose-
```
```
mary (Eriocephalus), hibiscus (Hibiscus), rose hip (Rosa), elderflower (Sambucus),
```
```
vanilla (Vanilla), green tea (Camellia), chili (Capsicum), carob (Ceratonia), lavender
```
```
(Lavandula), kelp seaweed (Laminariales), bay leaves (Laurus), shallots (Allium),
```
```
tarragon (Artemisia), poppies (Papaveroideae), various berries, ginger (Zingiber),
```
etc.
Current scientific advances regarding the slow fermented vinegars mainly focus
```
on the study of the process factors for the production of high-quality (and high-price)
```
```
traditional balsamic vinegars (TBVs), which can be summarized in three practical
```
```
steps (Solieri and Giudici, 2008):
```
```
(1) Raw material preparation (cooking of the grape must for concentration,
```
```
color development by browning reactions, and sterilization)
```
```
(2) Two-stage fermentation (alcoholic fermentation followed by oxidation of
```
```
ethanol to acetic acid)
```
```
(3) Ageing
```
```
FIGURE 6.1 Standard, slow (“Orléans”) vinegar making in a barrel designed to prevent
```
disturbance of the surface bacterial mat.
87Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
Solieri and Giudici (2008) suggested that despite the extended knowledge on TBV
```
yeast microbiota, further study is needed to screen yeast species suitable for fermen-
tation of the cooked must and to understand their metabolic activities and how they
can affect the quality of TBV. For example, in an effort to implement principles of
traditional concentrated grape must fermentation to the production of new genera-
tion balsamic vinegars, the isolation and molecular identification of the predominant
yeasts in concentrated grape must, their technological characterization, and their
```
fermentative aptitude were evaluated (Lalou et al., 2016). Specifically, tolerance
```
```
against 5-hydroxymethyl-furfural (HMF), furfural, acetic acid, and glucose concen-
```
tration was examined, as well as enological characteristics such as acetic acid and
H 2 S production, foaming, flocculation ability, key enzymatic activity, and formation
of key volatiles. Tolerance to both HMF and furfural was found to be strain and
```
dose-dependent; therefore, it was suggested as critical factor in yeast pre-selection
```
```
(Lalou et al., 2016).
```
Other studies have focused on the use of selected strains of acetic acid bacteria
```
for improvements in TBV production (Gullo et al., 2009). The phenotypic traits of
```
acetic acid bacteria relevant for starter culture selection in TBV production has also
```
been reviewed by Gullo and Giudici (2008), who pointed out that selected starter
```
cultures are the main technological improvement to innovate TBV production. The
selection criteria should consider the composition of the raw material, the acetic acid
bacteria metabolic activities, the applied technology, and the desired characteristics
```
of the final product; with the main traits being the preferred ethanol content, the
```
efficient ethanol oxidation, the rate of acetification, the tolerance to high acetic acid
concentration, sugar concentration, and low pH, the avoidance of overoxidation, and
the temperature range.
The structure of high-quality TBVs has also been a subject of vinegar research.
During ageing of TBV the density is increased mainly due to evaporation, and
```
changes such as crystallization, taste, and color alterations occur. Falcone (2010)
```
```
used high-resolution light microscopy (HR-LM) and X-ray diffractometry (XRD)
```
to study the bulk structure of the TBV of Modena, which may undergo solidifica-
tion through equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium phase transitions including crystal-
```
lization (due to the rearrangements of α-d-glucose molecules) and jamming (due to
```
crowding of amorphous colloids of unidentified substances including polymeric mel-
```
anoidins). Elmi (2015) also used XRD for an unambiguous identification of crystal
```
by-products in TBV. This work described the relationships between the sugar con-
```
tent, the total acidity (volatile and non-volatile acidity), and the crystal by-products
```
during TBV ageing, to suggest the best practice for controlling crystallization. The
XRD patterns showed presence of glucose crystals at the bottom of the bottles and
concluded that the glucose deposit could be related to the high concentration of the
```
substrate (cooked must), the imbalance of the glucose/fructose ratio, and the evapo-
```
ration of water -during ageing.
Also, many studies deal with the classification and authentication of vinegars,
which is especially important for the brand protection of high-quality Protected
```
Designation of Origin (PDO) vinegars and the prevention of adulteration and unfair
```
```
competition (Rios-Reina et al., 2017, 2018). Spectroscopic techniques, chemomet-
```
ric techniques, and their combinations are proposed for this purpose. For example,
88 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRs) (Rios-Reina et al., 2018), or multidimensional
```
```
fluorescence spectroscopy (Rios-Reina et al., 2017), or 2D-NMR (Graziosi et al.,
```
```
2017), combined with chemometrics, were demonstrated as suitable methodologies
```
for the classification and authentication of high-quality vinegars, as described in
more detail in Chapter 21.
Finally, a considerable amount of research aims to highlight the health benefits of
vinegars, as described in more detail in Chapter 18.
```
6.2.2 tHe quiCk (“generator” or “german”) metHods
```
The “generator” or “German” methods are improved vinegar production processes
in terms of rate and acetic acid yield. They were initially developed by German sci-
entists, especially Johann Sebastian Schüzenbach in 1823, and have been applied for
more than 100 years. The methods’ centerpiece is the generator, which consists of a
```
tall, upright, wooden (oak) or steel tank filled with wood shavings (mainly beech), or
```
charcoal, or grape pulp, or stalks, soaked with vinegar and serving as inert immo-
bilization carriers, on which the acetic acid bacteria are adsorbed as a surface film
```
(Adams and Twiddy, 1987; Mazza and Murooka, 2009; Plessi, 2003; Tan, 2005).
```
The production method is like earlier methods, with the main difference the
forced aeration applied either through holes at the sides or through the perforated
```
bottom of the generator, which also serves as support for the shavings (Figure 6.2).
```
The wine, or other alcoholic liquid, is sprayed from the top of the tank by a suitable
sprinkling mechanism, to increase the contact surface between the liquid and acetic
acid bacteria, and it passes under gravity through the bed of shavings. The time
required for complete acetification is about 3–7 days at the optimum temperature
range 27–30°C. The temperature of the generator must be controlled because oxidi-
zation releases heat that may damage the bacteria and cease the process. A part of
```
the produced vinegar (about 2/3) is then removed from the bottom of the generator
```
and is replaced by an equal amount of wine.
```
FIGURE 6.2 Types of quick (“generator” or “German”) vinegar making vats with wood
```
shavings.
89Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
These methods yield higher acetic acid concentrations (up to 14%) at higher rates,
```
and the final products, which are generally considered of good quality, are produced
by suitable dilutions with water. Therefore, the main advantage compared to the tra-
ditional slow methods is the smaller installation space and lower required capital and
operation costs. However, considerable amounts of yield may be lost due to evapora-
tion. Another problem is the replacement of the wood shavings, which must be done
at least once a year. The generator is still used in many parts of the world, and it has
been considerably improved through the years, evolving to the modern acetator that
is currently used worldwide for industrial submerged acetification.
6.2.3 tHe modern rapid suBmerged metHods
The rapid submerged acetification methods have been applied since the mid 1950s
and are currently the common methods used in industrial vinegar production.
These methods involve forceful supply of air into an alcoholic mash contained in a
```
suitable acetator tank, followed by acetification at about 26–30°C (Tan, 2005). At
```
the end of each batch, about 1/3 of the fermented liquid is discharged and the tank
is supplied by equal volume of alcoholic mash for a second acetification batch. The
acetators are large stainless-steel tanks equipped with air pumps that supply air
though the bottom of the tank. Nutrient supply, heating, and monitoring equipment
is also usually attached to the acetators. Finally, the produced vinegar, after each
discharge, can be supplied to a series of clarification, filtering, stabilization, and
bottling equipment.
The current industrial, rapid submerged processes differ mainly on the final acetic
acid content of the product. The higher the desired final acidity, the higher the preci-
```
sion required to control the process (FRINGS, 2018). The alcohol content is the main
```
variable that must be controlled during industrial vinegar production. Therefore, the
alcohol monitoring systems are integral parts of the modern industrial submerged
vinegar production processes, determining the rate of fermentation and the proper
discharge time. These systems are more sophisticated and specified in the case of
```
high-strength processes (> 17% acidity) to be able to provide a continuous overview
```
and secure the process control.
Various types of processes can be controlled to yield levels of acidity up
to or higher than 20% including batch and continuous processes, single-stage
high-strength processes, dual-stage processes for vinegar with no residual alcohol,
processes with automatic or manual mash preparation, etc. For a vinegar acidity
level up to 20.5%, two acetators are usually connected and operated in sequential
fermentation, and only highly sophisticated state-of-the-art instrumentation can
guarantee the best process control and viability of the acetic acid bacteria under the
```
stressful conditions of such processes (FRINGS, 2018).
```
```
Programmable logic control systems (PLCs) are currently the core of the process
```
control systems, evaluating all data received by the monitoring systems, to ensure
a cost-effective production, low product loss, and high quality. Finally, process
control and integrated software systems can be connected with several acetators
located anywhere in the world allowing communication from a central control room
```
(FRINGS, 2018).
```
90 Advances in Vinegar Production
6.3 ACETATORS AND ATTACHED EQUIPMENT
6.3.1 aCetator Configuration
The centerpiece of every vinegar production system is the fermenter or “acetator,”
which is now a synonym for vinegar fermenter worldwide. Companies currently
constructing acetator systems, such as Frings, may also provide the complete range
of technologies, starter cultures, consumables, know-how, and training required
```
to install and operate an industrial vinegar production plant (FRINGS, 2018). The
```
advantage of such technologies is that they can be adapted to all types of vinegar
```
(spirit, wine, fruit). Moreover, the production involves only biological steps, is highly
```
automated, easy to handle, and has low maintenance costs.
```
Acetators, such as the Frings acetators (Figure 6.3), generally consist of the fol-
```
```
lowing parts and attached equipment (CETOTEC, 2018; FRINGS, 2018):
```
• High-quality stainless-steel tanks with internal cooling coils
• High performance aerators
• Sensors to monitor filling level, temperature, pressure, alcohol, and acetic
acid concentration
```
• Piping to supply and circulate air including fresh air filters (e.g., with acti-
```
```
vated carbon)
```
• Charge and discharge pipes and pumps
• Defoaming systems with foam concentrate pipes
• Exhaust air pipes and condensers
• Overflow pipes with safety locks
• Cooling water pumps
• Tank attachment parts, such as overflow switch, pressure probes, etc.
6.3.2 indiVidual industrial equipment
Individual equipment is also available from vinegar technology providers, to com-
plete the acetator systems, and to allow industrial producers to improve their aceta-
tors performance and maintenance, or to convert old generators and wooden tanks
into acetators for rapid submerged vinegar fermentations. Such equipment includes
```
(CETOTEC, 2018; FRINGS, 2018):
```
• Aerators for the acetators
• Defoamers
• Exhaust air scrubber/condensers
• Stationary and mobile special pumps
• Air impulse mixers
• Consumables
• Auxiliary materials
6.3.2.1 Aerators
```
Aerators (rotor-stator-turbines) are the centerpieces of acetators. Oxygen
```
transfer and distribution are the most important factors in submerged vinegar
91Current Industrial Vinegar Production
fermentations, and the proper, intensive, and homogenous mixing of the air and
```
any additions (alcohol, water, nutrients) is the basic principle of modern, high
```
```
performance vinegar production (CETOTEC, 2018). Aerators can be designed
```
in an energy-efficient way to intensely blow and homogenously disperse fresh
air into the acetator directly from the environment, without the use of additional
```
air compressors (FRINGS, 2018). The performance of the aerators in deliver-
```
ing oxygen into the fermenting liquid is critical, as the vinegar bacteria would
immediately die without enough supply of oxygen. Therefore, the desired char-
acteristics of industrial acetator aerators are: optimum air bubble dispersion and
```
oxygen transfer into the acetator, good production efficiency (high space/time
```
```
yield), low energy consumption, low loss of alcohol and acetic acid due to evapo-
```
ration, reliability, durability, and adaptability to the various tank configurations
```
(FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.3.2.2 Defoamers
Defoamers are very important for the course of submerged vinegar fermentations
because the inevitably developed foam must be quickly and efficiently removed. The
foam contains insoluble substances from the raw material, dying bacteria due to
depletion of nutrients in the foam, and bacterial metabolites that can lead to reduced
```
fermentation performance and contamination problems (CETOTEC, 2018; FRINGS,
```
```
2018). Foaming depends on the type of the raw material. For example, malt, rice,
```
apple, and pear mashes can produce large amounts of foam, which in many cases
```
FIGURE 6.3 A modern submerged fermentation acetator (based on the Frings technology).
```
92 Advances in Vinegar Production
leads to complete fermentation breakdown. The defoamers are vertical machines
placed on the top of the acetator that can operate automatically when required, to
```
remove the concentrated foam from the acetator (by applying an upstream pressure)
```
```
to a discharge tank (FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.3.2.3 Exhaust Air Scrubber/Condensers
Exhaust air scrubber/condensers are used to clean the exhaust air and recover valu-
```
able resources, with function based on physical absorption (CETOTEC, 2018). They
```
are tightly arranged constructions of absorber columns and absorber reservoirs con-
nected to an automation system. The exhaust air, containing ethanol and acetic acid,
is cleaned though the absorber leading to up to 60–80% recovery of resources. In
```
combination with a condenser (cross-flow heat exchanger), this percentage can be
```
increased to 95%. The resources washed by the exhaust air scrubber are gathered in
the washing liquid, which can then be reused either for mash preparation or charged
back into the acetator.
6.3.2.4 Special Pumps
Stationary special pumps are used for the charging and discharging purposes of
the acetators. They must be reliable, robust, acid-proof, and able to pump liquids
mixed with high proportions of gas, as is the case of the “discharge pump” of
an acetator. Mobile pumps, including the required suction and pressure hoses,
are also useful for pumping liquids into tanks that are not equipped with fixed-
installation lines, as is the case of most vinegar factories due to cost reasons
```
(FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.3.2.5 Air Mixers
Air impulse mixers are used to quickly mix large quantities of liquids, as is the mix-
ing of the finished vinegar to guarantee homogenization before filling the storage
```
tanks. Air impulse mixers operate by bursting large air bubbles (filtered) that cause
```
```
intense circulation of the liquid as they ascend (FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.3.2.6 Consumables and Auxiliary Materials
Consumables and auxiliary materials used in the industrial vinegar production pro-
cess include nutrients for the acetous fermentation, clarification, and filtration media,
```
air filtration media, and consumables (e.g., filtration consumables such as filter lay-
```
```
ers, membranes, etc.), detergents, chemical analysis reagents and consumables, sta-
```
bilization media, and others, as discussed in more detail below.
6.3.3 pilot and laBoratory aCetators
Pilot and laboratory scale acetators are also offered by vinegar technology providers.
```
User friendly and automated pilot acetators are small-scale systems (6–1,000 L) that
```
are used to produce high-priced, specialty vinegars such as high-quality fruit, wine,
herbs, or honey vinegars. These systems are especially suitable for vineyards and
specialty vinegar producers that give special attention to the art of wine and vinegar
fermentations, respectively.
93Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
A pilot acetator generally consists of (CETOTEC, 2018; FRINGS, 2018):
```
```
(1) Stainless steel or plastic (transparent) acetator tank with internal cooling loop
```
```
(2) High performance aeration system
```
```
(3) Central process control (PLC) unit
```
```
(4) Sensors/probes (alcohol, filling level, pressure, temperature, online alcohol
```
```
and acidity monitoring)
```
```
(5) Vertical defoamer
```
```
(6) Charge and discharge pumps
```
```
(7) Fresh and return air lines including air filters
```
The annual production capacity of a 200 L Frings pilot acetator is about 20,000 L
```
(FRINGS, 2018) and about 157,000 L (10%) for a 100 L CETOTEC acetator
```
```
(CETOTEC, 2018).
```
A laboratory acetator can be used for the testing of raw materials, for sample-
batch production, as pre-culture fermenter to provide active biomass to larger pro-
duction acetators, and for vinegar research purposes. An automatically functioning
```
laboratory acetator generally consists of (FRINGS, 2018):
```
```
(1) Transparent container with internal stainless-steel cooling loop
```
```
(8) High-performance aeration system
```
```
(9) Central process control unit
```
```
(10) Alcohol, temperature, and pressure measuring probes
```
```
(11) Defoaming disc
```
```
(12) Charge and discharge lines and containers
```
```
(13) Fresh air line with air filter
```
An 8 L Frings acetator has an annual capacity of about 840 L of vinegar and can
produce about 2–3 L of vinegar daily, while a 6 L CETOTEC acetator can produce
```
about 900 L of vinegar (10%) annually.
```
6.4 PROCESS DESCRIPTION
```
All vinegar fermentations involve an alcohol containing raw material (wine, cider, or
```
```
spirits), acetic acid bacteria culture, and nutrients. There are specially designed vinegar
```
fermentation units and nutrients for the requirements of different industrial processes,
e.g., based on direct fermentation of a complete mash with added nutrients or on sepa-
```
rate addition of alcohol, water, and nutrients during the process (FRINGS, 2018). For
```
example, various types of submerged vinegar production processes can be supported
```
by the Frings technology, such as (a) the “Standard or Repeated Batch Process,” (b) the
```
```
“High Acid Strength Process,” and (c) the “Continuous Process” (FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.4.1 tHe standard or repeated BatCH proCess
The “Standard or Repeated Batch Process” is a simple charging process used to pro-
duce high-quality vinegars with an acidity up to 14.5%. The alcoholic raw material is
94 Advances in Vinegar Production
transferred into a mash tank, which is used to charge a suitable volume of mash into
the acetator that already contains a residual volume with active acetic acid bacteria
for initiation of the process. During each batch process the acetic acid concentration
increases and when the alcohol content decreases to a minimum of 0.3%, a part of
the produced vinegar is discharged, and a new batch begins in the same manner.
```
Therefore, the Standard Process is divided into three process steps: (1) the charging
```
```
step, (2) the acetification step, and (3) the discharge step (FRINGS, 2018).
```
A simplified overview of the Standard Frings vinegar production process is pre-
```
sented in Figure 6.4a, in which the acetator (presented above in Figure 6.3) is charged
```
with a complete alcohol containing mash with added nutrients.
6.4.2 tHe HigH aCid strengtH proCess
```
The single-stage “High Acid Strength Process” (sHAS) is a technology developed by
```
Frings that allows production of vinegar with acidity up to 17.5%. It is also known
```
as the “Single Stage, High Percentage Fermentation Process” (FRINGS, 2018).
```
The sHAS process also involves successive acetification batches as in the Standard
Process, during which alcohol is oxidized until the desired acetic acid concentration
is obtained. The main difference is that after the initial batch, a second step follows,
called the “elevated phase,” where highly concentrated alcohol is added, and the
alcohol content is monitored and kept constant, leading to significantly elevated ace-
```
tic acid yields (Figure 6.4b). In the following step, called the “fermentation phase,”
```
the addition of alcohol stops, and the residual alcohol is converted until it reaches
the “discharge” level, at which the fermented liquid is discharged from the acetator
FIGURE 6.4 Block diagrams of the steps of vinegar production according to the Frings
```
(a) Standard Process, (b) High Acid Strength Process, and (c) Continuous Process.
```
95Current Industrial Vinegar Production
leaving only a necessary volume with active biomass. The next production cycle
initiates in the same manner, with the “charging” of water, alcohol, and nutrients in
the acetator.
Therefore, the sHAS process is divided into five successive process steps, as also
```
depicted in Figure 6.4b: (1) charging, (2) initiation of fermentation, (3) elevation, (4)
```
```
fermentation, and (5) discharging (FRINGS, 2018). This cycle is carried out con-
```
tinuously for several months, and despite the apparent complexity of the process, all
phases can be programmed and controlled automatically, with the required manual
intervention kept to a minimum. The sHAS process, as well as the dual process
described below, are also known as “Repeated-Fed-Batch Processes.”
6.4.3 tHe dual HigH aCid strengtH proCess
```
The Dual High Acid Strength Process (dHAS) is a more sophisticated mechani-
```
```
cal and technical process, used to produce vinegars with higher acid strength (up
```
```
to 20.5%) than those obtained by the sHAS process (FRINGS, 2018). The process
```
involves the use of two acetators linked together as a single functional unit. The first
```
acetator (called the “donor acetator”) operates as in the case of the sHAS process
```
but at significantly higher “discharge” concentration. The volume discharged from
the first acetator is charged to the second, which is called the “acceptor acetator,”
and alcohol is then added for an additional “elevated phase.” The residual alcohol
“fermenting phase” is finally carried out afterwards, and then the acceptor acetator
is completely emptied and cleaned. The active biomass, which is necessary for the
acetous fermentation, is transferred each time with the discharge volume from the
donor to the acceptor acetator.
6.4.4 tHe Continuous proCess
```
The Continuous Process for vinegar production involves continuous charging (feed-
```
```
ing) of the mash into the acetator with simultaneous removal of fermented liquid at
```
the same rate, leading to a “steady state,” which lasts for several weeks or months
```
(Figure 6.4c). Although it is a simple process, it is not a common practice in indus-
```
```
trial vinegar production because it does not lead to high acid strengths (up to 9%)
```
```
and is therefore suitable for low alcohol wines or other mashes (FRINGS, 2018).
```
During the Continuous Process, the concentrations of acetic acid and alcohol and
other process parameters remain constant. Specifically, the alcohol concentration in
```
the acetator is kept at low levels (about 0.3%), and the acetic acid concentration is the
```
maximum that can be obtained.
6.5 CONSUMABLES AND AUXILIARY MATERIALS
Various companies worldwide currently develop and distribute consumables and
auxiliary materials suitable for modern industrial vinegar production. Useful infor-
mation for the manufacturers and the public, regarding product specifications,
intended uses, and application instructions, are provided by many of these compa-
nies on the World Wide Web. Below, information on specific nutrients, clarification,
96 Advances in Vinegar Production
fining, and stabilization agents for the vinegar industry, that can be easily retrieved
from the Web, is presented.
6.5.1 nutrients
Complete nutrient supplements are available on the market to aid the efficient pro-
duction of various types of vinegars. Nutrients are vital for the optimal growth of
acetic acid bacteria in the acetators. The combination of nutrients is selected accord-
ing to the type of raw material to improve its nutritive value and thus the production
```
yields (VOGELBUSCH, 2018). Most commercial supplements contain:
```
```
• Carbohydrates (dextrose, sucrose, etc.)
```
```
• Proteins and peptides (yeast extract, etc.)
```
```
• N, P, and S mineral sources (ammonium and potassium phosphate, magne-
```
```
sium sulfate, etc.)
```
• Trace elements
```
• Vitamin mixes (thiamine, etc.)
```
```
For example, Acetiactiv (SOFRALAB, 2018) is a nutrient developed for the
```
stimulation of acetic acid bacteria in spirit vinegar production. It is a complete
nutrient that ensures smooth and complete fermentation, avoiding nutrient defi-
ciencies of alcoholic solutions poor in minerals and organic sources. It contains
carbohydrates, proteins, minerals, and trace elements. Another supplement suit-
```
able for raw materials highly deficient in nutrients is Acetivin (SOFRALAB,
```
```
2018), developed for use in the production of white and red wine, cider, and honey
```
```
vinegars. It contains ammonium sulfate (54.9%), diammonium phosphate (44.9%),
```
```
and thiamine (0.2%).
```
```
The Acetozym series of nutrients (FRINGS, 2018; NUTRIENTS INC., 2018) is
```
distributed for the production of a wide variety of vinegars to promote bacterial
growth in the acetators. The supplying companies also claim to develop nutrients on
a continual basis to fulfill the specific requirements of modern high acid vinegar pro-
duction. For example, the types of nutrient supplements currently available by Frings
are the Acetozym series DS+, DS+2, GZ, and D products for alcohol vinegars, the
Nutritive Salt for wine vinegars, and the Biozym DS for organic vinegars.
Acetozym DS+2 is described as a nutrient that works well in all types of sub-
```
merged fermentations and is 100% soluble in vinegar (NUTRIENTS INC., 2018).
```
It contains ammonium/potassium phosphate, sucrose, magnesium sulfate, yeast
```
extract, and trace minerals. Acetozym GZA concentrate (two parts dextrose/one part
```
```
Acetozym GZ) (NUTRIENTS INC., 2018) contains ammonium/potassium phos-
```
phate, magnesium sulfate, yeast extract, and vitamin mineral mix. Acetozym DGZ+
```
(NUTRIENTS INC., 2018) is offered as more suitable for vinegars made by sub-
```
merged fermentation and with less than 17% acid. It contains dextrose, ammonium/
potassium phosphate, magnesium sulfate, yeast extract, and trace minerals.
For fruit wine, nutrients developed by Vogelbusch are available, containing diam-
monium phosphate and BREMOFERM®, a formulation rich in vitamins, minerals,
```
and other nutrients (VOGELBUSCH, 2018).
```
97Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
Cetotec GmbH (CETOTEC, 2018) produces nutrients suitable for both traditional
```
```
and modern submerged processes, such as the Nutracet®Complete (for alcohol vin-
```
```
egar) and the Nutracet®Wine for wine and fruit vinegars. These nutrients consist of
```
```
well-balanced mixtures of ingredients (minerals, dextrose, vitamins, trace elements,
```
```
and yeast extract), and their claimed advantages include high quality standards (e.g.,
```
```
DIN ISO 9001: 2008, HACCP, Kosher and Halal certifications), high efficiency for
```
more than 20% acid strength in the fed-batch process, full solubility, no residues, no
color, and cost-effective dosing depending on the desired acidity.
The Nutri-Go® series nutrients are also used to promote bacterial growth in the
```
acetators (NUTRIENTS INC., 2018). They contain varying mixtures of sugars, ammo-
```
nium/potassium/tricalcium phosphate, magnesium/potassium/sodium sulfate, potas-
sium chloride, yeast extract, and vitamins. Specifically, Nutri-Go®1000 is suitable for
```
use in packed generators; Nutri-Go®1500 (two parts dextrose/one part Nutri-Go®1500)
```
is used in submerged fermentations for acid strength up to 16%. Nutri-Go®2000 is the
same as Nutri-Go®1500 but with the dextrose already added. Nutri-Go®2500 is used
for corn sugar, malt, and cider vinegars to improve production cycle times. Finally,
Nutri-Go®3000 is used to improve the cycle times in standard vinegar production even
for vinegars with acid strength over 16%.
The adaptation of these nutrient supplements to the needs of each individual vin-
egar production process is critical for enhanced fermentation efficiency as well as
```
for better filtration (CETOTEC, 2018). For special processes and geographic loca-
```
tions, the nutrient manufacturers develop special formulations and production pro-
```
cedures, based on their customer requests or legal regulations (FRINGS, 2018). The
```
best quality nutrients are those that ensure best productivity, avoidance of product
coloration, and good storage stability. These attributes can be achieved by sophis-
```
ticated formulations as well as through suitable packaging (e.g., Advanced Packing
```
```
Technology; APT) (FRINGS, 2018) that prevents moisture and oxygen penetration
```
during transport and storage.
Finally, most nutrients are subjected to strict production and quality controls to
ensure reliable and stable fermentation and should be used according to the supplier
dosage instructions and in accordance with current regulations. For example, to pro-
duce organic vinegar in the EU, nutrient supplements are developed according to the
```
Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 of 28 June 2007 on organic production and
```
controlled by local control bodies or control authorities, such as the DE-ÖKÖ-013,
suitable for the production of alcohol, wine, and fruit vinegars in the normal process
```
(FRINGS, 2018).
```
6.5.2 ClarifiCation and fining
Clarification/fining agents are used to clarify vinegars from insoluble organic mat-
ter, avoid cloudiness in the final bottled product, remove oxidized and oxidizable
```
components such as phenolics (to refresh and improve flavor and remove bitterness),
```
```
and remove color (curative treatments). They are also used to improve the gustatory
```
appreciation by consumers, accelerate clarification, improve the lees compaction
and facilitate the subsequent filtration, reduce Maillard reaction products such as
HMF, remove pesticides, heavy metals, and other substances responsible for sensory
98 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
defects or health problems (e.g., biogenic amines), stabilize minor patulin and ochra-
```
toxin contents, and optimize stability during storage. The clarification/fining agents
are usually formulations based on:
• Bentonite/activated montmorillonite
• Activated carbon
```
• Animal proteins (caseins, albumins, gelatins, etc.)
```
• Plant proteins
```
• Colloidal silica (silica sol)
```
```
• Polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (PVPP)
```
Companies that develop or supply clarification media for the vinegar industry
```
also describe (claim) specific advantages for their products and provide information
```
```
(usually limited) on their composition, which is available on the Web in the form of
```
technical data sheets that describe the product functionality, formula, application,
dosage, safety, packaging type, etc. The proper dosage for most products is indicated
by the supplier, or it should be determined after suitable medium pre-tests depending
```
on the intended use (clarification, stabilization, tannin reduction, and taste harmo-
```
```
nization). The stabilizing and clarification capacity are affected by the combination
```
of pH and temperature effects and by the level of turbidity of the liquid to be treated
```
(ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
Pre-swelling and the way in which a product is added are also critical for a success-
```
ful clarification/fining (Figure 6.5). All clarification/fining agents require thorough
```
stirring during addition to break down large flocs into smaller particles. However,
continuous in-line dosage is also possible for products that are frequently used and
```
are characterized by very fine flocculation (ERBSLÖH, 2018). Therefore, the wetta-
```
bility and suspensibility should also be taken into account when choosing the proper
clarifying agent. Their use should also be permitted according to current laws and
regulations, such as the Codex Alimentarius, national food regulations, the Food
Chemicals Codex, etc. Products free from animal-derived ingredients, non-GMO,
```
and non-allergenic (e.g., plant proteins), are suitable for producing vegan foodstuffs
```
```
and are not subject to allergen labeling (ERBSLÖH, 2018). Most products are very
```
```
FIGURE 6.5 Preparation (pre-swelling) and use of clarification/fining agents.
```
99Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
sensitive to odor and moisture; therefore, they should be protected against both by
```
```
suitable packaging and storage conditions (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
6.5.2.1 Bentonites
The most commonly used fining agent for the clarification and purification of liquid
foods, such as wines, fruit juices, vinegars, and others, is food grade bentonite. It
functions as adsorbent and flocculent of proteins and other undesirable substances
```
(AMCOL, 2018). Bentonite suspensions combine with dissolved salts and form rap-
```
idly settling flocculates drifting other suspended solids as they sediment. Combined
```
with other clarification agents (alum, lime, polyelectrolytes, etc.), bentonite can
```
```
improve both the rate of settling and the compaction of lees (AMCOL, 2018).
```
There are plenty of clarification/fining commercial products based on bentonite
with technical information provided on the Web. For example, UltraBent PORE-
```
TEC UF (ERBSLÖH, 2018) is described as a highly pure and efficient granulated
```
Na-Ca-bentonite designed for protein adsorption in combination with specific cross-
flow microfiltration systems. Due to the defined particle-size distribution, it is suit-
able, after pre-swelling, for direct dosing into hollow fiber membranes, facilitating
a one-step clarification and stabilization process. The claimed advantage over con-
ventional bentonites is its purity and high protein adsorbance capacity. The recom-
```
mended dosages are in the range 25–200 g/hL. NaCalit® PORE-TEC (ERBSLÖH,
```
```
2018) is also a granulated Na-Ca-bentonite for the highest quality demands in the
```
beverage industry by adsorbing proteins and other colloids. It can be combined with
silica sol and protein-based fining agents to enhance flocculation of components,
which may cause later haze. Furthermore, it is claimed to have a positive impact on
the sensory properties of the treated liquids. It is an effective clarifying agent even in
problematic cases and at high pH values.
```
The CX Granular Bentonite (CORIMPEX, 2018) is a granular bentonite with
```
high deproteinizing power, used for clarifying wine, must, vinegars, and fruit juices.
It is particularly recommended for stabilizing clarification of wines that require final
stabilizing clarification before bottling. The dosage lies in the range 50–150 g/hL for
the clarification of juices and vinegars.
```
The Volclay® series of fining agents (AMCOL, 2018) consists of hydrous alumi-
```
num silicate mainly comprised of the clay mineral montmorillonite. They are used
for the fining of wine, juice, cider, and vinegar, to efficiently and rapidly remove
suspended solids and heat-sensitive proteins and prevent cloudiness. Their chemical
```
formula is the dioctahedral smectite, an expanding layer silicate (Na,Ca) 0.33 (Al1.67
```
```
Mg 0.33)Si4 O10 (OH)2·nH 2 O, with elemental composition (moisture free) of about
```
63.02% SiO2 , 21.08% Al 2 O3, 3.25% Fe2 O3, 0.35% FeO, 2.67% MgO, 2.57% Na 2 O,
```
0.65% CaO, 0.72% trace, 5.64% LOI, and pH 8.5–10.5 at 5% solids (AMCOL, 2018).
```
```
Another specially activated montmorillonite agent is the Acetibent (SOFRALAB,
```
```
2018) used for fining of vinegar with high amounts of proteins. It is a fining agent
```
with an exceptional clarifying and protein adsorption potential, mainly used with
difficult cider or white wine vinegars that would otherwise require large amounts of
```
bentonite to be treated efficiently. Much lower dosages (20 g/hL) are recommended
```
for vinegars that are already clear or contain small amounts of proteins and may
exceed 50 g/hL for vinegars that are very difficult to clarify due to high organic
100 Advances in Vinegar Production
matter content. Treatment with Acetibent produces a significant amount of lees
```
(about 4% volume for treatment with 20 g/hL with a settling time of at least 4 days).
```
```
It is used after sprinkling over water while stirring (~1 kg for 25–30 L water), leaving
```
to stand for 1–2 h, left to swell for 12–24 h, and then added rapidly and vigorously
```
using a metering pump (Figure 6.5). The lees should be allowed to settle for a few
```
days before racking or filtration and can be recovered and filtered to reduce their
volume.
Plenty of such bentonite-style clarification agents are offered in the global market
```
mainly for the stabilization of wines before bottling; however, bentonites are also
```
amongst the most commonly used fining agents in the modern vinegar industry.
6.5.2.2 Activated Carbons
Activated carbons work better in pre-clarified liquids because the substances to
remove are partially bound to the sediments formed during the clarification process.
Therefore, the best results are achieved when treating a filtrate. However, if a turbid
liquid is to be treated to skip the filtration step, the addition of activated carbon
must be done before the addition of other treatment agents. Periodic stirring is also
recommended to increase the efficiency of the treatment, which is also affected by
pH, temperature, and turbidity of the liquid to be treated. Depending on the intended
```
application, the proper dosage must be determined by pre-testing (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
There are also plenty of clarification/fining commercial products based on activated
```
carbon, with technical information provided on the Web, some of which (randomly
```
```
selected) are discussed below.
```
