```
For example, the Granucol® (ERBSLÖH, 2018) products are activated carbon pel-
```
lets of plant origin with correspondingly varying inner surface, thus specific adsorp-
tion capacity. According to the supplier, the special production process assures
excellent porosity distribution. Depending on the specific treatment, the individual
Granucol® types are applied for adsorption of undesired off-flavors, reduction of
tannins and polyphenols, and for the elimination of color due to browning reactions
in beer, juice, wine, and spirits. Typical dosages are 40–150 g/hL for vinegar and
20–100 g/hL for wine.
```
Ercarbon SH (ERBSLÖH, 2018) is an activated coconut carbon specially designed
```
for beverage treatment for adsorption of minimal color pigments, off-flavors, and
adsorption of critical substances during concentrate production. It works better in
pre-clarified liquids. However, if a cloudy juice must be treated to skip a filtration
step, the addition should be done before other treatment agents. It is also suggested
that it should be used in the temperature range of 45–55°C and at maximum 30°Brix
```
sugar concentrations (or below 20°Brix if the treatment temperatures are below
```
```
20°C). Usually, reaction times of 30–60 min are sufficient. Similarly, Ercarbon FA
```
```
(ERBSLÖH, 2018) is a chemically activated (with phosphoric acid) carbon of plant
```
```
origin that presents higher efficiency in filtered liquids. Its special (claimed) features
```
are the efficient adsorption of oxidized polyphenols, the optimized stability during
the beverage storage, and the low impact on flavor.
```
Another oenological activated carbon is CX Anti Color (CORIMPEX, 2018) used
```
```
for decolorization of must (even from red grapes), vinegar, and vermouth, for treat-
```
ment of oxidation, as well as for the reduction of fungal toxins. The proper dosage
101Current Industrial Vinegar Production
is determined by laboratory tests, and the legal limit is 100 g/hL. Treatment time is
at least 30 min.
At research level, there are various studies investigating the use of activated
```
carbons (biochars) produced by waste biomass as clarification agents for vinegars.
```
```
Such a technology was proposed by Zhong et al. (2012) for utilizing vinegar lees.
```
The preparation of the porous carbon involved carbonization in N2 and activation
in CO2 . The carbon had a large specific surface area and micropore volume, with a
phenol adsorptive capacity much higher than that of commercial activated carbon
from coconut shells. Other studies dealt with the improvement of the decolorization
```
capacity of activated carbons. For example, Lopez et al. (2003) modified the surface
```
activity and porosity of activated carbon obtained from olive stones by controlled
oxidation with air at 350°C, for applications in vinegar treatment.
6.5.2.3 Proteins and Silica Sols
Proteins such as gelatin have a high positive adsorptive capacity for negatively
```
charged tannins and residual pectins (EATON, 2018). Gelatin is mainly used to
```
reduce the amount of polyphenols which cause browning reactions and colloidal
and polyphenol hazes. To eliminate possible gelatin residues a combined treatment
with silica sol is usually recommended. Silica sols are aqueous colloidal solutions of
```
amorphous silicon dioxide (SiO2) with particle sizes of 10–1,000 Å, which at wine
```
```
pH are highly negatively charged (ESSECO, 2018). Their fining capacity is based
```
on the flocculation of their negatively charged SiO 2 particles with the positively
charged protein particles. The flocculates precipitate causing sedimentation of other
suspended substances responsible for product turbidity. Therefore, the combination
```
of proteins or isinglass (fish glue) with silica sols improves and accelerates clarifica-
```
tion, improves lees compaction and filterability, eliminates unstable polyphenolic
substances, and reduces overall time, effort, and costs in the fining of musts, fruit
```
juices, wines, and vinegars (ERBSLÖH, 2018; ESSECO, 2018).
```
```
An example of a commercial silica-based product is Klar-Sol Super (ERBSLÖH,
```
```
2018). It is an acidic special silica sol developed for clarification of wine, fruit juice,
```
```
fruit wine, and other beverages by causing complexation of proteins (including fining
```
```
proteins). It precipitates quickly forming compact fining deposits. When applied in
```
liquids with high hydrocolloid loads and low pH values, it performs more efficiently
than alkaline silica types. The required dosages are in the range 20–250 mL/hL of
beverage.
```
Acetisol (SOFRALAB, 2018) is a liquid colloidal silica solution (30% silicic acid)
```
used for the clarification of difficult wine vinegars and vinegars rich in mucilage and
colloids. It is an aqueous suspension of negatively charged silica particles that can
flocculate only through the mutual action with the protein fining agent with long
```
molecular chain such as Acetigel (described below). Acetisol accelerates clarification
```
avoiding overfining, improves lees compaction, and facilitates subsequent filtration
of the vinegars. It is applied at rates of 10–100 mL/hL combined with 10–100 mL/hL
of Acetigel. Specifically, the required amount of Acetisol is diluted in ten times its
```
volume of vinegar during pumping over (at least 1/3 of tank) with the aid of a meter-
```
```
ing pump. Acetigel (previously diluted in a small amount of cold water) is immedi-
```
ately added.
102 Advances in Vinegar Production
Similarly, the silica sol product Sol Di Silice works best in synergy with CX
```
Liquid Gel (CORIMPEX, 2018). When mixed, a rapid and complete clarification is
```
achieved as well as a reduction in deposit volume. The dosage may be from 25 to
100 g/hL.
```
Acetigel is a liquid, partially hydrolyzed gelatin formulation (molecular struc-
```
```
ture characterized by long chains) for wine vinegars in combination with Acetisol
```
```
(SOFRALAB, 2018). Due to its molecular homogeneity, purity, stability, and con-
```
trolled surface charge density, it is presented as a highly reactive agent specifically
```
developed for vinegar fining. Acetigel (diluted with cold water) can be used on its
```
own with tannic red wine vinegars, added directly during pumping over. Proper
homogenization during addition is highly recommended. Flocculation occurs rap-
idly, and perfect lees compaction can be achieved after a week’s rest.
```
ErbiGel and ErbiGel®Bio (ERBSLÖH, 2018) are gelatin-based products of
```
```
pork origin. ErbiGel is an acidically treated gelatin with 90–100 Bloom value (gel
```
```
strength measure), which is ideal for beverage treatment. Due to the acidic digestion
```
it has mostly positive charges in typical beverage media ensuring high reactivity
with polyphenols or silica sol. Typical dosages are 5–40 g/hL. ErbiGel®Bio is an
organic edible gelatin obtained from organic pork rind and certified according to EU
Regulation no. 834/2007. It reduces tannins and polyphenols and can be used in both
sedimentation and flotation due its good gelling ability. The dosage is 5–20 g/hL for
tannin reduction or more depending on pre-test results.
```
FloraClair® (ERBSLÖH, 2018) on the other hand, is a purified plant-based pro-
```
```
tein. Like animal-derived protein agents (gelatin, casein, isinglass) it shows good
```
reactivity towards tannic substances and suspended matter improving haze and color
stability in fruit juices, fruit wines, vinegars, tea extracts, etc. It is also suitable for
vegan products, for pre-clarification of musts, for tannin correction, and for reduction
```
of oxidized yellowish/brownish colorations. Similarly, Acetigreen (SOFRALAB,
```
```
2018) is a water-soluble plant protein (pea), used for red and white wine and cider
```
vinegar clarification. Plant proteins are offered as efficient alternatives to gelatin,
ensuring safety for consumers regarding the skepticism toward products of animal
origin. Plant proteins react with suspended particles present in vinegars, specifically
```
the most astringent tannins with high molecular weight (e.g., gallic tannins), to form
```
large aggregates that will flocculate and sediment. It is highly recommended to carry
out pre-tests to determine the proper dosages, and addition should be done homog-
enously in the proper volume of vinegar during pumping over.
Products based on milk proteins are also available as clarifying aids. For exam-
```
ple, Kal-Casin Leicht löslich (ERBSLÖH, 2018) is an effective tannin adsorption
```
agent based on pure milk protein components. It has good dispersion properties and
does not require laborious dissolving equipment. It is particularly effective for reduc-
```
ing excess tannins as well as off-flavors (bitter notes) caused by high polyphenol
```
```
contents (e.g., in the case of grapes subjected to great mechanical stress). It also
```
suppresses Maillard reactions and reduces oxidized, brown pigments. As tannins
are often bound to sediment particles, the most effective treatment is in pre-clarified
beverages. In the case of combined fining, it is usually introduced first unless acti-
```
vated carbon is used; then it should be added 1–2 h later. The dosage is 5–20 g/hL for
```
removal of tannic notes and 20–40 g/hL for reduction of slight volatile flavor notes.
103Current Industrial Vinegar Production
Regarding research studies, there is a growing interest in developing alternative
beverage fining agents to replace animal or plant derived proteins that are potentially
```
allergenic (Gazzola et al., 2017). For example, grape-derived fining agents would be
```
beneficial as they are fully compatible with wines and wine vinegars. For example,
grape seed flour, a by-product of the grape oil seed industry, was used to prepare an
```
extract as a novel wine fining agent (Gazzola et al., 2017). Its efficiency was com-
```
pared with that of patatin, pea proteins, PVPP, potassium caseinate, ovalbumin, and
gelatin, and it was concluded that grape seed extract can be considered as a valid
allergen-free alternative to most common wine fining agents.
6.5.2.4 PVPPs
PVPP is also highly effective for the specific removal of polyphenols, as well as
```
bitterness and herbaceous aromas (ESSECO, 2018). Products of pure, food grade
```
PVPP are available in the form of white/whitish, fine, hygroscopic powders, insolu-
```
ble in water and alcohol. For example, Stabyl (ESSECO, 2018) is an effective aid for
```
removing oxidizable and oxidized polyphenols and is used for treatment or preven-
tion of oxidation in white wine. It reduces phenolic bitterness, eliminates compounds
that combine with SO2 , improves the color of oxidized wine, and reduces tannins
that can cause protein instability. It can also be effectively combined, depending on
the intended application, with bentonite and potassium caseinate.
```
Another product, the X PVPP (CORIMPEX, 2018), also claims to have high and
```
specific adsorption capacity for tannic and oxidized phenolic substances. It is recom-
mended for the treatment of prestigious wines both to prevent and treat the effects of
phenolic oxidation, but it can also be used for beer and vinegar clarification.
```
Stabyl Met (ENARTIS, 2018) is a co-polymer of polyvinylimidazole/polyvi-
```
```
nylpyrrolidone (PVI/PVP) and silica, used to absorb heavy metals (high affinity
```
```
with Cu) and remove hydroxycinnamic acids and low molecular weight catechins.
```
It removes bitterness and prevents oxidation, browning and destruction of varietal
thiols, pinking, and formation of copper haze. The dosage range is 20–50 g/hL.
PVPPs are permitted according to current laws and regulations. They are usually
dissolved in water before use and allowed to swell, preferably with constant stirring.
The product/water ratio and the time required for swelling are applied according
to the supplier instructions for use. Swelling can be accelerated by the use of warm
```
water (40–50°C) (ESSECO, 2018). The resulting suspension is added by a dosing
```
```
pump to the liquid to be treated under stirring (Figure 6.5). A contact time of 1–2 h is
```
usually sufficient, and the residual clarifying product and sediment can be removed
by filtration. The maximum level allowed by EEC legislation in must and wine is
```
50 g/hL (EC 606/2009).
```
6.5.3 filtering
Limpidity is the first quality that consumers request in vinegars. Development of
haze or deposit inside the bottle is inevitably perceived by consumers as a sign of
product alteration and spoilage. The suspended or colloid particles in vinegars are not
passive, and limpidity or haze development depends largely on their electric charges
```
(SOFRALAB, 2018). Therefore, filtration is required to clarify vinegar (clarifying
```
104 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
filtration) and/or eliminate microorganisms (sterilizing filtration). Filtration is the
```
physical process consisting of passing a liquid through appropriate filters that retain
the suspended particles. Vinegar filtration can be achieved by the same means and
ways used for wine, juices, and other liquid foods, i.e., by deposition using appro-
priate additives such as diatomaceous earth, or using pads of cellulose or other
```
appropriate materials, or by porous membranes (microfiltration) (OIV, 2017). These
```
methods involve products based on:
• Diatomaceous earth
```
• Cellulose fibers (long, medium, and short)
```
• Perlites
• Combined mineral silica and cellulose
• Combined diatomite and cellulose
• Combined perlites and cellulose
• Membranes
```
These products are available for various types of filtration (fine, polishing, very
```
```
fine, coarse, pre-sterilizing, sterilizing, and vacuum filtration) of very turbid or
```
```
clear liquids (DAL CIN, 2018). There are also plenty of commercial media, means,
```
and integrated systems for vinegar filtration with technical information provided
```
on the Web, some of which (also randomly selected) are discussed below. All fil-
```
```
tering material must meet the requirements of Commission Regulation (EC) No
```
606/2009 of 10 July 2009 laying down certain detailed rules for implementing
```
Council Regulation (EC) No 479/2008 about the categories of grapevine products,
```
oenological practices, and the applicable restrictions. It should also conform to the
```
International Oenological Codex (OIV, 2017).
```
6.5.3.1 Diatomaceous Earth
```
Kieselgur or diatomite or diatomaceous earth (DE), is a sedimentary rock contain-
```
```
ing high amounts of hydrated amorphous silica shells (fossil remains) from diatoms
```
```
(microscopic brown algae) that lived in aqueous habitats (e.g., lakes) as phytoplank-
```
```
ton and sedimented after death (SOFRALAB, 2018). There are many such deposits
```
worldwide, mainly in Europe and South America, from which kieselgur is harvested
by mining. Kieselgur has a wide range of industrial applications. It is used as a
filtering agent for food liquids, and other water resources, and as an additive in con-
crete, toothpastes, paints, papers, fertilizers, pesticides, etc. In its recommendations,
```
the EU Expert Group for Technical Advice on Organic Production (EGTOP) con-
```
```
cluded that kieselgur complies with the organic objectives and principles; therefore,
```
```
it should be included in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 that lays down
```
detailed rules for the implementation of EC 834/2007 on organic production and
```
labeling and control of organic products (EGTOP, 2018).
```
Due to its structure, kieselgur has very good filtering characteristics. The quan-
tity and type of kieselgur used determines the filtering efficiency and the clarifying
sharpness of the finished product. Its filtration performance can also be improved
by combining with other filter aids, such as perlites, cellulose fibers, filter flakes for
pre-coat filtration, etc. As an active adsorbent substance, kieselgur can also adsorb
105Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
moisture and odors; therefore, it should be stored in dry, well ventilated places
```
```
(EATON, 2018). Many kieselgur-based products can be found on the Web, with
```
information provided in the form of technical data sheets that describe functionality,
applications, advantages, safety, packaging types, etc.
For example, kieselguhr filters for wine, vinegar, olive oil, fruit juices, and other
```
alimentary liquids are available from Enomet Impianti Srl (ENOMET, 2018). Their
```
claimed features/advantages are the very simple use and maintenance, the very high
panel stability also in case of interruption of the filtering operation, and the fast
opening to inspection and washing of the filtering screens.
```
Kieselguhr C200 (EATON, 2018) is a fine DE, claiming to provide particu-
```
larly high efficiency for the fine filtration of vinegar and other liquids. Its specific
claimed advantages include high clarifying sharpness, reliable filtration through
rapid formation of an adherent filter cake, economic filtration due to the optimum
ratio of flow rate/clarifying sharpness, and maximum purity. It is used in specific
```
filter devices (pre-coat plate/frame filters with washable support; pre-coat filters
```
```
with horizontal or vertical screen elements; cartridge filters with vertical filter car-
```
```
tridges) (EATON, 2018).
```
```
BECO filter pads for plate filtration (SOFRALAB, 2018) are also available for
```
the clarification of vinegars. The range of Standard pads are used for a separation
range of 4.0–0.1 μm, and their claimed advantages include reliable retention of
the target compounds due to an ideal porous structure, high level of clarifica-
tion, and extended lifetime. The range of Steril filter pads, used for sterile fil-
tration, have a high microbe retention capacity and are particularly suitable for
vinegar bottling or cold storage of liquids. Due to their high adsorption capacity
for colloidal compounds, these pads can be used as pre-filters before membrane
filtration. The range of Fine Filtration pads are used to achieve a high level of
clarification, efficiently retaining the finest particles and decreasing the concen-
tration of microbes. The range of Clarifying Filtration filter pads have a signifi-
cant alveolar structure, suitable for efficiently adsorbing particles responsible for
```
haziness (SOFRALAB, 2018).
```
A wide variety of similar commercial kieselgur-based filtering products/devices
are available in the international market to satisfy the different vinegar manufacturer
demands.
6.5.3.2 Cellulose Fibers
High-purity, finely fibrillated cellulose fibers are used to form depth filter sheets with
large internal surface. Such filters are available in the market for all filtration ranges
```
and clarifying sharpness/sterilization performances (EATON, 2018). Cellulose fibers
```
```
can be enhanced by different techniques and materials (e.g., combined with perlites
```
```
or kieselgur) to ensure variable porosity and large holding capacity. Fine particles of
```
the treated liquids are trapped in the interwoven fiber structure of the filter, while
microorganisms are absorbed by electrokinetic charges and entrapped in the interior
```
filter structure (ERBSLÖH, 2018). Filtration using filter sheets can be customized
```
```
with great accuracy for the specific vinegar or wine filtration requirements (clari-
```
```
fying or sterilizing filtration) and economic throughput volumes. Filter celluloses
```
```
should be stored in dry, odor-free places (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
106 Advances in Vinegar Production
Following, some commercial cellulose filters available for the filtration needs of
vinegar and beverage industries are briefly described. For example, FitoflocTM is
a commercial pre-dispersed pre-coat for fine to pre-sterilizing filtration. The pre-
dispersion technique is used to increase the adsorbing/filtering surface and thus the
```
pre-coat efficiency, as well as the dispersibility into the treated liquid (DAL CIN,
```
```
2018). FitoflocTM is made of very pure plant fiber with specifically re-elaborated
```
intermolecular structure of the cellulose chains, a modification that makes the spe-
cific surface of cellulose wider and increases the filtering capacity. It is particu-
larly suitable for the retention of unstable colloids, with dosages that can range from
```
0.5 to 2.0 kg/m 2 of filtering surface (DAL CIN, 2018).
```
CelluFluxx® is another commercial cellulose filtration aid, suitable for vari-
```
ous grades of fineness and specifically tailored for beverage filtration (ERBSLÖH,
```
```
2018). The fibers are extremely pure as the result of a complex extraction process
```
during manufacture, involving special milling and fibrillation of the fibers. These
products are 100% organic and biodegradable since they are obtained from sus-
```
tainable cellulosic raw materials (deciduous and coniferous timbers). Cellulose in
```
CelluFluxx® forms a loose filter cake with high-pressure surge elasticity, which is
very gentle on the treated product, preventing particle breakdown in the filter and
causing a highly increased total throughput. Therefore, it reduces the quantity of
filtration aid used as well as the product loss and the quantity of generated waste.
The filter quantities used may vary greatly depending on the initial turbidity of the
liquid to be filtered and the desired final degree of clarity. Kieselgur can be added
to the treated liquid to aid drainage in the growing filter cake during the filtra-
```
tion (ERBSLÖH, 2018). A wide range of CelluFluxx® cellulose filters have been
```
developed for different filtration requirements. Long cellulose fibers are used for
coarse filtration and for drainage formation in the filter cake. They strengthen the
filter cake and provide high-throughput rates with good turbidity reduction. They
are also specifically used for initial pre-coating. Medium to long fibers are used
for coarse clarifying filtration and are suitable for second pre-coating. Medium
length fibers are used for fine filtration. These fibers are strongly fibrillated and
are suitable for second pre-coating and for regular dosing. The strong fibrillation
creates a good internal structure in the filter cake, which leads to high turbid-
ity reduction and fine filtration. Short, cubic fibers have also been developed for
abrupt fine filtration. They are suitable as an admixture or in pure form for second
pre-coating. Extra-short fibers are used for abrupt filtration and antimicrobial
```
filtration (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
Various porosity range filter sheets containing pure cellulosic fiber as well as kie-
```
selgur are also available for a wide retained size range (e.g., 0.2–10 μm).
```
6.5.3.3 Perlites
Perlite is a vitreous, amorphous volcanic rock of the rhyolite group, made of about
70–75% SiO 2 , 12–15% Al 2 O3 , and lower amounts of other minerals, as well as
1–2% chemically bound water content. It is used for oenological purposes after
drying at 150°C, grinding, and “expanding” to 15–60 times its size by heating at
200–400°C, followed by exposure at 800–1,100°C. Perlite is a common filtration
aid for wine that must be stored in well-ventilated dry places, protected from odors
107Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
and moisture (OIV, 2017)). An interesting feature of perlite is that it does not con-
```
```
tain crystalline silica; therefore it is not considered a hazardous material to work
```
```
with (DAL CIN, 2018).
```
There are many commercial products available on the market with information
provided on the Web for the needs of the beverage industries, including vinegar fil-
```
tration, such as the Enoperlite range (DAL CIN, 2018). This range of perlite products
```
has been developed for vacuum drum filtration as well as an alternative to kieselgur in
pre-coat filtration. It is suitable for covering all the filtration ranges, from very coarse
to very fine. A typical dosage may be 0.5–2.0 g/L as body-feed or 1.0–1.5 kg/m 2
```
for vacuum drum filters (DAL CIN, 2018).
```
```
The Dicalite Perlite range (ERBSLÖH, 2018) has been developed after ground-
```
ing, annealing to 15–20 times the initial size by heating at 800–1,000°C, and re-
grounding to determine the desired fineness and structure. Coarse perlites are used
to form cavities in filter cakes, while fine perlites are used to make the filter cakes
denser, increasing their clarifying efficiency. The dosages vary greatly and depend
on the initial turbidity of the product to be filtered and the final degree of clarity
```
desired (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
6.5.3.4 Microfiltration Systems
Microfiltration systems are applicable for the filtration of different kinds of vinegars
```
(alcohol, wine, and cider vinegars). According to Lopez et al. (2005), membrane
```
technology combined with cross-flow microfiltration has and can lead to significant
innovation, making it possible to design, develop, and optimize innovative processes
and products in terms of quality, plant size, energy consumption, and environmental
impact. Cross-flow filtration involves mainly microporous hollow fiber membranes,
through which the vinegar is driven diagonally and at high speed to prevent the for-
mation of coating.
```
For example, Cetotec Microfiltration systems for vinegar (CETOTEC, 2018) are
```
based on the combination of cross-flow principles with high performance mem-
```
branes. Specifically, they consist of Liqui-Flux®-Modules of polypropylene (PP)
```
```
embedded in polysulfone (PES) housing and are suitable for capacities in the range
```
300–3,200 L/h. These systems are fully automated with an integrated process con-
```
trol, including automatic backflush for cleaning; they are arranged in a small com-
```
```
pact space and require no consumables (CETOTEC, 2018).
```
```
Similarly, C-CUT hollow fiber modules (BÜRKERT, 2018) are available for
```
microfiltration applications to properly remove vinegar bacteria and other microor-
```
ganisms. The membranes consist of polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), PES, and PP
```
and have been especially developed for applications requiring high filtration perfor-
mance and packing density. The C-CUT capillary modules are specifically used for
water, wine, and vinegar filtration due to their high stability and the possibility for
```
chemical and backwash membrane cleaning (BÜRKERT, 2018).
```
Various research studies also deal with aspects of vinegar clarification by
```
microfiltration. For example, Tamai et al. (1997) studied the cross-flow filtra-
```
tion of an acetous fermentation broth using a hollow fiber module to optimize
```
operating parameters (cell concentration, feed velocity, and pressure) and back-
```
washing operation. From their results they were able to calculate the membrane
108 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
area required for the bioreactor. Lopez et al. (2005) studied the clarification of
```
white, rosé, and red vinegars by cross-flow microfiltration at industrial scale,
```
using the Permawine Mini (Permeare S.r.l., Milan, Italy), consisting of a four-
```
module filter with a filtration area of 24 m 2 each. The membrane material was
```
PES (0.45 μm pore diameter). The system led to a significant reduction of tur-
```
```
bidity in all types of vinegars (lower than 0.5 Nephelometric Turbidity Units
```
```
(NTU)), with an acceptable effect on color and polyphenol content, concluding
```
that microfiltration can be simultaneously used to clarify and cold-sterilize vin-
```
egars (Lopez et al., 2005).
```
6.5.4 staBilization
6.5.4.1 Addition of SO2
```
Stabilization of the finished vinegar (microbial and oxidative stability) is necessary
```
before storage in tanks or bottling, in order for the product to enter the market with-
```
out any defects. The most commonly used stabilization products “contain” (liberate)
```
SO2 , acting as both antiseptic and antioxidant preventing browning and discoloration
by rapidly scavenging oxygen and other oxidative species. Care should be taken in
the use of SO 2 -releasing products to avoid the characteristic smell of SO 2 in the
```
treated product (SOFRALAB, 2018).
```
Various products for SO 2 release are available in the market, such as the Acetibak
```
(potassium bisulfite, KHSO3, E228) (SOFRALAB, 2018). The specific product con-
```
tains 150 g/L of SO2 in the form of KHSO3, and the amount needed to release 1.5 g
of SO2 in the treated liquid is 10 mL.
```
Other products contain potassium pyrosulfite (or potassium disulfite or potassium
```
```
dihydrogensulfite; K 2 S2 O5, E224; white powder), such as the Baktol P (SOFRALAB,
```
```
2018), used to inhibit all types of fermentation in musts and wines. It is also widely
```
used in vinegars. It is an easy-to-handle product, dissolving easily at up to 400 g,
yielding an amount of 200 g of SO2 .
6.5.4.2 Addition of Gum Arabic
Stabilization, regarding colloidal precipitates, is usually done by addition of selected
gum arabic, a polysaccharide with a high molecular weight commonly used in the
```
food industries (CORIMPEX, 2018). Gum arabic is the final treatment for colloidal
```
stabilization of vinegars, which restores the initial colloidal protection lost during
the acetification and clarification processes. Once treated with gum arabic, vinegar
can no longer be fined because the gum can clog the filters unless it is added at least
```
2 h before filtration (SOFRALAB, 2018).
```
In wine, gum arabic, such as the commercial Délite product from selected Acacia
```
Senegal nodules (DAL CIN, 2018), is used mainly to improve sensory characteris-
```
```
tics, by softening astringent (in red wines) and acidic (in white wines) sensations.
```
These results are obtained by reducing the tannin interactions with saliva proteins
and by increasing the fullness and sweetness sensations, respectively. Gum arabic
also affects aroma, making herbaceous notes less perceptible, thus unveiling fresh
and fruity notes.
109Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
Acetistab (SOFRALAB, 2018) is a gum arabic product suitable specifically
```
for the stabilization of red wine and cider vinegars to ensure color stability and
avoidance of cloudiness due to cold storage. It is made from specially selected,
solubilized, purified, and sterilized gums. Typical dosage is 1 L per 5–30 hL,
```
defined by cold tests (4–6 days at 2°C) according to the vinegar stabilization
```
requirements.
```
Another example is the CX Blanc Gum D (CORIMPEX, 2018), a gum arabic
```
product used as a colloid protector in wine and to prevent alterations caused by
ferric, copper, protein, and ferric phosphate as well as from colorant precipitates.
```
Similarly, HydroGum (ERBSLÖH, 2018) is a liquid gum arabic, obtained from the
```
dried sap of Acacia Senegal, that protects against colloid instability and heavy metal
turbidity. As a side effect, it is claimed to improve the mouthfeel and complexity
of wines. The dosage for stabilization and harmonization is about 40–100 g/100 L.
All the above products must be used according to current laws and regulations and
should be laboratory tested for purity and quality.
6.5.4.3 Addition of Tannins
```
Tannins for oenological use include products suitable for the treatment of wines (red
```
```
and white), vinegars, and distillates. Tannins may first be suspended in a little water
```
and then added to the liquid to be treated with vigorous stirring. Also, preliminary
tests are recommended, regarding dosage, the desired degree of clarity, and the
effect on flavor, especially when treatments with clarifying agents containing pro-
tein, such as isinglass or gelatin, are subsequently applied. Their stabilizing effect
may be enhanced by low oxygen absorption. Tannin products should be stored in
sealed containers away from odors, moisture, and light and should be quickly used
```
up after opening (ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
```
For example, Tannivin® Galleol (ERBSLÖH, 2018) is a specially selected and
```
purified gallnut tannin with high charge potential, suitable for the clarification and
stabilization of fruit juices and wines to improve structure and reduce oxidation.
```
The CX Tan Plus (CORIMPEX, 2018) is a mix of ellagic tannins obtained from
```
selected Quercus woods through exclusive hydroalcoholic extraction followed by
mild air drying to preserve the characteristics of the raw material. It is used in the
treatment of red wines, white wines, vinegars, and distillates. The CX Tan Skin
```
(CORIMPEX, 2018) has the tannic composition of mature grapes (procyanidic and
```
```
catechinic origin), which is highly reactive with proteins, including polyphenol
```
```
oxidase, and colorants. The CX Tan Stab (CORIMPEX, 2018) is also an ellagic
```
tannin obtained by hydroalcoholic extraction, used in wine maceration treatments,
for protein stabilization, and for the protection against oxidation. Finally, the CX
```
Tan Liqueur (CORIMPEX, 2018) is an aqueous preparation of selected French and
```
American oak tannins, used in the early stages of maturation in old barrels that
are no longer able to provide traditional, elegant tannins from ageing. The dosage
for vinegars of the above CX Tan series of products is in the range 10–40 g/hL
```
(ERBSLÖH, 2018).
```
Tannic stabilization aids should also be permitted according to current laws and
regulations and should also meet the purity requirements of OIV.
110 Advances in Vinegar Production
6.6 EXAMPLE: INDUSTRIAL PROCESS FOR VINEGAR
PRODUCTION FROM RAISIN FINISHING SIDE-STREAMS
The raisin finishing side-stream is the main raw material used for industrial vin-
egar production in countries that are major producers of raisins such as Greece.
Raisins are dried grapes produced by sun, shade, or mechanical drying. In Greece,
```
the famous variety Corinthian currants (small black Vitis vinifera L. raisins; referred
```
```
to as “currants” from this point on) is an old, historic product that played an impor-
```
tant role in the development of the Greek state, as an important exporting product.
Currently they account for about 80% of the total global production and are exported
worldwide, while the Greek market absorbs less than 2% of the total production. The
currants are a dual-use variety of grapes that can be dried and consumed as a snack
or used to produce wine and vinegar.
There are three main subvarieties of the product, the Gulf, the Provincial, and
```
the Vostitsa currants (Chiou et al., 2014), which are the top quality produced exclu-
```
```
sively in the area around Aeghion, Greece (Lat. 38°14′54″N; Lon. 22°04′54″E), where
```
```
the climatic conditions (effects of soil, altitude, sea breeze, and sunshine) are ideal.
```
Vostitsa is the highest quality of currants, standing out for its unique flavor. It is a PDO
```
(Ministerial Decision No. 442597, 1993; Commission Regulation No. 1549/98, 1998).
```
In recent years, companies working with this product have made a lot of progress
and innovation, including engagement in intense research activities to determine its
```
nutritional value. The published research shows that the Vostitsa currants are (1)
```
```
excellent sources of antioxidants (Chiou et al., 2007; 2014; Kaliora et al., 2009) and
```
```
(2) dietary fiber with potential prebiotic properties, (3) they present high bioavail-
```
```
ability of micronutrients (Kanellos, et al., 2013), (4) they have anticancer properties
```
```
(Kountouri et al., 2013), and (5) a moderate glycemic index, therefore they can be
```
```
consumed by diabetics (Kanellos et al., 2014).
```
A currant possessing company produces a large amount of a lower quality
```
side-stream (5% of total production) with ~70% invert sugar content. In Greece, this
```
side-stream is mainly used for vinegar production and to a lesser extent for raisin
```
syrup production. The process involves three stages: (1) extraction of raisins with
```
```
simultaneous alcoholic fermentation, (2) double stage acetification process, and
```
```
(3) post-fermentation treatments. The integrated vinegar production process from
```
raisin finishing side-streams is illustrated in Figure 6.6.
6.6.1 extraCtion/alCoHoliC fermentation stage
The raisin finishing side-stream is extracted with water at ambient temperature
without stirring and without SO2 addition. The extraction takes place either in open
cement tanks or in closed horizontal stainless-steel wine rotary fermenters as shown
in Figure 6.7.
The horizontal rotary fermenters are designed to be used for traditional red wine
vinification, or carbonic maceration, or cryomaceration, or as storage tanks. Special
```
features of such industrial fermenters include: (1) high versatility for the production
```
```
of different types of wines (e.g., through cryomaceration), (2) various utilizations
```
```
during the year, (3) very short extraction times (over 40%), (4) higher extract, which
```
111Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
gives more fullness and body to the wine, (5) almost no production of dreg (< 3%),
```
```
(6) possibility to ferment with the tank partially loaded, (7) possibility to control
```
```
the fermentation though controlled thermoregulation and oxygenation, (8) automatic
```
```
unloading of the exhausted marc, (9) possibility to arrange several fermenters in
```
```
stack, etc. (DESILLA, 2018; FRACCHIOLLA, 2018). Basic components of the hori-
```
```
zontal fermenters are: (1) automatic rotary mixer, (2) automatic discharge, (3) tem-
```
```
perature control in both heating and cooling, (4) breathing and sample valves, (5)
```
```
inlet/outlet, (6) level gauge, etc. (DESILLA, 2018; PRETTECH, 2018). The rotary
```
fermentation tanks constitute an innovative technology for the wine and vinegar pro-
ducer, as the horizontal configuration and the rotation mixing significantly increase
```
the contact capacity between the mash of the raw material (e.g., grape must) and
```
layer, allowing maximum maceration of tannins and anthocyanins and reducing
FIGURE 6.6 Industrial vinegar production from raisins or raisin finishing side-streams
involving sugar extraction and simultaneous alcoholic fermentation, followed by a two-step
```
acetification process (TC: temperature control).
```
FIGURE 6.7 Types of tanks for raisins extraction and simultaneous alcoholic fermentation
in vinegar production.
112 Advances in Vinegar Production
manual labor without compromising the extract quality. Another advantage of these
systems compared to traditional open cement tanks is that they are safer regarding
```
contamination issues (microbial, insect, etc.).
```
The raisin finishing side-stream extraction duration is about 1–2 days, until an
```
extract of 16°Be density (Baume hydrometer density) is obtained. At the end of the
```
```
extraction, the currants may be pressed to receive all the contained must (especially
```
```
those extracted in an open tank). The higher the content of skins, stems, and stalks of
```
the raisin finishing side-stream, the better the separation of the extract. Spontaneous
alcoholic fermentation takes place during the extraction, and a wine with more than
10% v/v alcohol is produced. Pure yeast culture can be used as starter, but it is gener-
ally avoided for cost reasons. The solid residues of the extraction are used as animal
```
feed. The produced wine is transferred to the wine tank (Figure 6.6) where it can
```
remain for 1–2 months until it is used for vinegar fermentation. In this specific pro-
cess, the wine is diluted with water before the acetous fermentation, up to a maximum
strength of 10–10.5% alcohol, so as not to inhibit the action of acetic acid bacteria.
6.6.2 dual stage aCetifiCation
For a production capacity of about 5 tn/day, the acetification process includes two
```
acetators (8 tn capacity each) connected in series, which are charged with wine from
```
```
the wine tank (Figure 6.6). The acetification is carried out at a strict temperature
```
```
range of 28–30°C. Outside this range (e.g., due to a technical problem), the fermen-
```
tation ceases and the viability of the specific oxidation cycle is seriously compro-
mised. Specifically, during fermentation, the temperature is maintained constant at
29–30°C. A drop to 28°C is an indication that the fermentation is completed. If the
temperature reaches the strictly marginal point of 30.8°C, then cooling water must
be immediately circulated. If the temperature is kept at this level for more than
20 sec, it is very possible that the whole batch will be destroyed.
In this system, each acetator produces about 4% acetic acid per day. When the
first acetator produces vinegar with ~8% acidity, 2/3 of the fermented liquid is dis-
charged and transferred to the second acetator to complete the fermentation, yield-
ing a final 10% acidity. The 1/3 of the liquid that remains in the first acetator acts as
starter for the next acetous fermentation cycle.
For this acetification process, the required air flow is ~3–4 m 3 of air per m 3 of
wine per hour. Lower oxygen flow leads to fermentation losses. More oxygen can
lead to cease of fermentation and conversion of the acetic acid into CO 2 and water.
An oxidation cycle duration is about 10 days. If for technical reasons the normal
```
course of fermentation is disturbed (e.g., problematic control of temperature and oxy-
```
```
gen), the specific production cycle is canceled, and the factory production is delayed
```
for about 10 days. If the produced vinegar has an acid strength lower than 10%, it
must be stabilized by SO2 addition.
6.6.3 post fermentation treatments
The vinegar produced from the raisin finishing side-stream is diluted with water to
```
at least 6% acid strength before bottling (or at least 4.5% for wholesale distribution).
```
113Current Industrial Vinegar Production
```
The final product is stabilized by addition of SO2 at about 40 mg/L (and not higher
```
```
than 170 mg/L), as indicted by the Greek Codex Alimentarius. Oxidation of excess
```
SO2 is done, if needed, by addition of food grade hydrogen peroxide.
The vinegar is clarified by passing through one or two diatomaceous earth fil-
ters. It may also require paper or cross-flow membrane filtration before bottling. To
produce white vinegar decolorization, activated carbon is used. The vinegar must
be kept at a constant low temperature during all finishing treatments and is also
```
pasteurized before bottling (e.g., at 65°C for 3 min). Finally, the vinegar is usually
```
analyzed before entering the market for acidity, solid residue, SO 2 content, and spe-
```
cific metal concentrations (Fe, Cu).
```

7
Advances in Immobilized
Biocatalyst Technologies
for Vinegar Production
Argyro Bekatorou
7.1 INTRODUCTION
Numerous cell immobilization techniques have been proposed for food production,
especially for wine, beer, cider, vinegar, distillates and ethanol production. These
techniques involve a variety of materials that serve as cell immobilization carri-
```
ers in a variety of processes and bioreactor configurations (Bekatorou et al., 2015;
```
```
Dervakos and Webb, 1991; Gotovtsev et al., 2015; Kosseva, 2011; Kourkoutas et al.,
```
```
2004). Cell immobilization is defined as the “physical confinement or localization of
```
intact cells to a certain region of space with preservation of some desired catalytic
```
activity” (Karel et al., 1985). Immobilized cell processes, in contrast to submerged
```
```
processes (with suspended, “free” cells) imitate the natural habitats of microbes,
```
where they are usually found attached on various surfaces. Such processes offer
numerous advantages and opportunities for industrial development compared to
```
conventional submerged, free cell systems, such as: (1) higher cell densities in the
```
```
bioreactors, leading to (2) higher productivities and shorter process times, (3) protec-
```
```
tion of cell integrity and viability (e.g., against stresses related to pH, temperature,
```
```
substrate concentration, toxic products, shearing forces, etc.), (3) ability to apply con-
```
```
tinuous processing, facilitating (4) easy product recovery and (5) reusability of the
```
