118 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
biocatalyst, (6) reduction of maturation times, (7) reduction of production costs, etc.
```
```
(Bekatorou et al., 2015).
```
Solid materials that have been used as carriers for cell immobilization in food
production, include:
```
(i) Organic materials, such as synthetic polymers, cellulose and chemically
```
```
modified celluloses (e.g., DEAE-cellulose) and other polymeric carbohy-
```
```
drates and proteins, natural sponges, agri-industrial residues (wood/saw-
```
```
dust, parts of fruit, cereal bran, etc.) and others
```
```
(ii) Inorganic materials, such as naturally occurring minerals and rocks
```
```
(polygorskite, montmorilonite, pumice stone, alumina, etc.), porous porce-
```
lain, porous glass and others
Some of these materials may also be chemically treated to improve their cell or
enzyme binding properties. These materials can be used in food production if they
present good stability against shearing forces, have proper surface area and poros-
ity characteristics and are easy to handle. Moreover, the immobilization technique
should be simple, inexpensive and suitable for scale-up. Finally, one of the most
important prerequisites for application of a cell immobilization technique is that it
should not degrade the quality of the final product. In fact, many published works
reported that cell immobilization improves both the nutritional and sensory prop-
```
erties of the products (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Kourkoutas et al., 2004). However,
```
industrial application of immobilized cells faces limitations related to the proper
design of scale-up processes, difficulty of handling, required training of personnel,
contamination issues and above all, the level of inclination of the industrial producer
towards innovation.
The available scientific literature on viable cell immobilization technologies, for
food production, which is associated mainly with alcoholic beverages, ethanol for
food, pharmaceutical and fuel uses, and controlled release applications, is extensive
```
and constantly increasing (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Kourkoutas et al., 2004; Mishra,
```
```
2015). In this chapter, a presentation of the main features and advantages of cell
```
immobilization technologies, and scientific data available on the development of
such processes for vinegar production, are highlighted and discussed.
7.2 WHOLE CELL IMMOBILIZATION TECHNIQUES
Whole cell immobilization techniques may be grouped into the following four major
```
categories (Figure 7.1) (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Gotovtsev et al., 2015; Kourkoutas et
```
```
al., 2004; Mishra, 2015):
```
```
(a) Cell immobilization on a solid carrier: the cell is attached by covalent bond-
```
ing between the cell and a solid carrier surface, or is entrapped into cavities
of the carrier surface, and/or retained by physical adsorption, electrostatic
```
forces and other weaker forces (Bekatorou et al., 2015) (Figure 7.1a). In this
```
type of immobilization, the cells may grow and escape, and free cells in
suspension may also be present in the fermenting medium. This technique
119Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
has been extensively used due to its simplicity and low cost. It can be easily
carried out by suspending the carrier particles and the cells into a nutrient
medium and allowing the cells to grow at a suitable temperature, with or
```
without agitation (Bekatorou et al., 2015; De Ory et al., 2004; Kourkoutas
```
```
et al., 2004; Koutinas et al., 2012).
```
```
(b) Immobilization in a porous matrix: the cells are either allowed to pene-
```
trate a porous matrix until their mobility is obstructed by other cells, or
the porous matrix is solidified in situ into a cell suspension thus entrapping
```
the cells (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Mishra, 2015) (Figure 7.1b). The nature
```
of the porous matrix must be such as to allow effective diffusion of both
substrates and products. This type of cell immobilization is the most popu-
lar for lab-scale research, with main advantages the simplicity, compatibil-
```
ity with living cells and the controlled cell densities in the bioreactors (as
```
compared with cell immobilization on a solid carrier by natural entrap-
```
ment). However, this technique is less suitable for large-scale application.
```
The most commonly used immobilization matrices are polymeric mate-
```
rials such as natural polysaccharide hydrogels (alginates, k-carrageenan,
```
```
agar, pectins, etc.), cellulose, chitosan, gelatin, collagen, as well as synthetic
```
```
polymers (polyacrylamide, polyvinyl alcohol, etc.) (Bekatorou et al., 2015;
```
```
Mishra, 2015).
```
```
(c) Carrier-free immobilization: the cells can be attached to each other by nat-
```
```
ural flocculation, forming large aggregates (self-aggregation), or by artifi-
```
```
cial cross-linking (Figure 7.1c) (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Mishra, 2015; Zhao
```
```
and Bai, 2009). In both cases, the aggregates can be used in both batch and
```
FIGURE 7.1 Schematic representation of the generic types of whole-cell immobilization.
120 Advances in Vinegar Production
continuous processes. Natural flocculation is a simple and cost-effective
technique, with main drawbacks the risk of cell leakage and the difficulty
to control, which is essential for process optimization. On the other hand,
artificial cross-linking can enhance shelf-aggregation or can help aggre-
gate cells that do not naturally flocculate. The yeast flocculation mecha-
nisms and their importance for the fermentation industry have been widely
```
reviewed (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Jin and Speers, 1998; Kourkoutas et al.,
```
```
2004; Mishra, 2015; Pilkington et al., 1998; Zhao and Bai, 2009).
```
Another type of carrier-free immobilization technique, which is also
simple and inexpensive, is bioencapsulation, where the immobilization
```
matrix comprises of one of the species to be co-immobilized (e.g., a fila-
```
```
mentous fungus) (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Garcia-Martinez et al., 2015).
```
```
(d) Containment behind barriers: the cells are restricted (and may grow)
```
```
behind a barrier, such as a semipermeable membrane (Figure 7.1b), or are
```
entrapped into a microcapsule, or on the interaction surface of two immis-
cible liquids. The major disadvantages of these techniques are mass transfer
limitations and membrane plugging and/or rupture due to excessive cell
```
growth (Bekatorou et al., 2015). Microencapsulation in polymeric micro-
```
```
spheres (1–1,000 μm) is one of the most important containment-behind-a-
```
barrier techniques, with many applications in biotechnological processes
```
and food production (e.g., immobilized biocatalysts for fermentation pro-
```
```
cesses, protective delivery of probiotics, bioremediation processes, etc.),
```
allowing better mass transfer, easier separation of the cells from the prod-
```
ucts and less cell leakage (Mishra, 2015; Rathore et al., 2013).
```
7.3 EFFECT OF IMMOBILIZATION ON CELL
PHYSIOLOGY AND METABOLIC ACTIVITY
Various effects on cell physiology and metabolic activity have been attributed to
cell immobilization. These effects, which in most cases are desirable and respon-
```
sible for the advantages of immobilized over free cell systems, include: (1) acti-
```
```
vated energetic metabolism, (2) altered growth rates, (3) altered intracellular pH
```
```
values, (4) increased substrate uptake and fermentation products and by-products
```
```
(e.g., flavor formation), (5) increased tolerance against inhibitors (ethanol, acids,
```
```
solvents, etc.) and process conditions (pH, temperature, shearing forces, drying/
```
```
freeze-drying), etc. These effects may result from variations in protein expres-
```
sion, storage polysaccharides, nucleic acid contents, etc., caused by mass transfer
limitations, surface tension, osmotic pressure, water activity, changes in cell mor-
phology and membrane permeability and other changes as have been previously
```
discussed and reviewed (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Junter et al., 2002; Junter and
```
```
Jouenne, 2004, 2011).
```
One of the most important effects of cell immobilization in food production is
the improvement of the flavor of fermented foods. A considerable fraction of aroma-
related compounds in fermented foods is produced during the primary fermenta-
```
tion (congeners). In the case of fermented beverages, these compounds are mainly
```
acetate esters of higher alcohols, ethyl esters of fatty acids and other esters with very
121Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
low odor threshold values and pleasant fruity/flowery aromas. Higher alcohols, fatty
acids, carbonyl compounds and sulfur compounds are also produced during fermen-
```
tation (Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2008; Mallouchos and Bekatorou, 2008).
```
```
Esters are either by-products of yeast lipid metabolism (alcoholysis of acyl-CoA
```
```
compounds) or produced by slow esterification reactions between alcohols and acids
```
```
during ageing (Figure 7.2). Important esters in fermented beverages such as wine
```
```
are ethyl acetate (fruity below 150 mg/L), isoamyl acetate (banana), benzyl acetate
```
```
(apple) and ethyl hexanoate (apple, aniseed), ethyl octanoate (fruity, fat) and ethyl
```
```
decanoate (brandy-like) (Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2014).
```
Higher alcohols are produced by yeasts during alcoholic fermentation by deami-
nation, and subsequent decarboxylation and reduction reactions, of the correspond-
```
ing amino acids (Figure 7.2). Alcohols mainly contribute to the aroma complexity
```
```
when present at relatively low concentrations (below 400 mg/L), otherwise they are
```
```
considered off-flavors (pungent) and may musk the flavors of other aroma volatiles
```
```
(Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2014).
```
```
Aldehydes and ketones may be found as by-products of (1) fermentation
```
```
(e.g., acetaldehyde by alcoholic fermentation and by incomplete acetous fermenta-
```
```
tion), (2) processing (e.g., 2-furfural and 5-methylfurfural by Maillard reactions), and
```
```
(3) ageing (e.g., cinnamaldehyde and vanillin extracted from the maturation vessels),
```
```
or (4) derive from the raw material (e.g., β-damascenone, α-ionone, etc.) (Bekatorou,
```
```
2016; Giordano et al., 2003; Jackson, 2014). Among carbonyl compounds, diacetyl
```
```
(2,3-butanedione) is a key aroma compound with a significant impact mainly on
```
```
beer flavor (buttery, nutty or toasty flavors) Diacetyl has a very low threshold value
```
```
(~1 mg/L), and may be undesirable for some products such as lager beers, which
```
```
must be matured at very low temperatures (~0°C) for diacetyl reduction into acet-
```
oin, an energy and space demanding process commonly known as “diacetyl rest”
```
(Figure 7.2).
```
FIGURE 7.2 Production of aroma-related volatile compounds during alcoholic fermentation.
122 Advances in Vinegar Production
Acidity is usually classified as volatile and fixed. The volatile acidity is expressed
as acetic acid concentration, since it is the major volatile acid found in fermented
```
beverages such as wine and vinegar. Other carboxylic acids may also be present (for-
```
```
mic, butyric, propionic and longer chain fatty acids). These minor acids have specific
```
odors but are usually found at detectable levels only as a result of microbial spoilage
```
(Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2014).
```
Finally, organic sulfur compounds found in fermented beverages include amino
```
acids (cysteine, methionine), peptides (glutathione), vitamins (thiamine, biotin), thi-
```
ols, etc., which may derive from both the raw material and the metabolic activity of
the fermentation microflora. They may also derive from non-enzymatic reactions
during fermentation and ageing. Inorganic sulfites are also found in wine and vin-
egar due to the deliberate addition of SO 2 , which is the most commonly used pre-
servative and antioxidant additive. Volatile sulfur-containing compounds, although
usually found in trace amounts, have a high sensory significance due to their very
```
low threshold values and usually undesirable odors (Bekatorou, 2016; Jackson, 2014).
```
During alcoholic fermentation, the formation of congeners is not only raw mate-
rial- and yeast-dependent, but it is also affected by temperature and pH as well as
by the application of immobilization techniques. Specifically, many published stud-
ies have pointed out the effect of cell immobilization on the formation of volatile
compounds, especially when combined with very low fermentation temperatures.
One of the most important observations was the improved ratio of esters-to-higher
alcohols and the reduced diacetyl content after the end of primary fermentation,
which can both lead to products with improved aroma and reduced maturation time
```
(Bekatorou, 2016; Kourkoutas et al., 2004; Mallouchos and Bekatorou, 2008).
```
Vinegar is produced mainly from wine and cider or any other raw material that
has been previously subjected to alcoholic fermentation. Therefore, the aroma of
vinegar is directly affected by the composition of the alcoholic mash. As discussed
in other chapters of this book, the vinegar flavor is a result of the composition of the
alcoholic mash, the compounds produced by acetic acid bacteria during acetifica-
tion, the compounds extracted from the wooden barrels and the chemical transfor-
mations that take place during ageing. Therefore, vinegars produced by traditional,
slow methods, such as the “Orléans” method, are characterized by more complex
aromas. The “generator” methods, although faster than the Orléans method, involve
```
the use of immobilized cells (e.g., on wood shavings) which is also expected to affect
```
the quality of the final products.
```
Wood shavings (chips) have been the most studied carrier for acetic acid bacte-
```
ria immobilization in vinegar production as described and discussed in more detail
below. The addition of wood chips has also been extensively used in oenology to
```
accelerate both wine and vinegar ageing (Cerezo et al., 2014). For this reason, vari-
```
ous studies have dealt with the discrimination of vinegars that have been traditionally
```
aged in barrels or using wood shavings. For example, Cerezo et al. (2014) evaluated
```
```
the effects of the addition of shavings from different wood species (acacia, cherry,
```
```
chestnut and oak), toasted and non-toasted, on the release of phenolic compounds
```
during vinegar ageing. They found that the wood markers naringenin and kaemp-
```
ferol (cherry), robinetin and fustin (acacia), and isovanillin (oak) were identified in
```
the vinegars, while toasting of the wood shavings decreased the concentration of
123Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
most flavonoid markers. These observations were considered useful for discriminat-
ing vinegars regarding the ageing method applied, as well as the wood species of the
shavings used to accelerate ageing. In a similar manner, the possibility to discrimi-
```
nate vinegars subjected to different ageing techniques (traditional or accelerated)
```
```
was evaluated by Morales et al. (2006), using sensory analysis.
```
```
Following, recent advances in the use of immobilized biocatalysts (cells and
```
```
enzymes) for wine and cider making (the most widely used raw materials for vinegar
```
```
production), as well as for the efficient production of good quality vinegars, are pre-
```
sented and discussed.
7.4 WINE AND CIDER PRODUCTION BY
IMMOBILIZED BIOCATALYSTS
7.4.1 Wine making using immoBilized Cells
```
The available literature on wine making by immobilized cells is extensive; however
```
industrial applications are still limited due to the drawbacks mentioned above, as
well as due to consumer suspicion regarding innovative interventions in strongly tra-
ditional, timeless production methods. The objectives of studying the use of immo-
```
bilized cells in wine making, and alcoholic beverages in general, are: (1) to improve
```
```
fermentation productivities and yields, (2) to reduce the time needed for product
```
```
maturation, (3) to reduce the production cost and installation size, (4) to improve
```
```
flavor, (5) to facilitate extremely low-temperature fermentation (0–10°C), and
```
```
(6) to increase the alcohol tolerance of the yeast (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Kourkoutas
```
```
et al., 2004). Moreover, immobilized cells can (7) facilitate continuous processing
```
```
(Genisheva et al., 2014), (8) allow repeated use of the biocatalyst in batch processing
```
```
for cost reduction as well as for culture adaptation purposes (Bekatorou et al., 2015;
```
```
Garcia-Martinez et al., 2015), (9) facilitate simultaneous alcoholic and malolactic
```
```
fermentation (Servetas et al., 2013; Simo et al., 2017), (10) produce sparkling wines
```
```
by the “Champenoise” method (Milicevic et al., 2017), (11) reduce the ethanol con-
```
```
tent in wine using selected immobilized non-saccharomyces yeasts (Canonico et al.,
```
```
2016) and (12) produce novel products with distinctive characteristics (Bekatorou
```
```
et al., 2015).
```
A variety of materials and techniques have been proposed for yeast, bacteria and
enzymes immobilization for wine making applications, including organic, inorganic,
natural or synthesized carriers, with or without chemical modifications to optimize
their performance. Inorganic materials that have been used as immobilization carri-
ers in wine making include kissiris, montmorilonite, polygorskite and other minerals
```
and clay materials, γ-alumina, porcelain, porous glass, etc. (Bekatorou et al., 2015;
```
```
Kourkoutas et al., 2004). Despite their advantages in process rates and yields, the
```
use of such materials is limited by the potential transfer of undesirable residues in
```
the final product (e.g., Al in the case of γ-alumina or kissiris), unless the product is
```
destined for distillates production, since these residues are not volatile and do not
```
distil (Loukatos et al., 2000).
```
On the other hand, natural, food grade materials have been found to be very
advantageous as cell immobilization carriers in wine making and brewing processes.
124 Advances in Vinegar Production
Such carriers can be prepared from wood and other types of cellulosic biomasses,
chitin, chitosan and other natural polysaccharides, gluten and other proteins, k-car-
rageenan, alginates, starch and other hydrogels, fruit pieces, cork, grape seeds, skins
and stems, corn cobs, cereal grains, brewer’s spent grains and other solid waste mate-
```
rials (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Benucci et al., 2016; Bleve et al., 2016; Hettiarachchy
```
```
et al., 2018; Kourkoutas et al., 2004; López de Lerma et al., 2018). The immobilized
```
biocatalysts based on these materials are cheap, easy to prepare and easy to handle
and can be easily accepted by consumers.
Viable, dried immobilized biocatalysts based on these carriers have also been
studied to produce light-weight, easy to store, preserve and commercialize products
```
for wine making and brewing applications (Bekatorou et al., 2015; Kandylis et al.,
```
```
2014; Kourkoutas et al., 2004; Tsaousi et al., 2011).
```
7.4.2 Wine making using immoBilized enzymes
Although the bulk of the literature on immobilization techniques refers to whole,
viable cells immobilization, the most recent research publications propose innova-
tions in wine making based on the use of immobilized enzymes. Generally, the
```
use of immobilized enzymes for a wide range of processes (chemicals, food pro-
```
duction, medicine, biofuels, wastewater treatment, textiles, advanced biosensors,
```
etc.) has been recently reviewed and discussed. In these studies, the widespread
```
use of immobilized enzyme biocatalysts over free-enzyme systems is attributed
to advantages such as ease-of-use, better control of the reaction process, enzyme-
free final products, lower cost, environment friendly processing and the ability to
develop stable commercial enzymes, novel microporous or nanostructured carriers
```
and novel techniques (Ferner et al., 2018; Franssen et al., 2013; Hettiarachchy et al.,
```
```
2018; Sirisha et al., 2016).
```
As in the case of whole cell immobilization, “immobilized enzymes are physically
confined or localized enzymes that retain their catalytic activity and can be used for
```
repeated and continuous processing” (Franssen et al., 2013). The enzyme immo-
```
```
bilization techniques can be classified into the following categories: (1) binding to
```
a solid support by adsorption due to hydrogen bonds, ionic binding or other forces
```
(e.g., hydrophobic interactions), (2) covalent bonding on suitable carrier groups (e.g.,
```
```
epoxy groups), (3) cross-linking (e.g., using bifunctional reagents such as glutaralde-
```
```
hyde) and (4) entrapment in hydrogels (e.g., alginates), membranes (e.g., hollow fiber
```
```
reactors), microemulsions, etc. (Franssen et al., 2013).
```
Some of the techniques for enzyme immobilization that have been used in oenol-
ogy research for production or treatment purposes are illustrated in Figure 7.3.
For example, immobilized enzymes have been used to release significant aroma
compounds, such as terpenes, in wines. Terpenes are usually bound in conjugates with
various sugars that constitute a significant source of aroma precursors. To break up
the sugar linkages of these conjugates and release the terpenes, various enzymes have
```
been tested such as β-glucosidases, α-arabinosidases and α-rhamnosidases (Ferner
```
```
et al., 2018). More specifically, a simple and cost-effective technique for immobili-
```
```
zation of multiple Aspergillus niger glycosidase activities (β-d-glucopyranosidase,
```
```
α-l-arabinofuranosidase, α-l-rhamnopyranosidase, β-d-xylopyranosidase) on magnetic
```
125Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
```
beads was developed by Ferner et al. (2018), for the treatment of a model wine prepara-
```
```
tion (control) and white wine (Figure 7.3a). The results showed that the treatment of
```
white wine with the immobilized glycosidases significantly increased the amount of free
terpenes compared to that of the control wine.
Proteolytic enzymes, covalently immobilized on solid supports, have also
```
been used to reduce the haze potential of white wines (Benucci et al., 2018).
```
Specifically, innovative composite supports based on chitosan and nanoclays
```
(including montmorillonite, sepiolite and bentonite at amounts of 1–5% w/w
```
```
with respect to chitosan) were produced by a solvent casting technique and were
```
```
evaluated as a covalently linked carrier for pineapple stem bromelain (as ref-
```
```
erence enzyme) in a wine-like medium (Figure 7.3b). The results showed dif-
```
ferent interactions with the polymeric matrix and a different enzyme loading
```
(Benucci et al., 2018).
```
```
The co-immobilization of cross-linked β-glycosidase aggregates (Figure 7.3c) for
```
the enzymatic release of aromatic terpenes in Muscat wine was also recently reported
```
(Ahumada et al., 2016). The co-immobilized enzymes presented high stability and
```
good technological potential for the reduction of enzyme cost in wine making.
FIGURE 7.3 Schematic representation of enzyme immobilization techniques that have
been applied in oenology research.
126 Advances in Vinegar Production
In another study, immobilized crude enzymes from Geotrichum species were
used to decrease the higher alcohol content in red wine. The optimum treatment
```
(35 g/L sodium alginate, 20 g/L calcium chloride and 3 mL crude enzyme) sig-
```
nificantly increased the ester content and the overall sensory quality of the wine
```
(Lu et al., 2017).
```
Lysozyme from hen egg white was also covalently immobilized on spherical
microbial chitosan supports to develop a system for continuous enzymatic lysis of
```
lactic acid bacteria (Oenococcus oeni) in white and red wines (Cappannella et al.,
```
```
2016). The objective was to limit the SO2 required to control malolactic fermenta-
```
tion. The immobilization technique was optimized in batch process with respect
to the enzyme loading, specific activity and kinetics in a model wine sample and
subsequently in a fluidized-bed bioreactor at the optimum conditions. The lysozyme
was more effective in immobilized form when the system was applied to real wine
treatment, suggesting that covalent immobilization increases the enzyme tolerance
```
to the wine flavans inhibition (Cappannella et al., 2016).
```
Pectinase extracted from A. niger was immobilized on a chitosan-coated chitin sup-
```
port using various techniques (immobilization by adsorption, adsorption on glutaral-
```
```
dehyde-activated supports and covalent bonding), for possible use in juice and wine
```
industries. The optimum pH, heat stability, enzyme concentration, and reusability were
determined, and the results showed that the immobilized biocatalysts retained 100% of
```
their original catalytic activity after nine repeated cycles (Ramirez et al., 2016).
```
```
Finally, the treatment of must with encapsulated glucose oxidase (GOX) in
```
Ca-alginate hollow beads was suggested as a biotechnological alternative to the
```
production of reduced-alcohol wines (Ruiz et al., 2018), to overcome the inhibi-
```
tive effect of low pH on the enzyme activity. An immobilization yield of 73% was
obtained with 22 g/L Na-alginate, 20 g/L carboxymethylcellulose and 12 g/L CaCl 2
```
(Figure 7.3d). The encapsulated enzyme maintained about 92% of the initial activ-
```
ity at pH 4.0. Moreover, the GOX beads could be reused for seven repeated cycles
in model must. The retention of activity at the acidic must pH makes the immobi-
lized biocatalyst promising for industrial use in the production of low-alcohol wines
```
(Ruiz et al., 2018).
```
The above, and many such other innovations, can also be applied to vinegar pro-
duction or may have an impact on vinegar quality, as they aim at improving the qual-
ity of wines and other raw materials that can be used for vinegar production.
7.4.3 Cider making using immoBilized BioCatalysts
Apple cider is another major substrate used for vinegar production. Cider production
is a complex process consisting of an alcoholic fermentation step by yeasts, followed
by malolactic fermentation by lactic acid bacteria. Traditional cider is produced by
natural fermentation of apple juice by wild microflora, leading to an unstable prod-
uct of variable quality. Information on cider making around the world, the general
production approaches, microbiology, commercial production, control of pathogenic
and spoilage microorganisms and biochemical transformations during fermentation
```
and ageing can be found in a recent review by Jarvis (2014) and is also discussed in
```
more detail in Chapters 5 and 12.
127Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
The use of immobilization techniques in cider making aims at increasing the
process efficiency, reducing the maturation time and improving the product quality
and stability. The impact of immobilized cell technologies on alcoholic beverages,
```
including cider production, has been recently reviewed by Nedovic et al. (2015),
```
focusing on carrier materials, immobilization methods, bioreactor design, operation
and scale-up potential, as well as on the effect on aroma.
Recent research efforts on immobilized cell biocatalysts for cider making include
```
the use of co-immobilized species (for example co-immobilized Saccharomyces
```
```
bayanus and Leuconostoc oenos, or mixed kefir microflora) for simultaneous alco-
```
```
holic and malolactic fermentation, in various bioreactor configurations (Bleve et al.,
```
```
2016; Nikolaou et al., 2017; Zhang and Lovitt, 2006). These systems offer many
```
```
advantages over conventional free cell systems that include: (1) elimination of non-
```
```
productive cell growth phases, (2) feasibility of continuous processing and (3) reus-
```
```
ability of the biocatalyst (Bleve et al., 2016). Although most efforts were efficient,
```
further research is needed for industrial application of immobilized cells in cider
making, as in the case of wine and other fermented products.
7.5 VINEGAR PRODUCTION USING IMMOBILIZED BIOCATALYSTS
As concluded in other chapters of this book, the current trend in vinegar research is
to fuse traditional techniques with state-of-the-art technologies, in order to increase
vinegar fermentation efficiency, to completely and efficiently utilize the available
raw materials, to reduce the production and installation costs and to reduce the fer-
mentation and ageing times, without negatively affecting the quality of the final
```
product (which in most cases is improved).
```
The proposed methods should and do focus on ensuring controlled process condi-
tions and mainly include the use of carefully selected starters and the design of novel
```
acetification systems (e.g., systems with recycling of the substrates during fermenta-
```
tion, application of successive batch fermentations, semi-continuous and continuous
```
processing and the use of immobilized cell or enzyme biocatalysts). Engineering
```
advances also include the design of scale-up acetators with improved oxygen dif-
```
fusion systems. Following, the recent research advances (compared to some ear-
```
```
lier efforts) on immobilization techniques, carriers and microorganisms for vinegar
```
```
production (alcoholic fermentation, acetification and ageing) are highlighted and
```
discussed.
7.5.1 Vinegar produCtion using immoBilized Cells
Most of the earlier research efforts to produce vinegar by immobilized cells for appli-
cation in the modern vinegar industry mainly studied the use of Acetobacter species
entrapped in Ca-alginate gels. However, the practical application of hydrogels as cell
```
immobilization matrices faces a few challenges such as (1) diffusion limitations for
```
```
oxygen, substrates and products, (2) low stability (e.g., disruption due to shearing
```
forces such as high hydrostatic pressures in large-scale reactors or due to substances
```
with high affinity for Ca 2+ such as phosphates or citrates, etc.), (3) high porosity that
```
```
can lead to leakage of nutrients, etc. (Mishra, 2015; Smidsrod and Skjak-Braek, 1990).
```
128 Advances in Vinegar Production
To avoid leakage of cells and nutrients, or to allow immobilization of more than one
microbial species, double-layered beads and composites of alginate gels with other
materials have also been developed for beverage fermentations.
```
For example, Fumi et al. (1992) were among the first who studied the immobiliza-
```
tion technique factors that affect the oxygen uptake, cell growth and viability and
the release of immobilized Acetobacter cells from the carrier. These factors included
the alginate concentration, the use of double alginate gel layers, the particle size, the
cell density in the gel and the time of gel incubation in the CaCl 2 solution. The study
```
concluded that (1) the maximum oxygen uptake rate and cell leakage were affected
```
```
by the alginate and cell concentrations in the gel, (2) the extended contact with CaCl 2
```
```
reduced the number of viable cells, while (3) the use of double alginate gel layers had
```
no influence on cell viability or on the maximum oxygen uptake rate and prevented
```
cell leakage (Fumi et al., 1992).
```
The addition of α-alumina to the aqueous solution of Na-alginate leads to the
production of denser beads that allow better oxygen transfer and increased acetic
```
acid production rates. This property was exploited by Dabdoub Paz et al. (1993) for
```
the immobilization of viable Acetobacter cells isolated from an ethanol plant. The
prepared biocatalyst was used in the continuous oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid
in a circulating three-phase fluidized-bed bioreactor. In a similar manner, De Araujo
```
and Santana (1996) studied the continuous oxidation of ethanol in a fluidized-bed
```
```
reactor with immobilized Acetobacter (as a model system of aerobic cells), to evalu-
```
ate the effect of gel particle density on the acetous fermentation. Particles of vari-
able density were prepared by adding different amounts of α-alumina to the gel
matrix. Specifically, the particles were composed of a denser core of α-alumina and
Na-alginate, coated with a thinner layer of Na-alginate with entrapped cells.
Acetobacter aceti cells, entrapped in Ca-alginate gel or adsorbed on pre-formed
cellulose beads, presented no significant alterations in cell numbers under chang-
ing temperature or pH conditions, whereas the acetic acid production was slightly
```
increased by immobilization compared to free cells (Krisch, 1996). On the other
```
hand, the immobilization matrix at higher temperatures caused a diffusion bar-
rier decreasing the oxygen supply and reducing the conversion of ethanol. In a
```
subsequent study by Krisch and Szajáni (1997), Saccharomyces cerevisiae and A.
```
aceti cells were also entrapped in Ca-alginate beads or adsorbed on pre-formed
cellulose beads and were treated with 0–20% v/v ethanol and 0–10% v/v acetic
acid to evaluate the ethanol and acetic acid tolerance of the entrapped, adsorbed
and free cells. Their results showed that 20% v/v ethanol was lethal for free yeast
cells, while 62–72% of the entrapped cells survived. Also, at 10% v/v acetic acid,
both free and adsorbed A. aceti cells could not grow, but 69% of the adsorbed cells
survived. Therefore, they concluded that gel entrapment compared to adsorption
can be more favorable against the toxic effects of substrates and products during
the vinegar fermentations.
```
Dias et al. (2016) proposed the production of jabuticaba (Myrciaria jaboticaba)
```
vinegar using A. aceti and Gluconobacter oxydans cells immobilized in Ca-alginate,
as a novel method to exploit the fruit surplus. Their method included extraction of the
jabuticaba must by mechanical pressing of the fruit pulp, adjustment of the soluble
```
solids to 16°Brix by addition of sucrose, addition of dipotassium disulfite (0.1 g/L) as
```
129Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
preservative/antioxidant and treatment with 1 g/L bentonite for removal on nonfer-
mentable solids. Alcoholic fermentation by a S. cerevisiae strain resulted in jabuti-
caba wine with about 9.5% v/v ethanol content at about 14 days. Acetification by the
immobilized mixed culture resulted in an acetic acid yield of 74.4% with 0.29 g/Lh
productivity. The produced vinegar had a suitable taste and flavor, and the whole
process was evaluated as an added-value, viable technology for the exploitation of
the harvest surplus of jabuticaba fruit.
Wood shavings are another widely studied cell immobilization carrier for vinegar
```
production. For example, Garg et al. (1995) produced mango vinegar by alcoholic
```
fermentation with S. cerevisiae that was recycled to improve the fermentation rate,
followed by semi-continuous oxidation with A. aceti immobilized on wood shavings.
```
The process resulted in 5.3% acidity (as acetic acid) with 60% conversion efficiency.
```
```
In a similar manner, Kocher et al. (2006) proposed the production of sugarcane vin-
```
egar by fermentation of sugarcane juice by S. cerevisiae to 8% v/v ethanol, followed
by acetification by A. aceti adsorbed on bagasse, corn cobs and wood shavings, or
```
entrapped in Ca-alginate (Figure 7.4). The performance of all three adsorbed bio-
```
catalysts was similar, resulting in 5.9–6.7% acidity in about 1 month of submerged
fermentation. By recycling the bagasse adsorbed cells, the time of acetic acid fer-
mentation was reduced to 13 days. The semi-continuous fermentation with cells
adsorbed on bagasse using a packed-bed column further reduced the fermentation
time to 80 h.
```
Subsequently, Kocher and Dhillon (2013) produced vinegar from sugarcane juice
```
```
(17°Brix) by alcoholic fermentation with S. cerevisiae to 9.5% v/v ethanol, followed
```
by semi-continuous acetification using A. aceti cells immobilized on wood shavings
FIGURE 7.4 Schematic representation of Acetobacter adsorption during an initial acetifica-
```
tion batch in the presence of a solid porous carrier (based on De Ory et al., 2004).
```
130 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
(2:1 cell-to-adsorbent ratio) in a packed column reactor (Figure 7.5). The sugarcane
```
```
ethanol (containing mother vinegar) with an initial acidity of 2% w/v was supplied to
```
the reactor at 50 mL/h, at the 2.5 L scale, producing vinegar of about 4.1–6.8% w/v
```
volatile acidity, in 3 days (compared to the 13 days of the batch process; Kocher et
```
```
al., 2006). The production was consistent for over 25 cycles, with a fermentation
```
efficiency of about 53–88% and an acetification rate of 5.8–2.8 g/Ld. The produced
vinegar had a good quality in terms of body and flavor, and thus the method was
proposed as economical, efficient and environmentally friendly for potential indus-
trial use.
```
De Ory et al. (2004) developed a complete experimental design to study the
```
properties of three different solid carriers for the immobilization of acetic acid
```
bacteria: Siran (commercial sintered glass; 1–2 mm spheres; 60% porosity;
```
```
10–300 μm pore size), wood (15 × 1 mm chips; 96.7% porosity; 15 μm pore size)
```
```
and polyurethane foam (1 cm cubes; 97% porosity; 400 μm pore size). The immo-
```
bilization was carried out during an initial acetification batch in the presence of the
```
carrier (Figure 7.6). The immobilized cells were then used for consecutive semi-
```
continuous fermentation cycles in order to evaluate their acetification properties.
Polyurethane foam was found to be the most successful carrier because it allowed
```
a large number of immobilized cells (~10.5 × 10 6 /mg) in a short time (300 h) and
```
```
resulted in the highest acetification productivity (4.74 g/Ld). These outcomes,
```
combined with the inert nature of the carrier and its low cost, made the proposed
```
process potentially suitable for industrial application (De Ory et al., 2004).
```
```
Kaur et al. (2011) reported the production of tea vinegar by batch and semi-
```
continuous fermentation using immobilized cells on sugarcane bagasse, in order
FIGURE 7.5 Flow diagram of sugarcane vinegar production using immobilized A. aceti
```
(based on Kocher et al., 2006).
```
131Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
to produce a product that combines the beneficial properties of both tea and vin-
egar. The duration of the batch process was 4–5 weeks, but less time was required
when a semi-continuous or continuous process with immobilized cells was applied.
Specifically, alcoholic fermentation of 1.0 and 1.5% tea infusions using S. cerevi-
sae was carried out, followed by batch acetification with A. aceti yielding 4.5 and
4.7% volatile acidity, respectively, in 24 days. The semi-continuous fermentation
```
with immobilized A. aceti produced 4.4% volatile acidity from 1.5% tea wine (8.9%
```
```
ethanol; 1.0% acidity), in nine flow cycles (4 h each) at 50 mL/h flow rate.
```
```
Jiang et al. (2015) screened various carriers (bagasse, wood shavings, corn cob,
```
```
peanut shells, rice husk) for the immobilization of acetic acid bacteria to optimize
```
the production of blueberry vinegar. Their results showed that after 7 days of labora-
tory-scale fermentation the highest acid content was obtained by cells immobilized
```
on bagasse (6.04% w/v), the fermentation process was more stable, and the products
```
had good sensory properties. Therefore, bagasse was proposed as a suitable immobi-
lized carrier for the fermentation of blueberry vinegar.
```
Kumar and Kocher (2017) used three types of Indian wood shavings, i.e., Melona
```
```
grandis (Mirindi), Tectona grandis (Sagwan) and Castania sativa (Italian teak), to
```
produce immobilized biocatalysts for good quality sugarcane vinegar fermentation.
The immobilization technique involved washing of the shavings with 0.1 N HCl,
autoclaving and drying at 60°C. For the adsorption of bacteria, the shavings were
mixed with an A. aceti culture at a ratio of 1:2, and the mixture was incubated for
24 h under shaking at 28°C. The wood shavings with adsorbed cells were gently
washed with water and were used for the acetification of sugarcane juice, which was
previously fermented by S. cerevisiae to ~9% v/v ethanol. The cell adsorption rates
for the M. grandis, T. grandis and C. sativa shavings were 66.6, 44.4 and 21.4%,
```
respectively. The optimum acetification process (5.0% w/v volatile acidity in 6 days)
```
was obtained by A. aceti immobilized M. grandis shavings of 15 mm size, followed
FIGURE 7.6 Schematic representation of Acetobacter adsorption on wood shavings for sug-
```
arcane vinegar production (based on Kocher et al., 2006).
```
132 Advances in Vinegar Production
by T. grandis and C. sativa. Scale-up of the process produced sugarcane vinegar
with 7.0 and 4.0% w/v acidity in 5 L and 50 L fermenters, respectively, in 6–10 days
```
(Kumar and Kocher, 2017).
```
```
Viana et al. (2017) proposed the production of kefir apple vinegar and evaluated
```
the fermentation process by using a Biospeckle Laser methodology. The vinegar
```
was produced by inoculation of apple must with Brazilian kefir grains (10% w/v;
```
at 28°C under static conditions for alcoholic fermentation and agitated for ace-
```
tous fermentation). The culture contained S. cerevisiae, Lactobacillus paracasei,
```
Lactobacillus plantarum, Acetobacter pasteurianus and Acetobacter syzygii as
identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight mass spec-
```
trometry (MALDI-TOF MS). The kefir grains were able to utilize apple must pro-
```
ducing ethanol, acetic acid, volatile alcohols and aldehydes. The acetic acid yield
```
in the final vinegar product was ∼79% (4.1% w/v). The described technology was
```
```
proposed as a novel application of a mixed immobilized cell culture (species immo-
```
```
bilized in the kefir grains polysaccharide matrix) for one-step vinegar produc-
```
tion, eliminating the need for centrifugation which is required in the conventional
two-step fermentation process.
```
Finally, Leonés et al. (2019) proposed the production of lemon vinegar directly
```
from lemon juice. For the alcoholic fermentation they used two different yeast strains
```
(S. cerevisiae) and two process types (free cells and immobilized cells in alginate).
```
The acetous fermentation variables were optimized for a semi-continuous process.
The best conditions for alcoholic fermentation were obtained when free S. cerevi-
siae var. bayanus cells were used. With regards to acetic fermentation, the use of an
unloading volume of 33.33% of the total volume produced lemon vinegar in 20–24 h
```
with an acidity of 13.3% w/v of vinegar (expressed as acetic acid).
```
Various published studies also report cell immobilization applications in vine-
gar production, for purposes other than to improve the fermentation efficiency or in
other processes that may also have an impact on vinegar technology. For example,
```
Kondo and Ikeda (1999) developed carbon-paste electrodes modified with immobi-
```
```
lized cells of acetic acid bacteria (A. pasteurianus) to measure the current caused by
```
```
the substrate-oxidizing activity of intact cells, with Fe(CN) 63− as electron mediator
```
between the electrode and the cells. The magnitude of the current depended strongly
on the metabolic activity of the immobilized cells, and the electrode had a good
response to acetaldehyde and lactic acid as well as ethanol.
Also, in order to evaluate the performance of cells immobilized in the pores of
macroporous carriers coated with porous membranes, a fixed-bed bioreactor was
used to study the oxidation of D-sorbitol to L-sorbose by Acetobacter suboxydans
```
(Müh et al., 1999). Comparisons were made between immobilized cells in a coated
```
and non-coated carrier, as well as with free cells in suspension. The findings of that
study indicated that the coated carriers could catalyze biotransformations at very
high rates and that oxygen was the key limiting factor. Therefore, oxygen supply and
```
cell confinement (reduced carrier size, increased porosity to 1 ± 30 μm and a thinner
```
```
coating layer with porosity < 0.2 μm) were proposed as issues for further investiga-
```
tion to improve the effective reaction rate.
```
Gandolfi et al. (2004) used an A. aceti stain to oxidize 2-phenyl-1-ethanol to
```
phenylacetic acid in aqueous systems. High oxidation yields were obtained, while
133Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
the use of a two-liquid phase system of water and isooctane allowed the produc-
tion of the corresponding aldehyde. Cells immobilized in Ca-alginate presented
better operational stability, specific activity and substrate tolerance compared to
free cells. Specifically, a fed-batch process with immobilized cells in an air-lift
reactor resulted in the production of 23 g/L phenylacetic acid in 9 days without
foam formation.
Another interesting study was the fabrication of living soft matter as a result of
```
the symbiotic relationship of two unicellular microorganisms (Das et al., 2016).
```
Specifically, the material was composed of bacterial cellulose that was produced in
```
situ by an A. aceti strain in the presence of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (a photosyn-
```
```
thetic microalgae). The microstructure of the produced living material depended on
```
the shape of the growth container and stirring conditions, which affect the oxygen
availability. The photosynthetic C. reinhardtii cells produce oxygen in the bacte-
rial cellulose matrix, which is generated by the Acetobacter. Therefore, such living
materials can be used in immobilized microalgae applications, such as biohydrogen
production, or in other applications that involve commercially important symbiotic
```
microorganisms (Das et al., 2016).
```
```
Finally, Veeravalli and Mathews (2018) proposed the production of acetic acid
```
```
and propylene glycol (PG) from whey lactose and whey powder (containing lactose
```
```
and protein) as an alternative to high cost nutrient media. They used a high cell
```
density fermentation with cotton cheesecloth serving as immobilization matrix for
the acid tolerant Lactobacillus buchneri. The strain was able to ferment lactose to
acetic acid and PG at pH ~ 4.2, each at 25–30 g/L, using lactose as carbon source,
while cell immobilization improved the productivity resulting in 57% conversion of
the whey powder lactose.
```
An integrated vinegar production process (including primary alcoholic fermenta-
```
```
tion, secondary fermentation/maturation and acetification steps) using immobilized
```
cells is depicted in Figure 7.7.

```
production process using immobilized cells (TC: temperature control; HE: heat exchanger;
```

134 Advances in Vinegar Production
7.5.2 Vinegar produCtion using immoBilized enzymes
Regarding the use of immobilized enzymes in vinegar production, only a few pub-
```
lished research studies are available. For example, Wang et al. (2017) used Na-alginate
```
and xanthan gum as carriers to prepare an immobilized esterification enzyme for use
in accelerating the maturation of Shanxi aged vinegar. The results showed that the
enzyme activity could be maintained at about 50% for 9 days, increasing the total
ester of vinegar by more than 28.1%.
Other applications of immobilized enzymes include the development of a flow
injection system for the determination of acetic acid in the 10–60 mM range, based
on coupled reactions of acetate kinase/pyruvate kinase/lactate dehydrogenase
enzymes immobilized in series. Two identical parallel enzyme lines were installed,
one for use and the other for calibration. Analysis of vinegar samples resulted in reli-
able results, more reliable than the reference HPLC method, in the range 0.5–1.5 M
```
after a 40-fold dilution (Becker et al., 1993).
```
```
Also, a carbon nanotube (CNT) gel composed of single-wall CNT mixed with an
```
```
ionic liquid and a thermostable d-proline dehydrogenase (DPDH) immobilized elec-
```
```
trode was used to determine d-amino acids in foods (Tani et al., 2009). The CNT/
```
DPDH electrode presented higher sensitivity and a lower detection limit of d-proline
compared with CNT, Ketjen Black and carbon powder. The CNT/DPDH immo-
bilized electrode was specifically used for the detection of d-amino acids in rice
wine and vinegar samples, showing concentrations of about 0.02 and 0.55 mmol/L,
respectively.
Finally, in a more recent study, an aptamer-based surface plasmon resonance
```
(SPR) biosensor was developed to detect aflatoxins, showing comparable interac-
```
tion with aflatoxin B1 and aflatoxin B2, which can be exploited for the simultane-
```
ous detection of both aflatoxins (Wu et al., 2018). Specifically, in the SPR system,
```
```
streptavidin proteins were immobilized on the surface of a CM5 (carboxymethyl-
```
```
ated dextran covalently attached to a gold surface) sensor chip as a cross-linker,
```
and biotin-aptamers were captured through streptavidin–biotin interaction. The
aptasensor showed high specificity towards aflatoxins B1 and B2 but did not
bind to other similar toxins such as ochratoxins A and B, zeralenone and T-2
```
toxin. Determination recoveries of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) in vinegar ranged from
```
96 to 118%, and the SPR assay was characterized as a simple, fast and sensitive
approach for the detection of aflatoxins in vinegars and agricultural products in
```
general (Wu et al., 2018).
```
7.6 CONCLUSIONS
Τhe plethora of research studies on the development of immobilization techniques
for application in alcoholic beverages production, and to a lesser extent in vinegar
production, is due to the many advantages associated with such techniques. These
advantages include increased fermentation rates and yields, feasibility of continu-
ous processing, ability to recycle the biocatalyst, easier product separation, etc.
The proposed methods in vinegar production mainly include the use of immobi-
lized Acetobacter cells to facilitate the operation of batch, semi-continuous and
135Advances in Immobilized Biocatalyst Technologies
continuous acetification systems. However, industrial application of vinegar fermen-
tations by immobilized cells is limited due to issues related to the design of scale-up
processes, oxygen diffusion, difficulty of handling, lack of trained personnel and
contamination problems.

8.1 VINEGARS PRODUCED BY SOLID-STATE FERMENTATION
8.1.1 Brief introduCtion to solid -state fermentation
Vinegar can be made from any raw material containing fermentable sugars or sub-
```
stances that can be converted into fermentable sugars (Xu et al., 2010; Li et al.,
```
```
2015a). Many characteristic vinegar production technologies have been developed
```

142 Advances in Vinegar Production
according to local history, geography, natural resources and living habits. Vinegar
production is complicated and mainly applies natural fermentation systems, which
highly rely on experience. Due to the adaption of submerged fermentation after
```
the 1940s, solid-state fermentation (SSF) was almost completely abandoned in the
```
```
Western countries (Pandey, 2003), whereas it has been used extensively in Asia and
```
in African countries.
Most of the traditional vinegars in Europe are fruit vinegars produced by sub-
```
merged fermentation (Tesfaye et al., 2002). In Asia on the other hand, SSF sys-
```
```
tems are mainly employed for vinegar production (Xu et al., 2011a). Due to its
```
numerous advantages, such as low energy requirements and capital investment,
```
SSF has also been used in the processing of agri-industrial residues (Pandey,
```
```
2003), especially from abundant, affordable and good quality agricultural crops.
```
```
In China, the traditional Chinese vinegars (TCVs) are mostly produced through
```
SSF. China has the leading role in this production system, which includes the most
famous vinegars and production techniques, like Shanxi aged vinegar, Zhenjiang
aromatic vinegar, Sichuan bran vinegar, Tianjin duliu mature vinegar and others
```
(Liu et al., 2004; Nie et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2018,). Due to the long history, wide-
```
spread and successful application and the special flavor of these products, TCVs
are now famous worldwide.
8.1.2 ssf systems of Vinegar produCtion
Insoluble solid substrates are used in SSF systems, which contain a certain level of
humidity but with little or no free water. Therefore, an SSF system of vinegar pro-
duction is a biological transformation process, which uses the gas phase as the con-
```
tinuous phase (Liu et al., 2004), and the solid substrates not only provide essential
```
nutrients to the microorganisms but also serve as solid supports for the cells.
A natural enrichment SSF system is an enrichment mixing fermentation process
```
involving naturally occurring microorganisms (Lu et al., 2018). Fermentations of
```
traditional vinegar do not require inoculation of microorganisms but depend on the
natural microbial flora of the environment and raw materials. Multiple microorgan-
isms evolve into each niche of the fermentation system, which is the most favorable
to growth, metabolism and symbiotic cooperation.
The technological characteristics of SSF vinegars can be summarized in the fol-
lowing seven points:
```
(1) There’s no flow of free water in the SSF culture media, and the content of
```
```
water in the media is low (Liu et al., 2004). The water activity in the culture
```
media is lower than 0.99, which is beneficial for the growth of microorgan-
isms with dry water activity ranging between 0.93–0.98.
```
(2) The microorganism absorbs nutrients from a wet solid substrate. Due to
```
the gradient of nutrient concentrations, the fermentation, bacterial growth,
nutrient absorption and metabolite secretion are uneven.
```
(3) The contact area between the culture media in SSF and gas phase is larger
```
than the contact area between the submerged fermentation liquid and air
bubbles, and therefore, the oxygen supply is more sufficient.
143Solid-State Fermentation Systems for Vinegar Production
```
(4) Degradation of macromolecule substrates and fermentation occur simulta-
```
```
neously in the solid substrates (Li et al., 2015b). This simplifies the working
```
procedure and saves energy consumption.
```
(5) The product mechanization degree is low, and the process control is rela-
```
tively difficult as a result of the lack of online sensors.
The microbial populations in the SSF systems of vinegars mainly include fungi,
```
yeasts and bacteria, mainly lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and acetic acid bacteria
```
```
(AAB). Among them, fungi mainly secrete multiple enzymes, such as amylases,
```
proteases, lipases, etc. Macromolecules in the raw materials are decomposed by
these enzymes into fermentable sugars, amino acids and other micromolecules, thus
```
providing nutrients and fermentable substrates to microorganisms. Aspergillus (e.g.
```
A. niger), Rhizopus and Mucor are important fungi in vinegar production. Yeasts
mainly transform the fermentable sugars into alcohol and include Saccharomyces,
Zygosaccharomyces, Candida, Hansenula and other species. LAB, which are found
in the SSF systems of vinegars include Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Weissella, etc.
```
AAB include mainly Acetobacter and Gluconacetobacter (Li et al., 2015b; Nie et
```
```
al., 2015).
```
8.2 PROTOCOLS FOR SSF SYSTEMS OF VINEGAR PRODUCTION
8.2.1 key parameters in tHe ssf of Vinegars
Key parameters in the SSF of vinegars mainly include substrate characteristics, water
activity, pH, mass and heat transfer coefficient. These key parameters are introduced
in the following paragraphs.
8.2.1.1 Substrate
Microorganisms grow on substrates and produce metabolites. This metabolism is
```
highly influenced by physical factors (size of the grain substrate, shape, porosity,
```
```
fiber content and diffusion rate among particles) and chemical factors of the sub-
```
```
strate (polymerization and electrochemical properties). However, the grain size and
```
humidity or water activity are the most important parameters for microorganism
growth and activity during SSF.
The grain size of the particles not only influences the reaction surface area directly
but also the bacterial growth, the oxygen supply and the migration of CO 2 among
the substrate particles. Generally, small substrate particles can provide large specific
```
surface area for the microorganism to attack the substrate and accelerate SSF; hence
```
they are viewed as the ideal selection. However, too small particles easily cause sub-
strate agglomeration in many cases, and the pores in the particles may be decreased,
making the substrate recalcitrant to microbial attack. Heat and mass transfer are
also obstructed, and ventilation of the microorganisms is inhibited resulting in poor
growth.
On the other hand, large particles, which have big spaces between them, facilitate
heat transfer and provide better conditions for ventilation. However, they offer small
specific surface area for microorganism attack.
144 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
The following factors determine the substrate utilization by microorganisms: (1)
```
```
the types of microorganisms and their enzymes, (2) the growth state of the microor-
```
```
ganisms and their zymolytic activity, (3) the available area of the substrate for attack,
```
```
(4) the substrate nonuniformity and (5) the inhibition by the final products.
```
8.2.1.2 Water Activity
Since SSF is characteristic of no free water, changes in the water content of the
system may significantly influence the growth and metabolic activity of the microor-
ganisms. The microbial growth on the substrate is therefore determined by the water
```
activity (Aw) of the SSF system.
```
Aw is a physiochemical index that represents the actual free water content acces-
sible to the microorganism. It is defined as the ratio of the water vapor pressure of
```
the substrate (p) to the equilibrium vapor pressure of pure water (p0) under the same
```
temperature and pressure conditions. If the substrate is in equilibrium with air, then
```
the Aw is equal to the equilibrium relative humidity (ERH) of the substrate (i.e., the
```
```
relative humidity of the atmosphere in equilibrium with the substrate):
```
A w = =ppERH
0 100
The Aw required for the proliferous growth of microorganisms generally ranges
between 0.6 and 0.998. The lowest Aw of different types of microorganisms is listed
in Table 8.1. Most microorganisms, except a few fungi, cannot grow in dry condi-
tions when the Aw is lower than 0.60–0.70. A dry environment can inhibit microor-
ganism activity and bring microorganisms into a dormant state and may even cause
cell dehydration and protein denaturation. As a consequence, microorganisms die.
As a typical natural enrichment SSF, the vinegar SSF involves complex micro-
bial populations, including multiple types of bacteria and fungi. Different microor-
ganisms have different requirements on Aw. Therefore, Aw is one of the important
environmental forces to drive microorganism succession during fermentation.
Aw decreases during the fermentation process due to evaporation and temperature
rise. To protect the normal growth of bacteria, Aw is controlled by regulating the
TABLE 8.1
Values of Aw under the Growth of Different Microorganisms
Community Lowest Aw
Bacteria General bacteria 0.98–0.99
```
Halophilic bacteria 0.75 (about 5.5 mol/L NaCl)
```
Yeasts General yeasts 0.87–0.91
Hypertonic yeasts 0.61–0.65
Saccharomyces rouxii 0.6
Molds General molds 0.80–0.87
Drought-resistant molds 0.65–0.75
Xeromyces bisporus 0.6
145Solid-State Fermentation Systems for Vinegar Production
water content, and Aw can be adjusted effectively by ventilation or increasing the air
humidity.
8.2.1.3 Ventilation and Mass Transfer
The vinegar SSF involves two typical processes, namely alcoholic fermentation and
```
acetic acid fermentation (Li et al., 2015b). The alcohol fermentation is an anaerobic
```
process. However, air ventilation is particularly important in the second process.
The surface humidity of the substrate is enough to form a layer of liquid membrane,
```
and it is the control factor of mass transfer. Periodically stirring (turning over the
```
```
media) is necessary and not only can provide oxygen for the microorganism but can
```
also eliminate the generated bioreaction heat and CO 2 , increasing mass transfer. The
```
frequency of stirring is determined by (1) the demands of oxygen for fermentation,
```
```
(2) the amount of heat produced during fermentation and (3) the thickness of the
```
substrate layer, including the porosity of the substrate, the humidity of the substrate
and the shape and size of the fermenter.
8.2.1.4 Temperature
Temperature is an important influencing factor for SSF vinegar. The microorgan-
```
isms require appropriate temperatures for growth and metabolism (the optimum
```
temperature range for fungal growth is 20–30°C, for alcoholic fermentation by yeast
```
is 18–25°C, for growth of AAB is 30–35°C and for LAB is 30–40°C). On the other
```
hand, a lot of heat is also produced during microbial growth and metabolism, and the
bed temperature is increased dramatically due to the poor heat transfer efficiency in
SSF systems. Lethal temperatures for fungi and bacteria are 50–60°C and 60–70°C,
respectively. High temperatures disturb the viability and activity of the microorgan-
ism by influencing the microbial membrane fluidity, the enzyme and protein activity,
as well as the structure and transcription of RNA. If the fermentation heat cannot be
dissipated in time, the temperature may influence the growth and metabolism of the
microorganisms as well as the product yields.
8.2.2 examples of ssf: sHanxi aged Vinegar
Shanxi aged vinegar is one of the representative vinegars made with SSF technol-
```
ogy. The major production procedures are shown in Figure 8.1 (see also Chapter 10,
```
```
Vinegar Production in China).
```
```
(1) Processing of raw materials. Sorghum, that is the main raw material, is
```
ground and then 100 kg are mixed with 50 kg water for more than 12 h so
as to absorb water fully. The raw material is then steamed for about 2 h,
```
subsequently transferred into an alcohol fermenter (traditionally an urn),
```
```
stirred homogenously with hot water (70–80°C) and then cooled.
```
```
(2) Saccharification and alcoholic fermentation. The pretreated sorghum is
```
```
mixed with grinded Daqu, and water is added (340 kg water/100 kg sor-
```
```
ghum/62.5 kg Daqu). Thus, the raw material is saccharified and fermented
```
gradually. Rakings are performed every day during the first 3 days. The
fermentation peak is on the 4th day and the urn is covered by a piece of
146 Advances in Vinegar Production
plastic cloth to perform the fermentation at anaerobic conditions. This stage
lasts for about 16 days. The alcoholic strength and acidity reach 6–7% and
```
1–2.5%, respectively (Solieri and Giudici, 2009; Wu et al., 2012; Li et al.,
```
```
2015a).
```
```
(3) Acetic acid fermentation. The mash (called Jiulao) that is gained from the
```
```
alcoholic fermentation of sorghum is mixed with wheat bran (73 kg/100 kg
```
```
of sorghum) and rice hull (73 kg/100 kg of sorghum) evenly. The mixture,
```
called Pei, is placed into an urn, and the acetic acid fermentation starts by
```
inoculating the seed vinegar Pei (fermented vinegar Pei from the previous
```
```
batch). In some cases, seed Pei is not inoculated, but the microflora derives
```
from the environment. The urns are covered by a straw mattress, and the
temperature increases because of the microbial metabolism. By the 4th day
```
the temperature will reach 45–48°C (Nie et al., 2017). The diagram and the
```
photos of the urns are shown in Figure 8.2. The materials in the urns are
turned over daily. After about 8 days the fermentation is completed.
```
(4) Smoking. At the end of the acetic acid fermentation, salt is added to vinegar
```
Pei to inhibit microbial metabolism. Then half of the vinegar Pei is trans-
ferred into a tank for smoking. The tank is heated gently to 80–90°C for
5–6 days. The vinegar Pei in the tank is turned over once a day. Smoking
should not last too long, or the final vinegar would taste bitter. After smok-
```
ing the vinegar Pei turns into a dark color (Xie et al., 2017).
```
```
(5) Leaching. Leaching vinegar is the process of adding water to dissolve
```
```
out any soluble components from vinegar Pei (Chen et al., 2009). The
```
```
unsmoked vinegar Pei is leached with hot water to obtain light vinegar;
```
then the smoked Pei is leached with the light vinegar. Normally, vinegar Pei
should be leached three times. Finally, about 400 kg of vinegar with acidity
of 6–7% is obtained from 100 kg sorghum.
```
(6) Ageing. The fresh vinegar is transferred into a tank for ageing by exposing
```
to the sun at ambient temperature. After ageing, 400 kg of initial smoked
vinegar can only produce 120–140 kg of aged vinegar. The total acid con-
```
tent is above 8% (except for losses caused by volatilization).
```

8.3 RAW MATERIALS AND PRETREATMENT IN SSF VINEGAR
In SSF vinegar production, the raw materials include principal materials, adjunct
```
materials and stuffing (which mostly are cereals as listed in Table 8.1) and additives.
```
The principal materials are rich in starch or sugars and commonly include amyla-
```
ceous grains or cereals (sorghum, sticky rice, rice and maize) that can be converted
```
```
into fermentable sugars (Xu et al., 2010). Adjunct materials usually include wheat
```
bran, rice or soybean shells, which supply important nutritional substrates and fla-
```
vor compounds (Chen et al., 2009). They absorb water, loosen the Pei, store air and
```
facilitate the acetic acid fermentation. Besides providing nutrients, these solid sub-
```
strates also serve as supports for the microbial cells (Couto and Sanromán, 2006).
```
Prior to fermentation, the raw materials are prepared through milling or crushing
```
(Li et al., 2015b), which aim at breaking down the raw materials to release starch
```
and sugar, to increase water absorption, to obtain a desirable cohesion of mass and
```
to expand the area of contact with the microorganisms (Chen et al., 2009; Zheng et
```
```
al., 2011). In raw material preparation, the important parameter is the particle size,
```
which not only influences the microbial attack but also the heat and mass transfer
```
(Krishna, 2005; Couto and Sanromán, 2006). Therefore, a proper particle size must
```
```
be selected for each particular process (Pandey et al., 1999).
```
Before saccharification, the milled or crushed raw materials are subsequently
always soaked and may be steamed to gelatinize starch. In addition, the raw materi-
```
als are partly sterilized during steaming (Table 8.2).
```
Saccharification in an SSF vinegar is always initiated by Qu, which is made from
grains such as rice, wheat and beans, in either loose or various pressed forms depend-
ing on the manufacturer. Several kinds of Qu are used in the production of TCVs,
such as Xiaoqu, Fuqu, Maiqu, Daqu and Herbal Qu, some of which are shown in
```
Figure 8.3 (see also Chapter 10).
```
• Daqu is made from barley and pea and shaped as a brick, which is often
used in the production of vinegars in North China.
• Xiaoqu is produced in South China and is made from rice and rice chaff in
an egg-shaped form.
FIGURE 8.2 The diagram and the photos of the urns used for acetic acid fermentation.
148 Advances in Vinegar Production
• Fuqu is made up of wheat bran.
• Maiqu is made up of wheat in brick-shaped form.
• Herbal Qu is made up of wheat or other grains and a variety of herbs.
```
The use of different Qu depends on the type of vinegar (Xu et al., 2010). In some
```
recipes, the ratio of Qu to the principal material can be up to 0.6:1. Qu can also be
regarded as a raw material.
Notably, Qu is also a fermented product. Figure 8.4 illustrates a typical flow chart
for Daqu preparation. The main microorganisms in Qu are molds, yeasts and LAB
