```
(Chen et al., 2009). Besides microorganisms, Qu also contains various enzymes
```
produced by the microbial cells, including α-amylase, glucoamylase, acid protease,
```
lipase, cellulase and esterase (Steinkraus, 2004; Xu et al., 2010). Before fermentation
```
it should be milled into powder and mixed with the raw materials.
8.4 SACCHARIFICATION AND ALCOHOLIC
FERMENTATION SYSTEMS
Alcoholic fermentation proceeds simultaneously with saccharification. In the pro-
cess, the dominant microorganisms are molds and yeasts. As described above,
starchy material is steamed with vapor for gelatinization and then mixed with Qu
powder and water. Sugars produced by the hydrolysis of starch will be converted into
ethanol by yeasts. The mash of the alcoholic fermentation is called Jiulao.
Generally, alcoholic fermentation needs to be kept in a controlled tempera-
ture range of 20–30°C and is divided into two stages: open fermentation and
```
closed fermentation (Solieri and Giudici, 2009; Li et al., 2015a). The whole
```
process of alcoholic fermentation is carried out in a semi-solid state. The Qu
is the most important source of alcoholic fermentation microorganisms, which
```
are subsequently enriched (Wu et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015b). Molds can secrete
```
many enzymes such as amylase, glucoamylase, protease and lipase, which play
important roles in hydrolyzing macromolecules. Although only a few molds are
involved in the initial stage of the alcoholic fermentation, they also play a piv-
otal role in the final quality of the vinegar, because they can produce various
secondary metabolites, including flavor and odor components, pigments and
```
compounds with antibiotic properties (Li et al., 2015b). Saccharomyces cerevi-
```
siae, Hansenula anomala and Candida berkhout are the main yeasts associated
```
with the alcoholic fermentation (Solieri and Giudici, 2009). In addition, LAB
```
also contribute to the flavor of vinegar. During alcoholic fermentation, the com-
position and diversity of the microbial community is dynamically changed. For
Shanxi aged vinegar fermentation, some microorganisms are eliminated, such
as Staphylococcus, Saccharopolyspora, Bacillus, Oceanobacillus, Enterobacter,
Streptomyces, Eurotium, Monascus and Pichia, whereas some microorganisms
FIGURE 8.4 Typical flowchart of Daqu preparation.
150 Advances in Vinegar Production
are enriched such as Weissella, Lactobacillus, Streptococcus, Saccharomyces
```
and Saccharomycopsis (Nie et al., 2017).
```
8.5 ACETIC ACID FERMENTATION SYSTEMS
After alcoholic fermentation, wheat bran, sorghum or rice hull is added for supple-
mentary nutrition and to increase the porosity for oxygen intake and heat discharge
in the solid-state acetic acid fermentation process.
```
The mixture (vinegar Pei), is transferred into urns and is stirred every day to
```
increase the mass transfer and eliminate the heat. This step generally lasts about
10–20 days, and the temperature and humidity of the fermentation system are main-
tained at 40–46°C and 60–70%, respectively. Most of the water in the fermented
grains is contracted and dissolved in the fermenting materials. The solid, gas and
liquid phases of the substrates co-exist with observable solid–gas, solid–liquid and
gas-liquid interfaces, which markedly affect the survival and selection of microor-
```
ganisms (Mitchell et al., 2000).
```
The water content should be controlled strictly in the vinegar Pei. Too much
water would lead to a decreased amount of gas, large thermal capacity, difficultly
in heat exchange during fermentation and reduced oxidation area for the acetic
acid fermentation. Subsequently, the maturity period would be extended, and the
color and taste of the final products would also be affected. When the water level
is too low, the fermented grains will be heated up drastically and cooled quickly,
resulting in low utilization of the raw materials. The temperature changes from
low to high and then gradually decreases. When the temperature falls below
36°C and the acetic acid content no longer increases, the acetic acid fermentation
basically ends.
The brewing process of TCVs usually involves spontaneous fermenta-
```
tion, which leads to the growth of diverse microorganisms (Li et al., 2015b).
```
As for Shanxi aged vinegar, after alcoholic fermentation has commenced, the
most abundant bacteria are still Lactobacillus with a relative abundance of
over 70%, but their relative abundance is decreased, while the abundance of
Acetobacter is increased from about 18 to 30%. Many other microbes, such as
Sinorhizobium, Enterobacter and Gluconacetobacter, also play a very important
role. Some bacterial species generally appeared at the early period of the acetic
acid fermentation. Pediococcus and Escherichia disappeared on the 9th day of
the acetous fermentation due to their low tolerance to acetic acid. Other bac-
terial genera such as Nocardioides, Propionibacterium and Enterobacter were
spontaneously enriched at the early period and disappeared at the late period
of acetic acid fermentation. Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas existed during the
whole acetic acid fermentation process, but their abundance was less than 0.1%.
To some extent, competition spontaneously occurs between Acetobacter and
Lactobacillus, as well as other microorganisms, with Acetobacter being highly
competitive in the succession of microbial community. Fungi, which mainly
include Saccharomycopsis, Dothideomycetes, Saccharomyces and Moniliella,
are involved in the acetic acid fermentation, and the whole process is dominated
```
by the last two genera (Nie et al., 2015; Nie et al., 2017).
```
151Solid-State Fermentation Systems for Vinegar Production
8.6 INNOVATIVE DEVELOPMENT OF SSF
FOR VINEGAR PRODUCTION
8.6.1 researCH on tHe BasiC prinCiples
8.6.1.1 Micro-Ecology Studies
The SSF technology has been used in China for thousands of years. Vinegars brewed
by this technology are uniquely fragrant and thick and possess various beneficial
```
health functionalities (Xu et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018).
```
SSF is a very complex system, and so far, the fermentation mechanisms involved
are not fully illuminated. The complexity, diversity and dynamic changes of the micro-
bial populations are still not comprehended thoroughly, and the correlation between
microbial communities and flavor formation is ambiguous. The whole process is
```
mainly accomplished manually and depends highly on experience (observation and
```
```
sensory evaluation). Recently, the omics and high-throughput sequencing technolo-
```
gies, especially the metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, are developing greatly,
providing powerful research tools to study the structure, diversity and evolutionary and
```
collaborative relationships of the microbial communities (Lu et al., 2018).
```
8.6.1.2 Flavor Formation Studies
```
The flavor of food is the comprehensive perception by the human senses (smell,
```
```
taste and chemesthesis). Eating does not cover only the physiological demands for
```
nutrients, health quality and wellbeing but is also a kind of psychological satisfac-
```
tion (Min and Choe, 2003). Therefore, the flavor substances in foods constitute an
```
important research topic for food scientists and engineers.
The flavor of vinegars is mainly formed by two ways: either directly by the metab-
olism of the present microflora or through chemical reactions between the vinegar
```
components (Furukawa and Kuramitsu, 2004). As discussed in other chapters, the
```
aroma of vinegars is mainly attributed to the highcontent of ester compounds and
```
some carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) as well as acetals. The types and
```
proportions of these components are directly related to the fragrance type and the
degree of elegance.
A systematic study on the types of flavor substances, the evolution of microorgan-
isms and the influencing factors during vinegar fermentation must be carried out
for an in-depth understanding of the vinegar flavor and the improvement of vinegar
quality. Future studies shall be devoted to innovations in the analysis and identifica-
tion of flavor substances in vinegars, the formation mechanisms of vinegar flavor
substances, the analysis of the typical flavor of vinegars and the development of
modern, accurate instrumental methods of flavor detection and analysis.
8.6.2 teCHnologiCal and equipment innoVations
8.6.2.1 Bioaugmentation Technology
Bioaugmentation technology was developed in the mid-1970s and has been widely
```
studied and applied since the 1980s (Chapelle, 1999). Initially the bioaugmentation
```
technology was applied to wastewater treatment, where, in order to improve the
152 Advances in Vinegar Production
treatment efficiency, some highly efficient selected natural bacteria or genetically engi-
neered bacteria were added into the system. The bioaugmentation technology has also
been widely studied in the fermentation of vinegars in the recent years, with respect to
```
three main problems: (1) the limited knowledge on dominant bacterial communities
```
and their functions due to lack of research data on vinegar fermentation microorgan-
```
isms, (2) the food safety issues that are attracting more and more attention in the food
```
production field. The potential safety problems in bioaugmentation studies based on
exogeneous bacteria or highly efficient genetically engineered bacteria are not solved
fundamentally, which restricts the application of bioaugmentation technologies in the
```
production of traditional fermentation foods and (3) the traditional fermentation foods
```
generally apply the multi-bacteria SSF, and the unique flavor of these foods depends
on the co-metabolism of these multiple species. Bioaugmentation based on single bac-
teria can easily cause imbalances in the original bacterial communities and thereby
may have adverse effects on the quality of the products. Research on these three issues
is going to be the core of associated technological fields in the future.
8.6.2.2 Artificial Microflora
Artificial microflora is a relatively simple microflora, which is formed by the co-
culture of several known microorganisms under specific conditions. In such systems,
the microorganisms can be assembled according to function-oriented requirements.
At present, artificial microflora has become a hot research area in the field of tra-
ditional fermentation. Compared with natural microflora, artificial microflora has
```
various advantages, such as (1) the microorganisms in the synthesized microflora are
```
```
known, and the culture is less complex and more controllable, (2) the microorgan-
```
isms can respond mutually, changing their behavior in accordance to the reactions
of the community, so the overall function of the microflora is more harmonious and
```
(3) the different microorganisms in the community can act synergistically, to accom-
```
plish tasks which cannot be accomplished by an individual species.
With in-depth study, it is possible to develop high-quality vinegar fermentation
systems using artificial microflora. It has been reported that mixed fermentation sys-
tems containing LAB and yeasts can benefit the yeasts to some extent when the lactic
acid is lower than 0.9%. Specifically, vinegar produced by co-culturing of LAB and
yeasts contains more non-volatile acids and esters. Nowadays, high-quality fermen-
tation systems based on multiple microorganisms have not yet been applied in the
vinegar industry. Nevertheless, the continuous development of screening technolo-
gies and in-depth studies may lead to important breakthroughs in the SSF vinegar
production technology based on artificial microflora.
8.6.2.3 Equipment Inventions
Progresses in innovation of equipment for vinegar brewing have been made with the
development of intelligent technologies and devices. Existing brewing devices in
the SSF systems are only equipped with single functions. Most of the SSF systems
require intense labor and are characterized by low utilization of the raw materials,
thus restricting the economic benefits for enterprises. The realization of equipment
computer-based automatic control to reduce labor intensity and improve vinegar
quality is an important issue to be studied in the future.

Current Trends in
Balsamic/Aged Vinegar
Production and Research
Antonia Terpou, Ioanna Mantzourani,
Argyro Bekatorou, Athanasios
Alexopoulos, and Stavros Plessas
9.1 INTRODUCTION
Balsamic vinegars have a long history of production in Italy and are mainly
categorized in two types, namely the traditional and industrial types. They are
both obtained from the alcoholic and acetic acid fermentation of cooked and
concentrated grape musts, and this is the main characteristic that distinguishes
```
balsamic vinegars from other vinegars (Ho et al., 2017). Traditional balsamic
```
```
vinegar (TBV) is a high-quality balsamic vinegar produced in Italy by surface
```
fermentation and with a long history of well-developed procedures for its pro-
duction. As presented in Chapter 2, the ageing of balsamic vinegars may occur
```
in wooden barrels made from various woods (chestnut, cherry, juniper, mulberry,
```
```
oak), while TBV may age up to 25 years (Cerezo et al., 2010; Daglia et al.,
```
```
2013). In this chapter the recent trends regarding balsamic vinegar production
```
and research are highlighted and grouped based on the available most recent
scientific literature.

9.2 CURRENT TRENDS IN BALSAMIC/AGED
VINEGAR PRODUCTION AND RESEARCH
9.2.1 Current BalsamiC/aged Vinegar produCtion
```
The origin of TBV production dates back to the middle of the 18th century (Verzelloni
```
```
et al., 2010). The term “balsamic” derived from the Greek word “βάλσαμο” (pro-
```
```
nounced: válsamo), which refers to a substrate that can sooth, restore, or comfort
```
```
(Giudici et al., 2009), as this type of vinegar was used for its medicinal properties.
```
Nowadays, the term “balsamic vinegar” has been globally adopted to describe this
type of vinegar as well as various vinegar-based sauces, condiments, and dressings
```
with a particular sweet taste (Torri et al., 2017; Verzelloni et al., 2010).
```
The production of TBV starts from grapes, which have just been squeezed, and
continues with must cooking, must alcoholic fermentation and acetification, and
finally maturation. The alcoholic fermentation and acetification steps take place in
the same barrel by indigenous yeasts and bacteria before the ageing of TBV in a bar-
```
rel battery for many years (see also Chapter 2). Therefore, TBVs are vinegars made
```
from a blend of wine vinegar and cooked grape must after a long maturation period.
Must is cooked directly over a fire for 12–24 h, and during this heating various physi-
cochemical processes take place, most notably:
• Concentration of the must
• Maillard/caramelization reactions of the grape must constituents
The desirable cooked must sugar concentration for TBV is about 30°Brix. The
biological transformations for TBV production occur in the stage after must cooking,
where the must, still hot, is transferred to a special cask called the “badessa.” In the
badessa, the must is fermented and acetified. An alternative way is to seal the barrel
and leave the content without any further treatments. In the badessa, the yeasts and
```
acetic acid bacteria (AAB) require different conditions to grow and act, which also
```
rely on the composition of the medium. Specifically, low concentration of volatile
acids favors the alcoholic fermentation. Although this process may take place annu-
ally, irregular fermentations may occur. The most serious problem occurs when the
process ends up in TBV with low volatile acidity. To avoid this issue fresh vinegar is
added as starter culture.
The barrels in which vinegar is placed after the badessa are made from different
```
types of wood (chestnut, mulberry, acacia, cherry, oak). All barrels contain a quan-
```
tity of the vinegar from the badessa. Only a portion of TBV is removed from the first
barrel, which is then refilled with vinegar from the next barrel, and eventually each
barrel contains a blend of vinegars of different ages. The process is called “rincalzo.”
In modern methods for TBV production, new barrels are used, which are filled with
wine vinegar and left to stand for 6 months before use in the TBV ageing process.
The real role of the wooden barrels, rather than affecting the sensory properties of
the products, is to act as semi-permeable means to inhibit molecules with dimensions
larger than water, such as alcohols and acetic acid, from passing through the wood
```
(Giudici et al., 2009).
```
157Balsamic/Aged Vinegar Production and Research
The variability of ingredients and ageing processes/times leads to the production
of a vast variety of balsamic vinegars worldwide. Specifically, in Italy, two types of
```
balsamic vinegars are available: balsamic vinegar of Modena (BVM) and traditional
```
```
balsamic vinegar of Modena (TBVM). They are both typical Italian products of
```
```
protected destination of origin (PDO) (Cocchi et al., 2007). Both types of balsamic
```
vinegars are obtained from the alcoholic and acetic acid fermentation of cooked and
concentrated grape must. In the case of BVM, producers can add wine vinegar at a
concentration of at least 10% v/v and caramel color at a concentration up to 2% v/v.
On the other hand, no such additions are allowed in TBVM, which is prepared by
cooked grape must through natural fermentation and aged for at least 12 years.
```
BVMs must be aged in wooden barrels for at least 60 days (Cirlini et al., 2009). In
```
both cases the mixing takes place in tanks with the aid of suitable mixing equipment
and at blending times that vary from a few minutes to a few hours in the case of
bulky and viscous batches. Ageing takes place in a series of casks of different woods
and sizes, and the final product receives a certification as BVM after the appropriate
```
governmental controls (Cirlini et al., 2009; Cocchi et al., 2007).
```
A current huge trend in the market of balsamic vinegars is the production of con-
diments, glazes, and creams, based on wine vinegars, raisin vinegars, cider vinegars,
honey vinegars, fruit vinegars, apple vinegars, etc. The production of these balsamic
condiments is similar to that of TBVs but without the time-consuming ageing stage.
They are produced by simple mechanical mixing or more complex temperature-
controlled processes, and their final price is much more affordable compared to the
```
balsamic vinegars (Garcia-Parrilla et al., 2017; Ho et al., 2017; Torri et al., 2017).
```
Balsamic glazes and creams are viscous and creamy, due to the addition of thick-
```
ening and stabilizing agents such as starch (including modified starches), gums (e.g.,
```
```
xanthan gum), and pectins. They are usually packed in squeezable plastic containers,
```
allowing easy control stream while dispensing. They contain mixtures of balsamic
vinegar with concentrated grape juice, glucose syrup, agave syrup, rice syrup, and
```
other sweeteners such as invert sugar (mixture of glucose and fructose), saccharose,
```
```
fructose, steviol glucosides, etc., and a vast variety of flavor ingredients (fruit juices,
```
```
marmalades, herbs, nuts, spices, mushrooms, etc.).
```
```
Depending on the color of the added ingredient, white products (glazes/creams)
```
```
are available (with white vinegar), yellowish-orange products (with citrus fruit), red
```
```
or violet products (with strawberries, raspberries, blood oranges, pomegranates),
```
```
dark red and purple products (with figs and plums), green products (with herbs or
```
```
mint), and even more. Balsamic glazes with mustard, honey, tomato, vanilla, etc.,
```
are also available.
Preservatives and antioxidants commonly used in these products include potas-
```
sium metabisulfite (K 2 S2 O5; E224; also known as potassium pyrosulfite) and potas-
```
```
sium sorbate [potassium (2E,4E)-hexa-2,4-dienoate; E202].
```
The most common color additive in balsamic condiments is sulfite ammonia car-
```
amel (E150d; also known as acid-proof caramel or soft-drink caramel) (Sengar and
```
```
Sharma, 2012).
```
According to the Persistence Market Research report Global Market Study on
Dressing Vinegar & Condiments: Apple Cider Vinegar and Red Wine Vinegar
Segments Projected to Gain High BPS Shares During 2016–2024, the balsamic
158 Advances in Vinegar Production
vinegar products will be widely preferred by consumers in the period beyond 2017.
Balsamic vinegar will continue to account for one-third of the global dressing
vinegar revenues, and over 60% of the global condiments volume for the projec-
```
tion period will be accounted for by vinaigrettes (Market Watch, 2019; Persistence
```
```
Market Research, 2019).
```
9.2.2 progress in yeasts inVolVed in BalsamiC Vinegar fermentations
The number of yeast species involved in the TBV fermentation is large and very
complex. Prevailing species include Zygosaccharomyces bailii, Z. rouxii, Z. pseu-
dorouxii, Z. mellis, Z. bisporus, and Z. lentus, Hanseniaspora valbyensis and
H. osmophila, Candida lactis-condensi, and C. stellata, Saccharomycodes ludwi-
gii, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, while many other slow-growing species may
contribute to the cooked must fermentation, as reviewed previously by Solieri and
```
Giudici (2008).
```
```
Solieri and Giudici (2008) suggested that despite the extended knowledge of TBV
```
yeast microbiota, further study is needed to screen yeast species suitable for the fer-
mentation of cooked must, to understand their metabolic activities and how they can
affect the quality of TBV. The selected yeast strains are of major importance for high
quality TBV production as their metabolism is responsible for major physicochemical
changes of the cooked must. As also shown in other fermented food systems, the con-
ventional culture-dependent methods can access only a small proportion from a large
```
number of yeast species associated with TBV production (Perin et al., 2017; Solieri
```
```
et al., 2006; Solieri and Giudici, 2008). New insights can be provided regarding the
```
fermentation process of TBV by understanding the yeasts’ ecology, their genetic and
```
physiological properties (Lalou et al., 2018), the specific role of each yeast strain in
```
TBV production, and their interactions with other species and with the environment
```
of each region or producer (Dakal et al., 2018; Solieri and Giudici, 2008).
```
In an effort to implement principles of traditional concentrated grape must fer-
mentation to the production of new generation balsamic vinegars, the isolation and
molecular identification of the predominant yeasts in concentrated grape must, their
technological characterization, and their fermentative aptitude were evaluated by
```
Lalou et al. (2016). Specifically, tolerance against 5-hydroxymethyl-furfural (HMF),
```
furfural, acetic acid, and glucose concentration was examined, as well as enological
characteristics such as acetic acid and H 2 S production, foaming, flocculation ability,
key enzymatic activity, and formation of key volatiles. Tolerance to both HMF and
```
furfural was found to be strain- and dose-dependent; therefore these compounds
```
```
were suggested as critical factors in yeast pre-selection (Lalou et al., 2016).
```
Recently, the effect of fermentation temperature and inoculation strategy on the
fermentation dynamics of balsamic-styled vinegar production was also investigated
```
(Hutchinson et al., 2019). A microbial consortium of five non-Saccharomyces yeasts
```
```
(Metschikowia pulcherrima, Candida zemplinina, Hanseniaspora guilliermondii
```
```
and H. uvarum, and Z. bailii strains) and 13 AAB (Acetobacter pasteurianus and
```
A. malorum, Kozakia baliensis, Gluconobacter cerinus, and G. oxydans strains) was
tested at various fermentation temperatures, using different inoculation strategies
```
(co-inoculation and sequential inoculation). The population dynamics of the more
```
159Balsamic/Aged Vinegar Production and Research
rapidly fermented product were confirmed using a 16S and 18S gene sequencing,
showing that about 51% of the Acetobacter species were abundant at the end of the
fermentation cycle, while about 40% of AAB were unculturable. A practical applica-
tion of the results of this study is that lower quality wine grapes could be converted
```
to an alternative high-priced product (balsamic vinegar), with low technological
```
input requirements, thus facilitating establishment of low capital start-up businesses
```
and boosting of the economy in the areas of interest (Hutchinson et al., 2019).
```
```
Lalou et al. (2018) adopted a systematic approach (Taguchi design) to optimize the
```
parameters of the alcoholic fermentation of concentrated grape must from Greek grapes
```
(Xinomavro) using the best-performing indigenous H. uvarum and S. cerevisiae strains
```
as multistarters. The optimum combination of H. uvarum/S. cerevisiae cell ratio, inoc-
ulum size and inoculation time of S. cerevisiae, fermentation time, and temperature
resulted in an alcoholic product with 79 g/kg ethanol and 164 g/kg residual sugar, suit-
able for further use in the production of balsamic-style vinegar. Also, the multistarter
fermentation affected positively the organoleptic properties of the fermented concen-
trated must. The HMF content was also recognized as a critical factor for the standard-
ization of this process. Scale-up experiments validated the laboratory scale results, and
```
the work was proposed as a prototype for further similar efforts (Lalou et al., 2018).
```
Zygosaccharomyces species have been recognized as the predominant yeasts
involved in the alcoholic fermentation stage of TBV production. They are osmo-
```
philic yeasts growing in media with high sugar concentrations (50–60%) as well
```
```
as in salty foods (Dakal et al., 2018; Sá-Correia et al., 2014; Solieri et al., 2013;
```
```
Solieri and Giudici, 2008). In addition to these significant osmo- and halo-tolerance
```
properties, they also exhibit strong fermentative ability and resistance to low pH
```
and to certain food preservatives, such as benzoic and sorbic acids (commonly used
```
```
in vinegar products) (Dakal et al., 2018). Therefore, xerophilic Zygosaccharomyces
```
yeasts constitute potential spoilage species for sugary food fermentations, such as
in TBV production using cooked must with high sugar content. Cooked must has a
sugar concentration ranging from 30 to 50% w/w, which decreases the water activity
```
(a w) to values lower than 0.9. The majority of yeasts require a minimum a w of 0.85,
```
```
while xerophilic food spoilage yeasts can grow at a w values of 0.61–0.75 (Solieri and
```
```
Giudici, 2008).
```
```
Solieri et al. (2013) recovered 14 yeast isolates recovered from two TBV samples
```
from Modena and Reggio Emilia, Italy. Phylogenetic analysis based on the D1/D2
domains of the 26S rRNA gene indicated that these strains represented a distinct
species of the genus Zygosaccharomyces, closely related to Z. rouxii and Z. mellis.
Physiological and morphological tests supported the recognition of a novel taxon of
halotolerant, osmotolerant, non-psychrotolerant, and maltose-fermentation-negative
yeasts, and a novel species, namely Zygosaccharomyces sapae sp. nov., was pro-
```
posed to accommodate these strains (Solieri et al., 2013).
```
9.2.3 progress in aaB inVolVed in BalsamiC Vinegar fermentations
As discussed in the previous chapters, the main species responsible for the production
of vinegar belong to the genera Acetobacter, Gluconacetobacter, Gluconobacter, and
Komagataeibacter because of their high capacity to oxidize ethanol to acetic acid and
160 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
their high resistance to the resulting acidic medium (Gomes et al., 2018). The species
```
most frequently reported in vinegar production are Acetobacter aceti, A. cerevisiae,
A. malorum, A. oeni, A. pasteurianus, and A. pomorum, Gluconacetobacter entanii
and G. liquefaciens, Gluconobacter oxydans, Komagataeibacter europaeus, K. han-
senii, K. intermedius, K. medellinensis, K. oboediens, and K. xylinus. The history
of taxonomy, the biochemical aspects, and the methods of isolation, identification,
and quantification of AAB, especially those related with important biotechnological
```
applications, were recently reviewed by Gomes et al. (2018).
```
Many studies have focused on the use of selected strains of AAB for improve-
```
ments in TBV production (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Lalou et al., 2018). In gen-
```
eral, AAB are known to be able to oxidize carbon substrates such as sugars and
alcohols. The sugar tolerance is an important factor of AAB growth in the case of
TBV production, as few species are able to grow at elevated sugar concentrations.
As a result, selection of the appropriate strain is a crucial factor in TBV produc-
tion since this product is made from cooked must with a high sugar concentration.
It is reported that few species are able to grow at very high sugar concentration
as is for example Gluconobacter diazotrophicus which is reported to grow at
```
30% D-glucose concentration (Gullo et al., 2006). Another important factor that
```
has to be taken into account for the selection of the appropriate strain for TBV
```
production is its tolerance to the acid environment (pH 2.5–3.5) that occurs dur-
```
```
ing the fermentation (Gullo et al., 2006). The phenotypic traits of AAB relevant
```
for starter culture selection in TBV production has been reviewed by Gullo and
```
Giudici (2008), who pointed out that selected starter cultures are the main techno-
```
logical improvement required in order to innovate TBV production. The selection
criteria should take into account the composition of the raw material, the meta-
bolic activities of AAB, the applied technology, and the desired characteristics
of the final product. Main traits are the preferred ethanol content, the efficient
ethanol oxidation, the rate of acetification, the tolerance to high acetic acid con-
centration, sugar concentration, and low pH, the avoidance of overoxidation, and
the temperature range tolerance.
```
As presented above, recently Hutchinson et al. (2019) studied the effect of an
```
inoculation strategy on the fermentation dynamics of balsamic-style vinegar pro-
duction, which included a microbial consortium of five non-Saccharomyces and 13
AAB strains, which were isolated from healthy grapes, grape pomace, experimen-
```
tal vinegar, Shiraz wine, and Kei apple. Two inoculation strategies were followed;
```
the first involved the simultaneous inoculation of yeast and AAB at the start of the
process, and the second involved inoculating the yeast only at the start followed by
inoculation of the AAB when the ethanol concentration reached 6% v/v. The alco-
holic/acetous fermentations were completed within 42 and 56 days for the co-inocu-
lation and sequential inoculation strategies, respectively. Yeast and AAB growth was
observed throughout the fermentation, except for the case of the sequential-inocula-
tion strategy, with minimal differences between yeast and bacteria growth kinetics,
indicating that they can coexist proportionally. 18S sequencing of the selected vin-
egar showed that 51% of the Acetobacter species were present at the end of the fer-
mentation with an insignificant quantity of yeasts, explaining the completion of the
ethanol oxidation. Based on the fermentation length, it was concluded that the use of
161Balsamic/Aged Vinegar Production and Research
a co-inoculation strategy with fermentation at 28°C could be adopted for industrial
```
scale fermentations (Hutchinson et al., 2019).
```
```
Finally, Giudici et al. (2016) studied the set-up of a fermentation process that
```
could improve the quality of balsamic vinegar using selected yeasts and AAB strains
able to oxidize glucose in grape must-based media with different sugars concentra-
tions. Specifically, selected S. ludwigii and A. pasteurianus strains were used as
starter cultures for small-scale fermentation of cooked grape must, to evaluate the
physicochemical parameters that could affect the formation of gluconic acid produc-
tion in vinegar. Gluconic acid is a non-volatile acid that has been detected as a main
oxidation product of Acetobacter and Gluconobacter strains and plays an important
role in TBV quality. Specifically, gluconate has an acidic but mild sweet taste and
influences the sensory complexity of the vinegar. High gluconate vinegars have a
greater physicochemical stability and are preferred by consumers as they are per-
```
ceived a less pungent (Giudici et al., 2016). In their study, Giudici et al. (2016) based
```
```
their hypothesis on two pieces of evidence: (1) yeasts show selective preference for
```
```
glucose or fructose, and (2) the direct oxidation of glucose by AAB contributes to
```
the reduction of the glucose content of the final vinegar and enhances its fixed acidity
and sensorial properties. Throughout the process, from cooked must to base vinegar,
the glucose/fructose ratio decreased from 1.08 to 0.28, the titratable acidity increased
from 1.5 to 6.06, and the pH decreased from 3.46 to 3.18. The final titratable acid-
ity mostly depended on the presence of gluconic acid and glucono-δ-lactone, whose
concentration was two-fold that of acetic acid. The strains used and the control of all
production process have been fundamental for obtaining the vinegar with the desired
```
characteristics (Giudici et al., 2016).
```
9.2.4 struCture of BalsamiC/aged Vinegars
The structure of high quality TBVs has also been a subject of vinegar research.
During the ageing of TBVs the density increases due to evaporation, and various
other changes occur such as component crystallization and flavor alterations.
Various researchers have investigated issues related with these alterations.
```
According to Falcone et al. (2017), the molecular structure of TBV undergoes solidi-
```
fication through equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium phase transitions including
crystallization due to rearrangements of α-D-glucose molecules, and shear-induced
and time-dependent jamming transitions due to self-assembling phenomena of
amorphous colloids of unidentified substances, including polymeric, high molecular
```
size melanoidins with very long relaxation times (12 to more than 25 years).
```
```
Falcone (2010) used high-resolution light microscopy (HR-LM) and X-ray dif-
```
```
fractometry (XRD) to study the bulk structure of the TBV of Modena, which may
```
undergo such changes during ageing. Furthermore, liquid and jammed TBV of
Modena were also investigated for their microstructure and elemental composition
by coupling two non-destructive techniques, environmental scanning electronic
```
microscopy (ESEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), for their
```
```
molecular size distribution by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), and for their
```
```
shear viscosity with a stress-controlled rheometer (Falcone et al., 2011). The TBV in
```
the jammed state behaved as a pseudoplastic fluid due to nitrogen-free polymers with
162 Advances in Vinegar Production
a molecular size dispersion lower than a liquid TBV, which behaved as a Newtonian
fluid. The solid particles in TBV close to jamming transition showed 2.5 and 3.7 C/O
ratios for the liquid and jammed TBV, respectively. The Fe and Mg content was
higher, and the pH was lower in the jammed TBV. The jamming transition in TBV
was suggested to be a result of the imbalance between the increase of the bulk vis-
cosity and the structure relaxation of nitrogen-free polymers, which are two time-
```
dependent phenomena (Falcone et al., 2011).
```
TBV of Modena was also probed for its microstructure and composition as well
```
as for its flow ability under low- and high-shear limits by Falcone et al. (2012). The
```
results indicated that vinegar concentration, temperature, and viscosity are three
independent variables that affect the extent of solidification in TBV. Polymer-
mediated mechanisms and diffusion-limited kinetics were hypothesized for struc-
ture development, and three main experimental evidences were used to provide
proof on the solidification phenomena observed in TBV based on the concept of col-
```
loidal jamming transition: (1) the simultaneous presence of fractal-like aggregated
```
```
colloids and polydispersed biopolymers, (2) the non-linear shear dependence above a
```
```
critical level of vinegar concentration, and (3) a modified Krieger–Dougherty model
```
that efficiently described the scaling trend of relative viscosity accounting for the
fractal dimension of the jammed structure. The jamming threshold in TBV was
defined in terms of critical concentration of the overall structure-active constituents
```
(72°Brix and 40% w/w of the main sugars) and maximum resistance to Newtonian
```
```
flow (onset for shear-thinning flow achieved with a low-shear viscosity of ~0.95 Pa s)
```
```
(Falcone et al., 2012).
```
```
Finally, Falcone et al. (2017) performed a descriptive and quantitative evaluation
```
```
of the relationships between the rheological properties (density, flow behavior, and
```
```
dynamic viscosity over a wide range of shear rates), the vinegar composition (sug-
```
```
ars, volatile acidity, fixed acidity, pH, Brix degree), and the perceptual assessment
```
of the sensory properties of PDO TBV according to official sensory protocols. The
results showed that the flow behavior of TBV is affected by jamming properties over
a wide range of shear rates, producing flow instability below a shear rate of 60 s−1.
Homogeneous, continuous flow was found at medium-high shear rates, and a com-
mon onset for the structure scaling was estimated to occur around 1.32 g mL −1
density. The comparative analysis of the rheological, compositional, and sensory
properties suggested that the colloidal jamming of the vinegar melanoidins domi-
nated the total sensory stimuli and determined the classification of vinegars that had
```
a higher dynamic viscosity but more homogeneous flow (the highest commercial
```
```
quality category) (Falcone et al., 2017).
```
```
According to Elmi (2015), crystallization, which appears mostly in homemade
```
balsamic vinegars, is an undesirable effect during ageing of the vinegar in barrels
or even when it is bottled. The main chemical compound of the crystals is glucose,
which is a more stable sugar at high temperatures compared to fructose. The concen-
tration of glucose in vinegars is primarily related to the cooking of the initial must
and the ratio of glucose/fructose. Specifically, when the temperature of cooking is
higher than 80°C and the cooking time is more than 10 h the glucose deposit in the
must is higher. In addition, during ageing the content of water decreases because
163Balsamic/Aged Vinegar Production and Research
of evaporation, resulting in more extended crystallization of glucose in the aged
products.
```
Elmi (2015) used XRD analysis to identify the crystal by-products in TBV. Her
```
```
work described the relationships between the sugar content, the total acidity (volatile
```
```
and non-volatile), and the crystal by-products formed during TBV ageing, in order to
```
suggest the best practice for controlling crystallization. The XRD patterns showed
the presence of glucose crystals at the bottom of the bottles and concluded that the
```
glucose deposit could be related to the high concentration of the substrate (cooked
```
```
must), the imbalance of the glucose/fructose ratio, and the evaporation of water that
```
leads to growth of glucose crystals during ageing. The appearance of the crystals
could be explained by considering the high concentration of sugar and the low total
acidity of the product. Crystallization is a serious problem for vinegars because it
```
finally affects the sensory properties ending in total loss. According to Elmi (2015)
```
```
the ratio of sugar/total acidity should be between 9.26 (ideal sweet taste boundary)
```
```
and 6.74 (ideal acid taste boundary) in order to obtain acceptable organoleptic char-
```
acteristics and avoid glucose crystallization in the final product. For homemade TBV,
filtering the crystalline mass and addition of fermented grape must can be useful for
inhibition of crystallization, without loss of the desirable organoleptic characteristics
```
(Elmi 2015).
```
9.2.5 ClassifiCation and autHentiCation of BalsamiC/aged Vinegars
The authentication of food products is a complex procedure since it has to consider
many aspects including the control of traditional protocols and geographical origin
```
(Cocchi et al., 2007). Moreover, traditional foods have to be considered in a com-
```
pletely different way than industrial food products. Likewise, many recent studies
deal with the classification and authentication of vinegars, especially for the brand
protection of high-quality PDO balsamic vinegars and the prevention of adulteration
```
and unfair competition (Graziosi and Bertelli, 2017; Ríos-Reina et al., 2017; Ríos-
```
```
Reina et al., 2018; Ríos-Reina et al., 2019a, 2019b), as discussed in more detail in
```
Chapter 21.
A variety of techniques have been employed for the evaluation of vinegar quality,
the verification of authenticity, and the classification of vinegars, including spec-
```
troscopic techniques (near-infrared spectroscopy, multidimensional fluorescence
```
```
spectroscopy, or two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, etc.),
```
chemometric techniques, and their combinations.
```
For example, in a study by Chinnici et al. (2016), 23 amino acids and 11 amines
```
were quantified in many premium quality European vinegars, including TBV of
Modena, balsamic vinegars of Modena, and vinegars of Jerez, by an HPLC with
Diode Array Detector method after derivatization with diethyl ethoxymethylenmalo-
nate. Proline, glycine, and γ-aminobutyric acid were the main amino acids, while
isoleucine was only found in balsamic vinegar of Modena. TVB had the lowest num-
ber of biogenic amines. Based on the results, the samples were successfully classified
by means of principal component and cluster analysis. Because the amino acid and
amine content in vinegars is influenced by the production process and raw materials,
164 Advances in Vinegar Production
they may be potentially used to characterize premium quality vinegars for authenti-
```
cation or anti-fraud purposes (Chinnici et al., 2016).
```
In another recent study, gas chromatographic–combustion–isotopic ratio mass
```
spectrometry (GC–C–IRMS) was used to determine the compound-specific 13 C/12 C
```
isotopic ratio of glycerol, which varies on the basis of origin, variety, or provenance,
```
for the classification of industrial and PDO TBVs of Modena (Sighinolfi et al., 2018).
```
Several marketable products were subjected to the measurements, and the experi-
mental results highlighted the particularities of the two different production pro-
cesses, suggesting that the determination of the carbon isotopic ratio of glycerol can
be an additional tool for balsamic vinegar authentication.
```
In a similar manner, Perini et al. (2018) investigated whether the combination
```
of 13 C/12 C of ethanol using isotope ratio mass spectrometry with 2H-site-specific
natural isotope fractionation–nuclear magnetic resonance, and minor sugars using
ion chromatography with pulse amperometric and charged aerosol detection, could
allow the detection of sugar addition in balsamic vinegar of Modena. A large number
of authentic Italian grape musts and balsamic vinegars with an increasing percentage
of added beet, cane, and sugar syrups were used for the investigation. The possible
degradation of sugars in the balsamic vinegar matrix versus time was also consid-
ered. While stable isotope ratio analysis remained the best method to determine
```
the addition of cane and beet sugar, the addition of minor sugars (mainly maltose)
```
proved to be very useful for detecting the sugar addition. Based on their approach,
```
Peirini et al. (2018) managed to identify 3 out of 27 commercial balsamic vinegars as
```
adulterated and suggested that the combination of stable isotope ratio and ion chro-
matography with pulse amperometric and charged aerosol detection analysis can be
a useful tool to detect the authenticity of balsamic vinegars.
```
Finally, the large potential of high-resolution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
```
```
techniques (through specific applications and by using different approaches) for the
```
authentication of foods including balsamic and TBV of Modena, with a particu-
lar focus on geographical origin characterization, ageing determination, and fraud
detection, were presented and discussed in a recent study by Consonni and Cagliani
```
(2018).
```
9.2.6 analysis of BalsamiC/aged Vinegar Composition
The chemical composition of TBV is really complex and not yet completely explored
as a result of the complicated chemical and biological modifications that take place
during fermentation and ageing. The best studied compounds are sugars and organic
acids, followed by polyphenols, end-products of the Maillard reaction, and volatile
compounds.
Among sugars, fructose and glucose are the main monosaccharides in grape
```
juice in approximately equal ratios (~1). Fructose is fermented by osmotolerant
```
non-Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeasts and is a more heat-labile sugar compared
to glucose. On the other hand, glucose is preferentially fermented by S. cerevisiae
```
strains (Solieri et al., 2006). In TBV, glucose and fructose define the viscosity of
```
```
the final product, and increased “R-factors” (sugar concentration/titratable acidity)
```
in balsamic vinegars are currently pursued, since sweeter vinegars are preferred
165Balsamic/Aged Vinegar Production and Research
```
by consumers (Falcone et al., 2007). Other minor sugars that have been detected in
```
TBVs include xylose, ribose, rhamnose, galactose, mannose, arabinose, and sucrose
```
(Cocchi et al., 2007).
```
The main organic acid of a wine vinegar is acetic acid. In the case of TBV, other
organic acids such as tartaric, gluconic, malic, and succinic acid may appear in simi-
lar amounts. These acids determine the sweet taste of TBV, since they are less pun-
gent than acetic acid. The organic acid concentration in vinegars has been evaluated
```
with different techniques (HPLC, GS, GS–MS, enzymatic). The results indicate that
```
tartaric acid exists in TBV at a low concentration, probably because of the forma-
```
tion of potassium or calcium salts, especially during ageing (Cocchi et al., 2002;
```
```
Sanarico et al., 2003). Succinic acid may be found in higher amounts in young TBVs,
```
and during ageing its concentration decreases due to esterification reactions. On the
other hand, gluconic acid can be generally found in old TBVs and represents a qual-
```
ity parameter in these vinegars (Lalou et al., 2015; Papotti et al., 2015). The content
```
of citric and malic acids is generally constant during all the stages of the production
```
process (Cocchi et al., 2002). The origin of acids also greatly varies depending on
```
```
the metabolism of ethanol and sugars by the TBV microflora (Caligiani et al., 2007;
```
```
Lalou et al., 2015).
```
Among molecules with antioxidant activity, polyphenols and melanoidins are the
most prominent. Phenolic acids, catechins, polymeric procyanidins, and flavonoids
may be present in TBV samples. Tannins may also be present in varying amounts
```
(~260–300 mg/kg TBV). The observed increased amounts in the aged vinegars
```
```
is due to the extraction of polyphenols from the barrel woods (Piva et al., 2008;
```
```
Tagliazucchi et al., 2007).
```
```
Regarding melanoidins, Falcone et al. (2007) suggested that TBV may con-
```
tain mixtures with molecular weights varying from 0.2 kDa to over 2,000 kDa.
Melanoidins accumulate during ageing, and along with some other biopolymers they
```
can be used as ageing markers for TBVs (Liu et al., 2017).
```
```
Finally, a plethora of volatile compounds (apart from ethanol and acetic acid)
```
```
have been detected in balsamic vinegars, including alcohols (1-propanol, 1-butanol,
```
2-methyl-propanol, 2-methyl-butanol, 3-methyl-butanol, phenyl ethyl alcohol, and
```
many others), carboxylic compounds (hexanoic, octanoic, decanoic, undecanoic,
```
```
2-methyl-butanoic, 3-methyl-pentanoic acids, etc.), aldehydes (mainly acetaldehyde),
```
```
esters (ethyl or diethyl esters of different carboxylic acids), etc. (Zeppa et al., 2002).
```
Many studies have been performed to determine the composition of these major
```
metabolites in balsamic vinegars. Pinu et al. (2016) first proposed the characterization
```
of the comprehensive metabolite composition of balsamic vinegars, through a metabo-
```
lomics study using gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC–MS). The
```
combination of three GC–MS methods allowed the detection of > 1,500 metabolites in
```
the vinegar samples (123 accurately identified, including 25 amino acids, 26 carboxylic
```
acids, 13 sugars and sugar alcohols, four fatty acids, one vitamin, one tripeptide, and
```
over 47 aroma compounds). Moreover, they identified for the first time five volatile
```
metabolites, namely acetin, 2-methylpyrazine, 2-acetyl-1-pyroline, 4-anisidine, and
1,3-diacetoxypropane. That study demonstrated the ability of metabolomics to detect
and identify a large number of metabolites, some of which could be used for the clas-
```
sification of vinegars based on their origin and quality (Pinu et al., 2016).
```
166 Advances in Vinegar Production
In an effort to assess the vinegar antioxidant and metabolic profiles and to iden-
tify the most appropriate features that influence their type and subtypes, Sinanoglou
```
et al. (2018), examined commercially available balsamic vinegars using a combina-
```
tion of spectrophotometric, chromatographic, colorimetric, and spectroscopic meth-
ods. The total phenolic content and profile, antioxidant activity, radical scavenging
```
capacity, color parameters, Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) absorbance spectra,
```
and 1H NMR spectra were comparatively studied. The combination of all the applied
techniques provided critical information on the compositional differences among
the tested vinegars and was proposed as an important application tool for similar
```
fermentation products (Sinanoglou et al., 2018).
```
```
Slaghenaufi and Ugliano (2018) analyzed the volatile compounds in wines associ-
```
ated with tobacco and balsamic notes, using headspace solid-phase micro-extrac-
```
tion (HS-SPME) GC–MS. The results showed that among other relevant volatile
```
compounds, sesquiterpenes appear to contribute potentially to balsamic and spicy
aroma notes.
The odor-active compounds in TBVs and PGI balsamic vinegars from Modena
```
were determined by gas chromatography-olfactometry (GC–O) using frequency of
```
```
detection methodology (modified frequency, MF, %) by Corsini et al. (2019). The
```
```
main compounds (mean MF > 60%) were 2,3-butanedione (75%), acetic acid (70%),
```
```
furan-2-carbaldehyde (62%), 1-(furan-2-yl)ethanone (62%), 2-methylpropanoic acid
```
```
(66%), butanoic acid (78%), 3-methylbutanoic acid (83%), 2-phenylethyl acetate
```
```
(65%), 2-hydroxy-3-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one (61%), 2-phenylethan-1-ol (84%),
```
```
3-hydroxy-2-methylpyran-4-one (60%), (5-formylfuran-2-yl)methyl acetate (68%),
```
```
2-phenylacetic acid (69%), and 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde (86%). These
```
compounds were categorized according to their aromatic character in cheesy-butter-
lactic, sweet, flower, empyreumatic, fruity, chemical, and miscellaneous groups. The
balsamic vinegars from Modena presented lower values for the sweet category and
higher values for the miscellaneous and chemical categories compared to the TBVs.
A principal component analysis showed that both types of vinegars from Modena
```
could be clearly differentiated based on these olfactometric data (Corsini et al., 2019).
```
9.2.7 HealtH Benefits of BalsamiC/aged Vinegars
Balsamic vinegar has been long associated with various health benefits, as are most
```
naturally fermented products (Bhalang et al., 2008; Pazuch et al., 2015). According
```
to many recent scientific studies, the acetic acid contained in balsamic vinegar in
addition to other metabolites and bioactive compounds produced by fermentation
can contribute to its various beneficial health effects such as on cardiovascular
disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cancer as presented and discussed in detail in
Chapter 18. For example, the phenolic compounds such as cinnamic acid, gallic acid,
and catechin identified in TBVs could improve the lipid metabolism or provide anti-
```
oxidant effects (Cho et al., 2010; Verzelloni et al., 2007). In addition, balsamic vin-
```
```
egar washings have been reported as suitable to reduce foodborne pathogens (Ramos
```
```
et al., 2014), while the variety of organic acids (acetic, formic, lactic, malic, citric,
```
```
succinic, and tartaric) also found in balsamic vinegars can contribute as antimicro-
```
```
bial agents (Caligiani et al., 2007).
```

172 Advances in Vinegar Production
10.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar, a ubiquitous acidic condiment in the world, has a variety of health-pro-
moting properties stemming from its many nutritional and bioactive ingredients
```
(Tamang et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2018). Vinegar is widely consumed and has an indis-
```
```
pensable position throughout Asia, especially in China (Lim et al., 2016), which is
```
one of the world’s major vinegar producers. The annual consumption per capita of
```
vinegar in China is more than 2.3 kg (Li et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018).
```
Traditional vinegar is available from food grains in China. Since discrepant
climatic conditions and main planted crops are displayed in different regions, the
Chinese in all parts have creatively developed distinctive vinegar brewing processes
in accordance with local characteristics and dietary customs. Simultaneously, each
region has established unique selection of raw materials and brewing technologies
for the vinegar production process through long-term practice and experience. The
result is diverse regional vinegar types, such as Shanxi aged vinegar, Zhenjiang aro-
matic vinegar, Fujian Monascus vinegar, Sichuan bran vinegar, Shaanxi Qishan vin-
egar, Tianjin Duliu mature vinegar, Zhejiang rose rice vinegar, Beijing rice vinegar,
```
Shanghai rice vinegar, and Dandong white vinegar (Wu et al., 2012a). Among these,
```
```
the first four are regarded as four famous traditional vinegars in China (Chen et al.,
```
```
2013b).
```
Considering social aspects, this chapter presents an overview of the subject
including the raw materials, properties, and quality characteristics, production tech-
nologies, and the new trends of Chinese vinegar, and aims to provide a better under-
standing of vinegar production in China.
10.2 RAW MATERIALS FOR VINEGAR FERMENTATION IN CHINA
Theoretically, any raw material that contains starch, fermentable sugar, or alco-
```
hol can be used to produce vinegar (Solieri and Giudici, 2008). However, for
```
economical industrialization, the following four basic requirements for the
```
raw materials selection should be taken into account: (1) high enough concen-
```
tration of fermentable sugars to ensure a specified amount of acetic acid in the
```
end-products, (2) the principle of adaptation to local conditions with rich resources,
```
```
(3) easy storage, processing, and conversion, (4) absence of harmful ingredients
```
for the human body and for vinegar quality, in concert with food hygiene stan-
dards. Generally, the common raw materials of Chinese vinegar are divided into
the following categories.

173Vinegar Production in China
10.2.1 main materials
The main materials mainly provide nutrition for the growth of microorganisms and
```
secondary metabolism to form the full taste of the finished product (Liu et al., 2004).
```
```
They can be classified into three types in terms of the main ingredient: (1) starch-based
```
```
cereals and potatoes (e.g., rice, corn, sorghum, wheat, sweet potato, and cassava), (2)
```
```
sugar-based vegetables (e.g., beets) and fruit (e.g., apples, sweet dates, and persimmon)
```
```
(Budak et al., 2014), (3) alcohol-based diluted spirit solution and fruit wine.
```
In general, starch-based materials are the most used type of raw material for tra-
```
ditional Chinese vinegar (namely cereal vinegar) fermentation. They largely derive
```
from local crops, such as rice in the south of China and corn, sorghum, wheat, and
```
millet in the north of China (Liu, 2010; Solieri and Giudici, 2009). More specifically:
```
• Rice with the properties of over 70% of starch content and easy pasting is
```
an excellent raw material for Beijing rice vinegar (Zhang et al., 2006).
```
• Sticky rice, which almost completely consists of amylopectin and delays
the gelatinization progress, is the main raw material of Zhenjiang vinegar
and Fujian Monascus vinegar, conferring a mellow and full flavor to the
```
matured vinegars (Sasaki et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2017).
```
• Shanxi aged vinegar is fermented with a mixture of sorghum, other cere-
```
als, and starter Daqu (accounting for about 60% of the raw material) (Wu
```
```
et al., 2012a).
```
```
• Uncooked pure wheat bran (rich in proteins, starch, cellulose, and hemi-
```
```
cellulose) as the only solid substrate, combined with a unique fermented
```
```
medicinal herb Qu, as saccharifying and fermenting agent (Koji mother of
```
```
vinegar), is the fermentation raw material for Sichuan bran vinegar produc-
```
```
tion (Liu et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2017).
```
Thus, the main materials play a decisive role in the fermentation of the different
types of Chinese vinegar.
10.2.2 auxiliary and paCking materials
Considerable auxiliary materials are integrated in the brewing of traditional Chinese
```
cereal vinegar by solid-state fermentation (SSF), which supplement important nutri-
```
```
ents (such as sugars, minerals, or amino acids) and hydrolytic enzymes (such as
```
```
β-amylase) to improve the color, aroma, taste, and appearance of the end-products
```
```
(Solieri and Giudici, 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2017). In addition, the auxiliary
```
material plays a pivotal role in maintaining homeostasis fermentation. Hence, those
auxiliary materials, such as bran coat, wheat bran, and soybean meal, materially
influence the quality of vinegar. Commonly, chaff, rice husk, sorghum husk, corn
stalks, and corn cob with the properties of large contact surface and hard-to-break
fibers are regarded as packing materials for brewing the solid-state fermented vin-
egar. Moreover, the cellulose-based auxiliary and packing materials provide a loose
```
and aerobic medium in the vinegar Pei (a mixture of all materials of vinegar) to
```
174 Advances in Vinegar Production
promote microbial growth. Furthermore, rice husk and sorghum husk with good
porosity and hydrophilicity are low value by-products and are preferred as packing
```
materials (Kennedy et al., 2004; Qiu et al., 2017).
```
10.2.3 additiVes
Additives, such as salt and sugar, are typically essential for enhancing the soluble
salt-free solid content proportion, adjusting the color and flavor in the matured vinegar,
```
and further improving the traditional vinegar quality (Doyle and Glass, 2010). Salt is a
```
crucial additive agent for vinegar brewing that can reconcile flavor, suppress the propa-
gation of spoilage organisms, and prevent the continued decomposition of acetic acid at
```
a definite period of fermentation (Solieri and Giudici, 2009). Sugar is commonly used as
```
```
vinegar sweetener to regulate the taste of vinegar (Mcdonald et al., 2016). Additionally,
```
spices including yam, aniseed, sesame, ginger, and other natural flavoring substances
confer unique aromas to vinegar. Finally, caramel pigments can add color and flavor
```
to vinegar, and preservatives (e.g., benzoic acid) can be used to extend the self-life of
```
```
the vinegar product (see also Chapter 16, Post-Fermentation Treatments of Vinegars).
```
10.3 PROPERTIES AND QUALITY CHARACTERISTICS
OF CHINESE VINEGAR
Traditional Chinese vinegar comprises plentiful nutrients including organic acids,
amino acids, minerals, and polyphenols that contribute to the sensory quality and
```
functional activity (Li et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2017). An ancient Chinese medical
```
```
text, the Compendium of Materia Medica (a book compiled by the famous physician
```
of traditional medicine Shizhen Li and considered the most comprehensive medical
```
book on traditional Chinese medicine), describes the vinegar’s medicinal functions
```
```
and advantages for human health (Solieri and Giudici, 2009; Xu et al., 2010). Modern
```
scientific research further confirmed that vinegar plays essential roles in improving
```
appetite (Shahidi, 2009), softening the vascular tone (Setorki et al., 2010), allay-
```
```
ing tiredness (Fushimi et al., 2001), regulating blood glucose (Ostman et al., 2005),
```
```
lowering blood pressure (Kondo et al., 2001), degrading cholesterol, and attenuating
```
```
obesity (Fushimi et al., 2006).
```
Thus, available as a common food condiment for flavor and due to its functional
properties, the regular consumption of vinegar is promoted by many nutritional
researchers. Furthermore, the national quality evaluation and grading of Chinese
vinegars is based upon standard sensory and physiological characteristics.
10.3.1 pHysiCoCHemiCal properties of CHinese Vinegar
The physicochemical properties of Chinese vinegar are commonly important indica-
tors for identifying the quality of vinegar and are evaluated by relative density, pH,
total acidity, reducing sugar, total sugar, soluble salt-free solid, total nitrogen, salt,
and ash contents. However, there are certain disparities in these indicators among
```
different vinegars (Table 10.1), mainly derived from the raw materials and the pro-
```
duction processes.
