210 Advances in Vinegar Production
as condiment and preservative, as well as for its healthy attributes. In some countries
```
it is consumed as a drink (Solieri and Giudici, 2009).
```
```
Nowadays, the Codex Alimentarius (1987) defines vinegar as “the liquid, fit for
```
human consumption, produced from a suitable raw material of agricultural origin,
containing starch, sugars, or starch and sugars, by the process of double fermenta-
tion, first alcoholic and then acetous.” Nevertheless, the European Commission
```
in 2015 recognized that acetic acid when diluted with water (4–30% by volume)
```
could be used as a food or food ingredient in the same manner as vinegars from
agricultural origin. However, some European Union Member States still consider
that only vinegars obtained from the fermentation of agricultural products can be
named “vinegars,” while in other states both products obtained from the dilution
of acetic acid with water or by fermentation of agricultural products are accepted
as “vinegars.” According to the United States Food and Drug Administration
```
(FDA) as well as Food Standards Australia and New Zealand, natural vinegars
```
```
must contain not less than 4% (v/v) of acetic acid (USFDA, 1977; Food Standards
```
```
Australia New Zealand Act, 1991). They also consider vinegars produced from
```
synthetic alcohol.
Therefore, there is a huge variety of vinegars produced around the world from
```
very different raw materials (Bamforth, 2005; Solieri and Giudici, 2009). Thus,
```
depending on the available crops in each country, different vinegars have been pro-
duced worldwide.
Vinegar from agricultural origin is produced following a two-step bioprocess:
```
alcoholic fermentation and acetification. Once the fermentable sugars (e.g., glucose,
```
```
fructose, and sucrose) have been extracted from the raw material, the first biotrans-
```
formation is the alcoholic fermentation, carried out by yeasts that convert the sugars
into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Through this transformation yeasts obtain carbon
```
and energy (in the form of ATP) under anaerobic conditions. Afterwards, acetifica-
```
```
tion (also named acetous fermentation although it is not a real fermentation process)
```
```
takes place by the activity of acetic acid bacteria (AAB), during which the ethanol
```
is transformed into acetic acid. This process is highly dependent on the availability
of oxygen as a final acceptor of electrons. AAB can be considered as strictly aerobic
microorganisms due to their dependence on oxygen.
The first conscious elaboration of vinegar was done from wine. Thus, wine
vinegar can be considered “grape” vinegar based on the initial raw material.
```
However, even the word vinegar itself derives from wine (in Latin “vinusac-
```
crum” was a kind of wine from which “vin aigre” in French or “vino agrio” in
```
Spanish derived). Therefore, the term “wine vinegar” is a redundancy. In fact,
```
```
acetification can occur spontaneously when wine is exposed to air (e.g., during
```
```
the last steps of wine making), and this has been traditionally the main cause of
```
```
wine spoilage (Joyeux et al., 1984). It is considered that most wines in old times
```
had higher concentration of acetic acid than those consumed nowadays and that
```
was the main reason for addition of different compounds (honey, sea water, tar,
```
```
spices, etc.) to make them more drinkable. In this chapter, current aspects of vin-
```
egar production from wines or raisins are presented and fields for improvement
are proposed.
211Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
11.2 ELABORATION OF VINEGAR FROM GRAPES
11.2.1 traditional metHods for Wine aCetifiCation
Until the 19th century it was believed that the acetification was a chemical process
of oxidation due to the contact of alcohol with the air. The first report on the micro-
bial role in the acetification process was made by Pasteur in 1864. It was the turning
point that marked a difference in the engineering of vinegar production, leading
```
to improvements in industrial product efficiency and vinegar quality (Llaguno and
```
```
Polo, 1991).
```
Different recipes for vinegar making were developed, according to the raw mate-
rial as well as the environmental characteristics and traditions of each region. Wine
making countries such as Spain, France, and Italy used to produce vinegar from
spoiled or low-quality wines.
There are several ways to process wines into vinegar, although they follow the
```
same principles (Figure 11.1). In small-scale traditional vinegar making, it was com-
```
mon to use a back-slopping method to initiate the acetification of wine, using the
“vinegar mother” as starter. The “vinegar mother” is a mixture of microorganisms,
```
mainly AAB entrapped in a cellulose matrix produced by themselves (Figure 11.2),
```
as also described in the previous chapters. After some weeks or even months, the
```
wine reached an acetic acid concentration of 4–5% (v/v), and other volatile com-
```
pounds were also generated as a result of bacterial metabolism. The resulting prod-
uct was considered vinegar. The mixture of microorganisms was conserved a long
time for successive processes of acetification, and the bacteria adapted to the high
ethanol and acetic acid concentrations were naturally selected.
FIGURE 11.1 Schematic representation of vinegar production from grapes using different
elaboration systems.
212 Advances in Vinegar Production
The Michäelis process, based on the Luxemburgish method to produce wine
vinegar, was performed in barrels with two compartments communicating
through a holey surface between them. At the top of the barrel there were wood
shavings and wine was periodically added to this cavity to feed the acetification
```
process (Figure 11.3a). The bottom compartment collected the wine that went
```
```
throughout the wood (Mecca, et al., 1979). This method was industrially adapted
```
```
by Schützenbach mainly for spirit vinegar production (Llaguno and Polo, 1991),
```
which was named the “German method,” as also described in more detail in the
previous chapters.
The traditional Orléans method, which is still performed in order to produce
high quality wine vinegars, is applied by the modern industry in larger volumes.
The vinegar is made in a static way, and the microorganisms tend to accumu-
late in the surface of the liquid. For that reason, this process is also called the
surface method, as opposed to the submerged methods where the bacteria are
```
dispersed in the fermenting liquid (Tesfaye et al., 2002b; Vegas et al., 2010). In
```
this method, the availability of oxygen is reduced, so it is performed in barrels
or vessels with an open hole, which allows the air contact with the surface of the
```
liquid (Figure 11.3b). To maintain the acetification process and the metabolic
```
activity of the AAB, it is necessary to discharge some vinegar periodically when
the expected acidity is reached. Thereby, new wine is added to the barrel to feed
the acetification process with more ethanol. According to these peculiarities,
in the Orléans method the barrels are not completely filled, and they are never
totally emptied and should always keep a considerable space of air to allow the
oxygen exposure.
FIGURE 11.2 Acetic acid bacteria entrapped in a cellulose matrix during surface acetifica-
tion for wine vinegar production.
213Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
11.2.2 industrial metHods for Wine aCetifiCation
The industry of vinegar production is commonly based on the development of fast
acetification techniques. Contrary to the traditional vinegar production, in vinegar
production for industrial scale, the intentional inoculation of AAB is commonly
performed to make the product more homogeneous and obtain a fast processing
```
(Sellmer-Wilsberg, 2009; Gullo et al., 2014). The bacterial immobilization on wood
```
shavings, although a common strategy, presents drawbacks such as: up to 10% loss
of volatile substance, risk of contamination in the support material, cleaning proce-
dures and systematic conditioning of the bacterial support, accumulation of AAB
over the wood shavings, growth of cellulose producing bacteria on the wood shav-
```
ings, infection of vinegar with “anguillulas” (vinegar eels), and evaporation of etha-
```
```
nol (Llaguno and Polo, 1991; Tesfaye et al., 2002b).
```
Some vinegars are produced with immobilized cells using the surface method
adapted to industrial scale, using pumps to recirculate the unfinished vinegar during
the process facilitating the aeration and temperature control systems. This process
```
can take several weeks until the final vinegar is ready (Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
For that reason, the most commonly used technique in the industrial envi-
ronment to produce vinegar is the submerged process, as described in detail in
Chapter 6. The AAB are submerged in the wine, and they are not fixed on a sur-
```
face (Figure 11.3c). The process is performed in fermenters equipped with tem-
```
perature control and forced aeration systems with or without the addition of extra
oxygen. The systems for acetification made with stainless steel are equipped with
temperature and pH control, cooling unit, aerator, and defoamer, as described in
more detail in Chapter 6. Several systems for submerged acetification have been
developed and patented, such as Frings acetator, cavitator, bubble column fer-
```
menter, etc. (Adams, 1998). However, the Frings acetator is the most widely used
```
system in vinegar production industries, because it is a completely automated
```
fermenter, obtaining a rapid acetification and a homogenous product (Tesfaye
```
```
et al., 2002b). Therefore, in these systems, the loss of volatiles and the risk of
```
```
FIGURE 11.3 Different acetators. (a) Michäelis acetator for Luxemburgish method; (b) Orléans
```
```
acetator for surface method; (c) acetator for quick submerged acetification method.
```
214 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
contamination are reduced compared with the immobilized techniques (Llaguno
```
```
and Polo, 1991; Tesfaye et al., 2002b).
```
In the quick submerged methods, the production can be performed in batch mode,
if the final vinegar is completely discharged after every acetification cycle. Although
the cycles could be reduced to less than 24 hours, this is the usual cycle time in
industrial vinegar plants. On the other hand, it is also possible to conduct continu-
ous fermentation, maintaining a part of the acetified product inside the fermenter
```
in order to inoculate the next cycle (Nieto et al., 1993). Continuous fermentation is
```
performed up to a maximum 9–10% of acetic acid due to the reduction in growth
```
rate of the bacteria when the ethanol concentration is decreased (Sellmer-Wilsberg,
```
```
2009; Gullo et al., 2014).
```
After acetification, the wine vinegar is conditioned by clarification treatments in
order to remove the excess turbidity, which depends on the wine used as raw mate-
rial and the production process performed. Moreover, filtration of the vinegar is also
carried out in order to enhance the stability and the desired brightness of the final
```
product (Mecca et al., 1979; Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
The use of fast technologies for wine vinegar production has a direct impact on
quality. Industrially produced vinegars present lower aromatic complexity. The tra-
ditional methods for vinegar production, on the other hand, are expensive due to the
long times required to carry out the acetification until the desired acidity is obtained
and due to the subsequent maturation steps that are performed to obtain the final
vinegar. However, the resulting product is associated with high quality and unique
organoleptic properties. For that reason, submerged acetification, followed by ageing
in wood, is a trend in industrial vinegar production to reduce the process time and
```
improve the quality of the final product, respectively (Tesfaye et al., 2002b).
```
11.3 TYPES OF WINE AND RAISIN VINEGAR
The wine vinegars are classified with regard to the raw material used for their pro-
duction. They are mainly produced from red wine, white wine, fortified wines, or
raisin wines. In general, the wines used for vinegar production should be:
• Sound and clear, but they can present acetic acid concentration higher than
the limit considered for direct consumption.
• With an ethanol concentration less than 8% v/v. However, the current tech-
nologies allow the use of wines even with 10–12% v/v of ethanol.
• Without residual sugars that can favor the contamination with yeast.
• With a moderate level of SO2 , as AAB are sensitive to high SO2
concentrations.
• With a pH above 3.5.
The temperature for acetification is normally maintained between 30–31°C, when
```
the temperature can be controlled (submerged methods); however, it could be per-
```
formed in the range 28–33°C but with lower efficiency. High temperature increases
the loss of ethanol and volatile substances and could be dangerous for AAB. Another
key factor in the process is the aeration due to the strict necessity of oxygen for the
215Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
growth of AAB. Each type of acetator requires a specific aeration ratio for a correct
```
performance (Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
```
The Codex Alimentarius (1987) establishes chemical differences between wine
```
vinegar and vinegar from other raw materials. Wine vinegar must present at least
60 grams per liter of acetic acid, higher than vinegars from other crops. Also, in wine
vinegar the residual ethanol can be up to 1% v/v, a bit higher compared with the 0.5%
v/v allowed for other vinegars. Moreover, wine vinegar can present less dry extract
```
(1.3 g/L per acetic degree) compared with other vinegars (up to 2.0 g/L).
```
It is noteworthy that wine vinegars contain chemical substances derived from
the wine that have been not metabolized. In grapes, tartaric acid and proline, for
instance, are quantitatively important compounds that are not metabolized by
yeast and are present in wines in considerable amounts. Later, during acetifica-
tion, although AAB could metabolize them, both compounds usually remain in
large quantities. Thus, their presence makes it easy to recognize their natural origin
```
(Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
11.3.1 WHite and red Wine Vinegar
Wine vinegar is produced either from the spontaneous fermentation of grapes or from
wines that are fermented by inoculation of grape musts with specific Saccharomyces
cerevisiae strains. In all cases, the wines can be used for vinegar production directly
after the alcoholic fermentation, and ageing in wooden barrels after fermentation
and before vinegar production will positively affect their aroma complexity. The
wines prior to acetification are diluted with water, and mother vinegar is added
as starter culture to create a mixture with the appropriate composition regarding
bacterial population and ethanol concentration for traditional vinegar production
```
(Vegas et al., 2010).
```
The traditional process allows simultaneous acetification and maturation, but it
```
takes a long time for the desired concentration of acetic acid to be reached (Tesfaye
```
```
et al., 2002b). However, an interesting approach was put forward with the modifica-
```
tion of the barrel shape to increase the surface/volume ratio that reduced the time of
```
acetification by 40–60% without any decrease of quality (Hidalgo el al., 2010b). This
```
```
was one of the aims of the WINEGAR EU Project (“Wood solutions to excessive
```
```
acetification length in traditional vinegar production”). The quality and complexity
```
of the wine used for acetification is related with the composition and aroma of the
```
resulting vinegar (Raspor and Goranovic, 2008). The selection of starters for vin-
```
egar production should include a mixture of species. In fact, during the WINEGAR
Project it was evident that during the production of vinegar there is a succession
of the AAB species: those adapted to low acidity but able to start the acetification
```
process (generally Acetobacter sp., such as A. pasteurianus), and others adapted to
```
high acidity that take over once the acetic acid concentration goes over 4–5% w/v
```
(generally Komagataeibacter sp., such as K. europaeus) (Gullo et al., 2009; Torija
```
```
et al., 2009; Hidalgo et al., 2010b; Vegas et al., 2010).
```
White and red grapes are commonly used to produce still wines selected for
vinegar production. Also, sparkling wines are used as substrate to produce vine-
gar. Champagne and Cava vinegars are produced in regions of France and Spain,
216 Advances in Vinegar Production
respectively. In some cases, vinegar is produced after the first alcoholic fermentation
of wine, or it is made using the disgorging product after the second fermentation
```
performed in the bottle (Lefebvre, 1999).
```
The submerged methods for vinegar production are performed in small fermen-
```
ters of 20–40 m 3 compared with those for alcohol vinegar production (Sellmer-
```
```
Wilsberg, 2009). In this case, the wine is used as raw material and selected cultures
```
of AAB are used as inoculum. Due to the forced aeration used in these systems, the
loss of volatile compounds is higher compared with traditional methods. However,
```
the process is faster and efficient (Tesfaye et al., 2002b).
```
A common practice in vinegar production is the use of flavorings to provide pleas-
ant aromas to the final product. The vinegar can be flavored with several substances
approved such as herbs, spices, whey, sugar, honey, or salt according to the Codex
```
Alimentarius (1987). Normally, there is a maceration step during maturation of the
```
final product that contributes to the complexity of the aromatic profile in vinegars
```
(Lefebvre, 1999). Indeed, the result of vinegar production is related not only with
```
the raw material but also with the metabolism of AAB involved in the process, the
```
interaction of vinegar with the wood from the barrels, and the ageing process (Mas et
```
```
al., 2014). Throughout maturation and ageing the integration of aromas occurs. The
```
interaction with wood and the chemical reactions that occur, such as ester formation,
combined with evaporation, are key events in this step. During ageing, the reduction
of the pungency of acetic acid due to a better integration of aromas and metabolites
```
in the final product results in higher quality vinegars (Mas et al., 2014).
```
11.3.2 sWeet Wine and raisin Vinegars
Special vinegars are produced using over-matured or sun-dried grapes. The vin-
egars from Sauternes wine in France, made using Botrytis infected grapes, present
higher sweetness and flavor complexity than vinegars made with wines from sun-
```
dried grapes. In fact, raisin vinegars have gained popularity in the Greek market (as
```
```
described in Chapter 6), due to their low pungency, an attribute that is considered
```
```
positive by consumers (Lalou et al., 2015). The high initial sugar concentration of the
```
must may lead to the production of wine with considerable residual sugars. During
the acetification process the sweetness from the raw material is equilibrated with the
acidity created by the metabolism of AAB.
On the other hand, common red and white wines used for vinegar production
```
can be supplemented with must with different sugar concentration (concentrated or
```
```
cooked must, caramel or must from raisin grapes) in order to provide additional
```
sweetness to the final product. This process must be not confused with traditional
balsamic vinegar production, in which the grape must is concentrated by cooking in
order to obtain a higher sugar content before the initiation of the alcoholic fermenta-
```
tion and acetification processes (Giudici et al., 2009).
```
Sherry vinegar is produced mainly by two different methods of maturation: static
system and dynamic system, also called the “solera” system. The static system
involves maturation carried out in a single butt. Conversely, the solera system is
based on the refilling of oak butts from less matured vinegar to more aged ones. The
refilling is repeated three to four times a year. The solera system is more commonly
217Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
used for the production of Sherry vinegars and allows acetification and maturation
at the same time. Regarding the ageing duration, these vinegars are differentiated in
Sherry vinegar with at least 6 months of maturation, Sherry Vinegar Reserva with at
least 2 years of maturation and Sherry Vinegar Gran Reserva with at least 10 years.
Moreover, depending on the grape varieties used to produce this special vinegar,
there are two extra appellations:
• Sherry Vinegar Pedro Ximénez: a raisin wine from Pedro Ximénez variety
grapes is added during the ageing process.
• Sherry Vinegar Moscatel: a sweet wine from Moscatel variety grapes is
added during the ageing process.
In both cases, the result is a semi-sweet vinegar that can present a maximum
residual alcohol of 4% v/v. This value is lower for the rest of Sherry vinegars that can
present up to a 3% v/v ethanol and higher acetic acid content.
11.4 CHEMICAL COMPOSITION OF GRAPE VINEGARS
Wine vinegars, independently from the origin of the grapes or raisins, can differ in
chemical composition and complexity. Besides the raw material, the starter culture,
production method, and ageing method used also affect the final product composi-
```
tion (Mas et al., 2014).
```
11.4.1 aCetiC aCid
Acetic acid is the main organic component of vinegars, with concentration com-
```
monly expressed as acetic degree (grams of acetic acid per 100 mL of vinegar).
```
Acetic acid is inhibitory for bacteria. Therefore, during vinegar production AAB
```
remain active just up to 12 grams of acetic acid per 100 mL (Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
The volatile acidity in the case of vinegars is mostly due to the presence of
acetic acid. In fact, the relation between volatile acidity and dry extract has been
```
used as standard for vinegars made from wine (Llaguno, 1972). Other analytic
```
```
techniques such as carbon-14 (14 C) determination have been used to determine the
```
organic origin of the acetic acid. Wine vinegars present unstable 14 C isotopes dur-
ing the growth of vines, which can be detected by liquid scintillation spectrometry
```
(Kaneko et al., 1973).
```
11.4.2 residual etHanol
The aim of vinegar producers is a total transformation of ethanol acid to get the high-
est quantity of acetic acid possible. The control of this process is important because
in absence of ethanol as substrate, AAB can degrade acetic acid transforming it into
carbon dioxide and water. Industrial production of vinegar is based on the conversion
```
of almost all the ethanol to acetic acid; however in traditionally made vinegars the
```
```
residual ethanol is commonly higher (2–3 grams of ethanol per 100 mL). Indeed, the
```
presence of a small ethanol content is required for two reasons: on one side, ethanol
218 Advances in Vinegar Production
inhibits the Krebs cycle, which uses acetic acid, and on the other side it is desired
if the product must undergo the ageing process. During the maturation of vinegar,
alcohol is combined with acetic acid or other acids to produce esters, which provide
```
aromatic complexity to the final product (Llaguno and Polo, 1991).
```
In the final wine vinegar, the ethanol content is limited to up to 1% v/v, except
```
in those cases where there is a regulation by Apellation of Origin (such as in Sherry
```
```
vinegars). Moreover, the amount of ethanol, expressed in mL per 100 mL, summed
```
to the amount of acetic acid, expressed in grams per 100 mL, is called total concen-
tration of the vinegar. In fact, it is the maximal concentration of acetic acid that can
```
be obtained after a complete fermentation process (Gullo et al., 2014). The yield of
```
vinegar produced in a process of acetification is the relation between vinegar con-
```
centration in the mash and the final vinegar (Ebner et al., 1996). Theoretically, this
```
quotient should be constant along the process but that is not always true due to meta-
bolic processes occurring throughout the acetification and also due to evaporation.
11.4.3 aCetoin
Acetoin is always present in wines and in vinegars, and its presence influences the
vinegar aroma. This substance can be oxidized to diacetyl having an impact on the
```
aroma profile of vinegars (see also Chapter 7). Acetoin contents in wine vinegars can
```
vary between 100–400 mg/L depending on the elaboration system used and may be
even higher in those made by the traditional method. The acetoin content in wine
```
vinegars is an important indicator of both quality and origin (OIV, 2000). Moreover,
```
```
this compound is a precursor of tetramethylpyrazine (TMP), a common food flavor
```
```
found in different traditional fermented foods (Zhao and Yun, 2016).
```
11.4.4 glyCerol
Glycerol is commonly produced during the process of alcoholic fermentation for
wine production. The glycerol content is related to the sugar concentration in must
```
and to the fermentation conditions such as temperature or sulfite level (Llaguno
```
```
and Polo, 1991). Normally, white or red wines present 5–10 g/L glycerol. However,
```
wines made with botrytized grapes may present much higher glycerol content, up to
20 g/L. Therefore, the glycerol content in vinegar can be related to the wine used
as raw material. Commonly, quality vinegars have glycerol contents varying from
```
0.6 to 6 g/L (Suárez et al., 1976).
```
11.4.5 free amino aCid and total nitrogen Contents
This parameter is very variable among different types of vinegars. However, positive
correlations have been made between the content of total nitrogen and free amino
acids and high quality of vinegars. Moreover, a distinctive characteristic of wine
```
vinegar is the presence of proline as major amino acid (Polo et al., 1976).
```
The ageing of wine used as raw material for vinegar production is expected to
significantly affect the nitrogen content in the final product. Nevertheless, Álvarez-
```
Cáliz et al. (2014) observed that Spanish vinegars made with biologically aged wine
```
219Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
```
(in which yeasts are present forming a biofilm on the surface of the liquid during
```
```
maturation in wooden barrels) presented a slightly lower rate of acetification com-
```
```
pared with those made from young (unaged) wines, due to the lower content of avail-
```
able nitrogen in the biologically aged wines. Despite that, the nitrogen composition
of both vinegars was very similar, with proline and cysteine being the major amino
acids.
11.4.6 polypHenoliC Compounds
Polyphenols are responsible for the color and astringency of vinegars. These mol-
ecules present high antioxidant activity and are commonly found in plant products.
In vinegars, due to the aerobic metabolism of AAB, the oxygen is a determinant
factor for the rate and outcome of the acetification. The rate of acetification is
related to the solubility of oxygen in the medium, which is decisive for the phenolics
composition. The submerged systems use excess oxygen to ensure and accelerate
the process, whereas in the surface methods the oxygen availability is continuously
limited because it is continuously taken up by the AAB. Each polyphenolic group
```
of compounds is differently affected by oxygen (García-Parrilla et al., 1998), so the
```
production method can generate a differential polyphenolic profile in vinegars. In
fact, in red wine vinegars, a decrease up to 50% has been reported in the contents
of individual phenolic compounds, especially in the case of monomeric antho-
```
cyanins (Andlauer et al., 2000; Cerezo et al., 2008). Conversely, in submerged
```
culture systems when the substrate of acetification was Sherry wine, the phenolic
compounds were not significantly altered either in laboratory or industrial fermen-
```
ters (Morales et al., 2001). Moreover, the antioxidant activity in wine vinegars has
```
found to be reduced when compared with red wines with the same polyphenolic
content. Thus, the process of acetification reduces the phenolic compounds with
higher antioxidant activity, and/or new phenolic compounds with lower antioxidant
```
activity are produced during the process (Dávalos et al., 2005). Furthermore, in
```
```
vinegars produced from Ulugbey Karasi grapes (Turkish variety commonly used
```
```
for raisins production), the surface and submerged production methods affected
```
the bioactive constituents of wine vinegars. The contents of catechin and epicat-
```
echin in industrial vinegar were higher than in traditional vinegar (Budak and
```
```
Guzel-Seydim, 2010).
```
During the ageing process, the polymerization and release of compounds from
the wood and losses by evaporation are common. Several factors affect the pro-
```
cess: ratio of contact between liquid volume and wood surface, type and roasting
```
```
of the wood, and time spent in ageing (Mas et al., 2014). In Sherry vinegars aged in
```
oak barrels for 90 days, there were significant differences in vanillin, syringalde-
```
hyde, coniferyl aldehyde, and cinnamic acid concentrations (Tesfaye et al., 2002a).
```
Moreover, different woods give certain flavonoids to vinegar during ageing. For
```
example (−)-taxifolin is typically released from cherry wood, and (+)-dihydro-
```
robinetin is a characteristic compound released from non-toasted acacia wood
```
(Cerezo et al., 2009). The type of wood used for ageing leads to differences in the
```
organoleptic properties that are also detected by sensorial analysis of the vinegars
```
(Cerezo et al., 2008).
```
220 Advances in Vinegar Production
11.4.7 Volatile aroma Compounds
In quality vinegars, a decisive characteristic is the aroma profile. Aroma derives
from a complex chemical fraction that includes a variety of compounds with differ-
ent volatilities, polarities, and concentrations. It is noteworthy that not all volatile
```
compounds contribute to vinegar aroma. For example, Charles et al. (2000) were
```
able to detect 30 volatile compounds related with aromas in industrial red wine vin-
egars using gas chromatography-olfactometry. Most of these compounds were pro-
```
duced during the acetification process; however, some were also identified in the red
```
```
wines. Later, Callejón et al. (2009) reported the presence of more than 100 chemical
```
substances responsible for Sherry vinegar aroma, including acids, alcohols, volatile
esters, ethers, acetals, lactones, phenols, and carbonyl compounds. In order to study
the individual contribution of each volatile compound to the final aroma, various gas
```
chromatography-based techniques have been developed (Callejón et al., 2008).
```
11.5 WINE AND RAISIN VINEGAR QUALITY
AND SENSORY ANALYSIS
The quality of vinegar depends on different factors that have an impact on the final
```
product chemical composition and physicochemical parameters (Morales et al.,
```
```
2001). These factors have been studied to correlate them with some parametric val-
```
ues in order to evaluate vinegar quality. One of the main hurdles to obtain an effi-
cient method for authentication of vinegars is the wide range of values obtained for
```
the main physicochemical and sensorial parameters (Carnacini and Gerbi, 1992).
```
One of the parameters used for vinegar characterization is the polyalcohol con-
```
tent, which has been considered as an origin discriminator. Antonelli et al. (1997)
```
used capillary gas chromatography–mass spectrometry to determine polyalcohols
```
(xylitol, erythritol, arabitol, mannitol, sorbitol, s-inositol, m-inositol). The results
```
allowed discrimination of the vinegar raw materials at least for white vinegars, mak-
ing it possible to distinguish white wine vinegar from alcohol vinegar and apple
vinegar. Moreover, the use of statistical methods such as multivariate analysis of the
phenolic composition resulted in satisfactory classification of different wine vine-
gars. These methods allowed the differentiation of wine vinegars regarding the type,
ageing time, and geographical origin of the wine used as raw material and also the
```
production system used (Guerrero et al., 1994; García-Parrilla et al., 1997; Tesfaye
```
```
et al., 2002b). Morales et al. (2001) established a method to differentiate Sherry vine-
```
gars produced in laboratory scale fermenter from those made by traditional methods
based on their aroma profile and organic acid content.
Volatile compound profiles have been used to distinguish between quality and
```
defective or adulterated samples of wine vinegars (Nieto et al., 1993). Indeed, the
```
production of the volatile components of vinegars is highly related with the bacte-
```
rial strains and the acetification processes used (Gerbi et al., 1995). Furthermore,
```
```
Sáiz-Abajo et al. (2006) determined 14 parameters using spectral measurement of
```
wine vinegars by near-infrared spectroscopy including total acids, non-volatile and
volatile acids, organic acids, l-proline, solids, ash, and chloride. This method was
proposed for industrial vinegar quality control.
221Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
In any case, one of the main aspects related with quality in vinegars is the sen-
sory character. The standardization of sensory analysis for this product is nec-
essary in order to convey reliable results that can be used for the evaluation and
discrimination of vinegars. Consequently, several efforts were made to normalize
the parameters and nomenclature as well as to train expert panels for vinegar tast-
```
ing (Tesfaye et al., 2010).
```
On the other hand, safety is also a parameter that must be taken into account
when evaluating the quality of vinegars. Generally, the vinegar composition cre-
ates a harsh environment for the growth of other microorganisms apart from AAB.
```
However, the presence of ochratoxin A (OTA) has been reported in commercial
```
red wines and vinegars from Mediterranean countries. The mycotoxin was previ-
ously detected in dried grapes such as raisins and sultanas from Greece and Turkey
```
(MacDonald et al., 1999; Akdeniz et al., 2013). Probably, OTA is present in the raw
```
material and its carry over into vinegars varies from year to year depending on the
```
environmental conditions (Markaki et al., 2001).
```
11.6 GRAPE VINEGAR MICROBIOLOGY
The vinegar production has been traditionally performed using the back-slopping
technique, in which the starter culture is an undefined and uncontrolled mixture
of bacterial strains. Even in industrial acetification, undefined cultures of AAB are
currently used. Although there are differences in the behavior among the different
```
strains of AAB, even those belonging to the same species (Wu et al., 2012), the selec-
```
tion of pure cultures in vinegar production is not always an option.
In order to select a bacterial strain for a production process, the first step is to
carry out ecological studies based on the isolation of strains on solid culture media
and their further identification and characterization. Therefore, genotyping tech-
niques are necessary for this purpose. Moreover, after the strain selection process,
pure cultures of the selected strains must be obtained and maintained to be used as
starter cultures. However, the cultivation and maintenance of pure cultures of AAB
also present hurdles.
As mentioned above, vinegars represent complex, harsh environments for the
```
growth of microorganisms. AAB can survive in these conditions; however their
```
direct recovery on common laboratory media is not always successful due to the
different conditions these media represent. Species derived from extreme environ-
ments that include high ethanol and/or acetic acid concentrations are difficult to
```
grow on common solid media (Sievers et al., 1992; Sokollek et al., 1998a; Millet and
```
```
Lonvaud-Funel, 2000). Therefore, several laboratory media have been designed for
```
the specific plate growth of AAB using different carbon sources such as ethanol,
```
glucose, or mannitol (Entani et al., 1985; Gullo et al., 2006; Vegas et al., 2013).
```
Moreover, for the recovery of AAB from vinegar samples, some specific solid media
```
have been developed that include acetic acid in their composition (Entani et al., 1985;
```
```
Sokollek and Hammes, 1997; Sokollek et al., 1998a). However, those based on glu-
```
```
cose and yeast extract (GY) are the most commonly used due to the better recovery
```
```
of AAB from grape wine or vinegar in comparison to specific vinegar media (Du
```
```
Toit and Lambrechts, 2002; Vegas et al., 2010; Barata et al., 2012).
```

223Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
Culture-independent techniques are also available and useful to detect and iden-
```
tify the presence of AAB species in vinegar bypassing the cultivation step (Gullo et
```
```
al., 2009; Valera et al., 2015). These techniques are based on a high-quality DNA
```
that is representative of all the microbial diversity in the sample. In the case of vin-
egar samples, this is one of the main hurdles for culture-independent approaches
```
(Streit and Schmitz, 2004; Jara et al., 2008). The presence of PCR inhibitors such as
```
polyphenols, tannins, and polysaccharides common in wine or wine vinegars affects
the isolation of DNA in the adequate quantity and quality, which interferes with the
```
efficiency of the molecular techniques (De Vero et al., 2006; Ilabaca et al., 2008;
```
```
Jara et al., 2008; Mamlouk et al., 2011). The use of combined culture-dependent and
```
culture-independent approaches allows a better understanding of the whole micro-
```
biota present in concrete ecological niches (Vegas et al., 2013; Valera et al., 2015).
```
Few ecological studies have been performed in raisin or grape vinegars.
Nonetheless, different species of AAB have been isolated from grapes or grape must
```
mainly belonging to Gluconobacter and Acetobacter genera (Table 11.1). The sound-
```
ness of the grapes is an important factor for the number of bacteria that can be
```
detected on the samples (Barbe et al., 2001). Healthy grapes allow poor recovery
```
of bacteria, and it is usually necessary to use enrichment steps before plating iso-
```
lation (Prieto et al., 2007). The comparison between AAB recovered from sound
```
and botrytized grapes from France resulted in a population one order of magni-
```
tude higher in infected grapes (Barbe et al., 2001). These results agreed with those
```
```
obtained by Joyeux et al. (1984) from French botrytized grapes.
```
The genera Acetobacter and Gluconobacter were also isolated and identified
```
from healthy grapes from the Canary Islands (Valera et al., 2011). Prieto et al. (2007)
```
recovered mainly the species Gluconobacter oxydans and Acetobacter cerevisiae
```
from the healthy grapes of Chile. Navarro et al. (2013) identified five different spe-
```
cies of Gluconobacter genus as well as three of Acetobacter genus from Spanish
grape musts. In this latter work, the authors also reported the presence of Kozakia
```
baliensis. Curiously, Mateo et al. (2014) detected, on healthy and spoiled grapes from
```
Australian vineyards, species belonging to Asaia and Ameyamaea genera, besides
the Gluconobacter and Acetobacter commonly recovered in these environments.
```
In the fermentation process from grape must to wine, González et al. (2004)
```
reported that the species G. oxydans was mainly present in grape must and was
significantly reduced in the first day of fermentation and subsequently disappeared.
Moreover, the population of Acetobacter aceti gradually increased throughout the
```
fermentation. Similar results were reported by Du Toit and Lambrechts (2002) dur-
```
ing white and red wine fermentations, performing the identification using biochemi-
cal and physiological tests.
In submerged vinegar fermentations, the main species obtained was
Komagataeibacter europaeus in both white and red wine vinegar from industrial
```
acetators (Fernández-Pérez et al., 2010). Moreover, in German vinegar acetators,
```
```
Komagataeibacter oboediens was firstly recovered and identified (Sokollek and
```
```
Hammes, 1997). On the other hand, in traditional wine vinegar, Vegas et al. (2010)
```
detected the presence of Acetobacter pasteurianus as the main AAB in the wine used
as substrate and throughout the vinegar acetification, also recovering K. europaeus
in some cases at minor proportions. Similar results were obtained in Turkish grape
224 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
vinegars produced by the traditional method (Yetiman and Kesmen, 2015). These
```
authors described the presence of Acetobacter indonesiensis, Komagataeibacter
hansenii, K. europaeus, and Komagataeibacter saccharivorans in mother vinegars
and these same species together with Komagataeibacter nataicola and Acetobacter
okinawensis in the final vinegar.
Among the limited information available on AAB ecology in vinegar production,
a few studies have been performed on traditional vinegar using selected AAB strains
```
to obtain a highly controlled production (Gullo et al., 2009; Hidalgo et al., 2010a,
```
```
2013a,b). The inoculation studies were developed using selected strains from previ-
```
```
ous ecological studies (Prieto et al., 2007; Vegas et al., 2010; Hidalgo et al., 2013b);
```
a practice that increased the process control, ensuring its correct development and
```
ending (Kersters et al., 2006; Hidalgo et al., 2013b).
```
Based on the results obtained in these studies, they proposed the use of more than
one AAB strain for the inoculation process: one strain belonging to Acetobacter
to ensure the fast beginning of the acetification, and one Komagataeibacter spe-
cies to finish the process, since, in general, the Komagataeibacter species are able
to grow at higher acetic acid concentration, preventing a possible stuck acetifica-
```
tion (Gullo et al., 2009; Hidalgo et al., 2013b). Species such as Gluconacetobacter
```
liquefaciens, Komagataeibacter xylinus, Komagataeibacter intermedius, K. euro-
paeus, and K. oboediens have been found in vinegars with high acetic acid concen-
```
trations (Joyeux et al., 1984; Sokollek et al., 1998b; Schüller et al., 2000; Du Toit
```
```
and Lambrechts, 2002). On the other hand, the Acetobacter population is usually
```
```
maintained during the process of vinegar production with low acidity (Nanda et
```
```
al., 2001). In summary, a good starter culture for vinegar production should be
```
a strain with a high productivity and tolerance to acetic acid and low nutrient
```
requirements (Gullo and Giudici, 2008; Gullo et al., 2014), especially for industrial
```
application.
Several enzyme activities have been studied in relation to the oxidation process
```
in vinegar production such as ubiquinol oxidase (Yakushi and Matsushita, 2010) and
```
```
the enzymatic complexes: alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and aldehyde dehydroge-
```
```
nase (ALDH). The alteration of ADH has been reported to cause a loss of resistance
```
```
to acetic acid for AAB (Takemura et al., 1991; Chinnawirotpisan et al., 2003; Trcek
```
```
et al., 2006). Other genes and proteins have been proposed for their possible role in
```
```
acetic acid resistance in AAB (Fukaya et al., 1993; Matsushita et al., 2005; Nakano
```
```
and Fukaya, 2008), although the whole mechanism remains unknown.
```
11.7 FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
One of the main concerns in the vinegar industry is the development of defined
starter cultures using selected AAB strains. The vinegar production is not station-
ary, and it is subjected to variation of the acetification conditions throughout the
year. Differences in the composition of wines used during the year, the uncon-
trolled parameters of acetification due to technological fails, and the accumula-
tion of pernicious mutations in the bacterial cultures after some acetification cycles
can cause loss of viability, stuck acetification, and unexpected final process results
```
(Holzapfel, 2002).
```
225Current Aspects of Wine/Raisin Vinegar Production
Moreover, the identification and typing techniques should be improved, especially
for the proper isolation of AAB. As previously commented, one of the main hurdles
of ecological studies is the total recovery of AAB on solid media, which is a key
step for the isolation and genotyping of all strains involved in the process. Therefore,
efforts should focus on improving this step, since identification of the main species
involved in the acetification process is currently well-covered.
Different techniques for the specific detection and identification of AAB have
```
been compared in vinegar samples. Vegas et al. (2013) obtained similar results in
```
different culture media and culture-dependent and -independent techniques in sam-
ples of traditional wine vinegar, probably due to the refining of molecular techniques
in the last years. Both types of methodologies are complementary in ecological stud-
```
ies for vinegar production (Valera et al., 2015).
```
As abovementioned, the main characteristics of AAB to be selected as acetifica-
```
tion starters are high productivity and resistance to high acetic acid content (Gullo
```
```
et al., 2014). Nowadays, the industrial production of vinegar is based on obtaining
```
vinegars with high acidity and their subsequent dilution to the acetic acid concentra-
tion required for human consumption. Therefore, higher obtained concentration of
acetic acid during the production process is important from the industrial point of
view, since it represents economic advantages and higher added value of the product.
During the last years, different studies have been performed to understand ace-
```
tic acid resistance mechanisms and high acidity vinegar production (Nakano and
```
```
Fukaya, 2008; Mullins and Kappock, 2013). Several Komagataeibacter species have
```
```
been described as highly resistant to acetic acid (Gullo et al., 2014). Moreover, ther-
```
motolerance is an additional characteristic of AAB strains that could be interesting
```
for their selection as acetification starters (Gullo and Guidici, 2008; Gullo et al.,
```
```
2014). For industrial conditions, the optimal temperature is approximately 30°C, but
```
during the process the temperature increases because acetification is a thermody-
```
namically favorable aerobic process (Gullo et al., 2014). Therefore, different studies
```
have also been carried out to isolate AAB strains that are able to produce acetic acid
at temperatures higher than the optimal ones. Specifically, some strains of the spe-
cies Acetobacter tropicalis and A. pasteurianus have been described as highly resis-
```
tant to acetic acid at 35 and 38°C, respectively (Ndoye et al., 2006). More recently,
```
thermo-adapted strains of A. pasteurianus were obtained by recursive cultivation
```
cycles. These strains are stable during acetic acid production at 40°C (Matsutani
```
```
et al., 2013).
```
Another feature to take into account for the selection of starter cultures is the
```
effective storage and recovery of the strains. Sokollek et al. (1998a) carried out stud-
```
ies, in which freezing in liquid nitrogen resulted in 100% viability. On the other
hand, after lyophilization the recovery was reduced to 90%. This work pointed out
that the storage must be done when the bacteria are in the exponential growth phase
and without high acetic acid content in the samples. However, losses of phenotypic
traits have also been described after freezing. A clear example is the loss of resistance
```
and capacity to produce acetic acid (Ohmori et al., 1982) that must be avoided in the
```
```
vinegar industry. This loss can be related to spontaneous mutations (Okumura et al.,
```
```
1985), as well as to the presence of a high number of transposons in their genomes.
```
```
Recently, Azuma et al. (2009) reported that 9% of the total genes in the genome of
```
226 Advances in Vinegar Production
A. pasteurianus are transposons, which may affect metabolism and response to envi-
ronmental stimuli. The use of cryoprotective substances such as mannitol has been
reported as useful for the maintenance of the phenotypical stability after lyophiliza-
```
tion (Ndoye et al., 2007).
```
AAB produce metabolites that, besides their contribution to the organoleptic
properties of the final vinegar, are able to inhibit the growth of undesirable microor-
```
ganisms and present potential nutraceutical properties (Gullo et al., 2014). Therefore,
```
the study and selection of specific strains with the best features is a promising topic
for the vinegar industry.
Finally, quality control and authentication are equally important for the vinegar
industry for pricing reasons of an added-value product such as vinegar. Therefore,
the development of new technologies to improve the characteristics of the final prod-
uct is imperative. Besides, techniques to detect adulteration or fraud must be refined
to protect the rights of both producers and consumers.

Cider Vinegar Production
Panagiota Tsafrakidou
12.1 INTRODUCTION
Cider vinegar or apple cider vinegar is the vinegar produced by the acetous fermen-
```
tation of apple cider, according to the Codex Alimentarius (FAO/WHO, 2000). In
```
other words, the primal raw material is apple juice or concentrated apple juice that
undergoes alcoholic fermentation, and after that, the produced cider is subjected to a
```
fermentation with acetic acid bacteria, for the final production of the vinegar (Joshi
```
```
and Sharma, 2009). Cider vinegar is consumed and produced in several countries
```
around the world, mainly in the United States of America, the United Kingdom, and
```
Switzerland (Qi et al., 2017).
```
Regarding the composition of cider vinegar in total acid content, it is stated in the
```
Codex Alimentarius (FAO/WHO, 2000) that for vinegars other than wine vinegar,
```
```
the total acid should not be less than 50 g/L (calculated as acetic acid) and not more
```
```
than the amount obtained through biological fermentation. Joshi and Sharma (2009)
```
categorized cider vinegar into “low-strength cider vinegars” and “high-strength
cider vinegars” depending on the acid and alcohol concentration of the cider that
was used for their production. For “low-strength cider vinegars,” a cider with a solute
concentration up to 8–9% is used, while for the “high-strength cider vinegars” this
percentage can reach 13%.
Apart from the food industry, which uses cider vinegar as a flavor enhancing
condiment and as a preservation agent, its consumption has also been associated
with several health benefits such as cardiovascular disease prevention, weight man-
agement, reduced blood sugar levels, reduction of oxidative stress, and pH balance
```
in the body (Halima et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2017). Moreover, its antimicrobial proper-
```
ties against pathogenic forms of bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus

```
aureus, and Candida albicans have been demonstrated recently (Yagnik et al., 2018)
```
with very promising findings for future clinical therapeutic applications.
12.2 CIDER VINEGAR PROCESSING METHODS
The production of apple cider vinegar is traditionally done at both industrial and
```
household scale (Stornik et al., 2016). Native microorganisms that are present on
```
the skin of apples or inoculation with previously brewed vinegar are used in the
traditional method. The spontaneous fermentation is the result of the biochemical
activity of these microorganisms, that float on the surface of the container in which
the fermentation takes place. Uncontrolled conditions and randomness of the raw
material microflora usually result in a time-consuming process and a non-standard-
ized product. On the other hand, the modern industries use bioreactors, also known
as acetators as described in the previous chapters, in order to conduct a controlled
submerged fermentation process with continuous aeration for oxygen supply. These
```
processes lead to reduced times for bioconversion of ethanol into acetic acid (Trček
```
```
et al., 2016). It should be noted, however, that modified traditional methods are also
```
used by certain industries. In the following Figures 12.1 and 12.3–5, the steps fol-
lowed in apple cider vinegar production are depicted.
Depending on the total acidity of the final product that is intended to be produced,
two types of fermentation can take place, either the “low-strength” or the “high-
strength” fermentation. The low acidity obtained from the first type of fermentation
may lead to contamination problems, while the second fermentation type results in
increased nutritional needs for the acetic acid bacteria.
FIGURE 12.1 Apple must production.
235Cider Vinegar Production
12.2.1 general aspeCts of apple proCessing
The first step of cider making is the production of apple juice or concentrated apple
```
juice. Apples are initially cleaned and milled in stainless steel mills (Figure 12.1).
```
The extraction of the juice from the pulp is affected by the pectin content of the
apples. Pectins are fibrous methoxylated galacturonic acid polymers that obstruct the
juice extraction and clarification processes and are also a major cause of membrane
```
fouling during cold microfiltration of apple cider (Kumar and Suneetha, 2016; Zhao
```
```
et al., 2017). The fouling effect is directly dependent on the pectin concentration in the
```
juice/cider. Pectin combines with polyphenols and proteins resulting in colloidal haze
formation with particles having low surface electrical charges, which seem to be the
```
major cause of the membrane fouling (Zhao et al., 2017). Pectin in fresh fruit is usu-
```
ally less soluble, compared to stored fruit, enabling thus an easier pressing process.
An increase of temperature to about 50°C can accelerate and enhance the process.
The extraction and clarification of the apple juice/cider can be improved by the
```
use of pectolytic enzymes (pectinases), which act on the homogalacturonan smooth
```
region of pectins, breaking down the cellular structures of apple tissues, thus facili-
tating the juice release and preventing haze formation. The pectinases can be classi-
```
fied into various categories based on their mode of action (Ramesh and Rosell, 2017;
```
```
Rebello et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017), for example:
```
```
(1) Endo-Polygalacturonase (endo-PG) (EC 3.2.1.15): a hydrolase acting on
```
pectic acid to produce oligogalacturonates
```
(2) Exo-Polygalacturonase (exo-PG) (EC 3.2.1.67): a hydrolase acting on pec-
```
tic acid to produce monogalacturonates
```
(3) Pectin methylesterase (PME) (EC 3.1.1.11): a hydrolase acting on pectin to
```
produce pectic acid and methanol
```
(4) Endo-Pectin lyase (PNL) (EC 4.2.2.10): a lyase acting on pectic acid to
```
produce unsaturated methyloligogalacturonates by transelimination
```
(5) Endo-Pectate lyase (PL) (EC 4.2.2.2): a lyase acting on pectic acid to pro-
```
duce unsaturated oligogalacturonates by transelimination
Commercial pectinases include PLs from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens and B. subtilis,
```
Aspergillus niger, Trichoderma reesei and T. longibrachiatum (with/without gene
```
```
donor; usually from Aspergillus sp.), PMEs from A. niger and A. oryzae, T. reesei
```
```
and T. longibrachiatum (with/without gene donor; usually from Aspergillus sp./A.
```
```
niger), and PGs from A. niger, T. reesei, and T. longibrachiatum (with/without gene
```
```
donor; usually from Aspergillus sp.) (AMFEP, 2018).
```
At research level many studies deal with the production of pectinases, suitable
for apple juice treatment, usually from Aspergillus sp. by solid state or submerged
```
fermentation processes. For example, Mahmoodi et al. (2017) studied the production
```
of pectinases using a wild type of A. niger, isolated from a rotten orange texture,
through solid state fermentation of orange pomace. They specifically optimized the
parameters that highly affect the exo- and endo-pectinase activities, such as tem-
perature, moisture, and C/N ratio. Finally, they evaluated the performance of the
produced pectinases on natural apple juice, showing that the concentration of soluble
236 Advances in Vinegar Production
sugar, clarity and viscosity of the juice, and the juice extraction yield were signifi-
cantly improved by the enzymatic hydrolysis of the studied pectinases.
```
In a similar manner, Zheng et al. (2017) produced highly reactive endo- and exo-
```
PGs by shake-flask production in tobacco industry wastewater using immobilized
Rhizopus oryzae, for applications in the treatment of pectin containing lignocellu-
losic biomass. The immobilized cells led to increased enzyme activity and reduced
production time, compared with free cells, and enabled the semi-continuous produc-
tion of the enzymes in repeated-batch mode in a scale-up bioreactor. More infor-
mation on the recent advancements in the production and application of microbial
```
pectinases can be found in a recent review by Rebello et al. (2017), discussing the
```
strategies adopted for high yield, better catalytic efficiency, and thermotolerance of
pectinases, their significance and industrial applications, the utilization of natural
and recombinant microbial species, and the metagenomic approaches, metabolic
engineering, site directed mutagenesis, and media engineering techniques adopted
in the field of pectinases.
```
According to Heena et al. (2018), the industries apply pectinase twice during the
```
```
apple juice production process (Figure 12.1): (1) in a pre-press treatment, where the
```
apple pulp is treated with pectinase at 30–35°C for 30 min to 2 h, in order to facili-
```
tate the juice extraction by solubilizing pectin, and (2) during the clarification step,
```
where the filtered juice is treated with pectinase to remove the soluble pectin and
with some amylases to remove starch from the juice that can also cause unwanted
haze and gel formation during storage.
A good quality raw material can yield up to 85–95% by weight of expressed juice,
depending on the extraction method. Apple juice normally contains 11% by weight
```
solids (10–11°Brix), 90% of which are carbohydrates and more specifically sucrose,
```
dextrose, and fructose. The juice can be further processed using evaporation, freeze
concentration, hyper-, and/or ultrafiltration to produce concentrated apple juice with
a concentration normally around 70°Brix. The concentrated apple juice can be gen-
```
erally safely stored at 10–15°C without risk of deterioration; however, the degree of
```
```
concentration defines the storage conditions (Ashurst, 2016). The juice is diluted to
```
the desired concentration, prior to the alcoholic fermentation. Water or apple juice
can be used for the dilution.
The juice concentration by evaporation is currently done mainly using thermally
```
accelerated-short-time evaporators (TASTE), where the evaporation takes place by
```
a single pass and short exposure of the juice to high temperatures, preserving the
```
organoleptic properties of the product (COOK, 2018). The juice must be clear; there-
```
fore, pretreatment with pectinases is essential before the concentration of the apple
juice. Another modern system for apple juice concentration is the multistage system
evaporator with tubular falling juice film, which is generally suitable for condensa-
tion of soft fruit juices. Evaporation takes place by distribution of the juice through
```
a series of heating pipes (down-flow) creating a thin film that boils and evaporates.
```
These systems may be suitable for a single pass and/or recirculation of the liquid,
as well as for operation under deep vacuum. They offer short processing times/high
evaporation rates, with low heat impact on the product quality, and can combine
```
pasteurization, aroma stripping, and concentration steps in one system (B&P, 2018;
```
```
Bucher, 2018; Sulzer, 2018).
```
237Cider Vinegar Production
Freeze concentration, on the other hand, is a method that preserves the volatile fla-
vor components of the juice. It is based on the removal of ice crystals from the juice
```
(by screening or centrifugation) after cooling at very low temperatures. Specifically,
```
the steps of a freeze concentration system include: fractional crystallization of water
contained in the juice into ice in a crystallizer, continuous circulation of the liquid
between the crystallizer and an ice crystal growth vessel, and removal of the large
```
ice crystals in a wash column (Figure 12.2) (Ashurst, 2016).
```
Hyper- and ultrafiltration for juice concentration are carried out by means of
selective membranes. Depending on the juice composition and the membrane used,
```
it is possible to lose some flavor components during the process (Ashurst, 2016).
```
Most industrial juice concentration technologies include volatile compound recovery
systems so that they can be returned to the product. Hyperfiltration, although less
efficient, may be advantageous in terms of capital costs, compared to other evapora-
tion systems.
12.2.2 alCoHoliC fermentation of apple JuiCe
Alcoholic fermentation of apple juice takes place under anaerobic conditions, where
the sugars are converted to ethanol by yeasts, usually strains of Saccharomyces cere-
```
visiae (Figure 12.3). The fermentation may be spontaneous, or it may occur by the
```
```
addition of a pure culture to the mash (Ho et al., 2017). Other yeast species that
```
can be found during the spontaneous alcoholic fermentation include Kloeckera sp.,
Hanseniaspora uvarum at the beginning of the fermentation, and Dekkera sp. and
Brettanomyces sp. during the maturation phase, whereas S. cerevisiae dominates at
```
the end of fermentation (Morrissey et al., 2004). The final alcohol content depends
```
on the sugar concentration of the mash and the dominant yeast strains. After the
fermentation, yeast cells and fruit pulp can be either left to settle at the bottom of
FIGURE 12.2 Apple juice cryo-concentration.
238 Advances in Vinegar Production
the tank before cider collection, or they may be removed by centrifugation, a method
that most manufacturers prefer.
12.2.3 aCetous fermentation of Cider
The transformation of cider to vinegar can be accomplished by various methods
that present important differences on the acetification rates and yields. The slower
```
process is the traditional Orléans method (Figure 12.4i). Naturally existing aerobic
```
bacteria from the raw materials, or inocula from a previous batch of cider vinegar
```
making (usually Acetobacter xylinum species), grow at the interface of the cider
```
```
liquid and the air. The oxygen availability is the limiting factor of the process; there-
```
fore, as in the case of wine vinegars, the wooden barrels used are filled to about
75% of the total volume leaving an adequate amount of headspace for contact with
oxygen. The oxygen also enters the body of cider through diffusion from the pores of
```
the wood (Raspor and Goranovič, 2008). The majority of ethanol oxidation to acetic
```
acid takes place at the surface of the liquid, and then the acetic acid slowly diffuses
into the fermenting liquid towards the bottom of the barrel. The acetification rate
FIGURE 12.3 Alcoholic fermentation for apple cider making.
```
FIGURE 12.4 Acetous fermentation processes for cider vinegar making i.) Orléans process;
```
```
ii.) Generator process; iii.) Submerged process.
```
239Cider Vinegar Production
is about 1% of acetic acid per week. This long production period increases the cost
per volume of product, but the high quality of the vinegar produced by the Orléans
methods and the low cost of equipment counterbalances the drawbacks.
The demand for more efficient production, along with the evolution of fermenta-
tion technologies and the better understanding of the processes, led to the develop-
ment of the generator processes, as also described in the previous chapters. These
```
methods involve the use of wooden or stainless-steel tanks (50,000–60,000 L capac-
```
```
ity), with basic operating principle the increased contact area between bacteria and
```
oxygen. This is achieved by using an immobilization carrier for the acetic acid bac-
```
teria (usually beech wood chips) packed in the tanks (generators) (Figure 12.4ii). The
```
cider is sprayed from the top of the generator, while an air blower placed at the bottom
```
provides the required oxygen (Raspor and Goranovič, 2008). A cooling coil for pre-
```
vention of overheating and a recirculation system are also integrated in this apparatus.
The vinegar is recirculated until it reaches the optimum acetic acid concentration.
Subsequently, about 90% of the vinegar is removed from the bottom of the generator
and new cider of equal volume is supplied. This method reduces the cider vinegar
production time compared to the Orléans method, reaching an acid production rate
```
of about 1% per day (Lea, 1989). Another advantage of this method is the continuous
```
```
operation (successive batches) for long time periods and the increased volume of the
```
raw material that is being treated. However, a bottleneck of the process is the cost of
the immobilization carrier, which must be frequently replaced to ensure the viability
of the acetic acid bacteria. Also, other disadvantages include the risk of clogging due
to bacterial cellulose production and the ethanol losses due to evaporation.
As in the case of wine vinegar production, the fastest method, which is preferred
by the cider vinegar industries, is the submerged process based on the modern vin-
```
egar acetator (Mazza and Murooka, 2009; Tesfaye et al., 2002), as described in more
```
detail in Chapter 6. The bacteria are freely dispersed in the fermenting cider and oxy-
gen is supplied, by an efficient and accurate aeration system, through a mechanical
```
agitation system located at the bottom of the stainless-steel acetator (Figure 12.4iii).
```
12.2.4 maturation and paCkaging
Many physicochemical changes take place during the maturation of cider vinegar
that drastically affect the quality characteristics of the final product. The pres-
ence of air, and therefore oxygen, inside the wooden or stainless-steel containers
```
(Figure 12.5), where cider vinegar is matured from 1 month to 1 year, is responsible
```
for the oxidation of vinegar constituents and the amelioration of its sensory charac-
ter. Ethyl acetate, which provides a fruity flavor, may be also produced from the slow
reaction of acetic acid and residual alcohol. In addition, alterations of the color of
cider vinegar appear during maturation. The vivid color of cider vinegar at the first
stages of the processing, which is attributed to the apple polyphenol oxidase, gradu-
```
ally fades as a result of the polymerization of polyphenols (Lea, 1989).
```
Finally, the packaging of industrial cider vinegar may be done either in bulk con-
```
tainers or in bottles, for wholesale or retail distribution (Figure 12.5). Pasteurization
```
of the product, prior to packaging, is mandatory to ensure microbial stabil-
ity. Pasteurization can be achieved by direct heating of the vinegar through heat
240 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
exchangers (e.g., at 66°C), or after bottling, by submerging the containers in hot
```
```
water until the content reaches a temperature of 60°C (Joshi and Sharma, 2009) (see
```
```
also Chapter 16).
```
12.2.5 ClarifiCation
Prior to packaging, a process called clarification is performed in industrial vinegar
production, as discussed in more detail in Chapters 6 and 16. Clarification is manda-
tory in order to obtain a clear product and is also a measure to improve microbial
stability, besides pasteurization. Turbidity of the vinegar is caused mainly by raw
material debris, microbial cells, and flocculated carbohydrates, proteins, and poly-
```
phenols (Joshi and Sharma, 2009; K Onsekizoglu et al., 2010).
```
Chemical agents such as bentonite, gelatin, silicon dioxide, or a mixture of
```
these compounds are used for this fining process. Onsekizoglu et al. (2010)
```
reported that depending on the nature of the turbidity cause, different chemical
agents present effective results. For instance, proteins are better stabilized with
bentonite, while gelatin is more effective with the negative charged polyphenols,
```
as it presents an opposite charge in low pH values. Joshi and Sharma (2009) pro-
```
posed specifically two standard protocols for cider vinegar clarification, involving
the combined addition of gelatin and bentonite or silicon dioxide and gelatin, as
detailed in Chapter 16.
It should be mentioned that the removal of polyphenols may negatively affect the
```
aroma and health benefits of vinegar (Lea and Drilleau, 2003), while the addition of
```
bentonite may influence the fermentation bacteria and reduce the fermentation rates
```
(Duenas et al., 1997).
```
Finally, as discussed in more detail in Chapter 16, the scientific and technological
evolution in the field of membranes led to the replacement of the conventional chemi-
cal clarification by ultra-filtration or micro-filtration using membranes in integrated
```
processes (Onsekizoglu et al., 2010). Membranes have been applied in the processing
```
of various products such as vinegar, beer, milk, and juices. Also, through the method
of cross-flow microfiltration both clarification and sterilization can be achieved in
```
one step (López et al., 2005).
```
FIGURE 12.5 Ageing and packaging of cider vinegar making.

12.3 CIDER VINEGAR COMPONENTS AND QUALITY ASPECTS
The composition of cider vinegar is listed in Table 12.1, based on the Codex
```
Alimentarius (FAO/WHO, 2000) and relevant literature (Joshi and Sharma, 2009;
```
```
Lea, 1989). Apple cultivars, cultivation techniques, and cider/cider vinegar produc-
```
tion technologies affect to a large extent the composition and quality of the final
products. In Table 12.2, testing methods of sampling and analysis for cider vinegar
are also presented.
12.4 RECENT RESEARCH TRENDS
Most of the available scientific research deals mainly with the production and quality
aspects of apple juices and apple ciders, while a very limited number of studies are
found on cider vinegars. The most recent research trends include the investigation of:

• The role of pectin and haze particles in membrane fouling, for the develop-
ment of efficient, commercially viable, cold microfiltration processes for
```
apple cider. For example, Zhao et al. (2017) found that depectinization was
```
```

```
```
fouling is dominated by cake layer formation) and had a negative effect for
```
pore sizes above 0.8 μm.
Specifically, regarding the cider vinegar production, recent studies include:
• The use of molecular techniques for isolation and identification of acetic
```
acid bacteria with specific properties (e.g., high acid tolerance), as well as
```
the monitoring of microbiota present in different types of cider vinegars and
```
their roles in the chemical and sensory properties of the products (Stornik
```
```
et al., 2016; Trček et al., 2016).
```
• The study of fermentation nutrient feeding strategies in order to find the
key substrates that can significantly influence cider vinegar production and
```
quality. For example, Qi et al. (2017) concluded that aspartate, glutamate,
```
proline, and tryptophan should be considered in detail for optimizing the
244 Advances in Vinegar Production
nutritional composition of cider, since their incorporation led to an acetic
acid yield from alcohol higher than 93% and increased the concentration of
most volatile flavor compounds.
• The identification of vinegars in blends through spectroscopic data
```
(Torrecilla et al., 2016a,b).
```
• The improvement in sensory characteristics, bioactivity, and overall qual-
ity of apple ciders with the addition of phenolic compounds that have been
```
recovered from apple pomace (Benvenutti et al., 2019).
```
To conclude, cider vinegar is produced worldwide using a variety of manufacturing
methodologies ranging from traditional methods to continuous automated fermen-
tations. It has a variety of applications, from food additive and preservation agent,
to therapeutic agent due to its bioactive constituents, such as polyphenols, and its
antibacterial activity. However, more research efforts should be conducted in order
to study and fully exploit its health boosting properties and to develop low-cost pro-
duction processes that will result in high quality and added-value products.

Vinegars Made with Kefir
Antonia Terpou and Ioanna Mantzourani
13.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar is defined as “a liquid fit for human consumption, produced from a suitable
raw material of agricultural origin, containing starch, sugars, or starch and sugars
by the process of double fermentation, alcoholic and acetous, and contains a speci-
```
fied amount of acetic acid” (Joint FAO/WHO Food Standards Program, 1987). The
```
word vinegar originates from the French term “vin aigre” which means “sour wine,”
and until the beginning of the 19th century it was thought that vinegar derived from
```
spontaneous acidification of wine (Conner and Allgeier, 1976). Today, despite some
```
small local differences, vinegar is described in food regulations as the result of a
```
double process (alcoholic fermentation and acetification) of any sugar substrate
```
```
(Mas et al., 2014). Modern vinegars can be produced from almost any fermentable
```
carbohydrate source, including wine, apples, pears, grapes, berries, molasses, sor-
ghum, melons, coconut, honey, maple syrup, potatoes, beets, malt, grains, whey, etc.
```
Traditional vinegar production (e.g., made by the Orléans method) requires matura-
```
tion in wooden barrels for lengthy periods in order to obtain a proper acetic acid con-
tent and flavor. The resulting products are generally of high quality and high price.
Nowadays new technologies have been designed for the production of good quality
vinegars, which are faster and with lower production costs.
In this chapter, the production of vinegar using kefir grains is described. Kefir
is a natural mixed culture consisting of small, cauliflower resembling, gelatinous,
white or slight yellowish grains, used to produce dairy beverages by mixed alco-
```
holic and lactic acid fermentation (Garofalo et al., 2015). The matrix that carries the
```
```
kefir microflora (yeasts and bacteria) is composed of an exopolysaccharide called
```
```
“kefiran” (Luang-In and Deeseenthum, 2016). As it is well established that vinegar
```
is produced by a two-stage fermentation process, i.e., the conversion of fermentable
sugars into ethanol by yeasts followed by oxidation of ethanol by acetic acid bacteria
