250 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
(AAB), it is obvious that kefir, which contains both types of species, can be used for
```
the production of vinegar.
The chemical and organoleptic properties of kefir vinegars are a result of the
starter culture and the fermentation substrate. Acetic acid, the volatile organic acid
that identifies the product as vinegar, is responsible for the tart flavor and the pun-
```
gent, biting odor (Mas et al., 2014). In addition to primary metabolic conversion
```
of ethanol to acetic acid, secondary metabolism is also responsible for the typical
vinegar flavor. Small quantities of volatile secondary metabolites are formed during
```
vinegar production, which vary from vinegar to vinegar (depending on the starting
```
```
material, the cultures, and the process conditions), affecting significantly the sensory
```
```
properties of the final product (Raspor and Goranovic, 2008).
```
Chemical analysis of kefir vinegars has revealed enhanced organic acid con-
```
tent and good sensory properties that add value to the product (Viana et al., 2017).
```
Therefore, kefir vinegars can be characterized as novel products of high added value,
and there is a considerable amount of information on the specific role of kefir starters
on vinegar production and quality.
13.2 KEFIR
13.2.1 kefir and kefir-like BeVerages
Fermented dairy products are the most common fermented foods worldwide since
antiquity. Specifically, kefir is a fermented milk beverage consumed for thousands
of years. It is believed to originate from Caucasus, Tibetan, or Mongolian mountains
```
and Anatolia regions (Guzel-Seydim et al., 2011b). The name kefir possibly comes
```
from the Slavic word “Keif ” which means “living well” probably due to the health
```
and well-being attributes provided by its consumption (Rosa et al., 2017). Kefir is
```
also known in different regions worldwide as kephir, kiaphur, kefer, knapon, kepi,
```
and kippi (Rattray and O’Connell, 2011).
```
Kefir is a milk beverage produced by the fermentative activity of kefir grains,
which contain a variety of lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, AAB, and other species, coex-
```
isting in perfect symbiosis, entrapped in a polysaccharide (kefiran) matrix. Kefir has
```
a distinctive fizzy, acid taste, tart and refreshing flavor, depending on the origin of the
grains and mainly attributed to the contained lactic acid, acetic acid, CO2 , ethanol,
acetaldehyde, acetoin, diacetyl, exopolysaccharides, and other fermentation products
```
(Dertli and Çon, 2017). One of its main technological features is that the grains can
```
be recovered after fermentation and be used for the next fermentation batch.
In addition, kefir and kefir-like beverages have been reported to have numerous
health benefits, including stimulation of the immune system, lowering cholesterol,
reduction of lactose intolerance symptoms, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, anti-
```
carcinogenic, and antioxidant properties (Chen et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2005;
```
```
Sharifi et al., 2017). Kefir is also an excellent source of probiotic species with poten-
```
tial health benefits. Recently, the scientific research in order to expand the use of
kefir and its beneficial health effects has focused on alternative ways to use kefir
cultures for fermentation of non-dairy substrates such as fruits, vegetables, molasses,
```
etc. (Fiorda et al., 2017).
```
251Vinegars Made with Kefir
```
Kefiran, the main polysaccharide of kefir grains, comprises 50% of the mass (dry
```
```
basis) of the grains. It is an exopolysaccharide, produced by the lactic acid microflora,
```
```
and can affect the rheological properties of the final product (Guzel-Seydim et al.,
```
```
2011b). The kefir grains microflora (bacteria and yeasts), which are mainly the auto-
```
lyzing type, cannot pass through the kefiran matrix. The production of kefiran can
be affected by fermentation temperature but not by fermentation time. Lactobacillus
```
kefiranofaciens is primarily responsible for the production of kefiran (Dertli and
```
```
Çon, 2017; Zajšek et al., 2011). However, the production of kefiran is also reported
```
by other species such as Lactobacillus kefir, Streptococcus mutans, Leuconostoc
mesenteroides, and Streptococcus cremoris. In addition, kefiran can exert immuno-
modulatory, antimutagenic, antiulcer, antiallergenic, and antitumor properties and
```
can act as a prebiotic substance (Exarhopoulos et al., 2018).
```
Due to the plethora of claimed health benefits, kefir is currently considered one of
the most important functional dairy products, and, consequently, its production and
non-dairy applications are being increasingly developed all over the world.
13.2.2 kefir miCroflora
Different reports on the microbiological composition of kefir grains show that it
```
strongly depends on the origin, culture conditions (medium composition and tem-
```
```
perature), storage, and type of processing (raw material, fermentation time, tempera-
```
```
ture, degree of agitation) (Dertli and Çon, 2017; Fiorda et al., 2017). The microbiota
```
present in kefir drinks and kefir grains include numerous bacterial species from the
lactic acid and acetic acid groups, as well as yeasts and filamentous fungi, which
develop complex symbiotic associations. Yeasts include both lactose-fermenting
```
(e.g., Kluyveromyces spp.) and non-lactose-fermenting species (e.g., Saccharomyces
```
```
spp.). It is not clear whether all kefir products originate from an original culture, since
```
microbial analyses of kefir products from different locations indicate that micro-
```
bial populations significantly differ (Chen et al., 2009; Dertli and Çon, 2017; Fiorda
```
```
et al., 2017). The total number of microorganisms (colony forming units; cfu) in kefir
```
produced by milk fermentation should be at least 10 7 cfu/ml for bacterial species,
```
while the yeast numbers should not be lower than 10 4 cfu/ml (Codex Alimentarius
```
```
Commission, 2011). The microbial species identified in kefir and kefir grains are
```
presented in Table 13.1.
Another important aspect is the composition and stability of the microbial popu-
lation of kefir grains, which are important for the successful production of functional
```
kefir products (Nalbantoglu et al., 2014; Vardjan et al., 2013). In kefir products, lactic
```
acid bacteria are responsible for the conversion of lactose to lactic acid, resulting in
pH drop and thus aiding product preservation through storage. Lactic acid is further
broken down by propionibacteria into propionic acid, which also acts as a natural
```
preservative. Lactose fermenting yeasts convert lactose to ethanol (up to 1–2%) and
```
CO 2 resulting in the bubbling and carbonated character of the product. Other micro-
bial constituents of kefir include non-lactose fermenting yeasts and AAB. Yeasts
produce vitamins, amino acids, and other essential growth factors that are important
for the bacteria. Likewise, the metabolic products of bacteria can be used as energy
```
sources for the yeasts (Miguel et al., 2010). The microbial diversity of kefir described
```

```
in the literature varies greatly (Table 13.1) and has been directly related to the quality
```

of the final product (Nalbantoglu et al., 2014).
```
Following fermentation, the kefir grains increase in biomass by approximately
```
5%, with new grains formed during the process (Dertli and Çon, 2017; Miguel
```
```
et al., 2010). Agitation can affect the microbial composition of kefir, favoring the
```
development of homofermentative lactococci and yeasts. Sugar containing fermen-
tation substrates favor the development of yeasts, lactic acid bacteria, and AAB. As
has been reported in many studies, the individual species found in kefir grains do
not grow in milk or other substrates, and in some cases, they present a significant
```
decrease of biochemical activity (Fiorda et al., 2017; Viljoen, 2001). Kefir grains,
```
on the other hand, due to the symbiotic associations between the different species,
can adapt to different substrates more easily compared to the single-species start-
ers. Therefore, research has recently focused on new substrates, other than milk,
for kefir fermentation, targeting the development of novel functional food products
```
(Kesenkaş et al., 2017).
```
13.2.3 produCtion of kefir
Kefir can be produced using various types of milks, such as bovine, goat, ovine, ewe,
```
and even soy, coconut, and rice milk (Gul et al., 2015). Typically, kefir is produced by
```
```
the incubation of kefir grains in milk at room temperature (25°C) for up to 24 hours
```
```
with a final pH of approximately 4.6 (Guzel-Seydim et al., 2011a). The process results
```
in a unique self-carbonated beverage with an acidic flavor similar to thin yogurt.
```

255Vinegars Made with Kefir
The various fermentation products such as lactic acid, ethanol, CO2 , bioactive pep-
tides, exopolysaccharides, antibiotics, and bacteriocins contribute to the flavor and the
```
functional properties of the final product (de Oliveira Leite et al., 2013).
```
Several methods exist for the production of kefir, while many modern industrial
techniques have been introduced. Various combinations of time and temperature
```
may be applied to the fermentation substrate (e.g., 85°C/30 min, 90°C/15 min,
```
```
90–95°C/2–3 min), which can be then inoculated with either kefir grains or with
```
```
“mother” culture (2–10% w/v), and the fermentation can take place at room tempera-
```
ture in about 24 hours. After fermentation, the kefir grains can be easily removed
by straining.
The traditional method allows production of small volumes of kefir and involves
several process steps. Several interactions determine the composition and activ-
```
ity of the microbial populations (origin and quality of kefir grains, ratio between
```
grains and substrate, duration and temperature of incubation, sanitation conditions,
```
and storage). Generally, traditional kefir has a relatively short shelf-life (2–3 days)
```
```
(Guzel-Seydim et al., 2011a). Also, the sensory properties of traditional kefir may
```
present variations, even among batches of the same process, due to variations in the
process or storage conditions. These quality issues have urged for the development
of more controllable production processes.
In order to standardize kefir products at industrial scale, the production of pure
kefir cultures has been proposed and developed. In addition, refrigerated storage
```
(4°C) can help extend the shelf-life of the kefir products for up to 10–15 days (Singh
```
```
and Shah, 2017). On the other hand, industrial production has altered the traditional
```
character of kefir and may lead to elimination of the wild kefir microflora, which
still has great potential for further exploration and exploitation, mainly regarding its
beneficial health properties.
13.2.4 alternatiVe dairy or non -dairy kefir BeVerages
Vinegar is one of the most widely used food ingredients, with an annual world-wide
production of about one million liters. It is mainly used as a condiment to enhance
```
the flavor and acidity of foods, as well as a preservative (Ho et al., 2017). Although
```
many types of vinegars are produced around the world from a variety of substrates,
some are produced from premium quality wines, carefully aged, and priced based on
their unique sensory properties.
As discussed before, there are two main biotechnological processes involved
in vinegar production: alcoholic fermentation by yeasts, followed by oxidation
of the ethanol to acetic acid by AAB. Any ethanol containing material can serve
as a substrate for vinegar fermentation. According to the Codex Alimentarius
```
(Codex Alimentarius Commission, 1987), vinegar for human consumption must
```
not contain less than 50 g/L acetic acid. The European Union has also estab-
lished specific regional standards that determine white distilled vinegars in the
range 4–7% acetic acid and cider or wine vinegars in the range 5–6% acetic
acid. Following these regional guidelines, a large variety of vinegar production
processes have been proposed, varying in terms of method, raw materials, and
the type of the final product.
256 Advances in Vinegar Production
The numerous positive health effects of kefir, as discussed above, have increased
```
the interest of scientists in its use in novel non-dairy applications (Corona et al.,
```
```
2016; Randazzo et al., 2016). An easy to prepare and most popular non-dairy kefir
```
```
beverage is “water kefir” or “sugar kefir,” which is prepared by fermentation (room
```
```
temperature for 48–96 h) of mixtures of water and sugar with kefir grains, with or
```
```
without the addition of fruit extracts (Laureys et al., 2018). Sucrose is the common
```
sugar used in water kefir production.
Fruits and vegetables, known for their numerous health promoting properties,
are also proposed as substrates for kefir beverages production. These substrates
contain water, sugar, proteins, amino acids, vitamins, and minerals, and in most
```
cases, they do not require extra sugar addition (Duarte et al., 2010; Koutinas et al.,
```
```
2009). Recent studies report the successful use of fruits and vegetables, such
```
as apples, pears, grapes, strawberries, kiwi, cocoa beans, pomegranates, beans,
quinces, carrots, fennels, melons, onions, and tomatoes, for the development of
```
novel, functional, non-dairy kefir beverages (Fiorda et al., 2016; Puerari et al.,
```
```
2012; Randazzo et al., 2016).
```
```
Other substrates, such as soy milk (Liu and Lin, 2000), coconut (Limbad et al.,
```
```
2015), walnut (Cui et al., 2013), rice (Deeseenthum et al., 2018), peanut (Bensmira
```
```
and Jiang, 2015), and cocoa pulp (Puerari et al., 2012), can be used for non-dairy kefir
```
production, after supplementation with sugars in order to stimulate the growth of kefir
microbiota. Other flavoring ingredients may be added to these products, such as cin-
```
namon in “Tapache,” a Mexican pineapple/brown sugar kefir beverage (de la Fuente-
```
```
Salcido et al., 2015). Kefir can also be made from grapes (Gaware et al., 2011), such as
```
```
the “Kefir d’uva” beverages produced by fermentation of diluted grape must (to avoid
```
```
excessive alcohol content) and addition of various aromatic spices. Finally, kefir start-
```
```
ers have been proposed for the production of whey beverages (Magalhães et al., 2011)
```
```
or other whey-based products such as the production of cheese starters (Kourkoutas
```
```
et al., 2006), potable alcohol, and baker’s yeast (Koutinas et al., 2007). Generally, in
```
sugar kefir fermentations, the final products are acidic, refreshing, slightly carbon-
ated, low alcoholic, and may also contain acetic acid as a result of the action of the
```
various symbiotic species present in the grains (Figure 13.1).
```
Some types of vinegars are classified based on the raw materials used. For exam-
ple, the rice vinegars “Komesu” and “Kurosu” are produced by saccharification of
polished or unpolished rice, respectively, alcoholic fermentation of the produced
```
sugars, and oxidation of the ethanol to acetic acid (Nanda et al., 2001). Komesu,
```
which is produced from polished rice, is a colorless vinegar with a plain taste and is
mainly used for sushi cooking. Kurosu, on the other hand, is a black colored vinegar
```
that contains more nutrients (vitamins, amino acids, etc.) and is used as a healthy
```
```
drink (Park, 2018). Another novel vinegar product with improved flavor and quality
```
and potential health benefits is “Elephant garlic” vinegar produced by acetic acid
```
fermentation of rice wine (Kim et al., 2018). “Sichuan” is another type of vinegar
```
produced by 108 different medicinal herbs, while a liquid extract from smartweed
leaves is used to initiate the vinegar fermentation process. Likewise, based on the
substrate of fermentation, many other different types of vinegars have been pro-
duced such as sorghum vinegar, bamboo vinegar, tomato vinegar, onion juice vin-
```
egar, sherry vinegar, apple vinegar, etc. (Ho et al., 2017).
```
257Vinegars Made with Kefir
Another methodology applied in modern vinegar production is the use of immo-
bilized cells in order to enhance the vinegar fermentation yields, as discussed in
more detail in Chapter 7. Immobilization mimics cell aggregation that normally
occurs when microorganisms grow in natural environments. For vinegar production,
```
the bacteria are mainly immobilized on wood chips (de Ory et al., 2004; Kennedy
```
```
et al., 1980; Kourkoutas et al., 2004). The vinegar passes through the bed of wood
```
chips and is collected at the bottom of the fermentation vessel, while it can be recir-
```
culated back to the same fixed-bed of wood chips with immobilized bacteria (Mas
```
```
et al., 2014).
```
Similar to AAB immobilization, immobilized mixed cultures isolated from kefir
grains have also been proposed in order to enhance vinegar production and reduce
```
production and installation costs (e.g., through eliminating the use of centrifugal
```
```
separators) (Viana et al., 2017). Immobilized cell techniques can lead to desired acid-
```
ity during vinegar production within a week and produce vinegar of good quality.
13.3 ΚEFIR-VINEGAR PRODUCTION
Vinegar does not generally reach the high prices of alcoholic beverages but has made
an important contribution to the quality and safety of foods. In addition, vinegar
has been demonstrated to possess health promoting properties mainly due to the
```
antimicrobial effects of acetic acid (Gullo et al., 2014). In the same manner, kefir
```
vinegar can provide the market with a novel and better priced food product with
potential health benefits. As shown in Figure 13.1, there are two main fermenta-
tion processes involved in kefir vinegar production: alcoholic fermentation by
yeasts, and acetification by AAB. AAB are occasionally found in milk kefir most
likely due to oxygen diffusion in the fermentation vessel that triggers their growth
```
(Schlepütz et al., 2013). A wide variety of AAB has been identified in kefir grains
```
```
(Table 13.1), and thus a selective approach should be followed for commercial kefir
```
FIGURE 13.1 Species/fermentations involved in sugar kefir vinegar production.
258 Advances in Vinegar Production
vinegar production. AAB are Gram-negative, strictly aerobic bacteria that belong to
the family Acetobacteraceae of Alphaproteobacteria. The most frequently identified
AAB in kefir grains are the Acetobacter species A. aceti, A. lovaniensis, A. syzygii,
A. orientalis, and other species, as shown in Table 13.1.
The cultivation of kefir microbiota for kefir vinegar production can be done on
```
many different substrates such as vegetables, fruit, and cereals (Fiorda et al., 2017;
```
```
Randazzo et al., 2016; Viana et al., 2017). The alcoholic fermentation usually pro-
```
ceeds rapidly, and most sugars are consumed within the first 3 weeks of fermentation.
The step of alcoholic fermentation has to be carried out under anaerobic conditions.
The second step in kefir vinegar fermentation is the oxidation of ethanol by AAB
to acetic acid under strictly aerobic conditions. The oxygen supplied to AAB will
influence the speed of acetification as well as the sensory quality of the final product
```
(Ubeda et al., 2011). Most kefir AAB microflora are capable of oxidizing ethanol in
```
```
neutral and acidic (pH 3.0–4.0) environments and thus are the main oxidative spe-
```
cies that are able to survive the high ethanol and acidic conditions of vinegar fermen-
```
tations (Li et al., 2015; Viana et al., 2017). The produced organic acids (lactic acid
```
```
and acetic acid) are the dominant flavor components of kefir vinegars (Randazzo
```
```
et al., 2016; Viana et al., 2017).
```
The use of kefir grains instead of selected cultures for vinegar production has the
```
advantage of eliminating the culture harvesting steps (e.g., centrifugation) since the
```
```
grains can be easily recovered and reused (Viana et al., 2017). During the production
```
of kefir vinegar, the evolution of kefir species populations is defined, among other
factors, by the final concentration of acetic acid.
In Figure 13.2, a general scheme is proposed for industrial kefir vinegar produc-
```
tion based on available published studies (Randazzo et al., 2016; Viana et al., 2017).
```
Specifically, the proposed process is based on submerged vinegar production that
involves suspension of the kefir culture in the acetification substrate with the applica-
```
tion of strong aeration. The main steps involved in this process are: (1) preparation of
```
```
raw materials (pressing—dejuicing—milling—saccharification, etc.), (2) loading of
```
FIGURE 13.2 A proposed general scheme for industrial kefir vinegar production based on
the available published studies.
259Vinegars Made with Kefir
```
raw materials for homogenization with or without addition of dilution water, (3) high
```
```
temperature pasteurization, (4) addition of the starter culture (kefir) and fermentation
```
```
of the substrate, and (5) clarification of the product by filtration (Figure 13.2). The
```
```
fermentation unit consists of stainless-steel fermentation tank(s), air supply system,
```
cooling system, and foam control system.
Industrial production of vinegar is mainly achieved by aerobic submerged fer-
mentation, which requires robust AAB able to oxidize ethanol and produce high
acetic acid yield under optimized conditions. Currently, in industrial vinegar pro-
duction, the submerged fermentation is usually conducted by non-selected AAB cul-
tures deriving from previous acetification batches and able to remain viable during
```
repeated cultivation cycles (Gullo et al., 2014). The key points for industrial applica-
```
```
tion of the proposed technology (Figure 13.2) depend on the promotion of submerged
```
fermentation to result in high ethanol conversion and high acid yield.
```
AAB deriving from kefir culture (Table 13.1) are the main microorganisms
```
responsible for kefir vinegar production. Acetic acid is recognized as an effective
antimicrobial compound that prevents the growth of pathogenic and spoilage micro-
```
organisms in fermented food products (Gullo et al., 2014). Therefore, increased
```
safety and shelf-life could be provided in kefir vinegar products by the antimicrobial
```
activity of acetic acid and viable kefir species (Ho et al., 2017; Krátký et al., 2017;
```
```
Viana et al., 2017).
```
13.3.1 sensory and quality CHaraCteristiCs of kefir Vinegars
As in the case of vinegar, the quality of kefir vinegar will be strongly determined by
its sensory properties. Sensory analysis is a valuable tool, by which the organoleptic
properties of foods and beverages can be analyzed by the human senses. However,
one of the difficulties of taste-testing vinegar is the strong contribution of acetic acid
to the overall sensation. Also, the consumer’s perception of a product is an important
factor. The pungency of the high acetic acid content masks other flavors, and for
proper sensory evaluation, a degree of familiarity with this specific type of product
is required by the evaluators. Thus, additional chemical analysis may be required to
properly determine the quality of vinegar.
As discussed in other chapters of this book, chemical analysis has shown that the
aroma-affecting volatile compounds of vinegar generally increase after the acetous
fermentation, when AAB metabolize other alcohols, in a similar way to ethanol, to
```
produce their respective acids (Callejón et al., 2009). Secondary metabolism pro-
```
duces typical flavors and aromas in vinegar, as small quantities of volatile substances
```
(with low threshold values) are formed such as ethane, acetaldehyde, ethyl acetate,
```
butanol, methylbutanol, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, etc. The synthesis and concen-
trations of these compounds vary among the different types of vinegars, depending
```
on the cultures and raw materials involved (Plessi, 2003). In recent years, there have
```
```
been significant advances in the determination of the compounds (including carbon-
```
```
yls, esters, lactones, acids, alcohols, phenols, and acetals) that are responsible for the
```
```
sensory properties of vinegars (Ho et al., 2017).
```
Likewise, in the case of kefir vinegars a large variety of volatile compounds may
be produced due to the large variety and metabolic activities of kefir microbiota
260 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
(Randazzo et al., 2016). Among them, esters are largely responsible for the fruity
```
```
aromas associated with kefir yeast cultures (Nambou et al., 2014). Thus, kefir vinegar
```
flavor will be influenced by the raw ethanolic material, the involved kefir microbiota,
and the applied fermentation process. A characteristic example is apple kefir vinegar,
```
which has been described by evaluators as a sour (acetic acid) product, limpid, and
```
with translucent appearance, and by consumers as a product that 95% of them would
```
purchase and consume (Viana et al., 2017).
```

266 Advances in Vinegar Production
14.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar has a history of more than 4,000 years. For example, in ancient Greece,
a traditionally wine producing area for thousands of years, wine vinegar had its
place in both cooking and medicine. Hippocrates of Kos, a Greek physician, also
known as the “Father of Medicine,” used vinegar to treat various health conditions
```
such as to manage wounds (Johnston and Gaas, 2006). However, vinegar was until
```
recently considered a low-quality product and in some cases not even seen as a food,
since it is made after fermentation of higher quality products, such as wines, fruit
juices, fruits, vegetables, cereals, etc. As discussed in other chapters of this book,
this standpoint has changed, and several recent scientific studies have revealed the
numerous health benefits of vinegar and its potential to be considered as functional
```
food (Samad et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2017; Ho et al., 2017).
```
Almost all materials containing fermentable sugars may be used to produce
vinegar, through a two-step fermentation process: alcoholic fermentation to pro-
```
duce ethanol by yeasts, followed by oxidation of the ethanol to acetic acid (vinegar)
```
by acetic acid bacteria. Vinegar is generally a low-price product, apart from some
```
special vinegars such as Sherry wine vinegars and aged balsamic vinegars; there-
```
fore, inexpensive raw materials can be used for its production, such as substandard
fruits and vegetables, agricultural surpluses and food wastes in general. Also, the
post-harvest losses of agricultural production are very critical for the income of
farmers and the economy in developing countries. Therefore, processing of these
materials into vinegar is a helpful strategy to reduce these losses and to produce
added-value.
Another reason for the exploitation of alternative raw materials and agri-indus-
trial by-products of plant origin is the production of novel types of vinegars with
```
improved organoleptic and nutritional properties, since flavor or functional (bioac-
```
```
tive) components of these raw materials are expected to be delivered to the final
```
vinegar products.
In this chapter, agri-industrial wastes and by-products and alternative raw mate-
rials that have been used, mainly in the scientific research, for vinegar production
are presented. Focus is specifically given to fruit and vegetable sources, excluding
the conventional wine/raisin vinegars, balsamic vinegars, cider vinegars and starch/
cereal-based vinegars.
14.2 FOOD WASTE AS RAW MATERIAL FOR
VINEGAR PRODUCTION
Nowadays the continuous improvement of agricultural practices and their intensifi-
```
cation has led to significant improvement of the availability of food worldwide; how-
```
```
ever it has also led to the generation of high amounts of food wastes (Matharu et al.,
```
```
2016). There are several different origins of food wastes. The so-called “food chain
```
supply wastes” derive from different stages of the supply chain, from production to
```
retailing; however their majority is due to the increasing global economic develop-
```
ment and consumerism. This life trend generates food wastes that are still edible and
267Innovative Vinegar Products
with nutritional value that are discarded due to retailers’ and consumers’ behaviors
```
(Aschemann-Witzel et al., 2015). The results of a study by the Food and Agricultural
```
```
Organization (FAO) suggested that almost one-third of food produced for human
```
consumption is lost or wasted globally. This amount corresponds to about 1.3 billion
tons per year and has a carbon footprint of about 3.3 billion tons of CO 2 equivalent
```
(FAO, 2011). The source of food wastes can also be distinguished according to the
```
economic status of each country. Therefore, food wastes produced at the consump-
tion stage are the case in the industrialized countries, while low-income countries
produce the majority of their food wastes during the first stages of the food supply
```
chain (Ong et al., 2018).
```
Food wastes contain carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and inorganic components,
which can be further digested into simpler organic compounds such as glucose,
amino acids, fatty acids, etc., and their composition varies depending on their source
```
(Lin et al., 2013). Therefore, food wastes can be used in a biorefinery manner and in
```
an environmentally sustainable way for energy, chemical, pharmaceutical, cosmetic,
```
food and other high value-added products (Ong et al., 2018). Following that trend,
```
several food wastes have been used as raw materials for vinegar production, which
are summarized in Table 14.1.
14.2.1 oliVe oil mill WasteWaters
```
In a recent study, olive oil mill wastewaters (OMWs) were used as raw material to
```
```
produce a novel phenol-enriched vinegar at laboratory scale (De Leonardis et al.,
```
```
2018), offering a new alternative for the exploitation of olive oil wastes. Olive oil
```
```
processing (especially the traditional methods) generates a large amount of wastes
```
in the form of wastewater and pomace, with high environmental impact when dis-
carded. On the other hand, these wastes have a high content of phenolics and other
compounds, that could be recovered or transformed into high nutritional and phar-
```
maceutical value (De Leonardis et al., 2007; 2009). De Leonardis et al. (2018) used
```
```
sterilized or crude OMWs enriched with sucrose (200 g/L) and yeast nutrient sup-
```
```
plement (0.5 g/L) for spontaneous fermentation or fermentation by selected yeast
```
and wine vinegar inoculum. The fermentation took place at 30°C for 28 days, and
the product was stored for 15 months in a dark and cool place. After 15 months the
novel OMW vinegar presented similar characteristics to other commercial vinegars
from apple or wine. The most important characteristic of this novel vinegar was
```
its high phenol content (> 3,600 mg/L), especially hydroxytyrosol (1,019 mg/L).
```
```
The latter is recognized as a compound with important antioxidant properties (De
```
```
Leonardis et al., 2007; 2009). The European Union has officially recognized the
```
nutritional importance of hydroxytyrosol, allowing the health claim: “Olive oil
polyphenols contribute to the protection of blood lipids from oxidative stress,”
when at least 5 mg of hydroxytyrosol and its derivatives are contained per 20 g
```
of olive oil (European Union Commission, 2012). In the produced novel vinegar,
```
```
this required content of hydroxytyrosol was reached (De Leonardis et al., 2018),
```
indicating the potential of the novel vinegar to be characterized as functional food
or even as a nutraceutical.

14.2.2 VegetaBle Wastes
Another type of wastes that has been used as raw material for novel vinegar
production is vegetable wastes. For example, potato, pumpkin, carrot and par-
wal wastes were used after boiling for alcoholic fermentation and subsequent
```
vinegar production (Chakraborty et al., 2017). The background of that work, as
```
in the case of OMWs, was that vegetable wastes contain high amounts of com-
pounds with significant nutritional value and potential health benefits, such as
phytochemicals, polysaccharides and pectin, which, if transferred into the novel
vinegar, would provide potential functional characteristics. The results of that
```
study showed that a novel vinegar with appropriate acetic acid content (5.7%)
```
may be produced after 3 days of alcoholic fermentation, followed by 3.5 days for
acetic acid fermentation.
Onion wastes have also been studied as raw material for a new type of vinegar
```
(Horiuchi et al., 1999; Horiuchi et al., 2004; González-Sáiz et al., 2008). This pro-
```
posed new onion vinegar had unique properties and a high potential to be character-
ized as a functional product with high mineral, amino acid and organic acid content
```
(González-Sáiz et al., 2008). The production process was separated in three steps:
```
```
the onion waste was separated to onion solid residues (40% of onion waste weight)
```
```
that could be used as compost after appropriate treatment (Horiuchi et al., 2004), and
```
```
onion juice (60% of onion waste weight). Then the onion juice was used as substrate
```
```
in a two-step fermentation process (alcoholic and subsequently acetic acid fermenta-
```
```
tion) for the new vinegar production. Depending on the onion variety, the content
```
of acetic acid was between 29.4 and 37.9 g/L. In addition, in order to ensure the
effective production of onion vinegar and to control both alcoholic and acetic acid
fermentation processes, a monitoring system was developed based on NIR spectros-
```
copy (González-Sáiz et al., 2008).
```
14.2.3 pineapple Wastes
Another type of wastes that has been used as raw material for novel vinegar produc-
tion is that of the pineapple processing industry. The solid waste from pineapple pro-
```
cessing is estimated to consist of approximately 75% of the fruit (mainly peeled skin,
```
```
core, crown end, etc.) (Abdullah, 2007). This high amount of waste, in combina-
```
tion with the fact that pineapple production is the second highest among all tropical
```
fruits in the world (FAO, 2017), results in massive waste generation. The pineapple
```
```
processing wastes are rich in sugars (sucrose, glucose and fructose) and other nutri-
```
```
ents (minerals and vitamins), and therefore, they have been used to produce several
```
```
products by fermentation, such as ethanol, lactic acid and citric acid (Abdullah and
```
```
Mat, 2008; Upadhyay et al., 2010). Furthermore, pineapple wastes, especially peels,
```
contain considerable amounts of insoluble fiber, mainly cellulose, pectin substances,
```
hemicellulose and lignin (Huang et al., 2011), which after an appropriate pretreat-
```
ment process can be transformed into fermentable sugar. Therefore, the composi-
tion of pineapple wastes makes them ideal as substrates for vinegar production. In
addition, pineapple wastes contain bioactive substances like phenolic compounds
```
(Upadhyay et al., 2010) that may be transferred into vinegar or may be transformed
```
270 Advances in Vinegar Production
into new antioxidant molecules during fermentation, increasing the functional prop-
```
erties of vinegar (Shahidi et al., 2008).
```
The proposed technologies for vinegar production using pineapple wastes consist
```
of four main stages: (1) pretreatment, (2) enzymatic saccharification, (3) alcoholic
```
```
fermentation and (4) acetic acid fermentation. The pretreatment step is necessary
```
```
in order to improve the accessibility of cellulolytic enzymes to their substrate (cel-
```
```
lulose) for the subsequent saccharification.
```
In a recent study, four physical pretreatments were investigated to reduce the
recalcitrance of pineapple waste biomass: microwave heating, boiling, cooking at
```
high pressure with a pressure cooker and with an autoclave (Roda et al., 2016). The
```
use of the autoclave proved to be the most efficient pretreatment to increase the
sugar yield, due to structural modifications induced by pressure on the fibrous matrix
of the pineapple peels and core, facilitating the enzyme accessibility and promot-
```
ing the hydrolysis step (Alvira et al., 2010). The hydrolysate contained only glucose
```
```
and fructose (in total more than 60 g/kg) after the autoclave pretreatment and no
```
```
compounds from non-enzymatic browning reactions (Roda et al., 2016). After the
```
appropriate pretreatment, saccharification follows in order to increase the content
of fermentable sugars for the following fermentation step. In the case of pineapple
wastes, the optimal conditions of enzymatic hydrolysis were at 50°C with cellulase,
hemicellulase and pectinase for 24 h, followed by a 3 h incubation with invertase.
The use of enzymes without pretreatment allowed a sugar yield up to 30 g/kg of waste
```
(Roda et al., 2014), while the highest sugar yield of 72.8 g/kg was achieved when the
```
```
enzymatic hydrolysis was applied after an autoclave pretreatment (Roda et al., 2016).
```
This hydrolysate was fermented by Saccharomyces cerevisiae for 7–10 days under
aerobic conditions at 25°C, yielding 7% alcohol, which was subsequently used for
acetous fermentation by Acetobacter aceti for 30 days at 32°C to obtain 5% acetic
```
acid (Roda et al., 2017). The final pineapple vinegar presented significantly higher
```
concentrations of L-lysine, mellein and gallic acid than the original wine. Another
approach that was used to improve the quality of pineapple vinegar was the use of
```
yeasts and acetic acid bacteria isolated by the pineapple juice (Sossou et al., 2009).
```
```
According to Praveena and Estherlydia (2014), the color of pineapple vinegars
```
varied from light yellow for pineapple fruit wastes, to light brown for pineapple peel
wastes, while their aroma was characterized as mild fruity and acetic. The anti-
oxidant content of pineapple peel waste vinegar was up to 2,077 mg acetate equiva-
lence/100 mL.
Finally, a cost analysis of pineapple vinegar production showed that saccharifica-
```
tion is the most expensive part of the whole process (> 90% of total cost); however, this
```
disadvantage may be eliminated considering the high quantities of pineapple waste
```
generated annually worldwide and the pineapple vinegar prices (Roda et al., 2017).
```
14.2.4 Banana peels
The use of banana peels as raw material to produce a new type of vinegar has
```
also been reported (Byarugaba-Bazirake et al., 2014). Banana peels are the main
```
waste generated during the production and processing of bananas. The peels con-
tain starch, and therefore they can be used for vinegar production. Initially, the
271Innovative Vinegar Products
banana peels were boiled in water to extract the sugars, recovering a solution of
about 7°Brix. After that, sucrose was added to increase the sugar content, and alco-
holic and acetic acid fermentations followed leading, after 28 days, to a vinegar
```
with pleasant aroma (according to consumer evaluation), 6% acetic acid content,
```
5.0°Brix and pH 2.9.
14.2.5 CoConut Water
```
Several varieties of coconut (Cocos nucifera L.) are planted in large areas at tropical
```
and subtropical regions, with a market size continuously increasing. As a result, the
coconut industry generates large amounts of waste, including mature coconut water.
Specifically, more than 200,000 tons of coconut water of overly mature coconuts are
```
disposed after dehusking for the production of coconut oil or coconut milk (Unagul
```
```
et al., 2007). A very promising way to utilize mature coconut water is fermentation
```
```
to produce valuable products such as organic acids (Unagul et al., 2007) and vinegar
```
```
(Truong and Marquez, 1987).
```
For example, in coconut water, sucrose was added to increase the sugar content
```
up to 14°Brix, prior to pasteurization (Othaman et al., 2014). S. cerevisiae was then
```
used for alcoholic fermentation, leading to 6% v/v ethanol after 7 days, while A. aceti
was used to produce vinegar with 4% acetic acid after 4 weeks. In a similar study,
```
coconut water supplemented with sucrose (120 g/L sugars) was fermented by baker’s
```
```
yeast (4 g/L) and A. aceti (5 g/L), resulting in approximately 6% v/v ethanol in 1 day
```
of alcoholic fermentation, and 6.27% acidity after 18 days of acetous fermentation.
The produced vinegar received acceptable scores for attributes such as appearance,
```
odor, sourness and overall acceptance (Ngoc et al., 2016).
```
14.2.6 deComposed fruit and fruit peels
Several studies have also been carried out to evaluate fruit wastes as substrates for
acetic acid production or as sources of acetic acid producing microorganisms for
potential use in vinegar production. As mentioned above, the utilization of fruit and
vegetable peels for vinegar production is economical since they contain considerable
amounts of carbohydrates, which could be converted by the organic acid produc-
```
ing microorganisms. In a recent study, several fruit peels (orange, banana, mango,
```
```
pomegranate and papaya) were screened for total sugar content of their hydrolysates
```
prepared by autoclaving, boiling and acid hydrolysis. The hydrolysates were used
for acetic acid production by A. aceti. The highest sugar content was reported for
banana peels and the lowest for pomegranate peels. Banana hydrolysate with oats
and coconut oil cake as carbon and nitrogen source, respectively, proved to be an
ideal medium, with effective antibacterial and antioxidant activity, to produce acetic
```
acid (Preethi et al., 2017).
```
In another study decomposed fruits like grapes, mangoes, pineapples, oranges,
safeda, etc., were used for the isolation of acetic acid bacteria for potential use in
vinegar production. The results highlighted the potential of several isolated bacte-
ria to be used for vinegar production due to their capability of producing adequate
```
amounts of acetic acid even at high temperatures (Diba et al., 2015).
```
272 Advances in Vinegar Production
In similar studies, Acetobacter strains from Iranian apricot, peach, white and
```
red cherries were isolated and identified (Maal and Shafiee, 2009; Maal et al., 2010;
```
```
Maal and Shafiee, 2010). The strain isolated from apricot showed the best techno-
```
logical characteristics, presenting tolerance against high concentrations of ethanol
```
(even after 4 days incubation) and high acetic acid production (up to 8.53%, after 144
```
```
hours). These characteristics indicated that this strain could be considered as a suit-
```
able industrial strain to produce a new type of vinegar, using apricot fruit or apricot
```
wastes (Maal et al., 2010).
```
14.3 ALTERNATIVE RAW MATERIALS FOR VINEGAR PRODUCTION
In this section, alternative raw materials that have been used in vinegar production
are presented focusing on fruit and vegetable sources, excluding the conventional
wine/raisin vinegars, balsamic vinegars, cider vinegars and starch/cereal vinegars
```
(Table 14.2).
```
14.3.1 Watermelon Vinegar
```
Watermelon (Citrulus lanatus) is a popular refreshing summer fruit with high annual
```
production. It is a highly nutritious fruit containing vitamins, minerals and specific
```
amino acids (Liu et al., 2018). More specifically, it is an excellent source of vita-
```
min C, a good source of vitamin A and B vitamins, especially B1 and B6, as well as
```
minerals such as potassium and magnesium (Quek et al., 2007). In addition, water-
```
melon juice is an ideal source of carotenoids, namely lycopene. It contains almost
```
40% more lycopene than tomato, the most widely known source of lycopene (Holden
```
```
et al., 1999). Therefore, watermelon and its products have a large market potential as
```
a kind of functional food, and for this reason it has also been evaluated as raw mate-
rial for the production of a new type of vinegar.
In a recent study, fresh filtered watermelon juice was used for vinegar production
```
(Chen et al., 2017). Sugar was also added to the juice to increase the sugar content,
```
which is a common practice for vinegar production using fruit juices. The alcoholic
fermentation was carried out at 30°C for 5 days resulting in 9.45% v/v ethanol con-
tent. The produced watermelon “wine” was used for acetic acid fermentation result-
ing in vinegar with about 5% w/v acetic acid content. The vinegar was clear, with no
haze or sediment and a pale-yellow color. The major volatile compounds identified
in the vinegar were ethyl acetate, phenylethyl acetate and phenylethyl alcohol. The
taste of vinegar was characterized as primarily sour, followed by sweet and umami,
and slight bitter, which was attributed to the high sweet and umami free amino acids
and high esters content.
14.3.2 tomato Vinegar
Tomato is the most widely produced and consumed fresh fruit in the world, with a
```
global production in 2017 of about 177 million metric tons (Statista, 2017). Therefore,
```
a lot of surplus, wastes and by-products are also generated. For this reason, toma-
toes have also been used as raw material to produce vinegar. For example, two
