275Innovative Vinegar Products
similar methods were developed for the production of tomato-based vinegar: in the
first method, the tomato juice was mixed with apple extract prior to fermentations
```
(Lee et al., 2013; Seo et al., 2014), while in the second, only tomato juice was used
```
```
(Koyama et al., 2017).
```
```
More specifically, in the first method (Lee et al., 2013), mature tomatoes, without
```
stems, were crushed, mixed with distilled water and fortified with an apple extract
```
(Figure 14.1). A two-step fermentation process was applied: alcoholic fermentation
```
with S. cerevisiae at 30°C for 2 days, followed by acetic acid fermentation with
Acetobacter sp. in a shaking incubator at 30°C and 200 rpm for 8 days, resulting in
tomato vinegar with a total acidity of 5.6%.
```
In the second method (Koyama et al., 2017), the protocol of Mizkan Co., Ltd.
```
```
(Handa, Japan) was followed. In this method the vinegar was made from raw tomato
```
juice by alcoholic fermentation and acetic acid fermentation. Tomato was crushed
```
with water (2.5 kg tomato/L) and after filtration and heat sterilization, the raw, clear
```
```
tomato juice was used for alcoholic fermentation (at 30°C, for 96 h) with S. cerevi-
```
siae as starter and pectinase as promoter of the fermentation, resulting in a product
with 3.6% v/v alcohol. The produced tomato wine and previously prepared unster-
ilized tomato vinegar, containing A. aceti and 7% acid, were mixed in the ratio
7:3, and then acetic acid fermentation was performed at 32°C for 110 h. In the final
product, water was added to adjust the acid concentration to 4%.
In both cases, the tomato vinegar was associated with several health benefits related
to functional compounds, which either derived from the tomatoes or were products
```
of fermentation (Koyama et al., 2017). Indeed, as abovementioned, tomatoes and
```
their products are rich in several health promoting compounds such as organic acids,
```
amino acids, minerals, phenolic compounds, carotenoids (lycopene, β-carotene) and
```
```
vitamins (A, C, E) (Beecher, 1998; Boggio et al., 2000; Alarcon-Flores et al., 2016;
```
```
Siddiqui et al., 2016). Therefore, tomato vinegar is expected to have several health
```
```
promoting effects. For example, in a study by Koyama et al. (2017), tomato vinegar
```
was found to contain anti-hypertensive compounds, such as γ-aminobutyric acid and
potassium derived from the tomatoes and acetic acid and pyroglutamic acid pro-
duced during fermentation. The vinegar also had stronger superoxide dismutase-like
activity than commercial vinegars due to tomato-derived compounds, such as phe-
nolic acids, flavonoids and glutathione. In addition, the tomato vinegar reduced fat
accumulation and insulin resistance, decreased hepatic triglyceride and cholesterol
levels and lowered plasma LDL-cholesterol level and atherogenic index in high-fat
```
diet induced obese mice (Lee et al., 2013; Seo et al., 2014). Therefore, tomato vin-
```
egar could be an effective dietary supplement to regulate body weight, with potential
preventive effects against cardiovascular diseases and obesity.
14.3.3 orange Vinegar
Oranges are fruit with a large production all over the world and have also been
proposed for the production of vinegar, driven by the high production surpluses and
their high nutritional value. Oranges are significant sources of bioactive compounds,
```
such as ascorbic acid (vitamin C), folate, phenolic compounds and carotenoids. The
```
phenolic composition of orange juice includes phenolic acids, mainly ferulic and
276 Advances in Vinegar Production
FIGURE 14.1 Steps involved in vinegar production from different fruit and vegetable
sources.
277Innovative Vinegar Products
```
gallic acid, and flavanones, whose most abundant component is hesperidin (Kelebek
```
```
et al., 2009), while the ascorbic acid content varies (20–100 mg/100 mL) depending
```
```
on the orange variety (Davies et al., 2017). All the above are known to be compounds
```
with high antioxidant activity, and their presence in orange juice has been associ-
ated with reduction of DNA damage and protection against cancer and prevention
```
of degenerative diseases, such as atherosclerosis and coronary heart diseases (Keli
```
```
et al., 1996; Tripoli et al., 2007; Rech Franke et al., 2013; Davies et al., 2017). In addi-
```
tion, alcoholic fermentation of orange juice induces an increase of melatonin levels,
```
which is involved beneficially in various biological processes (Fernández-Pachón
```
```
et al., 2014). All these health benefits associated with orange juice and orange wine
```
are also expected to be presented in the orange vinegar.
Orange vinegar production follows the two-step fermentation process as in tradi-
tional vinegar making. Alcoholic fermentation is performed using Saccharomyces
```
strains; however acetic acid fermentation can be performed either by surface or sub-
```
merged cultures. A comparison of these two methods showed that the final orange
```
vinegar presents different characteristics (Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2018). The vin-
```
egars made by surface fermentation had higher concentrations of polyphenolic com-
pounds, and therefore could be considered as having a higher nutritional value. On
the other hand, submerged fermentation vinegar presented higher levels of acidity,
which was obtained in a shorter time, had higher content of volatile compounds and
received higher scores in sensory analysis.
```
In another study, the effect of different raw materials was evaluated (Cejudo-
```
```
Bastante et al., 2016). More specifically, squeezed orange juice, peeled orange juice
```
and non-peeled orange juice were used as raw material for orange vinegar. Alcoholic
fermentation was completed after 4 days in squeezed and peeled orange juice result-
ing in 5% alcohol content and after 30 days in the case of non-peeled orange juice
resulting only in 2% alcohol. Acetic acid fermentation, using the surface culture
method, resulted in acidities of 4% in squeezed and peeled orange juice and less than
2% in non-peeled orange juice. The use of orange peel in the raw material increased
the polyphenolic and volatile profiles of the final vinegar, while in order to obtain an
optimum flavor of the orange vinegar the initial raw material should be sweetened.
Finally, in order to validate the hypothesis that antioxidant compounds present in
orange juice are also present in orange vinegar, a comparison was carried out with
```
orange vinegar after storage for 6 months (Davies et al., 2017). The results demonstrated
```
a reduction in the antioxidant activity that occurred during the acetification process,
probably due to excess of oxygen content, while during storage no significant differences
were observed. More specifically, after acetification the ascorbic acid was reduced by up
to 50%, the total phenolics by up to 55% and the carotenoids by up to 45%.
To summarize, oranges are a promising raw material for the production of novel,
```
good quality vinegars. According to Coelho et al. (2017), oranges can be used to
```
```
produce wines with relatively high ethanol content (11.5 ± 2.0%) and vinegars with
```
total acidity of 5.3 ± 0.3%. In addition, orange vinegar presents relatively high anti-
```
oxidant activity [11.0 ± 1.7 mmol/L expressed as equivalents of Fe2 (SO 4)3] and good
```
characteristics regarding the volatile compound profile and especially the presence
of monoterpene alcohols such as linalool, a-terpineol and b-citronellol, which are
correlated with orange and citric notes.
278 Advances in Vinegar Production
14.3.4 Bee Honey Vinegar
Bee honey with its numerous health benefits may also be an ideal raw material for
```
development of vinegar products. In a preliminary study (Ilha et al., 2000), the use
```
of bee honey resulted in vinegar that was characterized as similar to traditional wine
vinegars, indicating that it could be easily accepted by consumers. More specifi-
```
cally, during a sensory evaluation, all attributes of the honey vinegar (appearance,
```
```
color, odor and flavor) were highly appreciated. From a technological point of view,
```
approximately 5 L of honey vinegar with 9% w/v acetic acid were obtained from
1 kg of bee honey. The raw material was prepared by diluting honey in distilled
water to 21% total solids content. The alcoholic fermentation was carried out by
S. cerevisiae at room temperature for 84 h resulting in wine with 8% v/v ethanol
content. The acetic fermentation with mixed acetic acid bacteria culture resulted in
vinegar containing up to 9% w/v acetic acid and about 1% v/v residual ethanol.
14.3.5 WHey Vinegar
Another source of vinegar is whey, the bulk liquid by-product of the dairy indus-
try. Whey generation is huge and is continuously increasing worldwide, while the
most studied approach for its exploitation is fermentation. In this respect, whey has
also been evaluated as substrate for novel whey vinegars production. For example,
```
Parrondo et al. (2003) used sweet whey powder diluted with water and supplemented
```
with lactose to reach the desired sugar content. The final concentration of lactose was
139 g/L. The conversion of lactose requires a microorganism with β-galactosidase
```
activity; therefore, a lactose fermenting yeast (Kluyveromyces fragilis) was used for
```
the alcoholic fermentation instead of the commonly used S. cerevisiae. After the
alcoholic fermentation, an ethanol content of 5–6% v/v and a residual lactose of
10 g/L were obtained. Subsequently, acetic acid bacteria isolated from traditional
cider vinegar were used for acetic acid fermentation at 30°C and 250 rpm. The
```
obtained vinegar had an acetic acid content of 5–6% v/v (Parrondo et al., 2003).
```
14.3.6 star fruit Vinegar
```
Another fruit that has been used for vinegar production is star fruit (Averrhoa car-
```
```
ambola L. of the family Oxalidaceae), which is traditionally cultivated in the Indian
```
Subcontinent and Southeast Asia, as well as other parts of the world. The use of
this fruit for vinegar production was proposed due to its numerous health benefits
```
attributed to its high content in vitamin C, vitamin A, iron and fiber (Minh, 2014).
```
The first step in star fruit vinegar production is the removal of tannin to facilitate the
growth and metabolic activity of yeasts and acetic acid bacteria in the subsequent
alcoholic and acetic acid fermentations. Several methods for tannin removal have
been tested, but the combination of NaCl and gelatin proved to be the most efficient.
After tannin removal, the addition of molasses was necessary to increase the sugar
content. Alcoholic fermentation carried out by S. cerevisiae resulted in 7–8% v/v
ethanol content and the subsequent acetic acid fermentation by A. aceti in 43–48 g/L
```
acetic acid (Minh, 2014).
```
279Innovative Vinegar Products
14.3.7 palm Vinegar
Palm has also been used as substrate for vinegar production in the tropics. Several
kinds of palm have been used depending on the variety grown in each area. For
```
example, the juice of Palmyra palm (Borasuss flabelifer), which is native to Thailand,
```
Malaysia, Indonesia and India, is sweet, with neutral pH, oyster white in color and
```
translucent (Naknean et al., 2010). It also contains 110–130 g/L carbohydrates,
```
150–190 mg/L proteins, 0.4–0.8 g/L lipids, 30–40 mg/L ascorbic acid, as well as
```
minerals (Na, K, Ca and Fe), vitamins like A, B and C, amino acids, dietary fiber
```
```
and polyphenols (Barh and Mazumdar, 2008; Ghosh et al., 2012). Palm juice was
```
```
used directly for ethanol fermentation by S. cerevisiae at 32°C for 72 h (Ghosh et al.,
```
```
2014). The produced palm wine was used for vinegar production using A. aceti. In
```
order to increase the acetic acid content, the palm wine was supplemented with a
```
carbon source (glucose, sucrose and glycerol at a ratio of 12:15:2 g/L) and nitrogen
```
```
(diammonium hydrogen phosphate and urea at a ratio of 3:1 g/L) prior to the addi-
```
tion of A. aceti. The method resulted in a vinegar with high acetic acid content up to
```
71 g/L (Ghosh et al., 2014).
```
```
Another variety of palm, namely nipa palm (Nypa fruticans Wurmb.), is also tra-
```
```
ditionally used for vinegar production, by fermentation of “nira” (a nipa palm sap) in
```
```
the East Asian region (Yusoff et al., 2015). Several health benefits have been associ-
```
ated with the consumption of that vinegar, for example, an aqueous extract presented
significant blood glucose lowering effect and improvement of the serum insulin lev-
els up to 80%. Because its antihyperglycemic effect was comparable to metformin,
nipa vinegar was proposed as suitable for consumption by type II diabetes patients
```
(Yusoff et al., 2015; Samad et al., 2016).
```
Finally, in a recent study in Nigeria the production of a palm vinegar was pro-
posed, using palm sap and A. aceti isolated from rotten banana fruits. The palm sap
was fermented for 7 days at 30°C by the yeasts present in the palm sap, resulting in
10.0% v/v final ethanol content. The subsequent acetification by A. aceti for 4 weeks
```
resulted in vinegar with pH 3.5 and 7.1% acetic acid (Samuel et al., 2016).
```
14.3.8 prunus plants Vinegar
Prunus plants are well known for their delicious fruit that, however, have short
```
shelf-life (5–7 days). Therefore, the utilization of surpluses or ripe fruit as substrates
```
```
for vinegar production by solid state fermentation was recently proposed (Zhao et al.,
```
```
2017). The stages involved in the production of this novel vinegar included: clean-
```
```
ing of ripe fruit (Prunus armeniaca × P. sibirica and P. domestica × P. armeniaca),
```
```
ultraviolet disinfection, crushing, addition of sucrose to the pulp (2:5), alcoholic
```
```
fermentation (stationary) by S. cerevisiae (0.2%), addition of acetic acid bacteria
```
```
(1.0 mg/100 mL) and acetous fermentation at either 33°C for 5 days or at 25°C for
```
```
45 days (Figure 14.1). Three different types of vinegars were produced by the above
```
methodology. The content of proteins, fats and non-essential amino acids were lower
compared to kernel-apricot vinegar, but the essential amino acid content was signifi-
cantly higher. These results showed that the fermentation method is important for the
recovery of nutrients from the raw material. Specifically, the vinegar prepared from
280 Advances in Vinegar Production
P. armeniaca × P. sibirica cultivar Zhongren No.1 was rich in minerals and micro-
```
elements (Fe, Mg, Zn and Ca), while vinegar from P. domestica × P. armeniaca cul-
```
```
tivar Fengweimeigui was rich in amino acids (200 mg/L), especially non-essential
```
```
amino acids (188 mg/L). The combination of the above fruit pulps (1:1) resulted in
```
```
vinegar with milder characteristics and balanced nutrient profile (Zhao et al., 2017).
```
14.3.9 roselle Vinegar
```
Extracts of Hibiscus sabdariffa L. (Malvaceae) flowers have been used to produce
```
```
soft drinks as well as vinegar (Kongkiattikajorn, 2014). The dried Hibiscus flowers,
```
commonly called “Roselle,” are used in Chinese herbal medicine to treat hyperten-
```
sion, pyrexia and liver disorders (Tseng et al., 1997). For vinegar production, dried
```
Roselle powder was added to distilled water and supplemented with glucose. The
alcoholic fermentation was carried out by S. cerevisiae resulting in 63.5 g/L ethanol
content, and acetification followed by a mixed culture of A. aceti and Acetobacter
cerevisiae to produce vinegar with 65.2 g/L acetic acid. The Roselle vinegar had
increased content of bioactive compounds and antioxidant capacity compared to
```
Roselle extract and Roselle wine (Kongkiattikajorn, 2014).
```
14.3.10 onion Vinegar
```
Onions are among the vegetables with the highest global production (about 93
```
```
million metric tons in 2017), after tomatoes (Statista, 2017). However, about 15%
```
of their production is disposed as waste due to quality standards or surplus pro-
```
duction (Lee et al., 2017). The consumption of onions has been associated with
```
numerous health benefits like cancer and heart disease prevention, and alleviation
```
of effects associated with ageing or diabetes (Griffiths et al., 2002; El-Demerdash
```
```
et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2017). However, their distinctive organoleptic properties
```
```
(tear-inducing, acidic, spicy, bitter, sour) do not favor their transformation into
```
products easily acceptable by consumers. In order to combine the numerous health
benefits of onions with acceptable organoleptic characteristics, the production of
fermented onion products has been proposed, among which vinegar production
has also been evaluated.
```
For example, the first step in onion vinegar production by Lee et al. (2017) was the
```
```
preparation of vinegar extract, by heating of onions at 121°C for 15 min (Figure 14.1).
```
After filtration and sterilization, sucrose was added to increase the sugar content of
```
the extract (to 12°Brix). S. cerevisiae (1% inoculum) was used for alcoholic fermen-
```
tation at 28°C for 12 h, at 100 rpm and with an oxygen supply of 0.1 vvm. After cen-
trifugation and membrane filtration, onion juice was added to the fermented broth
```
to adjust the ethanol content to 5% v/v, and acetic acid bacteria culture (Acetobacter
```
```
orientalis) was added (5% v/v). The acetification took place at 28°C, 300 rpm and
```
0.2 vvm oxygen supply. The fermentation proceeded in a semi-continuous mode
```
(three-cycle charging–discharging), by removing 75% of the fermented broth and
```
adding the same amount of ethanolic onion juice with an initial acetic acid con-
centration of 1% and an initial ethanol content of 4–5%. The final onion vinegar
```
contained 4.35% acetic acid (reached at 48 h of fermentation), significant amounts
```
281Innovative Vinegar Products
of flavonoids and polyphenols, and antioxidant activity and improved organoleptic
properties compared to commercial onion vinegar.
```
In another study (Horiuchi et al., 2000), red onions were used in a two-step fer-
```
mentation system combining a repeated batch process with flocculating yeast with
a packed-bed charcoal pellet bioreactor, without the addition of any sugar. The use
of the natural onion sugars, compared to the addition of sucrose, is recommended
```
to produce better quality vinegars (Shin et al., 2002). The charcoal pellets were
```
produced from waste mushroom. Specifically, red onion juice with 67.3 g/L total
```
sugar was smoothly converted into onion alcohol (30.6 g/L), by repeated batch
```
operation using a flocculating S. cerevisiae strain. The system was stable for more
than 50 days of operation resulting in 37.9 g/L maximum acetic acid concentration
```
(Horiuchi et al., 2000).
```
14.3.11 pomegranate Vinegar
```
Pomegranate (Punica granatum L.), a fruit native to the Middle East and widely cul-
```
```
tivated in many parts of the world (Middle East, Caucasus, north and tropical Africa,
```
```
central and south Asia, the Mediterranean Basin and California), is well known for
```
```
its numerous health benefits and widely used as a source of nutraceuticals (Ok et al.,
```
```
2013). Pomegranate extract has been used as substrate for vinegar production, and
```
the results showed that the new pomegranate vinegar may exert beneficial effects on
```
adiposity as was proven in in vitro studies (Kim et al., 2013b), high-fat-diet-induced
```
```
obese rats (Ok et al., 2013) and overweight women (Park et al., 2014).
```
```
For pomegranate vinegar production, in a recent study by Kharchoufi et al. (2018),
```
the fruit were cleaned, carefully peeled, the juice was extracted with a domestic
```
juicer, and 100 mg/L of sodium metabisulfite (50 mg/L SO2) was added to prevent
```
spoilage. The initial pH was fixed at 3.5 by addition of 1 g/L tartaric acid, and alco-
holic fermentation was carried out by a commercial S. cerevisiae strain at 25°C, for
```
6 days. Acetic acid fermentation of the ethanolic broth (ethanol content 55–63 g/L)
```
was carried out in a semi-continuous submerged culture laboratory acetator at 30°C,
```
with stirring (450 rpm) and air supply (60 L/h). A Sherry vinegar was used as starter
```
for the first cycle, mixed at 50% with the pomegranate wine. When the acetic acid
content reached 50 g/L, 50% of the volume was discharged and replaced by an equal
volume of wine. Ten cycles were performed in a period of 10 days. The product had
an antioxidant capacity comparable or even better than that of aged wine vinegars
```
and a volatile profile rich in esters (50%) providing a red fruit character as shown by
```
```
the sensory analysis (Kharchoufi et al., 2018).
```
14.3.12 Berry Vinegars
Berries are another type of fruit that has been used to produce vinegar with poten-
```
tial health benefits. Specifically, blueberries (Vaccinium corymbosum L.) have been
```
```
used in traditional medicine due to their antidiabetic (Broca et al., 1999), antioxidant
```
```
(Kim et al., 2013a) and anti-inflammatory properties (Pervin et al., 2016). Blueberry
```
```
vinegar was prepared by Hong et al. (2018) using a two-step fermentation process. In
```
their study, the blueberries were cut, crushed, and water and sugars were added until
282 Advances in Vinegar Production
15°Brix was obtained. Alcoholic fermentation was then carried out by S. cerevisiae,
followed by acetification by Acetobacter sp., resulting in vinegar with 5.3% total
acidity and pH 0.98. The blueberry vinegar presented preventive effects on cognitive
```
functions in a scopolamine-induced amnesia model in mice (Hong et al., 2018).
```
Black raspberries have also been associated with numerous health benefits and
are traditionally used in vinegar production in several Asian countries. For example,
in Korea a traditional Muju black raspberry vinegar is produced with a spontaneous
microbial process that uses seed vinegar from a previous batch process. In that pro-
cess, sugars are also added, and a ripening period of up to 1.5 years usually follows
```
(Song et al., 2016). Blackberries have also been used for vinegar production with
```
```
the addition of sugars, in order to increase the alcohol content (Cunha et al., 2016).
```
As in the case of other berries, the blackberry vinegars were characterized by high
```
antioxidant properties (Hong et al., 2012; Cunha et al., 2016).
```
The berry that has been extensively evaluated for vinegar production is straw-
berry, mainly due to its high production, popularity among consumers around
the world and its nutritional and health benefits as demonstrated by several stud-
```
ies. Strawberries and strawberry-derived products are rich in vitamins (mainly
```
```
vitamins C, E and folic acid), minerals, fiber and phytochemicals, such as ellagic
```
```
acid, anthocyanins, quercetin and catechin (Ubeda et al., 2013; Hornedo-Ortega et
```
```
al., 2017). The phenolic compounds contained in strawberries are highly antioxidant,
```
with potential health benefits, such as antiproliferative effects against cancer cells
```
(Olsson et al., 2006), antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that reduce the risk
```
```
of cardiovascular diseases (Hannum, 2004).
```
Several studies have evaluated the use of strawberries as substrates for vinegar
```
production. In most of these studies, strawberry mash (purée) was used, since the
```
results demonstrated that fruit pressing should be avoided from a technological point
```
of view (Cerezo López et al., 2010). A simple method for strawberry vinegar making
```
```
involved only pasteurization of the strawberry purée (with a sugar content of about
```
```
34 g/L), without any other additions, and a two-step fermentation process (Hornedo-
```
```
Ortega et al., 2017). In a more complex process, to produce vinegar with better char-
```
```
acteristics, sulfite (60 mg/L) and pectolytic enzymes (3 g/hL) were added in the
```
```
strawberry purée (Hidalgo et al., 2013; Ubeda et al., 2013). In some cases, sucrose
```
was added to increase the sugar content, and the acetification was carried out in oak
```
or cherry barrels (Ubeda et al., 2013). However, the addition of sucrose is generally
```
not preferred, and an increase in sugar content could be obtained by concentration
```
of the strawberry purée (e.g., by heating at 80°C for 10 h). However, such a process,
```
although it was found to lead to higher antioxidant activity and total phenolic index
values, may cause practical problems at industrial scale as revealed by a pilot plant
```
experiment (Ubeda et al., 2013). The use of SO 2 and pectolytic enzymes at the begin-
```
ning of the vinegar production process contributed to the increased values in the
```
antioxidant activity, the total phenolics and the monomeric anthocyanins (Hidalgo
```
```
et al., 2013; Ubeda et al., 2013).
```
The type of acetic acid fermentation significantly affects the final aroma of vin-
egar. For example, the use of wooden barrels, and particularly cherry wood barrels,
had a positive effect on all the abovementioned parameters and affected significantly
the aroma of vinegar. Specifically, the use of wooden barrels increased the aroma
283Innovative Vinegar Products
complexity in vinegars, enhancing the sweet and fruity notes, compared to vine-
```
gars kept in glass containers that had “grassy” characteristics (Ubeda et al., 2016).
```
```
Finally, the type of alcoholic fermentation (spontaneous or inoculated) also has an
```
influence on the final aroma of vinegar, with vinegars from inoculated fermentations
```
presenting better characteristics (Ubeda et al., 2012).
```
The acceptability of strawberry vinegar and its market potential was evaluated
by a consumer acceptability test, in which the strawberry vinegars received higher
```
scores than commercial white wine vinegars (Ubeda et al., 2017).
```
14.3.13 persimmon Vinegar
```
Persimmon (Diospyros kaki) is one of the most important fruits cultivated in Japan,
```
Korea, China and Brazil but also in California and several Mediterranean countries
```
(Hidalgo et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2017). Persimmon spoils quickly, and, therefore, its
```
long-term storage is difficult. For this reason, alternative uses for exploitation have
been evaluated, including vinegar production.
Persimmon vinegar was produced by a two-step fermentation process of crushed
```
persimmon pulp after the addition of sulfite (60 mg/L) and pectolytic enzymes
```
```
(3 g/hL) (Hidalgo et al., 2013). Two different processes were carried out: a spontane-
```
ous alcoholic fermentation followed by spontaneous acetification, and an inoculated
```
alcoholic fermentation (with a wine S. cerevisiae strain) followed by acetification
```
without acetic acid bacteria inoculation. The results showed that, from a technologi-
cal point of view, in order to produce persimmon wine and vinegar fruit, pressing
should be avoided and fruit mash should be used instead. Also, inoculation is recom-
mended instead of spontaneous alcoholic fermentation.
The consumption of persimmon fruit has been associated with numerous health
```
benefits, and it has been used for traditional medicine purposes (Giordani et al.,
```
```
2011). Therefore, several studies have focused on the determination of the poten-
```
tial health benefits of persimmon vinegar. The crushed persimmon pulp has a high
antioxidant capacity, which was found to increase even more after the alcoholic and
```
acetic acid fermentations (Zou et al., 2017). Also, persimmon vinegar was found to
```
```
exert anti-obesity (Moon et al., 2010) and anti-inflammatory activities (Lee et al.,
```
```
2016), protection against cellular oxidative stress and inhibition of lipid oxidation
```
```
(Zou et al., 2018).
```
14.3.14 CasHeW Vinegar
Cashew is well known by the corresponding cashew nut, however, the major part
```
of the fruit (the juicy portion or peduncle) is not used. Therefore, an added-value
```
alternative to its disposal is the use for vinegar production. In a study by Silva et al.
```
(2007), after washing, crushing and filtering the peduncle juice, gelatin was added
```
```
(at 10% ratio) to clarify the juice by removing pectin. Pectin should also be removed
```
since during fermentation it is responsible for excess methanol production by the
action of pectin methylesterases. Prior to alcoholic fermentation, the juice was sup-
plemented with ammonium sulfate and potassium phosphate, and potassium metabi-
sulfite was added as preservative. Sugar was successively added in the juice during
284 Advances in Vinegar Production
fermentation to avoid sucrose inhibition. The alcoholic fermentation was carried out
```
by a commercial S. cerevisiae strain (20 g/L) for 48 hours, producing a cashew wine
```
with 102.9 g/L ethanol and 7.12 g/L sucrose contents. The wine was vacuum-filtered,
and it was used for acetic acid fermentation resulting in a cashew vinegar with more
```
than 4% acetic acid content (Silva et al., 2007).
```
14.3.15 JaButiCaBa Vinegar
```
The jabuticaba tree (Myrciaria jaboticaba Berg.) is a member of the Myrtaceae fam-
```
ily native to Brazil. It produces a berry-like fruit, with a smooth black-purple skin
when ripe, which is rich in antioxidant phenolics and vitamin C. Jabuticaba is tra-
```
ditionally used for the treatment of several diseases (Santos and Meireles, 2009).
```
However, its short shelf-life is responsible for wasted surpluses, and, therefore, alter-
natives such as the use for vinegar production have been proposed.
```
For example, Dias et al. (2016) used jabuticaba fruit after washing, crushing and
```
addition of sucrose to the pulp to adjust the sugars concentration to 16°Brix, dipotas-
```
sium bisulfite (0.1 g/L) as antioxidant and disinfectant and bentonite for clarification.
```
The alcoholic fermentation, carried out by S. cerevisiae at 22°C, resulted in a wine
with about 9.5% v/v alcohol after 168 h. The wine was incubated at 10°C for 40 days
```
to facilitate sedimentation; it was filtered through diatomaceous earth and cellulose
```
filters under vacuum and was used for vinegar production. The acetification was per-
formed using a mixed culture of immobilized A. aceti and Gluconobacter oxydans,
```
under controlled conditions (28°C, 0.05 L/min oxygen supply, initial pH 5.0, without
```
```
stirring), resulting in 7.8% acetic acid. Several other acids were also produced such
```
as citric, malic and succinic, which are important for the development of character-
```
istic vinegar taste and flavor (Dias et al., 2016).
```
14.3.16 mango Vinegar
Mango is another fruit that has been evaluated as substrate for vinegar production,
as an alternative to exploit the huge amounts of mango fruit that are lost post-harvest
due to deterioration. Commercial mango vinegars usually are wine or other types
of vinegars blended and flavored with mango puree or mango juice. In an earlier
research study, in order to improve vinegar production from mango and reduce fer-
mentation time, immobilized cells and a semi-continuous process were proposed
```
(Garg et al., 1995). More specifically, S. cerevisiae was recycled to improve the alco-
```
holic fermentation rate, while A. aceti was immobilized on wood shavings and used
in semi-continuous acetification, resulting in vinegar with 5.3% acidity.
```
Later, according to a method developed by Ameyapoh et al. (2010), mango fruit
```
were washed, peeled and cut, and the juice was extracted by mechanical pressure.
The juice was heated at 80°C to prevent microbial growth and to increase sugar con-
```
tent (up to 20°Brix). Alcoholic fermentation was performed at 30°C for 144 h, while
```
the subsequent acetic acid fermentation was carried out at the same temperature for
15 days, resulting in 4.7% acetic acid.
```
Finally, in a recent study by Adebayo-Oyetoro et al. (2017), mango was processed
```
into juice which was divided into two parts: one was supplemented with 20% sugar
285Innovative Vinegar Products
and one with no sugar addition. S. cerevisae was used for the alcoholic fermentation
of both juices at 30°C for 15 days, after which acetic acid bacteria isolated from
wine were added for acetification at 30°C for 15 days. The results showed that pH,
alcohol and gallic acid concentrations were 4.02, 6.17 and 0.513 g/mL, respectively.
The process was proposed as effective and efficient to produce vinegar from mango
juice. The produced vinegar had good physicochemical properties compared with
commercial vinegar and was stable for at least 7 months of storage.
14.3.17 ginger Vinegar
```
Ginger (Zingiber officinale Rosc.) is a well-known and one of the most extensively
```
used spices worldwide to flavor foods and beverages. Moreover, in several Asian
countries it is used in traditional medicine, to treat the symptoms of conditions such
as common cold, digestive disorders, rheumatism, neuralgia, colic and motion-sick-
```
ness. The ginger rhizomes contain gingerols (a group of volatile phenolic compounds)
```
```
and shogaols (the gingerol dehydration derivatives), which are responsible for the
```
characteristic pungent taste of ginger and for biological activities, such as antican-
```
cer, antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and anti-allergenic activities (Yeh
```
```
et al., 2014; Leonel et al., 2015; Semwal et al., 2015). Among the other uses of ginger,
```
the production of ginger vinegar has also been proposed mainly to deliver these
bioactive properties and health benefits into vinegar and to exploit the low-quality
rhizomes as raw material for added-value products. Commercial ginger vinegars are
usually apple, coconut, cane or other types of vinegar infused with ginger.
```
At research level, Leonel et al. (2015), studied the effects of various process
```
parameters for the efficient production of ginger vinegar. Specifically, they used a
suspension of ginger rhizomes containing 12% starch, which was subjected to enzy-
matic hydrolysis to obtain a solution with 8.56% of glucose. The alcoholic fermen-
```
tation of the hydrolyzed substrate was carried out by S. cerevisiae (1.5%) at 28°C,
```
for 48 hours to obtain a wine of 4.03% ethanol. The subsequent acetification of the
ginger wine followed a completely randomized factorial design, with three factors at
two levels. The independent variables were: temperature, addition of nutrients and
```
proportion of “strong vinegar” and alcoholic solution (initial acidity). The results
```
showed a variation from 2.27 to 4.82% for total acidity and residual ethanol levels
lower than 1%. Also, the produced ginger vinegars contained acetic, citric, malic and
```
succinic acids in all treatments (Leonel et al., 2015).
```
Based on the above examples, a general scheme of the steps that may be involved
```
in the production of vinegar from different fruit and vegetable sources (including
```
```
their wastes) is presented in Figure 14.1.
```
14.4 NEW TRENDS IN VINEGAR PRODUCTION
As concluded by the above-described efforts, the vinegar and in general the food
and beverage market is turning towards the development of novel products with dif-
ferent and improved characteristics compared to traditional products. In addition,
the increasing consumer awareness regarding the consumption of healthier prod-
ucts makes the development of new products with functional properties a necessity.
286 Advances in Vinegar Production
Following that trend, vinegar production and research have adapted new methodolo-
gies to produce novel vinegar products with improved sensory and functional char-
acteristics. These techniques include, apart from the use of novel raw materials such
```
as fruit and agri-food wastes, as discussed above, (1) the maceration of conventional
```
```
vinegar products with fruit, (2) the production of aromatized vinegars with fruit,
```
```
spices and vegetables, (3) the fortification of vinegars with dietary fibers and (4) the
```
development of methods to increase the fermentation efficiency and reduce fermen-
tation time or even mimic the storage in barrels, thus accelerating the ageing process.
14.4.1 maCeration WitH fruit
The combination of several traditional drinks with fruit is gaining attention for the
production of novel products with improved sensory properties and health benefits.
The same trend also applies in the case of vinegar, with the maceration with fruit
to increase the health promoting characteristics, alter the organoleptic characteris-
```
tics and generally influence positively the quality of vinegar (Cejudo-Bastante et al.,
```
```
2013a, 2010). The aroma of the final vinegar product consists of volatile compounds
```
already present in the traditional vinegar and those derived from the added fruit,
resulting in a totally new product. This method for improving the characteristics of
vinegar has been a common practice in Asian countries for a long time, where some
```
products can be found in the markets, but is still limited in the rest of the world (Wu
```
```
et al., 2007; Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2013a).
```
```
In a work by Cejudo-Bastante et al. (2013a), the maceration process consisted of
```
the addition of fruit in fresh vinegar for up to 7 days, at room temperature or heat-
ing up to 40°C. Only peels or a combination of peels and pulp were proposed for
addition to the vinegar. Specifically, the maceration of Sherry wine vinegar with
several fruits, such as orange, lemon, strawberry, grapefruit and lime, was evaluated
regarding the volatile profiles and the sensory characteristics of the final products.
The results showed that the use of different amounts of fruit led to vinegars with dif-
ferent characteristics. In general, the use of lemon, lime and orange resulted in the
increase of fruity volatile characters, with a high content of terpenic compounds. On
the other hand, the use of strawberry did not affect the volatile profile of vinegars.
The sensory evaluation revealed that the use of the highest amount of fruit during
maceration led to vinegars that received higher preference scores by the evaluators.
The work concluded that the use of maceration with fruit may lead to totally new
vinegar products with the addition of only 4 to 7 days processing, which may expand
```
the vinegar’s market (Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2013a).
```
14.4.2 aromatized Vinegar
A similar method to the maceration of vinegars with fruits is to aromatize them
with the addition of extracts and infusions from different sources, in order to pro-
duce vinegars with improved sensory characteristics, different flavors and improved
```
bioactive (e.g., antioxidant) properties. Several vinegar products are available in the
```
international markets, aromatized with extracts from fruit, spices, herbs, vegetables
```
and mushrooms (Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2013b). Some examples are the use of white
```
287Innovative Vinegar Products
and black truffle, raspberry, garlic, lemon, rosemary, tarragon, raspberry, bay leaf,
parsley, thyme, clove, fennel, basil, caper, red and green pepper, onion, tomato, car-
rot, chili and others. These raw materials have been selected mainly in order to
increase the content of phenolic compounds and the antioxidant activity of vine-
gars. Specifically, vinegars aromatized with black truffle and rosemary presented
the highest values of antioxidant activity, followed by those aromatized with lemon,
tarragon, aromatic herbs and vegetables. Vinegar with black truffle had a high con-
tent of 5-hydroxy-methylfurfural, followed by trans-caftaric acid and trans-coutaric
acid, while in vinegar with rosemary the main phenolic compounds identified were
tyrosol and caffeic acid. Therefore, it was concluded that the antioxidant activity
of a vinegar depends on the simultaneous presence of various phenolic compounds
```
(Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2013b). The aroma analysis of these vinegars showed that
```
each different vinegar presented a unique profile of volatile compounds, indicating
potential to develop novel distinctive products based on the same wine vinegar.
14.4.3 Vinegar WitH HigH dietary fiBer Content
The enrichment of vinegar with dietary fiber has also been proposed, due to the
increasing demands of the food and enological market for diversification and
improvement of the nutritional value. In a similar manner as in the previous meth-
ods discussed, the addition of fiber from fruit in Sherry vinegars, and especially
```
citrus fruit, was proposed by Marrufo-Curtido et al. (2015). The enriched vinegars
```
presented improved polyphenolic and flavor profile. Specifically, the addition of
orange fiber resulted in higher volatile compound content, while lemon fiber resulted
in higher polyphenol content. The characteristic citric flavor of the new vinegars
increased their acceptability during the sensory evaluations compared to traditional
vinegars.
14.4.4 optimization of Vinegar fermentation
In vinegar production, acetification is the most important step, regarding both con-
version efficiency and rate, while the alcoholic fermentation is easy to control and
usually proceeds at high rates. The main problem associated with acetic acid fer-
mentation is the inhibitory effect of acidity on the growth and activity of the acetic
acid bacteria, that may lead to stuck fermentation and low acidity vinegars with high
residual sugars content. Acidity levels up to 10 g/L allow the growth of acetic acid
bacteria, levels higher than 20–40 g/L are inhibitive, and above 60 g/L the bacterial
```
growth is limited (De Ory et al., 2002). Several methodologies have been adopted
```
to reduce this inhibitory effect in order to increase the acetic acid fermentation rate
```
and yield and to improve vinegar quality. According to Tesfaye et al. (2002), these
```
```
methods can be categorized into three groups: (1) the design of better acetification
```
```
systems, (2) the selection of more productive bacteria (resistant to high temperatures,
```
```
substrate densities and product concentrations) and (3) the optimization of process
```
parameters.
The submerged acetification, where the acetic acid bacteria are suspended in the
substrate and strong aeration is applied, is the predominant method used currently to
288 Advances in Vinegar Production
produce commercial vinegars. The submerged acetification systems can be operated
in batch, semi-continuous and continuous mode, and, as discussed in previous chap-
ters, several acetators have been designed and patented such as the Frings acetator,
the cavitator, the bubble column fermenter and fermenters with different aeration
```
systems like the jet or effigas turbine (vinegator) (Tesfaye et al., 2002).
```
Several studies have also been carried out to find and optimize the ideal condi-
tions for an efficient acetification process. For example, in semi-continuous sys-
tems, parameters that have been studied to obtain the ideal cell growth and to
increase the fermentation rate include the monitoring of the ratio of oxygen con-
```
sumption versus the acid yield (Qi et al., 2013), and the optimal discharge/charge
```
```
ratios (Qi et al., 2014a). The enzyme systems of the acetic acid bacteria have also
```
been studied in order to optimize the acetification process. More specifically, the
alcohol respiratory chain of acetic acid bacteria, which is located on intracellular
membranes, is directly responsible for the efficiency of the vinegar fermentation.
Therefore, acetification was enhanced by the addition of precursors of alcohol
respiratory chain associated factors, such as ferrous ions and β-hydroxybenzoic
```
acid, as well as by increasing the aeration rate (Qi et al., 2014b). In another study,
```
the rate-limiting enzyme, which is responsible for the ethanol oxidation route, was
```
identified [pyrroloquinolinequinone (PQQ)-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase
```
```
(ALDH)], and several coenzyme Q precursors were added to increase fermentation
```
```
rate, with isopentenyl alcohol providing the best results (Xia et al., 2015). In a sim-
```
```
ilar manner, Gómez-Manzo et al. (2015) presented evidence that the membrane-
```
```
bound alcohol dehydrogenase (ADHa) of Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus is a
```
double function enzyme, able to use primary C2–C6 alcohols and the respective
aldehydes as substrates. They also proposed a mechanism for massive conversion
of ethanol to acetic acid, without the intermediate accumulation of the highly toxic
acetaldehyde.
Finally, studies have been carried out to identify the optimal nutrient feeding
strategy for acetic acid bacteria in several types of vinegar production. For example,
the key nutrients, in a system for cider vinegar production with Acetobacter pasteur-
ianus, were found to be aspartate, glutamate, proline and tryptophan. Specifically,
an optimum nutrient feeding strategy was achieved by orthogonal experiment
design, proposing the simultaneous addition of 0.02 g/L proline, 0.03 g/L glutamate,
0.01 g/L aspartate and 0.005 g/L tryptophan, leading to a 93.3% yield of acetic acid
from alcohol and increased concentration of most volatile flavor compounds in the
```
cider vinegar (Qi et al., 2017).
```
14.4.5 ageing of Vinegar
Ageing is a common practice in the production of traditional vinegars. It usually
involves the use of wooden barrels, as for example, in the case of Sherry wine vin-
```
egars, balsamic vinegar and others (Tesfaye et al., 2004). The ageing process may
```
last for 6 months to several years, resulting in vinegars with improved characteristics
and high prices. During ageing in wooden barrels several changes occur in vin-
egar, the most important being the water loss through the wood pores, which leads
to increased acetic acid concentration, the extraction of phenolic compounds from
289Innovative Vinegar Products
wood into vinegar and the formation of aroma compounds, mainly esters through
```
slow esterification reactions between alcohols and acids (Tesfaye et al., 2004).
```
Regarding the recent research literature, in order to accelerate the ageing process,
```
Martínez-Gil et al. (2018) proposed the addition of oak or other wood shavings, a
```
practice that has also been successfully applied in wine ageing. The use of wooden
shavings is expected to reduce the ageing time by increasing the extraction rate and
```
quantities of extracted compounds, such as phenolics, 5-(hydroxymethyl)-2-furalde-
```
hyde and volatile compounds, and to induce chemical reactions and condensations
```
among the existing compounds (Góamez et al., 2006). Several studies have been
```
conducted to accelerate vinegar ageing with the addition of wooden chips resulting
```
in vinegars with improved flavor and other sensory characteristics (Morales et al.,
```
```
2004; Tesfaye et al., 2004; Góamez et al., 2006; Guerrero et al., 2011).
```
```
In another study by Wang et al. (2017), immobilized esterification enzyme sys-
```
tems were studied in order to accelerate the maturation of Shanxi aged vinegar, lead-
ing to an increase of the total ester content by more than 28.1%.
14.5 CONCLUSIONS
Vinegar is an acidic liquid product that is widely available in the global market,
prepared mainly through a two-step fermentation process: alcoholic fermentation by
yeast and subsequently acetification by acetic acid bacteria. Traditionally, it is pro-
```
duced using wine as raw material; however, as discussed in this chapter, it is also pro-
```
duced from a wide variety of raw materials available around the world, such as fruit
and vegetables, using similar or different methodologies depending on the substrate.
In addition, nowadays the increasing production rates of agricultural products result
in the accumulation of wastes, by-products, surpluses and losses due to deterioration
of the most sensitive products on the way from production to consumption. In order
to reduce these losses and the generation of wastes, and to create added-value, their
exploitation through fermentation, including vinegar production, is increasingly
gaining the attention of researchers and industries.
```
Traditionally, vinegar is used for food flavoring and preservation; however, sev-
```
eral studies have demonstrated its potential health benefits, characterizing vinegar
as a functional food. These findings, combined with the increasing consumer aware-
ness on the consumption of healthy products, has made the development of novel
vinegar products with functional properties a necessity. The functional properties
of the final vinegar product depend mainly on the raw material used. The design of
efficient industrial systems for the fermentation of these alternative raw materials is
also necessary, along with techno-economic studies. Finally, also important is the
investigation of the potential health benefits of the novel vinegars for humans.

15.1 INTRODUCTION
Biotechnology in general, and bioprocess engineering in particular, are currently
```
having a substantial economic impact in many countries (especially in the more
```
```
developed ones). This is an undeniable fact judging by the large number of existing
```
biotechnological businesses and their substantial contribution to the gross domestic
```
products, among other indicators, of such countries (OECD, 2018). Although the
```
biotechnological industry has traditionally played a variety of roles in the agri-food
and healthcare sectors, its scope has lately expanded to other priority targets such as
```
energy production and the environment (OECD, 2011).
```
Because many bioprocesses use microorganisms at some stage, providing the
microbes with appropriate conditions for survival and growth is especially important
for their development, control, and optimization. However, the high complexity of the
underlying mechanisms makes this task difficult and requires using effective tools
for this purpose. Simulations are especially useful in this respect as they allow tem-
```
poral changes in the target variables (typically substrate and product concentrations)
```

300 Advances in Vinegar Production
and some yield indices to be predicted by using computer algorithms. This allows
one to predict the performance of a bioprocess at each step from the supply pattern
```
for nutrients or raw materials (system inputs) in order to compare feeding strategies
```
```
or facilitate process design, control, or dimensioning (Julian and Whitford, 2007).
```
However, a process can only be simulated based on a previously developed math-
ematical representation in the form of a model accurately reflecting its expected per-
```
formance in terms of the particular purpose (Agger and Nielsen, 2001). Mathematical
```
models are especially useful for bioprocess design and control, and also for the
acquisition and integration of quantitative information about complex biological sys-
```
tems from data, whether experimental and otherwise (Agger and Nielsen, 2001).
```
As a rule, biotransformations are highly complex processes involving an intricate
network of reactions. The complexity of the mathematical models needed to simu-
```
late them depends on their particular purpose (Bogaerts and Hanus, 2001). In many
```
cases, a simple model providing a reasonably good quantitative approximation to
the target variables over a restricted range of conditions may suffice. Therefore, the
nature and complexity of the model to be used will depend on its intended use, and
the best choice can only be made by considering the following factors, among others:
```
• the precision with which general cell functions (e.g., substrate uptake, prod-
```
```
uct formation) are to be described
```
• whether cells are to be treated individually or as a whole, and, obviously
• whether a steady or non-steady state is to be used depending on the opera-
```
tional mode for the process (Agger and Nielsen, 2001)
```
```
There are three general categories of mathematical models for this purpose (Bogaerts
```
```
and Hanus, 2001), namely: mechanistic or white-box models, empirical or black-box
```
models, and hybrid or grey-box models.
Mechanistic models, also known as first-principles models, provide a mathemati-
cal formulation from elements and mechanisms of a system, usually by integrating
mass and energy balances, cell and/or reaction kinetics, and equilibrium relations
```
(Gernaey et al., 2010). These models are typically constructed from the fundamental
```
physicochemical and biological principles governing the process concerned by relat-
```
ing changes in biomass, substrate, and product concentrations (Julian and Whitford,
```
```
2007). As a result, mechanistic models have higher extrapolation capabilities and
```
```
afford better control of processes than empirical models; obviously, however, they
```
require a better knowledge of the particular problem. Mechanistic models use ordi-
```
nary differential equations (ODEs) or partial derivative equations (PDEs) to describe
```
```
balances in addition to algebraic equations for cell kinetics (Jiménez-Hornero, 2007;
```
```
Julian and Whitford, 2007; Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2009a). Depending on the way
```
the mechanisms behind the target process are described, mechanistic models can be
```
of the following types (Agger and Nielsen, 2001):
```
• Highly detailed models, which are used to represent key cell processes such
as metabolic pathways or genetic transcription.
• Whole-cell models, which account for the overall behavior of cells without
much detail about their metabolism. This type of model can be structured
301Modeling and Optimization of Acetic Acid Fermentation
or non-structured depending on whether it is intended to explain the target
processes as the result of activity in specific cell compartments.
• Non-segregated or segregated models. The former assumes cells to behave
uniformly, whereas the latter considers differences among subpopulations
or cell cycles, for example.
Non-structured and non-segregated mechanistic models are obviously simpler than
their respective counterparts. For this reason, they are often used for purposes such
```
as state estimation or controlling bioreactors (Bogaerts and Hanus, 2001). In addition
```
to balance equations, these models use macroscopic mathematical approximations
```
to relate design variables to operational variables (e.g., Monod kinetics to describe
```
```
the influence of substrates on specific cell growth rates) (Chhatre, 2012). One of the
```
greatest challenges in constructing these models is selecting the mathematical struc-
tures to be used in order to describe kinetics or pseudo-stoichiometries, which are
usually unknown beforehand. In fact, a given apparent behavior may be described
```
by more than one mathematical structure (Jiménez-Hornero, 2007; Jiménez-Hornero
```
```
et al., 2009a). Also, these models are usually non-linear and thus require numerical
```
```
integration for simulation purposes (Jiménez-Hornero, 2007). Moreover, determin-
```
```
ing their parameters (Banga et al., 2003; Gutiérrez, 2003) requires knowing whether
```
```
they can be uniquely estimated (i.e., if they can be determined accurately), a problem
```
which in turn has two different complementary approaches: structural or theoretical
```
identifiability (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2008) and practical identifiability (Jiménez-
```
```
Hornero et al., 2009b). Structural identifiability only concerns the mathematical
```
structure of a model, whereas practical identifiability encompasses the quantity and
quality of experimental data used for estimation and also the sensitivity analysis of
the model parameters. An appropriate experimental design makes it easier to check
whether a model is practically identifiable and hence facilitates more accurate and
```
precise estimation of its parameters (Box et al., 1978). In general, models involving
```
many parameters have frequent identifiability problems and need a large amount of
data for their estimation.
```
Empirical (black-box) models describe functional relationships between the
```
inputs and outputs of a process from experimental data without providing for internal
```
mechanisms (Ljung, 1987). The mathematical structure behind such relationships is
```
defined a priori, and its parameters are then determined by optimization. The param-
eters need not possess physical significance or coincide with any state variables of
the process. Therefore, empirical models do not rely on existing knowledge about the
```
target system; as a result, they have limited extrapolation capability and can rarely
```
provide a physical interpretation of the system, which can be a major restriction for
```
some uses (Chhatre, 2012). However, they usually provide highly accurate predic-
```
tions for the range of experimental data used to construct them. There are two broad
categories of empirical models, namely:
```
• Regression models (Miller and Miller, 2002; Santos-Dueñas, 2009), which
```
typically use polynomials whose coefficients are estimated to fit the out-
puts to the experimental data. The independent and dependent variables in
the polynomials are called “factors” and “response variables,” respectively.
302 Advances in Vinegar Production
The influence of the factors on the response variables is examined by using
```
experimental designs (e.g., complete or fractional factorial designs), which
```
take into account the interactions among factors. Optimizing the design
```
entails identifying the key factors (viz., those expected to have the greatest
```
```
influence on the target process).
```
```
• Artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2009a), which
```
are universal non-linear approximators and the most common black-box
models. Topologically, ANNs consist of elemental processing units oper-
ating in parallel that are mutually connected across a layered structure
```
(Figure 15.1). Mathematically, ANNs are simple combinations of basic func-
```
```
tions that are implemented in processing units called “neurons” (Bogaerts
```
```
and Hanus, 2001). The neurons in a network are distributed among an
```
“input layer” that connects process inputs, an “output layer” that delivers
the response variables, and a variable number of “hidden layers” lying in
between the input and output layers that endow the ANN with black-box
characteristics. Neurons in different layers are connected with associated
weights reflecting to what extent they influence one another.
```
ANNs must be “trained” for their specific task (e.g., modeling a process). The train-
```
ing or learning process typically involves estimating the weights of the neural con-
nections. This requires feeding the network with training patterns in the form of
```
input/output data defining the desired behavior (supervised learning) and using an
```
optimization algorithm to adjust connection weights in such a way as to minimize
```
errors between network outputs and the training patterns (e.g., the widely used back-
```
```
propagation algorithm) (Rumelhart et al., 1986).
```
The ANN architectures most commonly used to model bioprocesses are of
the feedforward networks, where information flows from input to output only, or
the recurrent networks, where outputs can be fed back as inputs in order to model
FIGURE 15.1 Example of ANN. The circles are representing neurons, u i are the inputs,
y i the outputs, w represents the connection weights, and f ij are the basis functions.
303Modeling and Optimization of Acetic Acid Fermentation
```
dynamic systems (Norgaard et al., 2000). Dynamic networks are feedforward ANNs
```
where some past inputs and outputs are used as new inputs. Neuro-fuzzy structures,
which endow models with increased robustness and extrapolation capability, result
```
from the combination of fuzzy logic systems and neural networks (Nelles, 2001).
```
```
Finally, hybrid models combine the structure of first-principles models (and hence
```
```
use existing knowledge about a process) and the characteristics of black-box models
```
```
as estimators of unknown parameters (usually kinetic equations and pseudo-stoichi-
```
```
ometries). Several parameters are thus determined from experimental data by using
```
appropriate optimization algorithms, which force the carrying out of identifiability
analysis.
15.2 MODELING ACETIC FERMENTATION—VINEGAR
PRODUCTION
The industrial production of vinegar is a typical bioprocess, which has been mod-
```
eled in several ways (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2009a, 2009b; Santos-Dueñas et
```
```
al., 2015), particularly as regards its biotransformation stage. Although a variety
```
```
of vinegar types and modes of operation exist (Valero et al., 2005; Maestre et al.,
```
```
2008; García-García et al., 2009), most industrially produced vinegar is obtained
```
by a semi-continuous procedure in fermentation tanks with a self-aspirating turbine.
This methodology provides increased yields, stability, and reproducibility. Basically,
complex, strictly aerobic microbiota transform ethanol in a culture medium into ace-
```
tic acid. In the semi-continuous operational mode used (Figure 15.2), the cycle ends
```
```
when ethanol in the medium has been used to a preset extent; then, the fermentation
```
tank is partially unloaded, and the residual content is used as inoculum for the next
cycle once the tank is replenished with fresh medium.
In practice, the process affords control of four operational variables, namely: the
initial concentration of ethanol in the culture medium, the extent to which ethanol
must be used for a cycle to be finished, the volume of medium that is then unloaded,
and the rate at which the fermentation tank is loaded with fresh culture medium.
FIGURE 15.2 Typical semi-continuous cycle in vinegar production.
304 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
The mean properties of the environment where acetic acid bacteria (AAB) work can
```
vary widely depending on these four variables, and so can the mean concentration
```
of ethanol and the production of acetic acid over a cycle as a result (Baena-Ruano et
```
```
al., 2010; Álvarez-Cáliz et al., 2014). Because AAB are highly sensitive to both com-
```
pounds, their concentration and activity can be strongly affected by the fermentation
```
conditions (Baena-Ruano et al., 2006, 2010a,b; García-García et al., 2007; Jiménez-
```
```
Hornero et al., 2009a; Álvarez-Cáliz et al., 2012).
```
For various reasons, the semi-continuous mode has become the preferred choice
for vinegar production. This mode allows part of the biomass produced in each cycle
```
to rapidly start the next; also, the operational variables can be used to maintain the
```
average substrate and product concentrations within appropriate ranges for AAB
to operate, which in turn facilitates self-selection and adjustment to the specific
medium.
In this situation, a question immediately arises as to whether the operational con-
ditions used are the best possible. Obviously, the answer will depend on the particu-
lar aim, and, industrially, such an aim is typically maximizing productivity. Whether
or not this is the case, the responses can only be obtained by modeling the target
system prior to optimization.
The difficulty involved in modeling these systems, and their advantages and
disadvantages, are illustrated in the following sections with an example of a
non-structured, non-segregated mechanistic model and a polynomial black-box model.
Whereas the former type of model is usually applicable over a wider range of oper-
```
ating conditions, it tends to be more complex (e.g., in developing kinetic equations
```
```
and, especially, determining kinetic parameters). On the other hand, black-box models
```
require no provision for the physicochemical principles behind the process to be mod-
eled, but only finding as simple a way as possible of relating the target variables.
15.2.1 a meCHanistiC approaCH
Mechanistic models require the following:
```
(1) A prior analysis of all attempts at assessing the variables potentially influ-
```
encing the behavior of the target system and thus requiring inclusion in the
kinetic equations to be used
```
(2) Estimating the kinetic parameters
```
```
(3) Optimizing the model by defining an appropriate target function
```
A number of kinetic equations have been proposed to model acetic fermentation
```
mechanistically (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2009a). Some assume that cell growth is
```
only influenced by oxygen availability in the medium, whereas others additionally
consider the influence of ethanol and acetic acid and also their synergistic effect.
Still others consider the effect of the presence of viable, non-viable, and dead cells,
as well as the rate of transformation of viable cells into non-viable cells. Although
non-viable cells cannot grow, they are assumed to use some substrate—which, how-
ever, has not yet been demonstrated beyond doubt. Some equations consider all the
previous effects, whereas others are restricted to those factors thought to actually
305Modeling and Optimization of Acetic Acid Fermentation
influence the results. A detailed discussion of these and other equations can be found
```
elsewhere (Jiménez Hornero et al., 2009a).
```
It should be noted that many reported equations have been developed from the
results of a limited number of experiments conducted under widely different condi-
tions usually departing from those typically used in industrial processes. A broader
experimental program, mimicking the industrial production of vinegar as closely as
possible, revealed the need to develop a new model integrating the effects of all main
variables in addition to a new one previously not considered: cell lysis. A detailed
discussion of how the ensuing model was developed is beyond the scope of this
```
chapter but can be found elsewhere (Jiménez Hornero, 2007; Jiménez Hornero et al.,
```
```
2009a). Basically, the model relies on the following assumptions:
```
• Non-viable biomass uses no substrate.
• The total concentration of cells is the combination of those of viable and
non-viable cells.
• Unlike previous models, cell lysis is considered because the variation of the
total concentration of cells can only be explained in its presence.
• Ethanol acts as a limiting substrate at low concentrations and as a cell
growth inhibitor at high concentrations.
• The acetification process is assumed to be limited by oxygen availability in
the medium. In fact, the fermentation rate increases with increasing oxygen
transfer, which makes it advisable to consider the limiting effect of oxygen
as a nutrient on cell growth. Additionally, in the experimental conditions
studied, no inhibition effect on growth has been detected from the oxygen.
• Cell death is influenced by the concentrations of ethanol and acetic acid.
• Acetic acid influences cell growth and death.
If thorough mixing is assumed, then the mass balance for a process working in
the semi-continuous mode can be formulated as follows:

The model included the following nine parameters:mmax , KSE , KIE , KIA, KSO ,md0 ,
K mE , K mA , andmlysis0 . Although the model is of the non-structured, non-segregated
type, it encompasses six differential equations and six kinetic equations containing
nine kinetic parameters and three yield-related factors. Solving a system like this is
```
fairly easy with the powerful software tools available today; the problem is estimat-
```
ing the kinetic parameters from experimental data.
15.2.1.1 Estimation of Model Parameters
The estimation of kinetic parameters with optimization techniques is one of the cru-
cial steps in the development of biotechnological models. Ideally, one should obtain
a unique set of parameters allowing experimental results to be accurately predicted
in order to be able to assign some physical significance to the parameters. This,
however, is not always possible, especially with complex models. In fact, accurately
estimating the parameters of a model requires examining their identifiability, both
structural and practical.
15.2.1.1.1 Structural and Practical Identifiability
For a kinetic model to lend itself to validation, its parameters should be easy to
estimate in an unequivocal manner, that is, the model should be “identifiable” in
```
structural (theoretical) and practical terms (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2008). Structural
```
identifiability is established on the sole basis of mathematical structure, whereas
practical identifiability requires considering the quantity and quality of the experi-
mental data used to determine the kinetic parameters. A kinetic model can thus be
```
(a) structurally and practically identifiable
```
```
(b) structurally but not practically identifiable or
```
```
(c) structurally unidentifiable and hence also practically unidentifiable irre-
```
spective of the amount of experimental data used and their quality
15.2.1.1.2 Structural Identifiability
```
The way theoretical (structural) identifiability in a model is assessed depends on
```
whether the model is of the linear or non-linear type as regards its parameters.
Laplace transformations, Taylor series expansion, and Markov’s parameter matrix
```
approximation, among others, are suitable for linear models (Jiménez-Hornero et al.,
```
```
2008), but linear models for bioprocesses are rare.
```
By contrast, available choices for non-linear kinetic models are more complex and
```
smaller in number; also, they require the use of software tools affording symbolic
```
computation and/or powerful hardware for implementation. The symbolic methods
```
include Taylor series expansion (Pohjanpalo, 1978), generating series (Dochain and
```
```
Vanrolleghem, 2001), local state isomorphism (Vajda and Rabitz, 1989), and dif-
```
```
ferential algebra (Ljung and Glad, 1994). Even with small-to-mid-sized or fairly
```
complex models, these methods have a high computational cost and are difficult to
309Modeling and Optimization of Acetic Acid Fermentation
implement. On the other hand, numerical methods are easier to use but only allow
local identifiability to be verified.
The authors’ group used Taylor series expansion, generating series, and local state
```
isomorphism (Jiménez-Hornero et al., 2008), but none provided conclusive results
```
about the structural identifiability of the target model, mainly because of the high
operational complexity of the methods. By way of example, Taylor series expansion
```
entailed examining combinations of coefficients for the output variables (viz., those
```
```
experimental variables for which data were available) in order to unequivocally con-
```
firm the presence of structural identifiability. However, the large number of potential
combinations, and the high computational cost of calculating the coefficients, con-
siderably hindered application of the methods and precluded concluding about the
structural identifiability of the model.
```
Dochain and Vanrolleghem (2001) found using generating series based on the
```
relationship between Lie derivatives and non-linear observability to meet with simi-
lar problems.
Local state isomorphism methods, also known as “similarity transformations,”
```
require checking that the controllability rank condition (CRC) and observability
```
```
rank condition (ORC) are both fulfilled (Tunali and Tarn, 1987; Vajda et al., 1989).
```
These conditions, however, could not be checked for reasons similar to those hinder-
ing application of the previous methods.
These difficulties led us to use numerical methods, which are known to allow
identifiability in highly complex models to be assessed at a reasonable computational
```
cost (Braems et al., 2001; Sedoglavic, 2002; Walter et al., 2004; Gerdin, 2006). The
```
```
method proposed by Gerdin (2006) allowed local identifiability in the target model
```
to be confirmed.
15.2.1.1.3 Practical Identifiability
Assessing practical identifiability entails considering some characteristics of the
```
experimental data used to estimate model parameters (particularly, their amount and
```
```
scatter, and the lack of correlation between measured variables). Estimating model
```
```
parameters requires optimizing a target function that is subjected to primary (model
```
```
equations) and secondary restrictions on the variables and parameters such as high-
```
est and lowest limits. This usually entails formulating a non-linear programming
problem with various differential and algebraic restrictions where the decision vari-
ables are the parameters to be estimated.
```
The core of practical identifiability is the Fisher information matrix (FIM).
```
Basically, the matrix provides information in compact form about the uncertainty
in measurements and the sensitivity of the model parameters. Practical identifiabil-
ity can initially be assessed by calculating the FIM rank. If the matrix is not full-
rank, then the model cannot be practically identifiable. Even if it is, however, the
parameters may be difficult to identify. The sensitivity of model parameters and their
correlations can be assessed with various tools, the most effective of which is the
correlation matrix of the parameter estimation, which can reveal linear dependences
among them. Therefore, the most suitable method for assessing local practical iden-
tifiability is a combination of the analysis of sensitivity functions and the correlation
matrix of the parameter estimation.
310 Advances in Vinegar Production
The sensitivity analysis is crucial in that it assesses the effect of changes in
```
parameter values on the model outputs (measured variables). The analysis relies on
```
sensitivity functions and is usually local in models for biological processes owing
to their non-linear nature. A graphical analysis of the sensitivity functions allows
```
the specific parameters most strongly influencing the outputs to be identified; the
```
greater the function is, the stronger will be the effect of its parameters and vice versa.
Likewise, if the sensitivity functions for different parameters have similar profiles
for an output variable, the parameters concerned may be highly correlated.
Unambiguously identifying all parameters is impossible if the correlation matrix
of the parameter estimation reveals any correlations. Even so, it is useful to iden-
tify those parameters that can be estimated in an unequivocal manner with a view
to developing a precisely calibrated model. However, ambiguity in the values of
unidentifiable parameters precludes assignation of physical significance.
The subset of identifiable parameters can be identified in various ways. Our group
used an improved version of FIM in combination with parameter estimation for this
purpose.
15.2.1.1.4 Application to the Proposed Model
We used the above-described methods to assess identifiability in the target kinetic
model and estimate its parameters. The conclusions about its theoretical identifi-
ability are stated above. The practical identifiability study needs experimental data
```
such as those of the X point cloud (viz., the concentration of total cells) for one of
```
```
the series of experiments carried out by Jiménez-Hornero et al. (Jiménez-Hornero et
```
```
al., 2009b) (Figure 15.3a).
```
Then, in the next step, the highest and lowest limit for each parameter must be
established. For instance, based on Equations 15.7–15.11, the specific growth rate,mc ,
was dependent on factors f e, f a , and f o , whose values should fall in the range 0–1 if
the maximum specific growth rate is to bemmax . Whereas the lowest possible value of
```

```

set as the highest possible value formmax .
Additionally, simulations such as those of Figure 15.4, which illustrates the effect
of changes in KIA on f a at a variable concentration of A, are necessary. Initially,
parameter K IA was used to represent the sensitivity of AAB to the concentration of
acetic acid in the medium. As can be seen from the figure, if the lowest value of K IA

Once a kinetic model for a bioprocess has been developed, the next step usually
involves optimizing the operating conditions for the process.
15.2.1.2 Dynamic Optimization
The overall performance of a bioreactor and the quality of the resulting product are
known to depend strongly on the operating conditions used. Identifying the specific
operations leading to the best possible results typically requires using an optimiza-
tion procedure. With dynamic optimization, the time profiles for the control vari-
ables are obtained to optimize a given target function such as that for fermentation
productivity.
Dynamic optimization methods are largely of the dynamic programming, indi-
rect, or direct type. By virtue of their simplicity, direct methods are usually more
efficient than those of the other two types. They use a discretization procedure to
convert a problem with infinite dimensions into one of finite dimensions that is sub-
jected to the restrictions imposed by the dynamics of the target system and any
others needed for the particular problem in order to enable the use of standard

15.2.2 BlaCk-B ox modeling —polynomial models
```
As noted earlier, black-box models are easier to develop than mechanistic models;
```
also, they require no prior identifiability analysis and are thus much more practical
with a view to optimizing and controlling processes. This type of model finds as
simple as possible relationships between experimental and process variables from
experimental data obtained under different operating conditions. However, the ensu-
ing model will be valid over a limited range owing to the restrictions imposed on the
operational variables.
Linear and non-linear models based on polynomials of variable order are the most
```
widely used in practice (Bezerra et al., 2008; Nguyen and Borkowski, 2008). Most
```
use first- or second-order polynomials, the second being more precise and widely
```
applicable as a result of their considering interactions between factors (operational
```
```
variables) (Packett and Burman, 1946; Abilov et al., 1975; Box et al., 1978).
```
Worth special note among first- and second-order polynomial models are the
```
Packett–Burman and Box–Behnken models, respectively. The latter (Equation
```
```
15.24) considers interactions between factors, whereas the former (Equation 15.23)
```
does not.
