The number of experiments needed to determine all coefficients in a model will
depend on the nature of the model. Thus, fitting a linear model will require k n experi-
ments, and fitting a non-linear one k n + k·n + 1, where k is the number of levels of
each variable and n that of independent variables.
The precision of a polynomial model depends on the number of terms it includes
```
and on the values of its coefficients; however, ensuring a high precision entails using
```
a large number of data to determine the coefficients. The experiments to be used can
be selected according to no specific criterion or, alternatively, by following a preset
experimental design, which, as shown below, has a number of advantages.
15.2.2.1 Experimental Design
Experimental designs are intended to facilitate the simultaneous assessment of the
```
influence of all factors involved in a process (Miller and Miller, 2002), and their inter-
```
```
actions (Brereton, 1990; Morgan, 1991), as well as to minimize the number of experi-
```
```
ments needed to estimate the target polynomial coefficients (Castro Mejías et al., 2002).
```
One of the most widely used experimental design strategies is factorial design.
As with any other strategy, it is crucial to establish the number of factors to be con-
```
sidered and their levels (values), which will dictate their ranges of variation. Usually,
```
```
factors are scaled from –1 (the lowest possible level) to +1 (the highest level) (Ramis-
```
```
Ramos and García, 2001). Factorial designs use a series of experimental points (a
```
```
design matrix) corresponding to specific combinations of factor levels. As a result,
```
the number of experiments required increases markedly with those of variables and
levels. With three or more factors, however, models can be simplified by neglecting
interactions of third and higher orders because their effects will usually be much
```
weaker than those of first- and second-order interactions (Miller and Miller, 2002).
```
One the most widely used factorial designs is the Box–Behnken or Doehlert
```
central composition design, also known as the face-centered cubic design (Ramis-
```
```
Ramos and García, 2001). This design uses three different types of experimental
```
points, namely:
• Those for a complete design with two levels per factor, which provides 2n
```
points (n being the number of variables). A design with three variables thus
```
uses eight points corresponding to the vertices of a cube whose coordinates
```
are combinations of the highest (+1) and lowest level (–1) of the factors
```
```
(Figure 15.6).
```
• The central point, whose coordinates correspond to level 0 for all factors.
```
• The projections of the central point on the planes (faces) of the design,
```
which adds 2n further points.
Therefore, the total number of experimental points for this factorial design will
be 2n + 1 + 2n, and the design will be appropriate for fitting the coefficients of a non-
linear quadratic polynomial.
317Modeling and Optimization of Acetic Acid Fermentation
Figure 15.6 shows the geometric location of the experimental points in a non-
linear factorial design with three independent variables, and Table 15.2 shows the
normalized values of the factors used in each experiment.
The results of the experiments are used to determine the coefficients for the dif-
ferent terms of the polynomial and also to identify those terms that are actually
significant.
```
Using these methods requires a prior analysis of variance (ANOVA) of the experi-
```
```
mental data to expose significant differences at a given probability level (usually
```
```
99.9%), as well as to verify that a given variable is dependent on the operational
```
conditions considered and can thus be included in the polynomial regression.
Basically, the methods used to determine the polynomial coefficients minimize
```
the residual sum of squares (viz., the difference between predicted and observed
```
```
values or, in other words, the prediction error). This is the basis for least-squares
```
methodology.
```
Most available statistical software suites (SigmaPlot, SPSS, BMDP) can be used
```
for this purpose. Thus, SigmaPlot allows calculation of polynomial terms by using
three different types of statistical fitting algorithms, namely: best subset regression,
backward stepwise regression, and forward stepwise regression. The best subset
regression algorithm establishes the combination of independent variables best pre-
dicting the dependent variables in terms of the multiple regression coefficient of
```
determination (R2) and incorporates independent variables one at a time until all
```
have been included in the polynomial. Subsequent Pareto analysis allows one to
```
identify those polynomial terms with statistical significance (Grierson, 2008), which
```
FIGURE 15.6 Diagram of the central composition design used to model the target opera-
tional variables.
318 Advances in Vinegar Production
will be those with a ratio of the statistical t to the critical value for Student’s t with
provision for the number of degrees of freedom of the polynomial and the desired
probability.
On the other hand, forward and backward stepwise regression methods include or
exclude independent variables from the model depending on whether the variables
contribute in a significant manner to facilitating prediction. Inclusion and exclusion
```
decisions are based on multiple correlation coefficients (R) or coefficients of deter-
```
```
mination (R2), both of which are measures of suitability of a regression model for
```
describing experimental data.
Once the terms to be included, and their coefficients, are known, the model can
```
be optimized by using various methods. One (Karush, 1939; Kukn and Tucker, 1951)
```
```
involves using the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions to be met by the opti-
```

15.2.2.2 Application of Black-Box Modeling to Acetic Fermentation
The procedure, which provides a systematic, rigorous approximation of the influence
of three operational variables affecting industrial vinegar production at a completely
automated laboratory plant operating in a semi-continuous mode, is described in detail
```
elsewhere (Santos-Dueñas et al., 2015). The three variables considered are as follows:
```
• The ethanol concentration in the medium at the time the reactor is unloaded
```
(E). The reaction is allowed to develop until the ethanol concentration falls
```
```
to 3.5, 2.0, or 0.5% (v/v), which represent the highest (+1), central (0), and
```
```
lowest level (–1), respectively.
```
```
• The unloaded volume (V). A proportion of 25, 50, or 75% of the volume of
```
```
medium (viz., 2, 4, or 6 L, respectively, since the reactor is loaded with 8 L)
```
is rapidly unloaded. These proportions correspond to the levels –1, 0, and
+1, respectively.
```
• The loading rate (C). The reactor is fed with fresh medium at a constant rate
```
of 0.01, 0.035, or 0.06 L·min –1, which correspond to a normalized level of
–1, 0, and +1, respectively.
Variables E, V, and C coincide with X1, X2 , and X3, respectively, in Table 15.2.

procedure one can obtain different polynomials for the dependent variables to be

15.3 CONCLUSIONS
Bioprocesses are not only an enormously important reality at present but also a
highly promising field for expansion in the future. Properly implementing a biopro-
cess requires a deep analysis of its fundamentals and of the methods to be used for
its design and optimization. The complex interrelationships encountered in address-
ing the ensuing multidisciplinary problems can only be solved with close coopera-
tion among professionals from different areas of knowledge and expertise. Only in
this way can models sophisticated enough to account for the observed behavior but
operationally simple enough to be useful in practice be developed. Such behavior
can be approximated with mechanistic models based on the inherent fundamental
biological and physicochemical principles or with simpler, black-box models merely
predicting the response of a system under a variety of operating conditions.
The previous sections describe the process by which the conversion of ethanol
into acetic acid, which is the main transformation in quantitative terms in vinegar
production from wine, can be modeled with both types of methods.
The non-structured, non-segregated mechanistic model discussed above uses
mass and energy balances in combination with kinetic equations for the production
and disappearance reactions involved, and also potential equilibrium relationships.
The ensuing equation system is intended to describe in simple terms some of the
```
main aspects of the target biological reaction (viz., substrate uptake, product forma-
```
```
tion, changes in cell biomass). Development of the model is not finished until the
```
```
kinetic parameters concerned can be unequivocally estimated (i.e., until the model is
```
```
theoretically and practically identifiable), which is the greatest problem to be solved
```
with mechanistic models. In fact, verifying identifiability in a model involves com-
```
plex mathematical computations that rarely provide a completely reliable answer;
```
very often, they only allow certain parameters to be estimated. Therefore, if one of
the main reasons for using mechanistic models is to explain the principles underlying
a bioprocess and to identify specific parameters that can be attached to some biologi-
cal or physicochemical significance, the difficulty in verifying identifiability makes
them impractical in many cases. If problems arise even with fairly simple models
involving a relatively small number of target parameters, developing more structured
models to explicitly account for a number of metabolic reactions, for example, will
foreseeably be a much tougher task. This is suggestive of the importance of math-
ematical problems in this field, which can be expected to increase with the level of
322 Advances in Vinegar Production
detail with which a biochemical process is to be explained or cell behavior to be
discriminated, for example.
Because of the foregoing, and the need to develop effective methods for optimiz-
ing bioprocesses, black-box models are increasingly being used to model the under-
lying processes. Polynomial models and experimental designs are among the most
```
common choices in this respect; in practice, they allow much easier identification of
```
the specific terms to be considered and their coefficients to be computed, with a view
also to their easier optimization with standard methods.

16
Post-Fermentation
Treatments of Vinegars
Francisco López
16.1 INTRODUCTION
The vinegar produced by any type of fermentation process will present or develop cloud-
iness since it contains acetic acid bacteria and suspended matter coming from the origi-
nal raw material, such as unstable phenolic compounds, pectins, and traces of proteins,
that can form haze or deposits. Therefore, clarification and/or stabilization of industrial
vinegars is usually imperative. The traditional method consists of adding a clarification
agent, such as bentonite, to facilitate the removal of the unstable compounds from the
product. Vinegars made by surface acetification methods usually have a few bacteria in
suspension, while vinegars obtained by the submerged method contain large amounts of
bacteria. The quality of vinegar may also be affected by chemical phenomena, as well
as by the actions of microorganisms, yeasts, and vinegar eels. Therefore, prior to con-
sumption, it is advisable to treat the vinegar in order to achieve the best possible color,
limpidity, and presentation results before it reaches the consumer.

16.2 ALTERATIONS OF VINEGAR
Once vinegar is elaborated, it can present chemical defects or biological diseases.
```
Among chemical defects, the so-called “iron or blue casse” (ferric tannate), “white
```
```
or persistent casse” (ferric phosphate), and “darkening or brown casse” should be
```
```
highlighted. Furthermore, microbiological diseases (such as the moldiness, weaken-
```
```
ing, and the presence of mucilage) must be distinguished by those produced by other
```
organisms such as eels, flies, and mites. Following, some of the common vinegar
alterations are described in more detail.
The iron or blue casse is produced by an excessive presence of iron, which reacts
with the tannins to form precipitates. The presence of excessive iron can also affect
the taste of vinegar. White or powdered casse occurs when the phosphate contents
```
exceed the tannin contents; then, iron reacts with phosphate to form white precipi-
```
tates. The darkening or brown casse is characterized by a brown color caused by the
```
contact of vinegar with air, or when vinegar is insufficiently sulfited (Casale et al.,
```
```
2006). The enzymes responsible for the brown casse are the so-called “enoxidases”
```
```
or “oxidases” (polyphenol oxidases, PPOs), which oxidize the polyphenols to qui-
```
nones in the presence of oxygen and, subsequently, the flavonols are responsible for
```
the development of turbidity and browning (Waterhouse and Nikolantonaki, 2015).
```
Regarding diseases of biological origin due to microorganisms, the so-called
“weakening” should be highlighted. Weakening is due to a phenomenon of over-
```
oxidation (acetic acid conversion to CO 2 and water) caused by the same acetic acid
```
bacteria and/or other bacteria that might be present, such as Acetobacter xylinus
```
(LeFevre, 1924; Mas et al., 2014). “Weakened” or “reduced” vinegar can be also pro-
```
duced due to the action of molds and mucilages. In addition, the preservative action
will decrease with the acetic acid loss, resulting in a less stable product.
The molds occur on the surface, spreading later to the whole vinegar body.
Deuteromycetes, pelleting yeasts, and lactic acid bacteria will destroy acetic acid,
when it is diluted, by oxidation. The destruction of acetic acid is the consequence of
a low alcohol content or an excess of ventilation. Other alterations may be caused by
microorganisms, such as Lactobacillus, which transform malic acid into lactic acid
```
and CO 2 , reducing the vinegar acidity (Bartowsky, 2009). Fortunately, these micro-
```
```
organisms are almost never pathogenic. Finally, butyric bacteria (genus Clostridium;
```
```
sporogenous and aerobic) transform the soluble carbohydrates into acetic acid,
```
```
butyric acid, CO2 , and H 2 (Murali et al., 2017).
```
Regarding other organisms that can cause alterations in vinegar, the vinegar eels
```
(Turbatrix aceti; synonym Anguillula aceti) should be highlighted. Vinegar eels
```
are ubiquitous nematodes, inhabiting damaged fruit, such as grapes and apples, and
consequently they can often be seen swimming on the surface of vinegars. Little is
known on the role and effect of vinegar eels on vinegar production, and only a few
```
studies have been carried out to clarify this issue (Rainieri and Zambonelli, 2009).
```
Vinegar eels are small worms, viviparous and harmless for humans, but which can
```
cause turbidity (they are perfectly visible with backlight) and flavor alterations in
```
vinegar. They usually appear in vinegars produced by surface acetification meth-
```
ods (Orléans and Shützenbach), feeding on the mothers of vinegars. Vinegar eels
```
can even destroy the bacterial mat when they become large enough, causing it to
329Post-Fermentation Treatments of Vinegars
sink and interfering with the acetification process. Moreover, their putrid decom-
position after they die generates bad odors in vinegar, making it not suitable for
consumption.
```
Vinegar flies, also known as fruit flies (Drosophila spp.), which breed in the
```
juices of decaying fruit, are also found around the openings of vinegar containers
or wherever they find vinegar exposed to the air. In the case of high populations, the
larvae of these flies can enter the reactors and destroy the mother of vinegar. They
may also be responsible for the introduction of Acetobacter xylinum, an undesirable
acetic bacterium.
Finally, in vinegar factories that do not maintain proper cleaning and disinfection
practices, mites can appear which are small and prolific. Mites breed in cracks of the
woods of the acetifiers, where the environment is temperate and humid, and can be
```
readily destroyed using hot water or steam (LeFevre, 1924).
```
16.3 VINEGAR TREATMENTS
Firstly, it is convenient to differentiate “fining” from “clarification.” Clarification
can be defined as the treatment used to diminish the turbidity of a liquid product
by removing the solid particles, while fining is the treatment used to maintain the
vinegar stability along time from a colloidal point of view. In Europe, the treatments
applied during the production of vinegar can be regulated. For example, the Spanish
legislation allows all practices as far as the post-fermentative treatments are indi-
cated in Article 4 of the Real Decreto 661/2012.
16.3.1 storage and maturation
Maturation of vinegar is required for the development of a high-quality product with
```
a pleasant flavor. Traditionally, the rough stock vinegar (that is, the resulting liquid
```
```
after acetification) could be stored for up to 1–2 years in wooden barrels, whereas
```
today vinegar is stored, at the most, for 1–2 months in barrels or in stainless steel
```
tanks before bottling (Lea, 1989; Heikefelt, 2011). At 1–2 months of maturation,
```
vinegar has a high level of acetic acid and a low level of alcohols, which can produce
esters. The concentration of these compounds has a significant impact on the unique
flavor and bouquet of the vinegar. Also, in the case of malt vinegars for example, the
pH has by this time dropped below 3 and various polyphenols and other compounds
will slowly drop out of solution, giving the final vinegar a much more stable charac-
```
ter (Grierson, 2009).
```
In the industry, the diminished maturation time of vinegar is due to the higher
production and storage costs. In some plants, the producers may conduct rough filtra-
tions at the initial stages of production.
Many changes occur during storage. For example, in the production of cider
vinegar, the harsh flavor changes to more a pleasant aroma and bouquet, probably
due to the oxidation of vinegar caused by air entering though the pores of the wood.
During ageing, acetic acid reacts with the residual alcohol to form ethyl acetate,
```
which has a fruity flavor. The color of vinegar also alters during ageing (Joshi and
```
```
Sharma, 2009).
```
330 Advances in Vinegar Production
For quality products, the ageing of vinegar is usually performed in wooden con-
tainers. In the production of traditional vinegars such as vinegars in Jerez or Modena,
the ageing procedures are well established and regulated. However, in recent years,
various studies have been carried out to accelerate the maturation and ageing of vin-
```
egars. For example, Wang et al. (2017) applied ultrasounds to accelerate Zhenjiang
```
```
vinegar maturation. In their study, the ultrasonic treatment (optimal conditions) was
```
determined to be equivalent to 2–3 years of natural aged Zhenjiang vinegar. That
study has showed that ultrasound is a promising technique not only in shortening
the ageing time and lowering the costs for the vinegar-making industry but also in
producing fine quality vinegar.
16.3.2 Vinegar ClarifiCation
One of the most important treatments in the elaboration of vinegars is the clarifica-
tion to improve the appearance and stability of the product. Turbidity is due to larger
particles, such as plant debris, yeast, and bacterial cells, and smaller size material
```
such as carbohydrates, polyphenols, and protein aggregates (García-García et al.,
```
```
2009; Heikefelt, 2011).
```
16.3.2.1 Spontaneous Clarification
Clarification can be accomplished spontaneously, called spontaneous clarification
or self-clarification. This methodology includes allowing the vinegar to rest for
precipitation of the suspended particles by gravity at the bottom of the tank. For
an optimal performance, it is convenient to avoid cloudiness. The process is slow
and requires large capacity recipients. In addition, self-clarification by sedimenta-
```
tion depends on the vinegar acidity and on the maturation time (Ormaechea-Landa,
```
```
1991). Cider vinegar with low acidity normally does not clear even after a long-term
```
storage, whereas high-strength vinegars usually do so within a couple of months
```
(Joshi and Sharma, 2009). The risk associated with uncontrolled self-clarification
```
is that vinegar may integrate unpleasant odors and tastes, and sometimes it is con-
venient to aid and accelerate the clarification by sedimentation using suitable adju-
vants, as described in more detail in Chapter 6.
16.3.2.2 Mechanical Clarification
Another way to clarify vinegar is mechanically by using the centrifugation tech-
nique, which consists of accelerating the deposition of particles through the effect
of centrifugal force. This can be achieved by different types of equipment, such as
```
hydrocyclones, centrifugal decanters, or clarifiers (plate separators):
```
```
• Hydrocyclones (or cyclones) are based on the principle of free fall, accord-
```
ing to which the liquid flows freely, following a spiral course along the coni-
cal body of the cyclone trunk. The solid particles are separated from the
liquid and adhere to the wall of the trunk. They then fall by gravity and are
collected in a thick chamber, while the clarified liquid rises to the top. The
advantages of cyclones are that they have relatively low maintenance and
operation costs, do not usually require a large space, have a high capacity
331Post-Fermentation Treatments of Vinegars
and a solid construction, and can operate in a short time and at high tem-
```
perature and pressure conditions (Razmi et al., 2019).
```
• Centrifugal decanters are useful equipment for the separation of solids and
the recovery of liquids. They are continuously working machines, which use
an internal screw for the transport of the moist cake out of the machine. The
suspension to be clarified flows axially into the machine and is accelerated
```
to approximately circumferential velocity (Gleiss et al., 2018). Centrifugal
```
decanters are specifically effective for the separation of coarse particles,
```
which is a handicap to obtaining a fully clarified product; however, they can
```
```
be useful as pre-filtration treatments, if this is the limiting stage (Mushtaq,
```
```
2018). However, modern centrifugal decanters have several advantageous
```
features for delicate food and beverage industries, such as low moisture
in the discharged solids, easy cleaning, low separation costs, high-quality
end-product, low power consumption, and automated control.
• Vertical centrifugal clarifiers, also called plate centrifuges, are the most
suitable equipment to obtain a good clarification of vinegar, since they
allow rapid elimination of suspended solids. The product losses are low as
is the generation of waste, allowing the regulation of the turbidity of the
vinegar with the speed of rotation. The advantages of these machines are
that they can be operated continuously and automatically, do not require
adjuncts, and can act quickly on the vinegar to be clarified. It is important
to note that vertical centrifugal clarifiers are very versatile since they can
be used, if necessary, before the acetic fermentation for the clarification of
the wine, as well as for the treatment of waste, either to concentrate or to
recover vinegar from the deposits. This equipment is compact, occupying
little space in the vinegar factory, and has a relatively low operating cost.
```
However, it has a high investment cost (Hagel et al., 2008).
```
Generally, the modern high-speed centrifugal separators have several advantages,
according to their manufacturers, such as gentle, effective removal of undesirable sus-
pended particles from a wide range of liquids during pre-fermentation as well as post-
```
fermentation steps; they do not require fining agents (compared to flotation), they ensure
```
```
consistent performance, they do not require the use of filter aids (compared to vacuum
```
```
filtration), thus they are more environmentally friendly, they can be used for rapid, on-
```
```
demand polishing (e.g., prior to bottling), they increase the cross-flow filtration capacity,
```
```
and above all, they do not cause changes in the product quality (Alfa Laval, 2005).
```
16.3.2.3 Clarification by Filtration
Finally, the vinegar clarification can be done by filtration. Plate and frame filtration
is an alternative method of clarifying rough vinegars. This process consists of mix-
ing a filtering powder, usually diatomaceous earth, with the vinegar, which is then
```
pumped through the filter. The powder builds up a fine filter bed on the plates (depth
```
```
filter bed) to enhance the clarity of the vinegar (Grierson, 2009). More details about
```
currently available commercial vinegar filtration aids are provided in Chapter 6.
Membrane filters may also be employed to produce the required clarity. The
use of membrane technology in tangential flow filtrations improves the vinegar
332 Advances in Vinegar Production
production process, reduces the environmental impact, and makes cold sterilization
possible, thus reducing the vinegar treatment to a minimum, preserving the vinegar’s
```
own qualities, and minimizing production cost (López, 2012). Nevertheless, very
```
few studies have been carried out on the application of membrane technology to
vinegar. The application of membrane filtration to vinegar has been reported mainly
by membrane manufacturers.
In industrial production, the filter modules used in cross-flow membrane filtra-
tion are hollow-fiber membranes or spiral-wound membranes manufactured with
```
organic materials (such as polysulfone or regenerated cellulose) and ceramic tubular
```
```
membranes manufactured with various materials (such as zirconia or alumina). The
```
pore sizes that are most commonly used are of 0.2, 0.45, and 0.65 μm, but the cur-
```
rent trend is to use 0.2 μm. Nevertheless, ultrafiltration (with a typical cut-off point
```
```
of 50,000 molecular weight) was used to replace normal filtration and sterilization
```
procedures in cider vinegars. To minimize the risk of bacterial contamination, the
vinegar is filtered immediately before bottling. Ultrafiltration does not prevent the
formation of non-microbiological post-bottling haze, since haze precursor molecules
```
(such as procyanidins) have molecular weights ranging from 500 to 2,500 and can,
```
```
therefore, easily pass through even the smallest of ultrafiltration membranes (Joshi
```
```
and Sharma, 2009).
```
```
López et al. (2005) conducted a study of the clarification of vinegars (white, rosé,
```
```
and red) by cross-flow membrane filtration at industrial scale, and the main conclu-
```
sions were as follows:
```
• The turbidity for the three kinds of vinegars was reduced considerably; for
```
filtered vinegars, it was less than 0.5 NTU.
• The reduction of total solids in suspension was complete.
• Membrane filtration could be used to simultaneously clarify and cold steril-
ize the vinegar.
• The effect of membrane filtration on color and polyphenol content was
acceptable.
• The reduction in color, expressed as a decrease in modified color intensity,
was practically negligible for white vinegars, 11% for rosé vinegar, and 37%
for red vinegar.
• The reduction in polyphenol content was less than 15% in all vinegars.
• The polyphenolic profile of the filtered vinegar was quite similar to that of
the initial vinegar.
16.3.3 Vinegar fining
Fining is an alternative or complement to clarification, that can be used at both small
and larger scale. This treatment further improves the clarity and decreases the risk
```
of turbidity development during storage (Lea, 1989; Heikefelt, 2011).
```
Physicochemical stabilization is based on the use of clarifying additives, which
```
usually require a subsequent treatment by filtration (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). In this
```
treatment, the first stage consists of the dispersion of the clarifier, followed by coagu-
lation, which causes an increase in turbidity, and finally flocculation, which consists
333Post-Fermentation Treatments of Vinegars
of an increase in the size of the particles that facilitates sedimentation at the bottom
```
of the tank (see also Chapter 6). The temperature of the treatment must be low, since
```
it favors the coagulation and the flocculation of the particles. For the realization of
this treatment the tanks must be suitable for the operation, in particular with smooth
walls. Another important feature is that the flocs formed are of high density.
The used clarifiers must be inert from an organoleptic point of view, in order to
not transmit strange odors and flavors to the vinegar. Another aspect to consider is
the acidity of the product, since it affects the clarification. It has been observed that
```
increases in acidity in wine (low pH) can cause defective clarifications for pH lower
```
```
than 3.2 (Molina-Úbeda, 2000). If the wines are acidic, the effect of adjuvants such
```
```
as gelatin is less efficient (Brugirard, 1997). However, each clarifier has its optimal
```
```
pH range. For example, at pH 4 gelatin works well; however, at pH 3 clarifiers such
```
```
as albumin, casein, and potassium caseinate are more suitable (Brugirard, 1997;
```
```
Molina-Úbeda, 2000).
```
Among clarifiers, two types can be distinguished: organic and inorganic. The
organic clarifiers are usually effective but can modify vinegar composition, so it is
```
advisable to monitor the dosage of the treatment (as also mentioned in Chapter 6
```
```
regarding specific currently available commercial clarifiers). The organic clarifiers
```
include traditional clarifiers, such as gelatin, albumin, casein, potassium caseinate,
```
complex clarifiers, antioxidant clarifiers (which have a double, clarifying and stabi-
```
```
lizing effect), enzymatic clarifiers, tannins, polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (PVPP), etc.
```
```
(Guzmán-Chozas, 1998; see also Chapter 6).
```
```
Joshi and Sharma (2009) proposed a fining procedure for cider vinegar, involving
```
the addition of gelatin, bentonite, and/or liquid silicon dioxide, following the two
main protocols described below:
```
(i) 260 g gelatin and 400 g bentonite are added per 1,000 L of cider vinegar,
```
and the suspension is stirred and left to settle for at least 1 week before
racking.
```
(ii) Liquid silicon dioxide (5 L at 30% solution for 5,000 L of cider vinegar)
```
```
followed by gelatin (1 kg per 5,000 L) are added to cider vinegar and left to
```
settle. A final filtration could be necessary to completely remove suspended
materials and bacterial cells.
The effect of the inorganic clarifiers is based on the formation of a gel that traps the
particles in suspension and favors their removal. They do not usually modify vinegar
composition. Bentonite and silica gel are the most notable inorganic clarifiers and
are often used together for greater efficacy of the treatment. Normally the choice and
```
dosage of clarifiers should be determined in laboratory tests (Ormaechea-Landa,
```
```
1991; Chapter 6).
```
16.3.4 miCroBiologiCal staBilization
Vinegar is a product that normally does not have to legally indicate the expiration
date due to its special characteristics. However, it can be associated with a shelf-life
and restricted stability, even if stored cold. In addition, an unprocessed product may
334 Advances in Vinegar Production
contain potentially dangerous microorganisms that may be present without signs
of spoilage. Various methods can be used to eliminate unwanted microorganisms,
including pasteurization, sterile filtration, and addition of various preservatives
```
(Heikefelt, 2011).
```
16.3.4.1 Pasteurization
Pasteurization is an operation that aims to destroy bacteria and inactivate enzymes
that may cause later alterations in vinegar. This treatment can also be used to kill
vinegar eels, followed by filtration to eliminate them. The treatment must be such
```
as to avoid modifying the organoleptic characteristics of the vinegar; however, heat
```
may downgrade the organoleptic quality by affecting both the color and flavor of
```
vinegar (Choi and Nielsen, 2005).
```
Within the pasteurization process, different steps can be distinguished,
involving heating the vinegar at temperatures that range between 50–85°C and
application of treatment times that vary according to the selected temperature
```
(Ormaechea-Landa, 1991). The standard procedure consists of heating the vinegar
```
to temperatures between 65–70°C and successively bottling, sealing, and slow-
cooling. Alternatively, vinegar can be bottled and sealed first and then heated to
65–70°C. Sterilization of vinegars produced by submerged cultures with high bac-
```
terial concentrations may require higher pasteurization temperatures (77–80°C)
```
```
(Webb, 2007).
```
```
Joshi and Sharma (2009) described a particular chemical pasteurization, called
```
the “silver process,” based on flowing cider vinegar through silver-bearing sand, to
```
reach a silver ion concentration (about 2 ppm) sufficient to sterilize the vinegar.
```
16.3.4.2 Membrane Sterilization
Membrane technologies, such as the cold sterilization method, have also been
applied to food products. Specifically, cross-flow microfiltration is a useful technique
```
because clarification and sterilization can be carried out simultaneously (López,
```
```
2012). Cold sterile filtration through a membrane with pore size less than 0.2 μm
```
is an effective alternative to pasteurization. However, this method should only be
```
applied to clear products; otherwise the fine membranes that are used will possibly
```
```
clog (Heikefelt, 2011). Nevertheless, membrane application in the vinegar industry
```
makes it possible to avoid a pasteurization step, which is still useful in this produc-
```
tion area (Ormaechea-Landa, 1991).
```
16.3.4.3 Addition of Sulfite
Sulfiting is an effective method for the inactivation of microorganisms. This chemi-
cal stabilization is usually carried out by adding SO2 up to a maximum permitted
```
dose of 170 mg/L [Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008]. Usually it is introduced in the
```
```
form of gas (E220) or as potassium metabisulfite (E224); however, its efficiency is
```
reduced to half and it is difficult to dissolve it cold as potassium metabisulfite. It is a
self-limiting additive in its use, since above a certain dose it alters the taste charac-
```
teristics of the product (Ormaechea-Landa, 1991). Finally, it is especially effective
```
in an acidic medium, inhibiting bacteria and molds and to a lesser degree, yeasts
```
(bactericidal action up to values of 5–10 mg/L).
```
335Post-Fermentation Treatments of Vinegars
16.3.4.4 Other Preservatives
In some Denomination of Origin products, other antioxidant additives such as ascor-
```
bic acid (E-300), which prevents oxidative browning, and potassium sorbate (E-202),
```
which is applied as an inhibitor of secondary fermentation in the wine industry,
allow the reduction of the dose of SO2 .
Ascorbic acid is an antioxidant and is less effective than SO 2 unless used in very
```
high amounts (> 250 ppm). However, the breakdown products of ascorbic acid (dehy-
```
```
droascorbic acid and diketogulonic acid) are carbonyls which have been found to
```
be potent pro-oxidants, encouraging browning reactions and haze formation unless
```
excess ascorbic acid is present. The addition of small amounts of ascorbic acid (<
```
```
100 ppm) to vinegar is probably useless (Joshi and Sharma, 2009).
```
Sorbates are low in toxicity, among the lowest compared to other preservatives,
```
which is why their use is authorized all over the world. Sorbic acid (E-200) is an
```
unsaturated fatty acid naturally present in some vegetables, but for use as a food
additive it is manufactured by chemical synthesis. It is used in the preservation of
acidic foods and beverages, since its action at neutral pH is almost nil. It has the
technological advantages of being active in low acid media and of practically lacking
flavor. The main drawback of sorbic acid is that it is comparatively expensive and
that it is partly lost when the product is boiled. It is especially effective against molds
and yeasts and less so against bacteria, and is commonly used in oenology combined
with SO2 or another antiseptic. Currently it is not authorized in vinegars, but it is in
condiments.
16.3.5 otHer treatments
16.3.5.1 Vinegar Coloring
The color of vinegar normally comes from the natural color of the raw material.
```
Caramel (E 150a,b,d: plain caramel, caustic sulfite caramel, and sulfite ammo-
```
```
nia caramel) is the only coloring authorized, and it is usually added to provide a
```
balsamic character to the final product. The authorized dose is usually quantum
```
satis [Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008], i.e., it can be used to the amount required to
```
achieve the desired result, as it is considered generally harmless. For example, the
dark color of dark malt vinegar derives from the addition of barley extract or caramel
```
to malt vinegar, which normally has a pale straw-like color (Grierson, 2009). Finally,
```
the balsamic vinegar of Modena is a flavored wine vinegar obtained by blending
cooked must with wine vinegar and, in some cases, by adding a small amount of
```
caramel (Giudici et al., 2009).
```
16.3.5.2 Vinegar Decolorization
It is a common practice in the vinegar industry to decolorize a fraction of vinegar and
blend it with colored vinegar in order to obtain a final product with standard charac-
teristics and quality. The total or partial decolorization of the coloring matter of vin-
```
egar is usually carried out using powdered oenological activated carbon (vegetable
```
```
origin), which is added to the vinegar, allowed to settle, and then filtered (see also
```
```
Chapter 6). This type of treatment usually takes a long time (between 48–72 hours)
```
336 Advances in Vinegar Production
for the sedimentation of the carbon particles. Normally, the consumption of activated
carbon is high, and the decolorizing process may require doses of 10–20 g/L of
activated carbon, which increase the production costs and vinegar losses, and cause
```
a significant generation of residues (Achaerandio et al., 2002a,b; López et al., 2003).
```
Another alternative to the decolorization of vinegar by powdered activated car-
bon is the use of activated carbons in pellets, which can be packed in columns, allow-
ing the process to be carried out continuously, thus minimizing product losses and
```
generation of waste (Achaerandio et al., 2002a; López et al., 2003).
```
In cider vinegars, the color is modified during the ageing step. Specifically,
```
the color, which is intensified by the activity of polyphenol oxidase (a constitu-
```
```
tive enzyme of apples) during the milling and pressing processes, fades during the
```
fermentation and maturation phases, probably due to the polymerization of procy-
anidins and other polyphenols. It is a general practice to use PVPP and carbon to
```
reduce the color by removing oxidized and polymerized procyanidins (Joshi and
```
```
Sharma, 2009).
```
```
Another alternative is the use of exchange resins (not currently authorized)
```
```
(Achaerandio et al., 2003, 2007) or using tangential nanofiltration. In vinegar
```
decolorization, nanofiltration can be an alternative processing technique to the
```
traditional process using activated carbon. Güell and López (2001) decolorized
```
vinegar on a small pilot-plant that operated with a titanium dioxide membrane
fused on a porous ceramic tube with a nominal molecular cut-off of 1 kDa. The
decolorization efficiency was 88.2 and 35.5% for red and white vinegars, respec-
tively. It was also observed that the membrane treatment affected the fixed acidity
and the dry matter content of the product but left the other parameters almost unaf-
fected. That study suggested that nanofiltration can be used successfully to reduce
the color of vinegar.
16.3.5.3 Vinegar Deodorization
Deodorization is the total or partial elimination of substances that give an unpleasant
odor to vinegar using deodorant charcoal. The treatment procedure is similar to that
used for the decolorization of vinegars by activated carbon powder.
```
Citric acid (E-330) forms a stable complex with metals, such as iron and copper,
```
which catalyze the oxidative polymerization of polyphenols, and acts as preservative
```
of the color, aroma, and the vitamin content of the vinegar (Joshi and Sharma, 2009).
```
Generally, citric acid is used in oenology to enhance the acid taste in low acid prod-
```
ucts (wines). It also adds a “liveliness” or “freshness” sensation by unmasking fruity
```
flavors and can also help adjust the acidity in order to make fermentation more vigor-
ous. However, its major disadvantage is that it is microbially unstable, and therefore,
it may promote the growth of undesirable bacteria.
Pectin and arabic gum can also be added to stabilize vinegar against haze forma-
```
tion (Joshi and Sharma, 2009) as described in more detail in Chapter 6.
```
```
Finally, potassium ferrocyanide is used as a fining agent (blue fining) to remove
```
```
iron from vinegars (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). Specifically, potassium ferrocyanide
```
```
reacts with ferric iron (Fe +3) to form a blue insoluble precipitate of ferric ferrocya-
```
```
nide precipitate Fe 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ]3 (Prussian or Berlin blue), which can be easily sepa-
```
```
rated by flocculation with gelatin or bentonite (Popescu-Mitroi and Radu, 2017).
```

Vinegar Aroma Profile
and Analysis
Cristina Úbeda, Rocío Ríos-Reina, María
del Pilar Segura-Borrego, Raquel María
Callejón, and María Lourdes Morales
17.1 INTRODUCTION
Aroma is one of the most important organoleptic properties of food and hence a
quality indicator. Aroma is composed of volatile substances that can excite olfactory
receptors in the nose, and a smell is perceived. Moreover, other volatile food com-
pounds that do not provide a characteristic odor can contribute to aroma by enhanc-
```
ing or masking other aromatic compounds (Gamero et al., 2014). Therefore, the
```
volatile fraction of food is a complex mixture of volatile compounds of which only a
part directly influences its odor. The aroma, therefore, depends on the concentration
of aromatic compounds and interactions between different volatile compounds, as
```
well as between volatile and non-volatile compounds (Polášková et al., 2008).
```
The relevance of the quality volatile fraction of vinegar and, therefore, its aroma,
reside in its use as a seasoning to add flavor to food. For this reason, the value and
quality of vinegar are related to its unique and complex volatile composition. The
primary variables defining the vinegar volatile fraction are the raw material used and

```
the production process (submerged or surface acetous fermentation, ageing process,
```
```
etc.) (Callejón et al., 2009, 2010). So far, the effect on the volatile fraction of vin-
```
egar of the microorganisms involved in the fermentation process has scarcely been
```
studied (Callejón et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017).
```
Further studies concerning the role of microorganisms in vinegar volatile composi-
tion are necessary.
17.2 VOLATILE COMPOSITION OF VINEGAR
17.2.1 CHaraCteristiC Volatile profiles of Vinegars
Vinegar is the resultant product of a two-stage alcoholic and acetous fermen-
tation. The volatile profile of vinegar is primarily formed by the volatile com-
```
pounds produced throughout these two fermentation processes (Callejón et al.,
```
```
2009). It must be taken into account, however, that fermentation processes with
```
```
strong aeration may result in loss of highly volatile compounds (Morales et al.,
```
```
2001b). Despite the profound changes that the vinegar production process implies,
```
some vinegars retain compounds from the raw material in their volatile profiles
```
(Cejudo-Bastante et al., 2016). Finally, the maturing and ageing processes, to
```
which high-quality vinegars are submitted, contribute to increasing the complex-
ity of their volatile profile. In these processes, chemical transformations take
place, and, when vinegars are aged in wooden barrels, simultaneous extraction of
```
compounds from the wood occurs (Callejón et al., 2010); this final phase provides
```
added value to the product.
Primarily, the volatile profile of vinegars includes alcohols, carboxylic acids,
ethyl esters and acetic acid esters, and, depending on the type of vinegar, differ-
ent proportions of aldehydes, ketones, acetals, lactones, terpenes, volatile phenols
```
or pyrazines are also present (Table 17.1). Characteristic volatile compounds of
```
vinegar, such as acetic acid, acetoin and ethyl acetate, are found in greater quanti-
ties than others. In aged vinegars, acetoin and ethyl acetate can reach quantities
```
higher than 1,000 and 3,500 mg/L, respectively (Callejón et al., 2008b; Guerrero
```
```
et al., 2007).
```
Most of the available literature concerning the analysis of volatile compounds in
vinegars expresses the results as a relative peak area or relative concentration with
respect to an internal standard. This makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the
real volatile composition of these vinegars. Therefore, in this chapter the volatile
composition of vinegars with real data in the literature is initially described, and
then those with semi-quantified data are discussed.
The real data of the volatile composition of red and white wine vinegars, balsamic
```
vinegars from Modena and Reggio Emilia (traditional and non-traditional), Sherry
```
vinegar from different categories and some fruit vinegars such as apple, pineapple
```
and strawberry vinegars are primarily included or discussed in this chapter (Callejón
```
```
et al., 2008b; Del Signore, 2001; Guerrero et al., 2007; Roda et al., 2017; Ubeda et
```
```
al., 2011).
```

362 Advances in Vinegar Production
17.2.2 aCids
```
In acetous fermentation, acetic acid bacteria transform ethanol into acetic acid; this
```
acid is the primary product of this fermentation process, except in the case of tra-
```
ditional balsamic vinegar (Giudici et al., 2009). Moreover, acetic acid bacteria also
```
transform other alcohols into their respective fatty acids, endowing vinegars with
other remarkable acids including isovaleric, isobutyric and hexanoic acid.
17.2.3 alCoHols
Although ethanol is metabolized by acetic acid bacteria, there is still a residual ethanol
content in certain vinegars, especially in those obtained by surface acetous fermentation.
```
In these cases, ethanol is the major alcohol (Callejón et al., 2008b). This residual ethanol
```
content favors the formation of ethyl esters, which improve the aroma of such vinegars
```
(Callejón et al., 2008b). As mentioned above, other alcohols are also metabolized by
```
```
acetic acid bacteria; thus the amount of these alcohols depends on the substrate content
```
```
and the type of fermentation. Callejón et al. (2009) observed that isobutanol decreases
```
in surface acetous fermentation only. Therefore, without taking ethanol into account,
```
3-methyl-1-butanol is the most abundant alcohol in most cases (Callejón et al., 2008b;
```
```
Guerrero et al., 2007), 2-propanol in balsamic vinegar (Del Signore, 2001) and 2-phenyl-
```
```
ethanol in pineapple vinegar (Roda et al., 2017). The content of methanol is usually high
```
```
in both fruit (Ubeda et al., 2011) and in red wine vinegars (Callejón et al., 2008b).
```
17.2.4 esters
Acetic acid esters stand out among the esters since their formation is favored due to
the high amount of acetic acid. Ethyl acetate is the major vinegar ester, characteristic
of traditional vinegar aged in wooden barrels such as Sherry or balsamic vinegars
```
(Callejón et al., 2008b; Morales et al., 2001a). Although it smells like glue and is
```
```
present at high quantities, ethyl acetate has a high perception threshold (Tesfaye,
```
```
2001) and is not considered an aroma defect. In addition to ethyl acetate, vinegar
```
contains other acetic esters, primarily isoamyl, 2-phenylethyl and isobutyl acetate,
whose quantity depends on the abundance of their precursor alcohols. Acetic acid
```
esters usually provide fruity aromas (Callejón et al., 2008b).
```
Vinegars also contain ethyl esters, but their concentration is usually lower than
```
that of the acetic acid esters (Callejón et al., 2008b). This may be due to a hydrolysis
```
process probably caused by the active consumption of ethanol by acetic acid bacteria
```
during the acetous fermentation (Callejón et al., 2009). In some vinegars, the quan-
```
```
tity of ethyl lactate and diethyl succinate (Guerrero et al., 2007) stand out, as well as
```
others that provide fruity aromas, such as ethyl isobutyrate, butyrate and isovalerate
```
(Callejón et al., 2008b), or ethyl benzoate in pineapple vinegar (Roda et al., 2017).
```
17.2.5 CarBonyl Compounds
Among ketones, as mentioned above, acetoin is one of the most abundant. This pro-
```
vides an aroma of dairy products (Callejón et al., 2008b), and its content increases
```
363Vinegar Aroma Profile and Analysis
during acetous fermentation by the decarboxylation of α-acetolactate by acetic acid
```
bacteria (Asai, 1968). Moreover, aged vinegars such as balsamic and Sherry vinegar
```
have a remarkable diacetyl content, 44.15 and 197 mg/L being the maximum values
```
observed, respectively (Callejón et al., 2008b; Del Signore, 2001). This compound is
```
```
produced by the oxidation of acetoin (Mecca et al., 1979), as described in Chapter 7.
```
The most important aldehyde in vinegars is acetaldehyde, which derives from
wine since yeasts produce acetaldehyde as a secondary product of alcoholic fermen-
```
tation (Bosso and Guaita, 2008). In the special case of Sherry vinegar, when the raw
```
material used to obtain vinegar is a wine with biological ageing under flor velum, a
high quantity of acetaldehyde is to be expected. This compound is a characteristic
```
metabolite of this kind of flor velum yeast (Zea et al., 2015). For this reason, Sherry
```
```
vinegar may reach an acetaldehyde content of up to 98 mg/L (Callejón et al., 2008b).
```
Acetaldehyde is, moreover, also an intermediary product of the transformation of
```
ethanol to acetic acid by acetic acid bacteria as well as by chemical oxidation (Ubeda
```
```
et al., 2011). High quantities of this compound have also been found in strawberry
```
```
vinegars (Ubeda et al., 2011). On the other hand, when acetous fermentation is per-
```
formed in an open acetification system, a loss of this highly volatile compound may
```
occur (Morales el at. 2001b, Valero et al., 2005). For this reason, vinegars produced
```
by acetous fermentation with surface cultures have higher quantities of acetaldehyde
than those obtained by submerged cultures.
Vinegar also contains other aldehydes, with 2-furfuraldehyde, vanillin and
5-hydroxymethylfurfural in Sherry and balsamic vinegars being worthy of note, the
```
latter especially in balsamic vinegars (Callejón et al., 2008b; Chinnici et al., 2009;
```
```
Guerrero et al., 2007). These compounds may derive from wood (Tesfaye et al.,
```
```
2002), but those classified as furans may also come from the legal addition of cara-
```
mel must in Sherry vinegar or from the cooked must that is used as raw material in
balsamic vinegar.
17.2.6 otHer Compounds
Some vinegars contain other furanic, pyranic and pyrazine compounds, character-
istic of the thermal processing of either the raw material or the vinegar, such as in
balsamic vinegar and traditional Chinese vinegar production, respectively. These
```
compounds are primarily a result of Maillard reactions (Chinnici et al., 2009; Zhou
```
```
et al, 2017).
```
Some compounds are characteristic of the plant raw material used to produce the
vinegar. Terpenes are, for example, present in the volatile profile of fruit vinegars,
```
especially orange vinegars (Cejudo-Bastante, 2016; Coelho et al., 2017; Ozturk et al.,
```
```
2015), and lactones in strawberry and mango vinegars (Coelho et al., 2017; Ubeda
```
```
et al., 2016). Moreover, Guerrero et al. (2007) observed that C6 volatile compounds
```
are characteristic of apple vinegars.
During ageing in wooden barrels, vinegars extract wood compounds and they
lose water. As a result, the vinegars are enriched with volatile phenols and lactones,
```
such as eugenol or β-methyl-γ-octalactone (Callejón et al., 2010).
```
Finally, high-quality vinegars such as Sherry vinegars, traditional balsamic vin-
```
egar (from Modena and Reggio Emilia) and traditional Chinese vinegar (mature
```
364 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
Shanxi vinegar or Zhenjiang aromatic vinegar) present characteristic volatile com-
```
pounds due to their special production process. Among them, sotolon can be men-
tioned as a characteristic volatile compound of Sherry vinegars, which reaches high
```
concentrations in the longest-aged vinegars (Callejón et al., 2008b). As mentioned
```
above, traditional balsamic vinegars have a high variety and quantity of furans and,
along with pyrazines, the same occurs in the case of traditional Chinese vinegar
```
(Chinnici et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2017).
```
Although extraction methods are different, a graphical comparison of the vola-
tile profiles of different vinegars is presented in Figure 17.1. In this figure, semi-
quantitative data have been depicted. As can be seen, esters reach high percentages
```
in Spanish vinegars with Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) and balsamic vin-
```
egars from Modena, acids in fruit and Chinese vinegars from submerged fermenta-
tion and furanic compounds in Chinese vinegars from solid state fermentation and
in traditional balsamic vinegars from Modena.
17.3 ANALYSIS OF VINEGAR AROMA
17.3.1 extraCtion/sampling metHods for gas CHromatograpHy analysis
```
The vinegar volatile fraction is analyzed by gas chromatography (GC). Currently,
```
```
the widespread use of a mass spectrometer (MS) detector coupled to a GC sys-
```
tem requires an extraction step prior to analysis. In the vinegar volatile component
FIGURE 17.1 Volatile profile expressed as percentage of chemical groups of different vin-
```
egars: vinegars from Spain with PDO (Ríos-Reina et al., 2018), fruit vinegars (Su and Chien,
```
```
2010; Ubeda et al., 2016), vinegar from Modena with Protected European Geographical
```
```
Indication (Marrufo-Curtido et al., 2012) and Chinese vinegars (Xiao et al, 2011; Yu et al.,
```
```
2012). LCP = Low pyrazines, HCP = high pyrazines and PX = vinegars with a percentage of
```
Pedro Ximénez wine.
365Vinegar Aroma Profile and Analysis
analysis, different extraction methods have been used such as liquid-liquid extrac-
```
tion (LLE) (Zhong, 2011), simultaneous steam distillation-extraction (SDE) (Fu-xian
```
```
et al., 2014; Yun-qing, 2013), solid phase extraction (SPE) (Durán-Guerrero et al.,
```
```
2008), solid phase microextraction (SPME) (Cocchi et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2016) and
```
```
stir bar (SB) extraction by immersion (SBSE) (Guerrero et al., 2006) or in headspace
```
```
(HSSE) (Callejón et al., 2008a).
```
In order to avoid the use of contaminant solvents and their attendant health risk,
LLE has been replaced by more “green” methods, although recently a new type of
```
LLE has been used, in which a very small amount of solvent is used (only 400 μL),
```
```
this being a liquid-liquid microextraction (Coelho et al., 2017).
```
SDE is one of the most traditional extraction methods, first applied to vinegar in
1992 by Blanch et al., to determine the volatile compounds in conventional wine vin-
egars and Sherry wine vinegars. This method uses a special apparatus, in which the
volatile analytes are extracted from the matrix by water vapor and transferred to an
extracting solvent, when the water and organic solvent condense together on a cold
tube. After their condensation, water and solvent are collected and returned to their
```
corresponding flasks, thus enabling continuous extraction (Augusto et al., 2003).
```
Lickens and Nickerson designed the first SDE apparatus, but later other research-
ers performed modifications to improve the extraction process. There are, there-
```
fore, different apparatuses for performing SDE; some even enable the use of a small
```
```
amount of solvent (Chaintreau, 2001). The SDE method has several drawbacks such
```
as the formation of artifacts due to the high temperatures applied during distillation
```
(Chaintreau, 2001). This method is still used for determining the volatile composi-
```
```
tion of different kinds of vinegars such as lychee vinegar (Zhencheng et al., 2011),
```
```
pineapple bran vinegar (Yun-qing, 2013), Shanxi mature vinegar (Jinrong, 2013) and
```
```
apricot dregs vinegar (Fu-xian et al., 2014).
```
Some researchers have employed LLE and SDE to study Shanxi mature vinegar
aroma components and concluded that SDE is a good extraction technique for deter-
mining low-boiling-point substances, and LLE for high-boiling-point substances
```
(Zhong and Zhebin, 2011).
```
Since it is performed using a vacuum pump, solvent-assisted flavor evaporation
```
(SAFE) is a low-temperature distillation method. This method has scarcely been
```
employed for the determination of volatile compounds in vinegars and, specifically,
```
for performing olfactometric analysis (Liang et al., 2016).
```
In the SPE method, analytes are retained in a sorbent and then eluted from the
sorbent using a solvent. There are different types of cartridges that may be used
depending on the kind of analytes under study. A C18 cartridge was used by Zeppa
```
et al. (2002) for determining volatile compounds in three acetification batteries
```
```
from Reggio Emilia (Italy). Chinnini et al. (2009) used a LiChrolut-EN cartridge to
```
```
characterize and compare Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (TBVM) and
```
```
Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (BVM) from Italy and Sherry vinegar from Spain.
```
In both types, a similar number of compounds was detected: over 100 and 93,
respectively. This last type of cartridge had previously been used by Morales et al.
```
(2004) to determine characteristic volatile wood compounds in vinegar. In the SPE
```
method, the procedure is performed in several stages and, usually, finishes with a
concentration step, which can be performed under vacuum or nitrogen stream. SPE
366 Advances in Vinegar Production
with a derivatization process has, moreover, been applied to analyze aldehydes in
```
high-quality vinegars (Durán-Guerrero et al., 2015).
```
```
All the abovementioned methods have the disadvantage of using organic solvents;
```
some are time-consuming, and, moreover, the number of samples that can be pro-
cessed simultaneously is not very high. Currently, there is growing interest in the
use of extraction methods that comply with the green chemistry concepts. Moreover,
another drawback of the use of organic solvents is that they produce chromatographic
interferences making it difficult to correctly determine those compounds with simi-
lar boiling points to that of the solvent.
Among solvent-free extraction methods applied to study vinegar volatile com-
```
position are static headspace (SHS), dynamic headspace (DHS), SPME, SBSE and
```
```
HSSE (Table 17.2).
```
In general, these methods are easier to use than the previous ones. SHS is a simple
sampling method, in which an aliquot of the gas phase above the sample, in a condi-
```
tion of equilibrium, is taken (Ettre, 2002). In most cases, the analytical equipment
```
performs SHS extraction automatically. This, however, has several disadvantages
such as low sensitivity and that it is only suitable for substances with high volatility.
Therefore, this method is useful for determining major volatile compounds when a
```
direct injection of the sample cannot be carried out (Ubeda et al., 2011). SHS has
```
scarcely been applied to vinegar analysis.
On the contrary, DHS, a similar extraction technique for studying volatile com-
pounds, is beginning to be used in vinegars. In this method, volatile and semi-vol-
atile substances are continuously extracted from the sample headspace by an inert
gas stream and retained in a trap. They are then desorbed into the analytical equip-
```
ment. DHS is a high-capacity extraction method; hence it provides low detection
```
```
limits (Soria et al., 2015). This, however, has the disadvantage of water retention
```
in the extraction phase when the sample to be analyzed is liquid. Despite that, this
sampling method has been successfully applied to Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di
```
Modena analysis for determining furfurals (Manzini et al., 2011), in Shanxi aged
```
```
vinegar for studying changes in volatile compounds during fermentation (Zhu et al.,
```
```
2016) and for comparing the volatile profiles of different strawberry vinegars (Ubeda
```
```
et al., 2016).
```
Another important trend in extraction methods is the miniaturization of the
extraction devices, thus diminishing the extraction phase quantity. Among them,
SPME is the most widely applied vinegar sampling or extraction method. SPME
is performed using a special device consisting of a fiber, coated with a thin layer
```
of extraction phase and fixed inside a needle of a syringe-like device (Wardencki
```
```
et al., 2007). This sampling method has been primarily applied to extract volatile
```
```
compounds from the headspace of vinegars (HS-SPME). Volatile substances accu-
```
mulated on the extraction fiber are directly introduced into a gas chromatograph by
thermal desorption in the injection port. There are different polymers used as extrac-
tion phases, the most frequently used in vinegar analysis being a 75 μm carboxen-
```
polydimethylsiloxane (CAR-PDMS) fiber. HS-SPME has been applied to study the
```
```
volatile fraction of different wine vinegars and cider vinegars (Pizarro et al., 2008),
```
```
vinegars obtained from different fruits, such as blueberry vinegar (Su and Chien,
```
```
2010) and pineapple vinegar (Roda et al., 2017), or traditional home-made Turkish
```

368 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
vinegar obtained primarily from fruits (Ozturk et al., 2015). This method has also
```
been used to research the effect of the ageing process on the volatile composition of
```
Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena (Cocci et al., 2008) and balsamic Modena
```
```
vinegars (Cirlini et al., 2011), to differentiate Chinese vinegars (Xiao et al, 2011)
```
and to determine characteristic volatile compounds of traditional Chinese Zhenjiang
```
aromatic vinegar (Yu et al., 2012). Although it is the most widely used extraction
```
technique in vinegar volatile composition analysis, it has lower sensitivity compared
to DHS or SBSE due to the smaller quantity of the extraction phase.
SBSE or HSSE are other fast, easy-to-use and miniaturized extraction methods,
in which the extraction is performed using a stir bar coated with extraction polymers.
Although recently stir bars coated with new extraction phases have been commer-
cialized, the PDMS stir bar has been the only one used in vinegars up to the present
moment. The extraction technique has been applied to study the volatile composition
of high-quality vinegars, both by direct immersion of the sorptive stir bar into the
```
sample (SBSE) (Marrufo-Curtido et al., 2012) and by placing it into the headspace
```
```
(HSSE) (Callejón et al., 2008b). Several authors have highlighted the advantages of
```
```
SBSE versus SPME (Guerrero et al., 2006) or HSSE versus DHS and SPME in order
```
```
to study volatile profiles (Ríos-Reina et al., 2018).
```
Once volatile compounds have been extracted using one of the abovementioned
methods, they are injected into the CG system. For this kind of sample, the most
frequently used are the polar phase analytical columns. To perform an unequivocal
identification of compounds, among other requirements, a MS detector is necessary.
This enables the compound mass spectrum to be obtained and to tentatively identify
```
this compound using a standard mass spectra library. Linear retention index (LRI)
```
```
or Kováts index (I) values are then calculated and compared to those of standards
```
analyzed using columns with a polarity similar to that of the stationary phase in
order to confirm the identification.
```
Comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography (GC × GC) is a powerful
```
and effective analytical technique for analyzing complex samples. This method has
been applied to study the volatile composition of aromatic Zhenjiang vinegar, tenta-
```
tively identifying a total of 360 compounds (Zhou et al., 2017). To date, this recent
```
```
analytical technique has hardly been used; it could, however, be very useful for gain-
```
ing in-depth knowledge of the complex volatile profiles of high-quality vinegars.
17.3.2 olfaCtometriC teCHniques
The aroma is a complex mixture of many volatile compounds, which are present in
```
concentrations above their odor perception threshold in the matrix (Delahunty et al.,
```
```
2006). In fact, food matrices may contain hundreds of volatile compounds, but only
```
a small number of them make a direct contribution to the aroma of the food. Thus,
a volatile compound contributes to the global aroma of a matrix depending on its
```
odor activity value (OAV), that is, if its concentration divided by its odor percep-
```
tion threshold is above 1. Therefore, compounds with a very low odor perception
threshold may contribute to a great extent despite their low concentration. Similarly,
it is possible that substances present in a high concentration may not contribute
to the global aroma of the sample due to their elevated odor perception threshold.
369Vinegar Aroma Profile and Analysis
In this context, it is important to have a method for defining or assigning the relative
importance of every volatile compound in order to identify the source of the aroma
```
(Delahunty et al., 2006). The compounds with the greatest contribution to the global
```
aroma are denominated “key aroma compounds.” The technique employed for the
```
analysis is GC with olfactometer (GC–O) working as the detector. The GC enables
```
the different volatile compounds present in the sample to be separated, and as these
```
compounds are eluted, they are perceived (or not) and identified by the human nose
```
```
(Blank, 2002).
```
Aroma determination is possible through a special device, the sniffing port, which
is located at the end of the chromatography column. It is important to mention that
the GC is usually coupled to another detector in addition to the olfactometer, usu-
```
ally detectors such as the MS or the flame ionization detector (FID) (Plutowska and
```
```
Wardencki, 2008). Therefore, GC–O is a hybrid technique because it is possible both
```
```
to determine the chemical structure of the compound and to define its odor (Brattoli
```
```
et al., 2013) (Figure 17.2).
```
As mentioned earlier, compound identification is carried out using the LRI of
each compound. These are calculated by injecting a mixture of alkanes in the GC
under the same conditions as the sample analysis.
The different olfactometric techniques that have been developed are based on the
```
ability of the human nose to measure the odor length (from when it is perceived until
```
```
it disappears), to describe its quality and to quantify its intensity. These techniques
```
```
are:
```
Dilution to threshold. These techniques are used to quantify the compound odor
potency based on the relationship between odor concentration and its perception
```
threshold in the air (Acree, 1993). Among the most applied techniques, aroma extract
```
```
dilution analysis (AEDA) and combined hedonic aroma response measurement
```
```
(CHARM) differ from each other mainly in the way in which data are registered.
```
AEDA. This technique determines the maximum dilution of an extract in which
the odor of the compound analyzed can still be perceived. This value is employed to
```
calculate the dilution factor (van Ruth, 2001). CHARM, on the other hand, records
```
```
FIGURE 17.2 Gas chromatography-olfactometry (GC–O) analysis.
```
370 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
the length of the aroma needed in order to create chromatographic peaks (Plutowska
```
```
and Wardencki, 2008).
```
Time-intensity. These techniques record the presence or absence of an odorant
and the intensity with which it is perceived. To measure the intensities of odorants
perception, different scales of measurement will be used.
What differentiates the three techniques is the manner of registering the intensi-
```
ties: Later Intensity, Osme and Finger-Span. In general, the main drawback of time-
```
intensity techniques is the intense training that panelists require in order to obtain
reproducible results.
```
Frequency detection, also called nasal impact frequency (NIF). In these tech-
```
niques, a panel analyzes the same extract of the sample, noting the absence/presence
of the odorant and describing its aroma. The percentage of panelists who can detect
```
the odorant in a specific retention time is then calculated (Pollien et al., 1997). It is
```
considered that the compounds that were detected most frequently are those that have
a greater relative importance in the aroma of the sample. In addition, it is assumed
that the results obtained are related to the intensity of the smell perceived in the con-
```
centration at which the analyte is present in the extract (van Ruth, 2001). An odorant
```
that has been detected by the entire panel will, therefore, have an intensity value of
100%. Moreover, it is also usual to use a combination of intensity and frequency of
```
detection through the modified frequency (MF), which is the geometric mean of the
```
```
detection frequency of an aromatic zone (expressed as a percentage) and the aver-
```
```
age intensity (expressed as a percentage of the maximum intensity) (San-Juan et al.,
```
```
2010). The fundamental advantage of these techniques is their simplicity; they are
```
less time-consuming than the other techniques, a good reproducibility is obtained,
```
and the panelists do not require much training (Plutowska and Wardencki, 2008).
```
To date, there is no universal method or technique for determining the relative
importance of the volatile compounds identified as “active aromas,” since each of the
olfactometric techniques has advantages and disadvantages that must be considered
in order to apply the technique that best fits with our proposal.
In general, all these techniques employ an extract of the sample to perform the
analysis, and, therefore, this is an important issue to consider. The food flavor pro-
file is closely related to the isolation procedure, which should be representative of
```
the sample (d’Acampora Zellner et al., 2008). Depending on the properties of the
```
food product, the extraction procedure may include, among others, centrifugation,
```
solvent extraction (SE), headspace (HS) techniques and solid phase micro extraction
```
```
(SPME) (d’Acampora Zellner et al., 2008).
```
17.3.2.1 Olfactometric Analysis of Vinegar
Olfactometry has been applied widely in several food matrices such as coffee,
```
cheese, meat and strawberries, among others (Drake et al., 2001; Guth and Grosch,
```
```
1994; Semmelroch et al., 1995; Ubeda et al., 2012). However, it has been scarcely
```
employed in vinegar aroma analysis.
Sherry vinegar is the most studied using the GC–O technique. Callejón et al.
```
(2008b) defined the typical aroma of this vinegar and established that diacetyl, iso-
```
amyl acetate, isovaleric acid, sotolon and ethyl acetate are characteristic odor active
compounds in Sherry vinegars. The vinegars employed were representative samples
371Vinegar Aroma Profile and Analysis
of vinegars from the three existing qualities according to ageing time in oak bar-
```
rels: Vinagre de Jerez (minimum of 6 months), Reserva (at least 2 years) and Gran
```
```
Reserva (at least 10 years). In that study, the extract for GC–O was obtained employ-
```
```
ing different solvents (hexane, ether and dichloromethane) and applying a frequency
```
detection methodology. Later, the same authors restricted the responsibility for the
```
typical aroma of Sherry vinegars, diacetyl (odor description: butter), ethyl acetate
```
```
(glue) and sotolon (curry/liquorice), to three compounds, emphasizing their impor-
```
```
tant contribution to aroma (Callejón et al., 2008c). In this case, they employed aroma
```
```
extract dilution analysis (AEDA) and a representative sample of Sherry vinegar from
```
the Reserva category.
```
Afterwards, Aceña et al. (2011) employed the HS-SPME technique for extract-
```
ing the aroma compounds in vinegars aged for 6 months in oak barrels and AEDA
methodology for acquiring data. They established that the compounds with the
OAV higher than 1 were: ethyl isovalerate, ethyl isobutyrate, isoamyl acetate,
2-phenylethyl acetate, 2-phenyl ethanol, 4-ethylguaiacol, 4-ethylphenol, isovale-
ric, 2-methylbutyric and isobutyric acids. This difference was mainly attributed to
the different extraction method employed. In addition to Sherry vinegars, red wine
vinegar has also been studied, resulting in a representative extract employing solid
```
phase extraction technique and frequency detection method (Charles et al., 2000).
```
In this case, 2-phenylethanol, 2,3-butanedione, a mixture of 2- and 3-methylbuta-
```
nol, 3-hydroxy-2-pentanone, 3-(methylthio)-1-propanal and acetic, 3-methylbutyric,
```
butyric, 2-methylbutyric acids were defined as the most important contributors to red
wine vinegar aroma.
GC–O not only has been applied to wine vinegars but also vinegars produced
from other raw fruit materials. This is the case of a GC–O analysis of blueberry vin-
```
egar, where Su and Chien (2010) found acetic acid, 2- and 3-methyl-butanoic acid,
```
2-phenylethyl acetate, 2-phenylethanol, octanoic acid, eugenol and phenylacetic acid
to be the most important contributors to blueberry vinegar aroma. They extracted
the volatile compounds employing HS-SMPE analysis and performed an Osme pro-
cedure, which provides a description of odor, time, odor intensity and peak area of
time–odor intensity plot.
```
Moreover, strawberry vinegar has been analyzed by Ubeda et al. (2012), looking
```
for typical characteristic strawberry aromas present in the final sample and search-
ing for differences between strawberry vinegars produced via spontaneous alco-
holic fermentation and from inoculated fermentation. A total of 12 odor zones were
described as impact odorants in strawberry vinegars: acetic, butyric and isovaleric
```
acids, methional, 3-nonen-2-one, 2-phenylethanol, pantolactone + furaneol (impact
```
```
odorant in strawberry), p-vinylguaiacol, sotolon, phenylacetic acid and vanillin.
```
Furthermore, in order to check the effect on their aroma profile, that research team
```
analyzed strawberry vinegars produced in different containers (Ubeda et al., 2016).
```
Isovaleric acid, pantolactone + furaneol, p-vinylguaiacol, phenylacetic acid and van-
illin were the most important active aroma compounds in these strawberry vinegars.
Apart from fruit substrates, other vinegars made from cereals have also been
```
analyzed such as Zhenjiang aromatic vinegar, made from rice, koji (a specific
```
```
fermented cereal containing molds, yeasts and bacteria) and wheat bran (Zhou
```
```
et al., 2017). In that study, they designated methanethiol, 2-methyl-propanal,
```
372 Advances in Vinegar Production
2- and 3-methyl-butanal, octanal, 1-octen-3-one, dimethyl trisulfide, trimethyl pyr-
```
azine, acetic acid, 3-(methylthio)-propanal, furfural, benzeneacetaldehyde, 3- and
```
2-methyl-butanoic acid and 2-phenylethyl acetate as the most potent odorants of that
vinegar.
17.4 CONCLUSIONS
Vinegar is a seasoning usually added to give flavor to food. For this reason, the
quality of both volatile fraction and aroma are important. Characterization of the
complex vinegar volatile fraction requires analytical methods with high sensitivity
such as GC coupled to MS. For this purpose, vinegars are submitted to a previous
extraction process. For determining the volatile profile of vinegar, the most widely
used extraction technique has been SPME. Recently, however, several authors have
showed better results using PDMS stir bar by immersion as well as in headspace.
The volatile profile of vinegars includes primarily alcohols, carboxylic acids,
ethyl esters and acetic acid esters, and, depending on the type of vinegar, different
proportions of aldehydes, ketones, lactones, terpenes, volatile phenols or pyrazines
are also to be found. The major compounds in most vinegars are acetic acid, acetoin
and ethyl acetate. Although most vinegars have the same volatile compounds, these
are present in different quantities. Moreover, due to their specific production method,
traditional balsamic vinegars are rich in furans, traditional Chinese vinegars are
rich in pyrazines, and those vinegars aged in wooden barrels are rich in wood com-
pounds. Therefore, from all the above it can be deduced that the volatile profile of
vinegars from the same raw material depends primarily on the production method.
Among all volatile compounds present in vinegars, only some will be important
to vinegar aroma. There are few works on olfactometric analysis for describing the
aroma of vinegars. The results have shown that the vinegars studied have some com-
mon impact odorants, such as acetic or isovaleric acid and 2-phenylethyl acetate,
as well as others characteristic to each vinegar, such as methanethiol, 2-methyl-
propanal or trimethyl pyrazine in Chinese cereal vinegar or furaneol in strawberry
vinegars.
Therefore, further studies on aroma and impact odorants of a greater variety of
vinegars using olfactometric analysis will be necessary. Moreover, future research
applying two-dimensional chromatography will enable further insight into the vola-
tile profile of different vinegars.
