18
Health Benefits
of Vinegars
Jin Wei Alvin Ling, Sue Lian Mun, Shazrul
Fazry, Azwan Mat Lazim, and Seng Joe Lim
18.1 INTRODUCTION
Vinegar has been widely used for its health benefits, which are continuously investigated
and scientifically proven and emphasized. The functional, therapeutic effects of vinegar
arise from the content of inherent bioactive components such as acetic acid, gallic acid,
catechin, ephicatechin, chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, p-coumaric acid, and ferulic acid,
which are able to induce antioxidative, antidiabetic, antimicrobial, antitumor, antiobe-
```
sity, antihypertensive, and cholesterol-regulating responses (Budak et al., 2014).
```
For example, it has been reported that vinegar can help regulate the blood pres-
sure, improve the digestive system function, stimulate appetite, lower the lipid levels,
```
and alleviate fatigue symptoms (Fushimi et al., 2001; Qui et al., 2010). Moreover,
```
vinegar constituents such as polyphenols have been reported to prevent hyperten-
```
sion, inflammation, hyperlipidemia, lipid peroxidation, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)
```
```
damage, and even cancer (Chou et al., 2015; Osada et al., 2006; Prior and Cao, 2000).
```
These bioactive functions have been associated with several beneficial health effects,
```
such as anti-ageing (attributed mainly to antioxidants) and general health well-being.
```

380 Advances in Vinegar Production
Although the main component is acetic acid, vinegars also contain diverse bioac-
tive compounds, depending on the raw materials and the production methods used,
which may impart various effects on human health. The health benefits of vinegar
consumption have been mentioned in many chapters of this book. In this chapter,
these effects, the responsible bioactive components of vinegars, and the most recent
scientific studies are in more detail highlighted and discussed.
18.2 ANTIOXIDANT ACTIVITIES OF VINEGAR
Antioxidant compounds in food are considered capable of reducing health degenera-
```
tion caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as superoxide, hydrogen per-
```
```
oxide (H 2 O2), and the hydroxyl radical. These species have been reported to have
```
negative impact on DNA, proteins, and lipids, leading to brain degenerative disor-
```
ders, accelerated ageing, and cancer (Budak et al., 2014; Maes et al., 2011). Several
```
epidemiological studies have shown the protective effects of the consumption of food
rich in anthocyanins, flavonoids, and other phenolic compounds against diseases
```
(Almeida et al., 2011). During food digestion, the postprandial elevation of plasma
```
lipid hydroperoxides can be minimized by the dietary antioxidants, while oxidative
```
stress in the human body may be caused by low food antioxidant levels (Candido
```
```
et al., 2015; Verzelloni et al., 2007). Oxidative stress and postprandial hyperlipemia
```
are well-defined risk factors of atherosclerosis and other inflammatory, chronic, and
degenerative diseases including accelerated ageing process.
Recent studies have indicated that polyphenols and vitamins are among the bioac-
tive, antioxidant components in vinegars that can reduce such degenerative effects
```
(Pandey and Rizvi, 2009). More specifically, carotenoids, phytosterols, phenolic
```
compounds, and vitamins C and E are the bioactive compounds that contribute to
vinegar antioxidant capacity. Therefore, the detection and analysis of these compo-
```
nents in vinegars is also essential. According to Etherton et al. (2004) the bioactive
```
compounds present in vinegars impart beneficial health effects by affecting physi-
ological and cellular activities with potential to alter the risk of disease. In addition,
the polyphenolic compounds can act as quality determinants regarding the antioxi-
```
dant activity of vinegar, as well as its flavor (astringency) and color (Mas et al., 2014).
```
The determination of the antioxidant capacity of vinegars is usually carried out
```
by methods such as: (1) the DPPH radical scavenging assay (2,2-diphenyl-1-pic-
```
```
rylhydrazyl radical), which involves DPPH reagent (violet) absorbance reduction
```
```
(to yellow) measured at 517 nm after reaction with the sample antioxidants, (2) the
```
```
ABTS radical scavenging activity [2,2’-azino-bis-(3-ethylbenzthiazoline-6-sulfonic
```
```
acid) radical cation; ABTS·+), which involves measurement of the absorbance of
```
```
the green-blue radical at 734 nm after reaction with the sample, and (3) the cupric
```
```
reducing antioxidant capacity (CUPRAC) method, which involves reaction of the
```
```
sample antioxidants with Cu 2+ and neocuproine (2,9-dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline;
```
```
a heterocyclic, chelating organic compound) and measurement of the absorbance
```
at 450 nm. The results in these methods are usually expressed as mg ascorbic acid
```
equivalents or as Trolox (6-hydroxy-2,5,7,8-tetramethylchroman-2-carboxylic acid)
```
```
equivalents (mg per volume of vinegar), using L-ascorbic acid or Trolox as the refer-
```
ence antioxidant compounds, respectively.
381Health Benefits of Vinegars
```
Also, (4) the ferric reducing antioxidant power assay (FRAP) is used, which
```
```
involves reduction of the ferric iron (Fe3+) to the ferrous iron (Fe2+) by the sam-
```
ple antioxidants and measurement of the absorbance of the developed blue color at
594 nm. The antioxidant capacity is determined using a Fe2+ standard curve and is
```
expressed as Fe2+ equivalents (μM) or FRAP value.
```
The total phenolics in vinegars are usually assayed by the reduction of the Folin–
```
Ciocalteu reagent (mixture of phosphomolybdate and phosphotungstate) by the anti-
```
oxidant phenols and polyphenols that are contained in the sample and measurement
of the absorbance at 750–765 nm. The results are usually expressed as mg gallic acid
```
(GAE) equivalents per volume of vinegar.
```
Total flavonoids content of vinegar samples has been analyzed by colorimetric
```
assays, e.g., by the reaction of the samples with NaNO 2 , Al(NO3)3, and NaOH and
```
measurement of the absorbance at 510 nm. The results were expressed as mg rutin/mL
```
of vinegar (Xia et al., 2018a).
```
The analysis of individual phenolic compounds in vinegars is usually carried
out by HPLC methods, most commonly employing a diode array detector with UV
```
wavelength set at 278–280 nm and a reverse-phase column (e.g., C18 type) (Chung
```
```
et al., 2017). Phenolic compounds have also been analyzed in vinegars by selec-
```
```
tive ion monitoring GC–MS, after solid phase extraction and derivatization (e.g.,
```
silylated with N,O–bis-trimethylsilyl-trifluoroacetamide to form trimethylsilyl
```
ethers) (Sinanoglou et al., 2018).
```
Antioxidant vitamins such as vitamin E have been analyzed in vinegar after suit-
```
able extraction with organic solvents, using gas chromatography (GC) equipped with
```
```
a flame ionization detector (FID) (Chung et al., 2017). Vitamin C has been estimated
```
```
in vinegars colorimetrically, e.g., by the indophenol method (deep blue dye), which
```
involves reaction of ascorbic acid and metaphosphoric acid in acetic acid solution
and titration of the indophenol dye until a rose-pink color is formed as the end point
```
(Ho et al., 2017a). Total vitamin C has also been determined in wines and vinegars
```
```
by reaction with dithiothreitol [or Cleland’s reagent; (2S,3S)-1,4-bis(sulfanyl)butane-
```
```
2,3-diol] and N-ethylmaleimide (1-ethylpyrrole-2,5-dione), color development by
```
addition trichloroacetic acid, phosphoric acid, 2,2’-bipyridine, and FeCl 3, and mea-
```
surement of the absorbance at 525 nm (Xiang et al., 2013).
```
```
Finally, high molecular weight melanoidins (Maillard reaction products), which
```
```
highly contribute to the antioxidant activity of heat-treated vinegars (balsamic vin-
```
```
egars), are usually analyzed after extraction by ultrafiltration, washing (diafiltra-
```
```
tion), and drying. Characteristics of the isolated melanoidins, such as their content in
```
proteins, phenolic groups, total carbohydrates, glucose, fructose, and hydroxymeth-
```
ylfurfural may also be evaluated (Verzelloni et al., 2010).
```
18.2.1 reCent researCH on tHe antioxidant properties of Vinegars
A major part of the scientific literature on the bioactive and health promoting prop-
erties of vinegars is related to their antioxidant components and activities. While
earlier studies dealt with the analysis of antioxidant compounds and the antioxidant
capacity of vinegars in vitro, most of the recent scientific literature investigates the
effects of vinegar consumption by in vivo experiments. The available studies are
382 Advances in Vinegar Production
extensive, and in this section some characteristic works published in recent years
are presented.
```
For example, Shimoji et al. (2002) studied the traditional Japanese rice vinegar
```
Kurosu, made from unpolished rice and rice bran, and compared it with common
rice vinegar made only from polished rice. They reported that Kurosu vinegar con-
tained significant amounts of dihydroferulic acid and dihydrosinapic acid suggesting
that both acids were released from rice bran during the fermentation. The superior
antioxidant activity of Kurosu vinegar compared to common rice vinegar was attrib-
uted to these acids. Specifically, Kurosu was found to have 1.95 times higher DPPH
radical scavenging activity compared to that of rice vinegar.
```
Also, according to Nanda et al. (2004), Kurosu vinegar can inhibit the growth
```
```
of human cancer cell lines (breast adenocarcinoma, lung carcinoma, colon adeno-
```
```
carcinoma, bladder carcinoma, and prostate carcinoma), in a dose-dependent man-
```
ner. Ferulic acid, an antioxidant phenolic compound contained in rice bran, was
considered able to hinder the development of human breast and colon cancer cells.
Moreover, the ethyl acetate extract of Kurosu showed ability to restrain the growth
```
of different human cancer cells in vitro (Shimoji et al., 2004). The antioxidative
```
```
activities of the extract helped increase glutathione S-transferase (GST) and quinone
```
reductase activities and suppressed the formation of aberrant crypt foci, which is a
precursor lesion for colonic adenocarcinoma. These findings suggested that the ethyl
acetate extract of Kurosu has the potential to prevent colon carcinogenesis.
```
Other than Kurosu, Kibizu (a sugar cane vinegar produced in Japan) was also
```
found to be able to inhibit the growth of typical human leukemia cells due to its
```
potent radical scavenging activity (Mimura et al., 2004).
```
```
A study by Su and Chien (2007) showed that the fermentation of rabbiteye blue-
```
berries with the skin led to higher antioxidant activities of the product, due to higher
amounts of anthocyanins in the skin that exhibit stronger antioxidant activity com-
pared to other phenolic compounds.
The antioxidant activities of red wine vinegar, balsamic vinegar, and tradi-
tional balsamic vinegar are also strongly correlated to their total phenolic contents.
However, the antioxidant activities of balsamic vinegar and traditional balsamic
vinegar are attributed to phenolics other than flavonoids and to Maillard reaction
```
products, such as melanoidins (Verzelloni et al., 2007, 2010). Melanoidins are col-
```
ored polymeric compounds formed in the final stages of the Maillard reaction and
```
have a wide range of molecular sizes (from 2 to > 2,000 KDa). The high molecu-
```
lar weight melanoidins, which accumulate during traditional balsamic vinegar age-
ing, may contribute to 40–50% of the total antioxidant activity of the aged vinegar
```
(Verzelloni et al., 2010).
```
The antioxidant properties of vinegars among other functionalities have been
```
reviewed by Budak et al. (2014) and others. Following, some examples of the most
```
recent scientific literature are presented.
The hypouricemic and antioxidant effects of soy vinegar extracts in potassium
```
oxonate-induced hyperuricemic mice were investigated by Pyo et al. (2018). The
```
soy vinegar was made from soybeans fermented with a Monascus pilosus strain.
Specifically, soy vinegar extracts, which contained free isoflavones, ubiquinones,
gamma-aminobutyric acid, gallic acid, and acetic acid, reduced the level of uric
383Health Benefits of Vinegars
acid by decreasing its production through xanthine oxidase inhibition and increas-
ing its excretion through uricase activity in the hyperuricemic mice. Moreover, soy
vinegar extract administration increased the hepatic antioxidant enzyme activities in
a dose-dependent manner, suggesting that this vinegar can be used to prevent and
treat hyperuricemia.
```
Zhao et al. (2018) studied the differences in the chemical composition and anti-
```
oxidant activity of traditional and industrial Zhenjiang aromatic vinegar, during the
ageing process. Zhenjiang aromatic vinegar is a well-known Chinese condiment pro-
duced by solid-state fermentation. They found that the organic acids, total phenolics,
total flavonoids, total antioxidant activity, and individual phenolic compounds con-
tents in the vinegars were increased during the ageing process. The values of total
phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant activity were higher in the traditional vinegar
when the ageing was more than 3 years. Moreover, rutin and p-coumaric acid were
detected only in the traditional vinegar. These findings could also provide a means
for the characterization of traditional and industrial Zhenjiang aromatic vinegars.
Shanxi aged vinegar is another famous Chinese vinegar, and during its brewing
process a large number of nutrients and bioactive compounds are produced. Xia et al.
```
(2018a) determined the contents of nutrients (proteins, fats, carbohydrates, organic
```
```
acids, and amino acids) in Shanxi aged vinegars, as well as the evolution of antioxi-
```
dant compounds and properties of the vinegars during ageing. The results showed
```
that the contents of the basic nutrients (proteins, fats, carbohydrates) did not change
```
```
during ageing, but the total contents of amino acids (mainly alanine) and organic
```
```
acids (acetic and lactic) were increased. The total phenols, flavonoids, and browning
```
index were also increased with ageing, with a corresponding increase of the antioxi-
dant activities of the vinegars. The contribution of the polyphenolic fractions and
```
high molecular weight melanoidins to the total antioxidant activities was similar (49
```
```
and 48%, respectively). These findings were evaluated as significant for the develop-
```
```
ment of novel vinegar-based functional foods (Xia et al., 2018a).
```
```
Sinanoglou et al. (2018) examined commercially available common and balsamic
```
vinegars, using a combination of spectrophotometric, chromatographic, colorimet-
ric, and spectroscopic methods, to compare the total phenolic content, antioxidant
activity, phenolic profile, and color parameters. Red grape balsamic vinegars exhib-
ited the strongest antioxidant profile. The combination of all the used analytical
techniques was evaluated as critical to provide information on the compositional
differences among vinegars and similar fermentation products.
```
In another study, the antioxidant properties (ABTS and DPPH radical scavenging
```
```
capacities), the global polyphenolic composition, and the evolution of the polyphe-
```
nolic and volatile compositions of a new functional pomegranate vinegar product
were evaluated and compared with those of commercial Sherry and Rioja red wine
```
Spanish vinegars (Kharchoufi et al., 2018). The results showed that pomegranate
```
vinegar had an antioxidant capacity comparable to, or even better than that of the
aged wine vinegars. The global phenolic content was similar to those of the red wine
vinegars and higher than most white wine vinegars.
```
Zou et al. (2018) prepared and characterized persimmon vinegar polyphenols and
```
investigated their protective effect on H 2 O2 -induced oxidative stress in HepG2 cells
```
(a human immortal liver cancer cell line). The results showed that flavon-3-ols were
```
384 Advances in Vinegar Production
the predominant persimmon vinegar polyphenols and that treatment with these poly-
phenols significantly decreased the H 2 O2 -induced cell damage in a dose-dependent
manner, in addition to the decrease of lactate dehydrogenase leakage, aminotrans-
ferase activities, and ROS accumulation, the upregulation of the expression of anti-
oxidative enzymes, and the increased levels of glutathione. The results indicated
that the persimmon vinegar polyphenols effectively protected HepG2 cells against
oxidative stress via activation of the antioxidative pathway of the nuclear factor ery-
```
throid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2; a protein that regulates the expression of antioxidant
```
```
proteins that protect against oxidative damage).
```
In a similar manner, bamboo vinegar powder was tested on the activities of
antioxidant enzymes in the blood and liver and the gene expression of antioxidant
```
enzymes and Nrf2 signaling in the liver of pigs (Yu et al., 2018). The results also
```
showed that bamboo vinegar powder supplementation improved the antioxidant abil-
ity of the pig by increasing the activity of some antioxidant enzymes and decreasing
the activity of oxidative stress enzymes, due to the activation of the Nrf2-antioxidant
```
responsive element (Nrf2-Are) pathway.
```
Because synthetic antioxidants have shown contradictive results compared to nat-
ural dietary antioxidants that generally show beneficial effects on oxidative stress,
```
blood pressure, and serum lipid composition, Halima et al. (2018) studied whether
```
a daily dosage of apple cider vinegar can affect the cardiovascular risk factor. For
```
this reason, high-fat diet (HDF)-induced hyperlipidemic obese rats were tested. The
```
```
vinegar significantly improved all associated factors [serum total cholesterol (TC),
```
```
triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol, very low-density lipo-
```
protein, atherogenic index, and oxidative stress], and normalized various biochemi-
```
cal and metabolic changes (e.g., antioxidant enzyme activities, vitamin E levels, and
```
```
lipid peroxidation). These results suggested that apple cider vinegar can be beneficial
```
for the suppression of obesity-induced oxidative stress and atherogenic risk by modu-
lating the antioxidant defense system.
Finally, the protective effects of Shanxi aged vinegar on ethanol-induced liver
injury, and the underlying molecular mechanisms, were studied by Xia et al.
```
(2018b). The results showed that the vinegar attenuated the ethanol-induced hepa-
```
```
totoxicity in LO2 cells (a spontaneously immortalized human cell line) and in mice
```
livers. In addition, 2.500 mL vinegar/kg body weight significantly decreased the
ethanol-induced ROS and subsequently inhibited cell apoptosis and malonalde-
hyde levels in mice livers, and improved the ethanol-induced oxidative stress and
inflammation by down-regulating the expression of cytochrome P450 2E1 enzyme
```
and NADPH oxidase (NOX). These results suggested that Shanxi aged vinegar is a
```
health-promoting antioxidant food that can exhibit hepatoprotective effects associ-
ated with the alleviation of ethanol-induced oxidative stress.
18.3 ANTIMICROBIAL PROPERTIES OF VINEGAR
Vinegar has been used since antiquity for its medicinal purposes. For example, in
Ancient Greece, Hippocrates used vinegar to treat wounds. Back in the 10th cen-
tury in China, Sung Tse used vinegar as a hand washing agent to reduce spread of
infections. Even in the US, vinegar was used by medical practitioners to treat many
385Health Benefits of Vinegars
ailments such as poison ivy, high fever, and edema. Vinegar is also used for cleaning
and treating nail fungus, head lice, warts, and ear infections. Therefore, vinegar has
been useful for many applications, through the centuries and around the world, due
```
to its antimicrobial properties against a wide range of living organisms (Budak et al.,
```
```
2014; Cortesia et al., 2014; Johnston, 2009) (see also Chapter 1).
```
Furthermore, vinegar can also be used as a natural preservative to inhibit the
growth of foodborne pathogenic microorganisms, as well as for the pickling of fruits
and vegetables, and the production of mayonnaise, salad dressings, and a vast variety
```
of other food condiments (Budak et al., 2014; Pooja and Soumitra, 2013; Tan, 2005).
```
Generally, the use of organic acids as preservatives in food is a common practice,
as it is a cheap, simple, fast, and effective treatment. Organic acids, such as acetic,
malic, tartaric, citric, lactic, succinic, and propionic acids, are approved by the FDA
```
as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) for various food products, and most of them
```
have no limitations regarding daily intake by humans. However, sensory changes in
```
food (effect on color and flavor) should also be considered (Mani-López et al., 2012;
```
```
Zhitnitsky et al., 2017). Organic acids and their salts are considered weak acids that
```
```
do not fully dissociate in water. Their dissociation is pH-dependent; therefore, their
```
antimicrobial activity is stronger when the food pH is lower than their dissociation
```
constant (pKa) values. Specifically, the lower the pH, the higher the concentration
```
of protonated acid, which increases the diffusion of the molecule into the cytoplasm
through the microbial cell membrane. However, a balance should be kept between
```
protonated acids and their cation-substituted forms (Na+, K+, Ca+2) as the latter are
```
```
more soluble in aqueous systems (Mani-López et al., 2012).
```
The antimicrobial activity of organic acids has been mainly associated with two
```
mechanisms: (1) the cytoplasmic acidification, which leads to uncoupling of energy
```
```
production and regulation, and (2) the accumulation of dissociated acid anion at lev-
```
```
els toxic to the cells (Mani-López et al., 2012). When an undissociated acid diffuses
```
```
through the cell membrane into a higher-pH cytoplasm (more alkaline environment),
```
it is dissociated leading to establishment of a transmembrane gradient. The cell reac-
```
tion is to try to efflux the increasing free protons by active transport of cations (Na+,
```
```
K+) in order to maintain pH homeostasis in the cytoplasm (Mani-López et al., 2012).
```
Another theory suggested uncoupling of electron transport from oxidative respira-
```
tion; however, no theory completely explains the antimicrobial action of organic
```
acids. The presence of an uncoupling effect suggests that other inhibitory effects
possibly follow the diffusion of undissociated acid across the cell membrane, such as
accumulation of the acid anion in the cytoplasm, and adverse effects on enzymatic
activities, protein, and DNA/RNA synthesis, increased permeability of the mem-
```
brane, and interference with membrane proteins (Mani-López et al., 2012).
```
Vinegars containing considerable amounts of acetic acid have strong antimicro-
bial activity against both bacteria and fungi. The antimicrobial activity of organic
acids, including the acetic acid of vinegars, is generally affected by temperature, pH,
acid concentration, the type of the targeted microorganisms, and the ionic strength
```
(Wu et al., 2000; Rhee et al., 2003; Budak et al., 2014; Chang and Fang, 2007; Entani
```
```
et al., 1998; Mani-López et al., 2012; Zhitnitsky et al., 2017; Medina et al., 2007; Pinto
```
```
et al., 2008; and many others). Following, some of the most recent research works
```
and trends on the antimicrobial activity and applications of vinegars are highlighted.
386 Advances in Vinegar Production
18.3.1 reCent researCH on tHe antimiCroBial properties of Vinegars
Various studies have reported on the usefulness of vinegar in inhibiting pathogenic
bacteria on vegetables and fresh fruit, as well as on the comparison or synergistic
effects of vinegar with other antimicrobial acids such as lactic, citric, and malic
acid, as well as lemon juice, etc. For example, acetic acid was found able to inhibit
```
most bacterial strains when compared to hydrochloric acid (HCl) under the same pH
```
```
and concentrations (Entani et al., 1998). Specifically, 0.1% of acetic acid had strong
```
```
bacteriostatic activity when enhanced with sodium chloride (NaCl; salt) or glucose
```
except for the case of Vibrio parahaemolyticus. The effects of the presence of salt
and glucose were studied because they are both essential ingredients in cooking. The
combination of vinegar and salt has found to be highly synergistic on inactivation of
microorganisms.
Vinegar and lemon juice are commonly used as flavorings and were also found
to be effective alternative disinfectants to remove pathogens that could be harmful
```
to human health, such as Salmonella typhimurium, from vegetables (rocket, spring
```
```
onion, and carrots) (Sengun and Karapinar, 2004, 2005). The treatment of carrot
```
samples with lemon juice or vinegar alone caused significant reductions in the col-
```
ony forming units (CFU), while the number of pathogens was reduced to an unde-
```
tectable level after treatment for 30 min by combined use of lemon juice and vinegar.
```
In Budak et al. (2014) and Chang and Fang (2007) it is reported that acetic acid
```
is the most lethal acid against E. coli O157:H7, followed by lactic, citric, and malic
acids. The treatment of inoculated lettuce with commercial vinegar containing 5%
```
acetic acid (pH 3.0) for 5 min was found able to reduce by 3 logs the population of
```
E. coli O157:H7 at 25°C (Chang and Fang, 2007).
```
According to Ozturk et al. (2015), around 90% of tested traditional and industrial
```
vinegar samples showed antibacterial activity against Bacillus cereus, as the most
sensitive strain, at varying levels.
With regards to removing Listeria monocytogenes from lettuce, balsamic vinegar
from Modena displayed similar and even better effectiveness than chlorine-based
```
sanitizers at home or retail environments (Ramos et al., 2014). It was specifically
```
```
suggested that mixing vinegar with water (1:5), is enough to clean vegetables after
```
dipping for only 15 min. Food pathogens on the surface of food products can be
```
inhibited by balsamic vinegar due to its low pH range (3.26–3.38). The stronger anti-
```
microbial effect of balsamic vinegar has also been attributed to the presence of other
compounds that derive from either the grapes or the fermentation process. A variety
of grape phenolics, for example, are known for their antilisterial activities, such as
```
resveratrol, vanillic acid, caffeic acid, gallic acid, and flavonoids (rutin and querce-
```
```
tin) (Oliveira et al., 2013; Plessi et al., 2006; Vaquero et al., 2007).
```
```
Vinegar was also found effective against Candida spp. (Mota et al., 2015; Pinto
```
```
et al., 2008). For example, apple cider vinegar and red wine vinegar were found suit-
```
able to inhibit denture-related stomatitis caused by Candida albicans.
Vinegar and acetic acid solutions were used to inhibit E. coli, S. typhimurium, and
L. monocytogenes in meat (Rhee et al., 2003) and lettuce (Oramahi and Yoshimura,
```
2013), in order to assure product quality and consumer preference without altering
```
the nutrients content or the sensory properties of the products.
387Health Benefits of Vinegars
Generally, fruit are easier to decay by fungi. The best post-harvest fruit treat-
```
ment was found to be the fumigation technique using vinegar (Sholberg et al., 2000),
```
which functions by causing the vaporized undissociated acid to penetrate the fungal
conidia cell membrane, thus inhibiting microbial growth. It was also shown that vin-
egar in both liquid and vapor phase can reduce Klebsiella pneumoniae on vegetable
```
leaves (Krusong et al., 2015). Another example from Tzortzakis et al. (2011) was
```
the disinfection of tomatoes with vinegar vapor, which maintained their firmness
and acidity after the treatment. Therefore, the fumigation of vinegar on fruit or veg-
etables can be a potential alternative to replace common liquid sterilants.
All these efforts have been reviewed and discussed in some earlier reviews on the
```
antimicrobial effects of vinegars, such as the works by Ho et al. (2017b), Ali et al.
```
```
(2016), and Budak et al. (2014).
```
```
In a more recent study, Campos et al. (2019) investigated whether different
```
```
Acinetobacter spp. isolated from human and food samples (lettuce, turkey meat,
```
```
apple, and pear) were resistant to vinegar exposure, among other treatments.
```
Acinetobacter spp., such A. baumanni and A. lwoffii, are recognized as important
agents of nosocomial infections. Treatment with vinegar was effective against all
clinical and food isolates. Due to the limited knowledge on this field, the results
of that study were considered important for the understanding of the behavior of
Acinetobacter spp. when exposed to treatments commonly applied to foods, such as
the treatment with vinegar.
```
In another recent study (Yagnik et al., 2018), the antimicrobial capacity of apple
```
cider vinegar against E. coli, S. aureus, and C. albicans was evaluated based on the
concept of finding alternative antimicrobial means to avoid the global escalation in
antibiotic resistance. The minimum effective dilution of vinegar varied depending
on the targeted species, showing higher activity against E. coli, followed by S. aureus
```
and C. albicans (1/50, 1/2, and 1/25 effective vinegar dilutions, respectively). Also,
```
co-culture of the microbes with vinegar resulted in dose-dependent downregulation
```
of inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and impaired cell integrity, organelles, and
```
protein expression, demonstrating that apple cider vinegar has multiple antimicrobial
potentials with clinical therapeutic implications.
```
Stratakos and Grant (2018) studied the antimicrobial effects of multiple physical,
```
biological, and natural interventions on pathogenic E. coli in raw beef. Among the
```
natural interventions, washes with vinegar and lactic acid (5%) for 5 min caused
```
reductions of ∼1 logCFU/g immediately after treatment, whereas lactoferrin and
nisin treatments, separately or in combination, had insignificant antimicrobial effects.
These findings suggest that vinegar, similar to other treatments such as cold plasma,
```
bacteriophages, lactic acid, carvacrol (a monoterpenoid phenol present in the essen-
```
```
tial oil of oregano, thyme, and other plants), and thyme oil nanoemulsions, could
```
potentially be used in the beef industry to control pathogenic E. coli contamination.
Vinegar, along with H 2 O2 and sodium bicarbonate solutions were evaluated for
```
the disinfection of pacifiers (Pedroso et al., 2018). Different types and concentrations
```
of these agents were screened in planktonic and biofilm for antimicrobial activity
against Streptococcus mutans, Staphylococcus pyogenes, S. aureus, and E. coli. The
most effective substance was also tested against polymicrobial biofilms aiming to
mimic the multispecies colonization found in a pacifier. Based on the agar diffusion
388 Advances in Vinegar Production
test, the minimal inhibitory concentration, and minimal microbicide concentration
assays, 70% apple cider vinegar and 70% H 2 O2 were selected. The tested solutions
were able to significantly reduce the viable cells of S. pyogenes, S. mutans, and
E. coli in the biofilms. A statistically significant reduction of viable cells in S. aureus
biofilms was observed after treatment with 70% apple cider vinegar in comparison
to the other treatments.
```
Lee et al. (2018) produced tomato vinegar by mixing different ratios of tomato
```
wine and Makgeolli seed culture made using Acetobacter pasteurianus. The lyco-
```
pene content (the tetraterpene, carotenoid, pigment of tomatoes), which was higher
```
in tomato vinegars than in tomato wine, decreased with increasing amounts of seed
culture. However, the total phenolics content increased with increasing amounts of
seed culture, while the antioxidant activity showed a decreasing tendency. These
results showed that the antioxidant activity was more influenced by the lycopene
content. The antimicrobial activity of the vinegar was highest when the seed culture
content was 40% and was dependent on the total acidity.
Edible coating solutions, containing chitosan and bamboo vinegar, were devel-
oped to investigate their effect on the quality and shelf-life of ready to cook pork
```
chops stored at 4°C for 12 days (Zhang et al., 2018). The antioxidant effects against
```
lipid oxidation and antimicrobial activity against total viable counts, lactic acid bac-
teria, Enterobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonas spp. were analyzed. The results showed
that chitosan and bamboo vinegar coating treatments tended to retard lipid oxidation
```
by inhibiting the increase in thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) and
```
improved shelf-life by about 3 and 6 days, respectively. Therefore, bamboo vinegar-
based edible coating treatment could be applied to pork meat products to improve
their shelf-life and safety.
```
A final example, by Kadiroğlu (2018), was the discrimination between commer-
```
cial apple, rice, balsamic, red wine, rosé, white wine, grape, and pomegranate vin-
egars according to their antimicrobial activities, total phenolic contents, antioxidant
activities, and color parameters and the prediction of the quality characteristics using
FTIR spectroscopy. The results showed that the highest total phenolics content was
found in balsamic vinegar whereas the lowest was in rice vinegar. The antioxidant
activities of vinegars were correlated with the total phenolics content. The grape-
based vinegars exhibited higher antimicrobial activity against S. aureus, E. coli,
and P. aeruginosa, with no statistically significant differences among vinegars. The
results of that study indicated that FTIR could be used as a rapid method to estimate
the antimicrobial activities, total phenolic content, color, and antioxidant activities
of vinegars.
Many such other examples can be found in the recent research literature regard-
ing the antimicrobial properties of vinegar. The aims and trends of these efforts
```
show the significant concern of scientists, consumers, and the industries, to (1)
```
develop effective post-harvest treatments and ensure the microbiological safety
```
of fresh produce, (2) find alternative antimicrobial means in order to avoid the
```
```
global escalation in antibiotic resistance, (3) replace synthetic sterilants in food
```
```
and health care disinfection with safe products such as vinegar, and (4) apply mod-
```
ern techniques such as edible coatings and nanoemulsions in order to achieve the
above aims.
389Health Benefits of Vinegars
18.4 ANTIDIABETIC EFFECTS OF VINEGAR
Diabetes is a chronic disease characterized by the inability of the pancreas to pro-
```
duce enough insulin (a peptide hormone produced by beta-cells of the pancreas,
```
```
which regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins), which brings
```
the patient to a state of hunger or with high blood glucose levels after consuming a
meal. Type 1 diabetes is characterized by lack of insulin production due to the dam-
aged pancreatic cells resulting in hyperglycemia. Type 2 diabetes is the ineffective
use of insulin in the body, which causes the blood glucose concentration to increase
```
(WHO, 2014). Many choose to either reduce the carbohydrate intake or to consume
```
```
low glycemic index (GI) food. However, another possibility is to reduce postpran-
```
```
dial glycemia (glycemia occurring after a meal consumption) by consuming com-
```
```
plementary foods, such as vinegar, that lower the dietary glycemic load (Johnston
```
```
and Buller, 2005; Johnston and Gaas, 2006). Complementary food is a simple diet
```
improving approach, without having to avoid or reduce carbohydrates. The chronic
postprandial hyperglycemia is a strong predictor of cardiovascular disease risk in
```
both type 2 diabetes and prediabetes because it damages blood vessels (Bonora and
```
```
Muggeo, 2001).
```
Vinegar has antidiabetic effects and can improve the insulin sensitivity of both
humans and animals. Several mechanisms for this effect have been proposed, such
```
as (1) the interference with the enzymatic digestion of complex carbohydrates (sup-
```
```
pression of disaccharidase activity), (2) the delayed gastric emptying, and (3) the
```
```
enhanced peripheral glucose uptake and conversion into glycogen (Fushimi et al.,
```
```
2001; Liljeberg and Björck, 1998; Salbe et al., 2009). It was also shown that vinegar
```
ingestion at bedtime decreased fasting blood glucose levels the following morning,
leading to the conclusion that vinegar may alter the glycolysis/gluconeogenic cycle
```
in the liver, and that (4) vinegar ingestion may enhance satiety, as suggested by the
```
```
decreased energy intake at subsequent meals (Salbe et al., 2009).
```
18.4.1 reCent researCH on tHe antidiaBetiC effeCts of Vinegar
Various types of vinegars, including wine vinegars, balsamic vinegars, apple cider
```
vinegars (Hlebowicz et al., 2007), ginseng vinegars (Yun et al., 2007), and tomato
```
```
vinegars (Lee et al., 2018; Seo et al., 2014), were found capable of minimizing post-
```
prandial blood glucose, alleviating insulin resistance, and elevating insulin produc-
```
tion (Darzi et al., 2014; Derakhshandeh-Rishehri et al., 2014; Kohn, 2015; Petsiou
```
```
et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2016). Also, many placebo-controlled experiments have
```
```
confirmed the antiglycemic effect of vinegar (Johnston et al., 2004; Leeman et al.,
```
```
2005; Liljeberg and Björck, 1998). For example, vinegar showed significant reduc-
```
tion of postprandial fluxes in glucose and insulin in both control and insulin-resistant
```
subjects (Johnston et al., 2013). Acetic acid was shown to suppress disaccharidase
```
activity in high glycemic load foods in the small intestinal epithelium and also to
```
increase glucose-6-phosphate concentrations in skeletal muscle (Johnston and
```
```
Buller, 2005; Mitrou et al., 2015).
```
Researchers have also denoted that post-meal glycemia of healthy subjects can be
```
reduced by more than 30% after consuming a pickled cucumber (1.6 g acetic acid)
```
390 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
instead of a fresh cucumber (0 g acetic acid) in a test meal that included bread, butter,
```
```
and yoghurt (Östman et al., 2001). For individuals with type 2 diabetes and prediabe-
```
tes, the treatment using vinegar as supplementation improved insulin sensitivity by
```
19 and 34%, respectively (Johnston et al., 2004). Fushimi et al. (2001) also showed
```
that a diet containing acetic acid helps in enhancing glycogen repletion in liver
and skeletal muscle. Specifically, acetic acid could be immediately absorbed once
administered orally. The uptake occurred in the liver and peripheral tissues, and
acetic acid stimulated glycogenesis by increasing the influx of glucose-6-phosphate
into the glycogen synthesis pathway through the increase in citrate concentration,
which inhibits glycolysis.
```
Östman et al. (2005) studied the effect of vinegar in lowering the postprandial
```
responses of blood glucose and insulin, while increasing the rate of satiety on human
subjects. It was explained that acetic acid is able to lower the glucose response of
bread meals by decreasing the rate of starch hydrolysis in the upper small intestine.
The higher the acetic acid level, the lower was the metabolic response. Liatis et al.
```
(2010) suggested that the postprandial hyperglycemia can be lowered by consuming
```
```
vinegar in high GI meals but not in low GI meals. Mitrou et al. (2015), on the other
```
hand, supported that vinegar can boost insulin sensitivity by consuming vinegar
```
along with high and low GI meals. In addition, Johnston et al. (2010) stated that con-
```
suming 10 g of vinegar is better in lowering postprandial blood glucose compared
to 2 or 20 g of vinegar. Also, it was found that consuming vinegar 2 hours prior to
meals had better response than 5 hours prior to meal.
```
Salbe et al. (2009) hypothesized that by suppressing the endogenous insulin
```
secretion, they could estimate the glucose absorption rate after an oral carbohy-
drate administration and determine the effects of vinegar ingestion on this rate.
For that reason, they tested subjects who received placebo and apple cider vinegar
after a potato meal. At the beginning of the meal, an oral octreotide/insulin sup-
```
pression test was begun (octreotide is an octapeptide that inhibits growth hormone,
```
```
glucagon, and insulin), which suppressed endogenous insulin secretion. During the
```
testing time, the rate of glucose rise was modestly but significantly higher after
vinegar ingestion compared to the placebo, suggesting that vinegar does not act to
decrease glycemia by interference with enteral carbohydrate absorption. The study
also concluded that further modifications of the octreotide/insulin suppression test
are needed to confirm its effectiveness as a tool to investigate glucose absorption
after oral carbohydrate load.
In another trial, type 2 diabetes individuals were also examined to find whether
```
vinegar ingestion at bedtime altered waking glucose concentrations (White and
```
```
Johnston, 2007). The fasting glucose concentrations were recorded every morning
```
after the participants had been provided with a standardized diet including apple
cider vinegar or water. The vinegar treatment for 2 days significantly reduced the
fasting glucose level in comparison to the water treatment, proposing that the anti-
glycemic effect of vinegar can be exhibited besides meal time.
```
Hlebowicz et al. (2007) studied the effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric
```
emptying rate on diabetic patients with diabetic gastroparesis, which was measured
using standardized real-time ultrasonography. The results showed that the effect
of vinegar on the rate of gastric emptying was statistically significant. This study
391Health Benefits of Vinegars
showed that vinegar has the potential to affect insulin-dependent diabetic patients by
```
reducing the gastric emptying rate even further; however, this might be a disadvan-
```
tage regarding their glycemic control.
```
According to Johnston et al. (2004), vinegar may exhibit equal effectiveness with
```
```
anti-diabetic drugs used to treat diabetes mellitus type 2, such as acarbose (inhibits
```
```
alpha-glucosidase which releases glucose from larger carbohydrates) and metformin
```
```
(a biguanide compound that decreases glucose production by the liver and increases
```
```
the insulin sensitivity of body tissues). The study of Johnston et al. (2013) also
```
showed that fasting glucose levels can be minimized by receiving one tablespoon of
vinegar with meals twice a day.

```
An aqueous extract of Nypa fruticans Wurmb. (nypa palm) vinegar signifi-
```
cantly amplified beta-cell production and boosted beta-cell differentiation and thus


```
rally occurring alkylating antineoplastic agent) that induces diabetes by destroying
```

```
the insulin-producing beta-cells of the pancreas in mammals. Yusoff et al. (2017)
```

```
A recent study was carried out by Mohamed et al. (2018) to investigate the effect
```

```
of acetic acid on blood glucose, TG, and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and
```

```
The results indicated that acetic acid (and vinegar) could be used as an adjunctive
```

treatment.
```
Ali et al. (2018) conducted a double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled
```
study to evaluate the impact of date vinegar consumption on blood biochemical
and hematological parameters in patients with type 2 diabetes. Specifically, gly-
cated hemoglobin, fasting blood sugar, HDL, LDL, TC, creatinine, urea, complete

```
Karim et al. (2018) focused on the antiglycemic and antihepatotoxic effects of
```
mangosteen vinegar rind from Garcinia mangostana, on HFD-diet/streptozotocin
```

```
diabetic drug that causes cell membrane depolarization in the beta-cells resulting
```
in increased intracellular calcium and stimulation of insulin release) significantly
```

sitivity. Moreover, oxidative damage markers were also improved in both induced
diabetic groups compared to the diabetic control group.

```
Karta et al. (2018) analyzed the active content of Sibetan salacca (palm) vinegar
```
to evaluate its potential in antidiabetic and anticancer treatments. The results showed
```
that salacca vinegar contains high levels of acid (6.68%), as well as considerable
```
392 Advances in Vinegar Production
amounts of total phenols, total tannins, flavonoids, antioxidant capacity, and vitamin
C, at levels that could serve in lowering blood sugar levels, scavenging free radicals,
curing of damaged beta-cells, and protecting from oxidative damage. Zubaidah et al.
```
(2017) also explored the potential of salacca vinegar, made from various Indonesian
```
salacca fruit extracts, as a therapeutic agent for hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia for
streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats. Parameters such as blood glucose, TC, HDL,
LDL, TG, malondialdehyde, superoxide dismutase, and pancreas histopathology
were evaluated. The results demonstrated that all salacca vinegars were capable of
increasing HDL and reducing all other parameters in the induced diabetic rats. Also,
some salacca vinegars were capable of regenerating pancreatic cells. Among them,
the ability of Swaru salacca vinegar to manage hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia
```
appeared to be superior; therefore, that vinegar was considered a potential therapeu-
```
tic agent to manage these conditions.
```
Takao et al. (2018) studied the antidiabetic potential of acetic acid-free red vin-
```
egar containing a candidate bioactive compound, 6-O-caffeoylsophorose, in sponta-
neously diabetic rats. Daily intake of vinegar led to a significant reduction in fasting
blood glucose levels, in 28-week-old rats, while no antidiabetic effect was obtained
in rats fed from 27 weeks of age. These results demonstrated that acid-free red vin-
egar has a physiological potential to suppress the promotion of diabetes but not to
improve the development of onset.
```
Finally, Lim et al. (2016) reviewed the use of vinegar as a functional ingredient to
```
improve the postprandial glycemic control based on human intervention findings and
molecular mechanisms. The molecular mechanisms discussed, by which vinegar can
improve glycemic control, and which appear to be more effective in healthy subjects
```
than in diabetics, included: (1) activation of free fatty acid receptors 2 localized in
```
the enteroendocrine L-cells of the intestinal lumen, leading to increased glucagon-
```
like peptide 1 secretion, (2) increased adenosine monophosphate-activated protein
```
```
kinase (AMPK) activation, leading to increased fatty acid oxidation and decreased
```
```
hepatic gluconeogenesis, (3) lowering of free fatty acid in circulation, leading to
```
```
improved insulin sensitivity, (4) increased blood flow to the peripheral tissues, and
```
```
(5) increased satiety, leading to lower food intake.
```
18.5 ANTI-VISCERAL OBESITY PROPERTIES OF VINEGAR
As discussed in the previous section, vinegar ingestion may also have anti-obesity
effects by reducing the food intake through satiety caused by reduced glycemic
```
effect of meals (Mermel, 2004; Salbe et al., 2009). The intra-abdominal deposition
```
of visceral adipose tissue is a type of obesity associated with conditions such as
type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and coronary heart disease.
```
Structural and functional changes in the heart (known as obesity cardiomyopathy)
```
are strongly associated with obesity through mechanisms such as altered cardiac
metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, excess visceral adiposity, cardiac fibro-
```
sis, and hypertrophy (Bounihi et al., 2017). Visceral fat promotes obesity cardiomy-
```
opathy through the active production of numerous immunomodulatory factors such
```
as the tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), leptin, and other circulating inflammatory
```
```
biomarkers (Bounihi et al., 2017).
```
393Health Benefits of Vinegars
The possible mechanisms by which vinegar affects obesity attenuation have been
```
studied and proposed by various researchers. In Bounihi et al. (2017) it is explained
```
that AMPK, a kinase enzyme that plays a significant role in lipid homeostasis,
increases as the AMP/ATP ratio increases due to vinegar consumption. The phos-
phorylation of AMPK induces upregulation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated
```
receptor alpha (PPAR-α) that regulates mRNA expression of fatty acid oxidation
```
enzymes, such as acetyl-CoA oxidase and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 alpha
```
(CPT-1a), which may enhance fatty acid beta-oxidation. AMPK also affects lipolysis
```
```
as it induces upregulation of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) facilitating lipid break-
```
down. Therefore, vinegar can be used as a natural anti-obesity agent by promoting
```
fatty acid oxidation, enhancing lipolysis, and inhibiting lipogenesis (Bounihi et al.,
```
```
2017; Yamashita et al., 2007; Yamashita, 2016).
```
18.5.1 reCent researCH on tHe anti -VisCeral
oBesity properties of Vinegar
Although acetic acid has been identified as the main component in vinegar that con-
tributes to its anti-obesity effect, studies have shown that vinegar possesses different
```
degrees of bioactivity (Beh et al., 2017). Vinegar can reduce visceral fat weight, with-
```
out altering the amount of calorie intake, by interfering with preadipocyte prolifera-
tion and lipid accumulation. In addition, fat pad weight can be lowered by a consistent
```
ingestion of acetic acid without reducing skeletal muscle weight (Chou et al., 2015;
```
```
Park et al., 2014; Park and Lee, 2013; Petsiou et al., 2014; Seo et al., 2014).
```
```
Östman et al. (2005) tested subjects that were fed with bread and vinegar and
```
found that the lowest rating of satiety was when bread was consumed alone, and
a linear relationship was observed between satiety and the acetic acid content in
```
the test meals. Kondo et al. (2009) reported that mice fed with HFD demonstrated
```
significant reductions in weight as well as mesenteric, perirenal, and retroperitoneal
```
white adipose tissue, after receiving both high (1.5%) and low doses (0.3%) of acetic
```
acid supplementations.
```
Based on Fushimi et al. (2006), a diet rich in cholesterol and dietary acetic acid
```
significantly reduced the levels of serum cholesterol, TG, liver ATP citrate lyase
```
(ATP-CL) activity, liver 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA, liver mRNA levels of ste-
```
rol regulatory element binding protein-1, ATP-CL, and fatty acid synthase. On the
other hand, the serum secretin level, liver acyl-CoA oxidase expression, and fecal
bile acid contents were significantly higher in the cholesterol and acetic acid-fed
group than in the cholesterol-fed group of rats. The results indicated that dietary
acetic acid reduced serum TC and triacylglycerol due to the inhibition of lipogenesis
in the liver and due to the increase of fecal bile acid excretion.
```
Lim et al. (2009) evaluated the anti-obesity effects of vinegar extract from Panax
```
```
ginseng (ginsam) on obese insulin-resistant rat subjects. They found that the rats
```
that ingested ginsam possessed lower body weight and lower fasting, postprandial
glucose, and plasma insulin concentrations than the controls.
```
Moon et al. (2010) reported that persimmon vinegar can ameliorate blood lipid
```
profiles. Specifically, serum and hepatic TG and TC concentrations were signifi-
cantly decreased in all vinegar-administered groups compared with the control
394 Advances in Vinegar Production
HFD-group. The liver acid insoluble acylcarnitine was significantly higher in the
```
group fed with the highest amount of vinegar (2 mL/kg body weight). The acetyl-
```
CoA carboxylase mRNA levels tended to be lower in all the vinegar-administered
groups. These results suggested that persimmon-vinegar has anti-obesity properties.
```
According to Lee et al. (2013), the total visceral fat can be reduced when consum-
```
ing tomato vinegar on regular basis, as indicated by experiments on HFD-induced
```
obese rats. Lee et al. (2018), in addition to other functional properties, also studied
```
the anti-obesity effects of tomato vinegar made by varying amounts of Makgeolli
seed culture, based on lipid accumulation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes and assessed by Oil
Red O staining. The test revealed that lipid accumulation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes was
inhibited by increasing amounts of seed culture, enhancing the suggestion that the
Makgeolli tomato vinegar is a healthy, functional food product.
```
Bounihi et al. (2017) investigated the preventive effects of three types of Algerian
```
```
fruit vinegars (prickly pear, pomegranate, and apple) against obesity-induced car-
```
diomyopathy and its underlying mechanisms. The vinegar treatments significantly
attenuated the HFD-induced body weight increase, and visceral adipose tissue, and
increased the plasma levels of C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, leptin, TNF-α, aspar-
```
tate aminotransferase, creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) isoenzyme, and lactate dehy-
```
```
drogenase (LDH), while the myocardial architecture and attenuated cardiac fibrosis
```
were preserved. The great anti-obesity potential of pomegranate vinegar was also
reported, through the reduction of both plasma and hepatic TG levels, upregulation
of PPAR-α and CPT-1a mRNA expressions, including phosphorylation of AMPK
```
(Kim et al., 2013; Ok et al., 2013).
```
The scientific research on the therapeutic properties of vinegars, including the
possible mechanisms of these therapeutic actions, was reviewed by Samad et al.
```
(2016), where a daily intake of 15 mL vinegar (750 mg of acetic acid) was reported as
```
efficient to improve lifestyle-related diseases, such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia,
and obesity.
In a more recent study, a new beverage was developed from dates vinegar and
```
garlic juice in order to reduce obesity (Ali et al., 2018) and tested on obese adults who
```
received beverage or placebo daily for 10 weeks. Body weight, body mass index,
waist circumference, visceral fat area, serum lipid profile, serum leptin, alanine
transaminase, aspartate transaminase, urea, and creatinine levels were analyzed.
The results indicated that the new beverage reduced body weight, body fat ratio, and
serum leptin and could therefore play a critical role in preclusion of metabolic syn-
drome, which is a serious case of obesity characterized by increased cardiovascular
```
risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance (Halima
```
```
et al., 2018).
```
```
In this respect, Halima et al. (2018) studied whether apple cider vinegar could
```
affect cardiovascular risk factor associated with obesity in HFD-induced hyperlip-
idemic rats, that presented increased levels of serum TC, TG, LDL-cholesterol, very
low-density lipoprotein, and atherogenic index. The apple cider vinegar significantly
improved all these parameters. Oxidative stress that was developed after 6 weeks
of HFD was also significantly reduced by daily doses of vinegar. Also, administra-
tion of vinegar normalized various other biochemical and metabolic changes, such
as reduction in malondialdehyde levels and increase in thiol group concentrations
395Health Benefits of Vinegars
```
and antioxidant status (superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase, and catalase
```
```
activities and vitamin E concentrations). These findings suggested that apple cider
```
vinegar could be beneficial for the suppression of obesity-induced oxidative stress by
enhancing the antioxidant defense system and reducing the risk of obesity-associated
disorders.
```
Furthermore, Kherzi et al. (2018) conducted a randomized clinical trial to exam-
```
ine whether apple cider vinegar can result in dietary modifications that are ben-
eficial to manage body weight and serum metabolic profiles in obese individuals.
The vinegar significantly reduced body weight, body mass index, hip circumference,
visceral adiposity index, and appetite score. Plasma TG and TC levels significantly
decreased, and HDL-cholesterol concentration significantly increased in the vinegar
group. Thus, apple cider vinegar, along with a restricted calorie diet, could be con-
sidered as an effective strategy for reducing anthropometric parameters, TG and
TC levels, visceral adiposity index, and appetite and increasing HDL-cholesterol
concentration in overweight or obese individuals.
```
Beh et al. (2017) compared the anti-obesity and anti-inflammatory effects of syn-
```
thetic acetic acid vinegar and Nipa vinegar in HFD mice. Although both synthetic
and natural vinegar reduced food intake and body weight, a high dose of Nipa vin-
egar was more effective in reducing the lipid deposition, improving the serum lipid
```
profile, increasing adipokine expression (cytokines secreted by the adipose tissue),
```
and suppressing inflammation in the obese mice.
```
Finally, Yatmaz et al. (2017) quantified a new functional ingredient in vine-
```
```
gars, namely 5-hydroxy-4-phenyl-butenolide (Fraglide-1), by LC–MS/MS in mul-
```
tiple reaction monitoring mode. Fraglide-1 is a butenolide compound. This class
of compounds are known to have anti-cancer, bactericidal, fungicidal, antiviral,
anti-inflammatory, antitumor, and anti-obesity properties. Fraglide-1, which was dis-
```
covered in aromatic Zhenjiang vinegar (Kozu), is thought to move from the sticky
```
```
rice husk to Kozu during long-term ageing (6 months to 8 years). It was found in
```
```
all tested Kozu samples, as well as brown rice vinegar (Kurosu) samples, and the
```
Chinese sticky rice husk used for the production of Kozu.
18.6 ANTIHYPERTENSIVE ACTIVITIES OF VINEGAR
Hypertension is a major public health problem worldwide and an important risk fac-
tor for cardiovascular diseases such as coronary artery disease, stroke, heart failure,
atrial fibrillation, peripheral vascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and athero-
```
sclerosis (Yousefian et al., 2019). Both hereditary and environmental factors are
```
```
associated with hypertension (Na et al., 2016). Certain food components, such as
```
natural phenolic compounds, have been found to have regulatory effects on blood
pressure. Among foods, vinegar has also been assumed as capable of reducing blood
```
pressure, although scientific evidence is limited (Na et al., 2016).
```
It is well established that blood pressure is regulated by the renin–angiotensin–
```
aldosterone system (RAAS), in which the effect of angiotensin II (Ang II) on blood
```
```
pressure is mediated by Ang II type 1 receptors (AT1Rs). Inhibiting or blocking
```
```
AT1Rs decreases blood pressure (Na et al., 2016). Studies have also reported that
```
```
gamma PPAP (PPARγ) plays an important role in the regulation of blood pressure
```
396 Advances in Vinegar Production
by affecting AT1R. Specifically, the activators of PPARγ decrease the AT1R expres-
sion levels. On the other hand, activation of AMPK, an upstream agonist of PPARγ,
upregulates PPARγ expression. As mentioned above, acetate has been found able to
induce AMPK phosphorylation and activation in diabetic animal subjects, suggest-
ing that an acetate/AMPK/PPARγ/AT1R pathway contributes to the blood pressure
```
control (Na et al., 2016).
```
Furthermore, there is strong evidence that excess ROS-derived NADPH oxi-
```
dase (NOX) is an important agent in hypertension (Yousefian et al., 2019). NOX
```
increases blood pressure in the presence of other pro-hypertensive factors such as
```
Ang II. Vasodilating agents such as nitric oxide (NO) can interact with ROS such
```
```
as O2˙− and H 2 O2 in cardiovascular cells; therefore, ROS reduce the NO bioavail-
```
ability affecting the endothelial function in the cardiovascular system. Antioxidants
such as glutathione peroxidase, vitamin E, or superoxide dismutase exert protective
effects against ROS. In search of natural treatments to avoid the chronic use of anti-
hypertensive drugs and their adverse health effects, natural phenolic compounds
have been increasingly studied in order to understand the underlying mechanisms of
```
their action on hypertension (Yousefian et al., 2019).
```
18.6.1 reCent researCH on tHe antiHypertensiVe aCtiVities of Vinegar
In several previous studies on animal subjects, angiotensin-converting enzyme
```
(ACE) was found to be inhibited by vinegar. For example, rice vinegar has been
```
```
found able to inhibit ACE activity and reduce blood pressure in vitro (Kondo et al.,
```
```
2001; Nishikawa et al., 2001). Also, potential antihypertensive activity could be
```
attributed, besides acetic acid, to the melanoidins that are formed during the final
```
stage of the Maillard reaction in traditional balsamic vinegar production (Kondo
```
```
et al., 2001). The ingestion of vinegar (with 0.57 mmol acetic acid) was found
```
to help in the reduction of plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone, which
```
are variables related to blood vessel constriction in rats (Honsho et al., 2005).
```
```
In Japan, persimmon juice and vinegar (Kakisu) and Kurosu vinegar have been
```
```
used as traditional medicines to reduce blood pressure (George, 2008; Tong et al.,
```
```
2010). Many other studies have shown that regular vinegar (acetic acid) ingestion is
```
capable of affecting ACE concentrations, reducing plasma Ang II levels, promot-
```
ing vasodilation, and improving the blood pressure in human subjects (Johnston,
```
```
2009; Kondo et al., 2009; Nakamura et al., 2010; Nandasiri and Rupasinghe, 2013;
```
```
Samad et al., 2016).
```
```
More recently, Na et al. (2016) investigated whether vinegar exerts an antihy-
```
pertensive effect by activating the AMPK pathway in spontaneously hypertensive
```
rats, after oral administration of vinegar, acetic acid, nifedipine (a calcium chan-
```
```
nel blocker medication used to manage high blood pressure), nifedipine + vinegar,
```
and distilled water. Vinegar and acetic acid decreased blood pressure, decreased
```
serum renin and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activities and Ang II and
```
aldosterone concentrations, and increased AMP/ATP ratios and expression levels
```
of pAMPK, PPARγ coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), and PPARγ, while inhibiting AT1R
```
expression. The results led to the conclusion that vinegar activates AMPK by increas-
```
ing the AMP/ATP ratios; thereby it increases the expression of PGC-1α and PPARγ
```
397Health Benefits of Vinegars
and inhibits AT1R expression. Acetic acid was considered responsible for these anti-
hypertensive effects of vinegar.
```
Lee et al. (2016) prepared a formulation of a red ginseng fraction, enriched in
```
```
hypotensive components, with persimmon vinegar (12:1 against the red ginseng frac-
```
```
tion; reacted at 80°C for 18 h) and evaluated its ability to improve the hypertension in
```
```
spontaneously hypertensive rats. The formulation (with four-fold more Ginsenoside
```
```
Rg3 and 24-fold more arginine–fructose contents) led to reduction of systolic and
```
diastolic blood pressure as well as renin activity, while Ang II was not affected.
However, ACE inhibition and NO levels were significantly increased, indicating that
the formulation has a potential to be used as a new material for functional food pro-
duction with anti-hypertensive properties.
```
Yousefian et al. (2019) reviewed the scientific evidence that the natural phenolic
```
```
compounds (such as berberine, thymoquinone, catechin, celastrol, apocynin, res-
```
```
veratrol, curcumin, hesperidine, G-hesperidine, and quercetin) are NOX inhibitors
```
in hypertension. In comparison to other plant phenolics, the structural variability
of flavonoids exerts different impacts on oxidative stress in hypertension, such as
inhibition of NOX and scavenging of free radicals. The most active NOX inhibi-
tors are flavonoids bearing a hydroxyl group, a methoxy group in the ortho position
in the second aromatic ring, and a saturated 2,3-bond in the third ring. Especially,
hesperidin and G-hesperidin have a high potential as NOX inhibitors, preventing
ROS production by disturbing the NADPH complex assembly, mainly the p47phox
```
(phagocyte oxidase), therefore playing an important role in the prevention of cardio-
```
vascular diseases such as hypertension.
18.7 THERAPEUTIC PROPERTIES OF VINEGAR
The bioactive compounds present in vinegars, that are described in the previous sec-
```
tions, may also contribute toward the various therapeutic effects of vinegars (Samad
```
```
et al., 2016). Several therapeutic applications of vinegars were discussed above. For
```
example, vinegars have been reported to be capable of improving oxidative stress,
```
hypertension, and blood lipid profiles and preventing cardiovascular diseases (Budak
```
```
et al., 2011; Estruch et al., 2013; Halima et al., 2018; Kondo et al., 2009; Lee et al.,
```
```
2013; Pazuch et al., 2015; Zubaidah et al., 2017), improving lipid metabolism, man-
```
```
aging body weight and visceral adiposity index in obese subjects (Cho et al., 2010;
```
```
Khezri et al., 2018; Seo et al., 2015), delaying gastric emptying in diabetic patients and
```
```
generally exhibiting therapeutic effects on diabetes (Hlebowicz et al., 2007; Petsiou
```
```
et al., 2014; Yusoff et al., 2015), and exerting antimicrobial activities against various
```
```
pathogens (E. coli, S. aureus, and C. albicans, etc.) (Mota et al., 2015; Yagnik et al.,
```
```
2018) and displaying anti-cancer properties (Baba et al., 2013; Bhalang et al., 2008).
```
In addition, when vinegar is consumed regularly it can help balance the pH levels
```
in the body (Brown and Jaffe, 2000). It has also been shown that acetic acid bacteria
```
can produce alkali-stable lipids, which can significantly affect the cognitive ability
```
acting as precursors to several sphingolipids such as gangliosides (Fukami et al.,
```
```
2010). These sphingolipids are made up of sialic acid and ceramide-conjugated oli-
```
gosaccharides and have been reported to have impressive effects in improving the
symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease.
398 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
Nakhaee et al. (2015) compared, by a crossover randomized clinical trial, the
```
```
effects of Avena sativa (oat), diluted vinegar, and hydroxyzine (an anti-histamine
```
```
medication) on the reduction of uremic pruritus, a common complication in patients
```
with chronic kidney disease. Oat, vinegar, and hydroxyzine were effective in decreas-
```
ing pruritus; therefore, diluted vinegar and oat could be used as a complementary
```
treatment to hydroxyzine.
```
Shen et al. (2016), investigated the preventive effects of vinegar (5% v/v) and
```
```
acetic acid (0.3% w/v) on ulcerative colitis in mice. They found that vinegar sig-
```
nificantly reduced the disease activity index and histopathological scores, attenuated
body weight loss, and shortened the colon length in a murine experimental coli-
tis model induced by dextran sulfate sodium. Further mechanistic analysis showed
that vinegar inhibited inflammation through suppressing T h1 and T h17 responses
```
(T helper cells that play an important role in the immune system by releasing T cell
```
```
cytokines), the NLRP3 (a subset of the NLR inflammasome family; multiprotein
```
```
oligomers responsible for the activation of inflammatory responses), and the mito-
```
```
gen-activated protein kinase signaling activation (MAPK; a serine/threonine-spe-
```
cific protein kinase that affects diverse cellular responses including proinflammatory
```
cytokines). Vinegar also inhibited endoplasmic reticulum stress-mediated apoptosis.
```
The results indicated that vinegar supplementation may be a good dietary strategy
for the prevention of ulcerative colitis.
The anticancer properties of vinegar products such as Kibizu, Kurosu, and Izumi
```
(made from sugar cane, rice, and unpolished rice, respectively) were shown by inter-
```
```
ference on the differentiation of human cancer cells, programmed necrosis (necrop-
```
```
tosis), and apoptosis (Baba et al., 2013; Johnston, 2009; Mimura et al., 2004; Nanda
```
```
et al., 2004). Budak et al. (2014) also stated that hindering of cell proliferation can
```
```
be aided by Kurosu vinegar; thus it can be used as a complementary treatment for
```
```
various cancer cells. Bhalang et al. (2008) proposed that because of the specificity,
```
reliability, and sensitivity of acetic acid, it could be applied in oral cancer examina-
tion at just 5% concentration. Moreover, vinegar could be used for cancer diagnosis
because it is of low cost and has no side effects compared to toluidine blue and
metachromatic dye, which are commonly used for that purpose. In the same manner,
```
Limpaphayom et al. (2014) proposed the use of 5% acetic acid for visual inspection
```
of cervical cancer.
In a recent study, Euphorbia kansui stir-fried with vinegar was shown to have
promising biological activities toward treating malignant ascites with reduced toxic-
```
ity compared to crude kansui (Zhang et al., 2018). The mechanism of this activity
```
was interpreted through a UPLC-qTOF/MS based rat serum and urine metabolo-
mics strategy, coupled with network pharmacology. A total of 17 compounds were
considered as the potential active ingredients in the vinegar kansui. Metabolomics
revealed that this vinegar could be a promising and safe therapeutic medicine for the
excretion of ascites.
```
Vinegar baked Radix Bupleuri (VBRB), which originates from Bupleurum
```
chinense D.C. or B. scorzonerifolium Willd., is a widely used traditional Chinese
medicine. VBBR has been reported to exhibit higher potential activity for reliev-
```
ing the effects of a depressed liver than Radix Bupleuri (Lei et al., 2017). The
```
```
inhibitory effect of VBRB on the activity of glutathione S-transferase (GST)
```
399Health Benefits of Vinegars
was investigated in vitro, and an effective extract was selected that could effec-
tively enhance the liver-targeting efficiency of polymeric micelles loaded with
```
10-hydroxycamptothecin (DNA topoisomerase I inhibitor; cytotoxic anti-tumor
```
```
compound against a broad spectrum of cancers) after oral coadministration (Wu
```
```
et al., 2018). This simple strategy may enlighten on the potential use of meridian
```
guided drug, together with modern drug delivery systems, for optimized drug
targeting. Furthermore, behavioral studies, along with biochemical assessments,
as well as 1 H NMR analysis of the hippocampus and liver were employed to
systematically assess the pathology of depression and the therapeutic effects of
```
Radix Bupleuri and VBBR (Lei et al., 2017). The behavioral studies demon-
```
strated that treatment with VBBR resulted in better antidepressant effects than
Radix Bupleuri.
```
Finally, according to Lee et al. (2016), acidification of the skin surface has
```
been suggested as a therapeutic strategy for skin disorders such as atopic der-
matitis. Therefore, an animal study was performed to evaluate the usefulness
```
of acidification of the stratum corneum (the outer layer of the skin consisting
```
```
of keratinized cells) to inhibit atopic dermatitis and whether the therapeutic
```
effect of vinegar is attributed to other constituents besides acetic acid. The mice
subjects were treated for 3 weeks with control and vinegar or HCl containing
creams of different pH values. The results showed that application of topical
acids, regardless of their origin, inhibited the development of atopic dermatitis
lesions in murine model.

19
Dilution Water in the
Vinegar Industry
Hrissi K. Karapanagioti
19.1 INTRODUCTION
In food or beverage industries, water plays a crucial role in the quality of the final
```
product (Cribb, 2005a, 2005b; Lachenmeier et al., 2008; Platikanou et al., 2013;
```
```
Karapanagioti and Bekatorou, 2014; Karapanagioti, 2016). Nevertheless, water
```
```
quantities consumed receive more attention than water quality (Valta et al., 2015).
```
Depending on the type and number of the end-products, the capacity of the plant,
the type of the processes applied, the equipment employed, the level of automation,
and the system used for cleaning, the water quantities used vary considerably. Water
usage in the food and beverage industries is expressed either in volume of water con-
sumed per end-product or per raw material processed.
