410 Advances in Vinegar Production
In some cases, metals found in water have been reconsidered as taste adding
agents of particular importance to the local identity of the final product. In other
cases, large-scale industries, wanting to avoid packaging problems related to salts
found in tap water or changes in taste due to the variable quality of water that may
change due to weather conditions, treat the incoming water to secure a stable water
quality. Usually, they tend to deionize the incoming water. In vinegar, it does not
work the same way since the raw material contains many salts, being a fermentation
and not a distillation product. Wine conductivity for example can reach values up to
```
3,300 μS/cm (Henriques et al., 2019). In addition, SO2 is commonly added in the final
```
```
product as preservative and antioxidant (Chapter 6), and sulfites are formed possibly
```
increasing the conductivity of the final product. Nevertheless, it is recognized that
secondary constituents found in vinegar, and playing an important role regarding its
flavor and preservative qualities, have their origin not only in the raw material and in
```
the added nutrients but also in the water used for dilution (Sellmer-Wilsberg, 2009).
```
```
For the purpose of this chapter, vinegar is an acidic liquid (pH generally between
```
```
2 and 3) obtained by the oxidation of ethanol into acetic acid. Common vinegar has
```
a concentration of about 5–8% acetic acid, but tartaric acid and citric acid are also
```
found in lower concentrations in natural vinegar (European Commission, 2014).
```
19.2 WATER IN VINEGAR PRODUCTION
There are several steps during vinegar production for which water is required as it
```
happens with most food and beverage industries (Valta et al., 2015). Water is not
```
added as an ingredient of the product in all these steps. In some steps, water is used
as a means of heating or cooling or even as an air lock. There are two or three points
of entry for water into the vinegar production process. As an ingredient, water is
mainly used for soaking of the raw material and for diluting the final product to
```
reach the desired concentration of acetic acid (for a summary, see Table 19.1).
```
TABLE 19.1
Water Used as an Ingredient in Vinegar Production
Vinegar Type Before Fermentation End-Product
Wine Wine is diluted with water if the alcohol is higher than 12 degrees Yes
Wine and spirit Alcohol is mixed with water and nutrients Yes
Raisin Raisins are soaked in water Yes
Rice Steamed rice and starter are mixed with water
Malt Milled grains and hot water are mixed Yes
Cider Concentrated apple juice is diluted with water Yes
Cider Cider with a high alcohol content is adjusted to 7–8% v/v by adding
water
Yes
Mango Mango pulp is diluted in water and filtered
Sorghum Ground grains are mixed with water and a yeast starter
Banana Banana slices are boiled with water
Date Dates are boiled with water
Cereals Crushed cereals are soaked in water
411Dilution Water in the Vinegar Industry
19.2.1 Water as a means of Heating or Cooling
Sometimes water is required for cleaning, sterilizing the utensils used for the pro-
```
duction, or as an air lock in fermenting tanks (Hailu et al., 2012). In malt vinegar
```
production, the mashing vessel should be preheated by covering the perforated bot-
```
tom plates with hot water and heating the remainder of the vessel by steam (Grierson,
```
```
2009). The hot water is run off immediately prior to starting the mashing process.
```
Hot water can also be used to pasteurize bottled vinegar by immersion inside a con-
```
tainer to attain a temperature of 60°C (Joshi and Sharma, 2009). In distilled malt
```
```
vinegar, a water-cooled condenser is used (Grierson, 2009). During fermentation,
```
a temperature increase of 2–3°C can cause serious deterioration in both the aceti-
fication ratio and the efficiency. In submerged cultures, large amounts of heat are
generated, so that cooling costs become rather high. The need for cooling of the
```
bioreactors (which is normally performed with ordinary water) increases the overall
```
cost of vinegar production. This is especially true in African countries in which run-
```
ning water is not readily available (González and De Vuyst, 2009).
```
19.2.2 Water addition Before fermentation
As part of the product, water is added to the raw material to lower the degree of alcohol
in wine if it is higher than 12 since this may kill the cultures needed to produce vin-
egar. For example, according to the Greek regulation, denatured ethanol that is enter-
ing a vinegar factory must be diluted with water to reach 15% v/v. If raisins are used as
the raw material, raisins are soaked in water. During fermentation, water is also added.
```
The same is true for rice vinegar; in one ceramic pot, steamed rice, starter (e.g.,
```
```
koji), and water are mixed and fermented (Murooka et al., 2009). For malt vinegar
```
during the mashing step, the conversion of the grain starch to sugars, the milled
```
grain is mixed with hot water (Grierson, 2009). For wine and spirit vinegars, alcohol
```
```
is mixed with water and nutrients for the fermentation to start (Sellmer-Wilsberg,
```
```
2009). For cider vinegar before fermentation, concentrated apple juice is diluted with
```
water, or cider with a high alcohol content is adjusted to 7–8% v/v by adding water
```
(Joshi and Sharma, 2009).
```
```
For mango vinegar, mango pulp is usually diluted in water (in a pulp:water ratio
```
```
of 1:5) and filtered through a filter cloth to obtain the juice before fermentation
```
```
(González and De Vuyst, 2009). For sorghum vinegar, the ground grains are mixed
```
with water and a yeast starter culture before fermentation. For banana or date vin-
egar, banana slices or dates are blended and boiled with water and then filtered.
For cereal vinegar, the starchy raw materials, such as corn, wheat, and barley, are
crushed into pieces and are soaked in water for about 12 h in summer or 24 h in win-
ter. The materials are steamed with vapor to turn the starch granules into a sol-shaped
form to make the starch hydrolyze more easily. In addition, the raw materials are
```
partly sterilized during steaming (Chen et al., 2009). Cereal vinegar production also
```
involves a step called leaching vinegar. Water is added to cereal vinegar to dissolve
out any soluble components such as acids, amino acids, sugar, and other metabolites.
This process involves three steps that require leaching with old vinegar, and water is
only used in the third step to immerse the residue and to get the third-level vinegar.
412 Advances in Vinegar Production
19.2.3 dilution Water
For dilution of the final product in some of the fermentation methods that result in
very high acetic acid content, often as high as 14%, water must be added to bring the
```
acetic acid content to a range of 5–6% (Hailu et al., 2012). Formally, the formula-
```
tions made from vinegar commonly consist of an average 5–8%, and in some cases a
maximum of up to 20%, acetic acid in water. Vinegar is a common foodstuff, largely
commercially available. Since there is no unique recipe for vinegar, only dilution in
```
water is described in European Commission (2014). When vinegar (5–10% acetic
```
```
acid) is diluted in water and the desired dilution is 50% of vinegar in the prepara-
```
```
tion, the dilution is performed as 1 to 1 (i.e., 1 L of vinegar and 1 L of water) and the
```
produced concentration of acetic acid is 25–50 g/L.
Other vinegars also require dilution at their final step, e.g., sake-lees vinegar
```
(kasuzu) requires sake lees to ripen for 2 years and then be dissolved in water
```
```
(Murooka et al., 2009). For malt and grape vinegar, water is added to adjust the
```
```
strength to 5% total acidity (Grierson, 2009; Sellmer-Wilsberg, 2009).
```
The Greek legislation for vinegar production and quality does not indicate any
quality criteria for the dilution water. Nevertheless, there are general guidelines and
regulations that determine the drinking water quality. In the textbook describing the
```
vinegars of the world by Solieri and Giudici (2009), it is mentioned that the water
```
used for preparing mashes/juices must be bacteriologically clean, clear, colorless,
odorless, and without any sediment or suspended particles. In extreme cases, water
must be demineralized or fixed by the addition of the required minerals. Especially
for African countries, the amount of water available is also a technological consider-
ation for vinegar production.
19.2.4 Water in artifiCial Vinegar
```
Water is very important for imitation (artificial) vinegar or in other words for solu-
```
```
tions of acetic acid (E260). This is a substitute for vinegar and can be produced by
```
```
diluting acetic acid in water (4–30% by volume) and/or with original vinegar, and it
```
is suitable for human consumption. In Korea, the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety
calls this kind of solution synthetic vinegar that is manufactured by diluting glacial
```
acetic acid or acetic acid with drinking water (Ho et al., 2017).
```
19.3 MUNICIPAL WATER SUPPLY AND TREATMENT PROCESSES
Usually the water that is used in the food industries originates from the municipal
water supply. It is either used as it is or after further treatment. The municipal water
supply usually follows the drinking water guidelines valid in each region or coun-
try. Depending on the water source there are different treatment processes that take
place before water distribution. Municipal drinking water sources include groundwa-
```
ter (springs or wells), surface water (rivers and lakes), and seawater (Katsanou and
```
```
Karapanagioti, 2016; Katsanou and Karapanagioti, 2017). The basic treatment pro-
```
cesses commonly used are described below. New innovative methods still tested in the
```
laboratory and aiming at treating water are described in the book of Gil et al. (2019).
```
413Dilution Water in the Vinegar Industry
19.3.1 groundWater for muniCipal drinking Water
If the drinking water source is from groundwater, there are usually limited processes
that are required for its treatment. The most common treatment, and in most cases the
only treatment, is chlorination for water disinfection from microbes including bacte-
ria, protozoa, and some viruses. The most common technique for chlorination is the
```
introduction of chlorine gas (Cl 2), a small volume of a sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl)
```
```
stock solution, tablets of calcium hypochlorite [Ca(OCl)2], a combination of chlorine
```
and ammonia to produce chloramines, or a combination of chlorine and sodium chlo-
```
rite (NaClO2) to produce chlorine dioxide (ClO2). Chlorine should last in the water
```
supply pipeline network. There should be a maximum concentration of chlorine so
that the consumers that are close to the treatment plant get water that is drinkable and
does not contain high concentrations of chlorine. At the same time, there should be a
minimum concentration of chlorine that will allow water to reach the end of the sup-
ply network having enough chlorine for its disinfection. If the supply network is too
long there might be intermediate points where chlorination is repeated.
Other treatment processes used to treat groundwater are the removal of hardness
```
(softening), aeration, or chemical precipitation of metals, usually iron (Fe) or manga-
```
```
nese (Mn). Odor and flavor are also removed with these techniques. More metals can
```
```
be possibly found in groundwater such as chromium (Cr) or arsenic (As). In this case,
```
more sophisticated treatment techniques are required to lower the concentration of
toxic metals, or a change of the drinking water source is necessary.
19.3.2 surfaCe Water for muniCipal drinking Water
If the drinking water source is from surface water such as a lake or river, more pro-
cesses are required to treat water than in the case of groundwater sources. The water
treatment that is common in all cases is disinfection and most commonly chlorina-
tion as discussed above. Surface water is usually less hard than groundwater, and
softening is not required, but it usually contains a high number of suspended solids
that need to be removed. Some of the suspended solids can easily be removed by
sedimentation due to gravity, but most of them are so small that will never settle by
gravity only. These suspended solids are called colloids. Since they have the same
charge on their surface, they repel each other. So, in this case, coagulation is needed
to destabilize the surface of the colloids and help them to flocculate with each other
to form bigger size particles that will sediment easier by gravity. The most common
coagulants used are inorganic salts of aluminum or iron such as aluminum sulfate
```
[Al 2 (SO 4)3], iron(III) chloride (FeCl 3), iron(III) sulfate [or ferric sulfate; Fe2 (SO 4)3],
```
```
and iron(II) sulfate [or ferrous sulfate; FeSO 4·xH 2 O]. A mixing tank with high mix-
```
ing rates is required for coagulation, whereas a sedimentation tank is required for
the particles to create the flocs and then sediment to the bottom of the tank. After
the sedimentation tank, usually sand filters are required to filter water, such as tanks
filled with sand that allow water to flow in a vertical direction. These sand filters
remove the finest flocs which formed but did not settle in the sedimentation tank as
well as the destabilized particles that have been affected by the coagulant and are
ready to flocculate with the sand particles. In order to remove any organic compounds
414 Advances in Vinegar Production
diluted in water, aeration is applied after sand filters or the sand filters contain a bed
of activated carbon that is capable of removing dissolved organic compounds. At the
end of the treatment plant, there is always the disinfection step that is performed as
described above for the groundwater.
19.3.3 seaWater for muniCipal drinking Water
If the drinking water source is seawater, even more processes are required to treat
water than in the case of surface water sources. Suspended solids need to be removed
in a similar fashion as for surface water. Then, water flows through a reverse osmosis
membrane filter that allows water molecules to pass through a membrane and retains
```
salt in the other side (more details are provided below). Such a treatment can result in
```
```
about 300 mL of clean water from 1 L of seawater (Simonic, 2009), while the rest of
```
the water with an increased concentration of salt can be returned into the sea. Most
consumers are not used to the taste of water resulting from desalination.
19.4 LOCAL WATER SUPPLIES AND TREATMENT
Municipal water supplies in most cases can result in high quality water, but poorly
maintained water systems can become polluted with microorganisms. Bacteria can
multiply in water distribution systems, especially when water remains still for a long
time in storage tanks or in pipes that are not used regularly. The problem will be even
greater if the water system is not kept clean. The resulting microbiological contami-
nation can then spread to other parts of the system and be transferred to food. In such
cases, local water supplies including private wells or springs seem more desirable
for a vinegar producing industry, but local treatment of water is necessary. For some
food products such as soft drinks, local treatment is necessary, to meet product qual-
```
ity requirements before being used in the manufacturing process (Ait Hsine, 2005).
```
Disinfection is needed in all cases, but since water does not have to pass through the
water supply system, other techniques besides chlorination can be applied. A com-
mon process for compact industrial systems is filtration. It is commonly used to sepa-
rate solid and suspended matter from water. There are two common techniques: filter
beds and membrane filters. A summary of the common local treatment processes
and their targets is provided in Table 19.2.
19.4.1 disinfeCtion
For water that will be used as a food ingredient, if bacteria are suspected, then a
disinfection step should be included such as ozone, chlorine, or ultra-violet systems
```
(Bowser, 2016). Nevertheless, taste and odor due to chlorine need to be removed
```
using an activated carbon filter.
19.4.2 Bed filters
Bed filters or sand filters are beds with layers of different materials. In the entrance,
which is commonly at the bottom of the sand filter, there are the higher grain
415Dilution Water in the Vinegar Industry
materials with loose packing. Other feeding schemes also exist to minimize back-
```
washing (Simonic, 2009). The upper layers consist of materials with grain size that is
```
finer, and the packing is denser. This type of filtration is commonly used for particles
```
with grain size in the range of 5–1,000 μm (Bowser, 2016).
```
Surface filtration can be performed with metal sieves, clothes, or other synthetic
films. It is used for the removal of suspended sediments.
19.4.3 aCtiVated CarBon filters
Activated carbon filters are commonly used to remove chlorine from tap water. This
involves water flow through an activated carbon bed with granular material usually
in the grain size range of 1–2 mm. The removal mechanism is basically oxidation of
the activated carbon surface by the chlorine. The result is the formation of chloride
ions and oxygen containing surface groups for the material. The removal mechanism
may also involve sorption on the material surface. In any case, this is a very effective
method to remove chlorine. At the same time, microbes and micropollutants are also
sorbed on this filter.
Usually the commercial producers suggest that such filters, besides chlorine,
can also remove lead, algae, odor/flavor, pesticides, asbestos fibers, and polyaro-
matic hydrocarbons. The activated carbon filters are used to remove agents that
can foul subsequent treatment techniques like deionization or reverse osmosis
```
(Bowser, 2016). These filters are usually certified by government or international
```
agencies.
The problem with this technique is that the material has a certain life-time, and
after that new filling material is needed for the filter. This life-time is specified by
either a certain time period or by a certain volume of water that has passed through
the filter. If the filling material is not replaced regularly, a biofilm may form on the
TABLE 19.2
Summary of Local Water Treatment Processes and Their Targets
Water Treatment Process Target
Disinfection Bacteria, Protozoa, Virus
Bed filters Particles 5–1,000 μm
Activated carbon filters Chlorine, microbes, lead, algae, odor/flavor, pesticides, asbestos fibers,
polyaromatic hydrocarbons, etc.
Deionization Cations, anions, hardness
Microfiltration Particles > 10−1 μm, colloids and suspended solids
Ultrafiltration Particles 10 −2–10−1 μm, humic acids, dyes, viruses
Nanofiltration Particles 10−3–10−2 μm, some salts, organic compounds, bacteria,
protozoa, viruses
Reverse osmosis Particles 10−3–10−2 μm, dissolved solids, organic compounds, colloids,
bacteria, viruses
Electrodialysis Cations, anions
Distillation Salts
416 Advances in Vinegar Production
surface and microbes will start to grow and eventually be released in water. This is
not desirable, and thus, the filling material guidelines should be strictly followed.
New filling materials for such filters have been developed and can be found in the
market. These include hybrid materials that can also disinfect water or prevent bio-
```
fouling of the material. The most common bacteriostatic agent is silver (EPA, 2005).
```
19.4.4 deionization
Another bed filter using the appropriate material is deionization. This process is
based on the ability of some materials to exchange ions existing on their surface
with ions present in water. Such materials can be natural such as zeolites or syn-
thetic such as polymer resins, and they can selectively remove cations or anions.
For water treatment, both kinds of resins should be used to remove both cations
and anions, especially the ones causing hardness. The water produced by this
technique is called deionized water, and its conductivity can be around 17 μS/cm
```
(Karapanagioti and Bekatorou, 2014). The flow through the bed is usually down-
```
wards, and the backwashing is performed upwards. Regeneration is performed in
either direction of flow.
The problem of this technique is that after some time or after a certain volume
of water has passed through, the material is spent and requires regeneration by
replenishing its surface with easily exchanged ions, e.g. hydrogen or hydroxide. To
increase the life-time of the filter and avoid clogging of the filter bed, water with
low suspended solids concentrations should pass through ion exchange filters. This
suggests that a process removing suspended solids should be placed before the ion
exchange filter.
19.4.5 memBrane filters
```
For the removal of smaller grain size (10 −3 –10 −1 μm) particles, the processes of
```
```
microfiltration, ultrafiltration, and nanofiltration are used (Ibanez et al., 2007).
```
These processes can help with water softening and colloid, algae, bacteria, protozoa,
```
viruses, color, solids, and micropollutants removal (Bowser, 2016). Such technolo-
```
gies are used in the food industries for various separation and purification processes
```
(Kotsanopoulos and Arvanitoyannis, 2015). They rely on the use of a membrane and
```
application of a pressure difference between the two sides of the membrane as the
driving force. Particles bigger than the membrane pores are retained on one side of
the membrane, and clean water passes through the membrane.
Microfiltration and nanofiltration can be used as pretreatment for nanofiltration
```
and reverse osmosis (see below). Microfiltration is used to remove the remains of
```
colloids and suspended solids. This type of filtration is commonly used for particles
with grain size higher than 10 −1 μm. Ultrafiltration is used to remove macromol-
ecules, such as humic acids and dyes, as well as viruses. This type of filtration is
commonly used for particles with grain size in the range of 10 −2 –10 −1 μm.
Nanofiltration is used to remove some salts, organic compounds, bacteria, proto-
zoa, and viruses. It is a form of disinfection. This type of filtration is commonly used
for particles with grain size in the range of 10 −3 –10 −2 μm.
417Dilution Water in the Vinegar Industry
19.4.6 reVerse osmosis
Reverse osmosis is the ultimate filtration method. It is commonly used to remove salts
```
from seawater (desalination) to produce drinking water. The term osmosis describes
```
the tendency of the water molecules to pass through a membrane that separates a
concentrated solution from a dilute solution. The water molecules pass through the
membrane from the diluted side towards the concentrated solution side tending to
balance the chemical potential of water in both sides. By applying hydrostatic pres-
sure from the concentrated side, water molecules will pass through the membrane
in the opposite direction and clean water can be obtained from the other side of the
membrane. Reverse osmosis can also be used to remove dissolved solids, organic
compounds, colloids, bacteria, and viruses. This type of filtration is commonly used
for particles with grain size in the range of 10 −3 –10 −2 μm. The water produced by this
technique is characterized as ultrapure water and is used in many industrial applica-
tions, such as vinegar production.
The most common problem for all filtration processes is clogging due to waste
accumulation, and backwashing is the common technique to reverse this problem.
Another problem is the development of biofilms, which can be solved with the use
of disinfectants in the water. Nevertheless, additional processes are required in order
to protect the membranes, which are quite expensive, from substances such as sus-
pended solids including sediment and/or algae. Such processes include coagulation,
flocculation, and sedimentation, or sand filtration depending on the raw water qual-
ity. Also depending on the desired pH and taste of the produced water, the addition
of different chemicals may be necessary.
19.4.7 eleCtrodialysis
Electrodialysis can be described as a membrane procedure employing electricity.
Ions are transferred through ion exchange membranes under the effect of an electri-
cal potential. Cations move toward the negatively charged electrode, whereas the
anions move toward the positive. Since membranes are impermeable to ions, the lat-
ter are accumulated at both sides of the membrane. Thus, this technique is used for
desalination. The main problems associated with this technique are the blockage of
the membrane pores and the relatively high cost of equipment.
19.4.8 distillation
Water distillation is an easy process to produce water low in salt content. Water is
boiled in a container until evaporation, and it is then condensed in a cooling devise.
```
The water produced by this technique is called (once)-distilled water and its conduc-
```
```
tivity can be around 40 μS/cm (Karapanagioti and Bekatorou, 2014). If the process
```
is repeated, an even cleaner water can be obtained. If the process is repeated three
times, the water is called triple-distilled water, and its conductivity can be around
```
3 μS/cm (Karapanagioti and Bekatorou, 2014).
```
The main problem associated with this technique is that in order to cool the
vapors, flowing water is usually used, and high amounts of water are spent this way.
418 Advances in Vinegar Production
Energy consumption is also another problem that can be solved if solar or wind
energy is used instead of electricity.
19.5 A TYPICAL WATER PURIFICATION SYSTEM
Based on commercially available water purification systems for the food and bever-
age industries, such a system for a vinegar facility could combine bed filters and
reverse osmosis. The typical system components include sediment and carbon
```
absorption filters and a reverse osmosis unit (see Figure 19.1).
```
Bed filters are used as pre-treatment in membrane systems for reducing the feed
water suspended solids in the 10–20 μm range and above. Activated carbon filters
are used for removal of off-tastes, odors, chlorine, chloramines, low molecular-
weight organics, and possible chlorination toxic by-products, called trihalomethanes
```
(THMs), through sorption. Activated carbon filters are designed based on the time
```
required for removing chlorine and chloramines from the supply water. Reverse
```
osmosis systems are used for the removal of monovalent and divalent ions (e.g., alka-
```
```
linity, sodium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, etc.), viruses, bacteria, and pyrogens.
```
Typical applications include low-sodium and low total dissolved solids soft drinks
and bottled water.
19.6 CONCLUSIONS
Water is one of the main ingredients of vinegar, used before fermentation for soaking
the raw materials and before packaging to bring its acetic acid content to the suitable
```
range (usually 5–8%). Water used in vinegar can derive either from the municipal
```
supply or from local sources after suitable treatment. There are several techniques to
treat water on-site in the vinegar production industry and before usage, and selecting
one depends on the quality of the water entering the industry. In most cases, local
FIGURE 19.1 A typical water treatment system for a vinegar facility.
419Dilution Water in the Vinegar Industry
treatment can be sufficient if it includes a combination of sand and activated carbon
filter beds and a reverse osmosis unit.

20.1 INTRODUCTION
Monitoring of bioprocesses, such as fermentation processes, where many physico-
chemical parameters change during their course, is crucial for ensuring productivity,
efficiency, and reproducibility. Generally, the methods used for monitoring biopro-
cesses are off-line methods, mainly including chromatographic techniques, such
```
as high-pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC), gas chromatography (GC), and
```
spectroscopic techniques. The most used spectroscopic techniques are near-infrared
```
(NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy or in combination with Fourier trans-
```
form instruments, for the determination of acetic acid, total acid content, ethanol,
```
aroma compounds, sugars, and other substrates, as well as biomass (Chen et al., 2012;
```
```
Durán et al., 2010; González-Sáiz et al., 2008; Ji-yong et al., 2013; Kornmann et al.,
```

```
2002; Sáiz-Abajo et al., 2006; Suehara and Yano, 2004). UV-VIS spectroscopy, fluo-
```
```
rescence, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, as
```
well as mass spectroscopy, have also been widely exploited in food analysis. In most
cases, extended sample preparation is needed prior to analysis, due to the complexity
of the food matrices.
Common titration has been mainly used for the determination of total acidity for
```
the off-line monitoring of vinegar fermentation (de Ory et al., 2004; Fregapane et al.,
```
```
2003). HPLC equipped with a refractive index detector has been used for the detection
```
```
of organic acids (lactic, acetic, tartaric, malic, and succinic acids), glycerol, ethanol,
```
```
and carbohydrates (glucose, fructose, and sucrose) during alcoholic and acetic acid
```
fermentation with mixed cultures of Acetobacter aceti and Gluconobacter oxydans
```
(Dias et al., 2016). GC has been utilized for the simultaneous off-line detection of
```
```
ethanol, acetic acid, acetoin, and diacetyl during vinegar fermentation (Akasaka et al.,
```
```
2013; de Ory, 2004; Schlepütz and Büchs, 2013), while GC has been, early enough,
```
```
coupled to MS for extensive online process monitoring (Matz et al., 1998) and for
```
```
volatile compounds determination in vinegar fermentation broth (Kocher et al., 2014;
```
```
Pinu and Villas-Boas, 2017; Roda et al., 2017). Moreover, the volatile organic compo-
```
sition of balsamic vinegars has been monitored using the solid-phase micro-extrac-
```
tion as sampling technique in GC analysis with a flame ionization detector (FID). The
```
```
obtained data, after principal component analysis (PCA), were in good concordance
```
```
with the data from HPLC coupled with a UV detector (Cocchi et al., 2008).
```
Advances in UV-VIS spectrophotometers that cover the whole range from the UV
```
to the near-infrared region, and the use of charge-coupled devices (CCD) or photo-
```
diode arrays instead of expensive photomultipliers, made these instruments useful
in bioprocess monitoring. Specifically, they have been applied to determine soluble
solid contents and pH, enabling the fermentation process and quality control of white
vinegar production. CCD cameras also allow the simultaneous detection of different
```
analytes (Bao et al., 2013; Beutel and Henkel, 2011).
```
NMR spectroscopy with the help of chemometric tools has been applied in dif-
ferent substrates, such as wine and vinegar, using various techniques for sample
pretreatment and extraction of analytes or in direct analysis to obtain a metabolomic
```
fingerprint (Fotakis et al., 2013). NMR was also combined with a bioreactor for
```
online monitoring of a bioprocess. Glycerol, glycose, and lipids were successfully
```
identified by this system (Kreyenschulte et al., 2015).
```
Raman spectroscopy with chemometric methods were applied to vinegar samples
for the determination of glycose, fructose, ethanol, and acetic acid during vinegar
fermentation. The results showed good correlation with the reference method of
```
HPLC (Uysal et al., 2013).
```
```
Capillary electrophoresis (CE) has also been dynamically introduced for chemi-
```
cal characterization and monitoring of fermentation broths. Several organic acids,
which are the main metabolites of the fermentation process, as well as other metabo-
lites and substrates such as sugars, have been determined by this technique. CE
provides a rapid analysis, from a few seconds to a few minutes, along with great
```
resolution (Alhusban et al., 2013).
```
```
Recently, a novel thermal infrared enthalpimetry (TIE) method combined with
```
disposable microplates and an infrared camera was developed for determination of
423Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
the total acidity of vinegar samples to increase the high-throughput of the analysis.
The results were in good agreement with conventional techniques such as titration
```
(Barin et al., 2015; Tischer et al., 2017).
```
```
A novel chemosensor based on a surface plasmon resonance (SSR) taste sensor
```
and a metal oxide odor sensor was also developed for the quality control of the vin-
```
egar fermentation process (Nanto et al., 2002).
```
```
Finally, selected ion flow tube–mass spectrometry (SIFT–MS) was recently intro-
```
duced as an alternative method to traditional GC–MS for the detection of volatile
compounds, due to its potential for real-time monitoring of the fermentation prog-
ress. Ethanol and acetoin in sourdough fermentations were detected by this tech-
```
nique (Kerrebroeck et al., 2015).
```
Fermentations are, however, vulnerable regarding microbiological stability and
contamination. Thus, the accurate and continuous real-time control of specific
parameters is essential for a successful outcome, as well as to ensure and improve the
quality of the product. The traditional off-line methods used to control the fermenta-
tion process are usually methods that include sample collection and pretreatment,
are time-consuming, and carry the risk of contamination. The best way to eliminate
the risk of contamination at all process steps is the online monitoring, providing
automatic, real-time, rapid, precise, consistent, robust, sensitive, reproducible, and
multi-analyte detection of variables and aseptic determination of the course of fer-
```
mentation, with no sample preparation and low consumption of reagents (Peris and
```
```
Escuder-Gilabert, 2013; Tamburini et al., 2014; Tosi et al., 2003).
```
```
Following, the main types of available online monitoring methods (chromato-
```
```
graphic, spectroscopic, chemical techniques) are highlighted and discussed.
```
20.2 CHROMATOGRAPHIC TECHNIQUES
```
20.2.1 gas CHromatograpHy (gC)
```
GC is a traditional analytical technique that is robust and reliable for the online moni-
toring of volatile compounds during a fermentation process. GC is a technique that is
applied for the separation of volatile substances. The compounds are passed through
```
a chromatographic column (usually a capillary tube) and are eluted by means of an
```
inert gas, such as He, Ar, or N2 , called the carrier gas. The separation depends on
the boiling point of sample components, the temperature of the column, the interac-
```
tions between the compounds and the stationary phase (column type), and the speed
```
of the carrier gas. At the exit of the column, all eluted substances are detected by a
proper detector depending on the nature of the substances being analyzed. GC usu-
ally involves the use of FIDs for the analysis of fermentation products.
GC has been successfully applied for the real-time monitoring of the progress of
vinegar fermentation. For example, a gas chromatograph was attached to the head-
```
space outlet of a fermentation system (González-Sáiz et al., 2009). The pressure in
```
the headspace of the outlet was controlled by a valve placed to the air exhaust line.
Several organic volatile compounds, such as ethanol, acetic acid, ethyl acetate, and
acetoin, were simultaneously analyzed at real-time by this GC system, which was
equipped with two columns, two detectors, and an electro-valve to control the gas
424 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
flow (Figure 20.1). Oxygen was detected by a thermal conductivity detector (TCD)
```
while the organic volatile compounds were analyzed by an FID detector.
This model fermentation process explained well the steady and semi-steady states
reached in the pilot fermenter, within a broad range of conditions, although the ini-
tial cell population was not known. The model includes the effect of oxygen transfer
and the hydrodynamics by the fermentation medium, which depend on hydrostatic
pressure, agitation, aeration, and temperature. These data are necessary for develop-
ing scale-up fermentation processes. A future simulation of the environment of the
fermentation will be useful for the design of processes in industrial-scale fermenters
```
(González-Sáiz et al., 2009).
```
```
Liquid chromatography (LC) and HPLC have also been connected through an
```
auto-sampling device for online monitoring of ethanol and glycose using a refrac-
```
tive index detector (RID) and automatic control of the ethanol fermentation process,
```
```
enhancing the fermentation yield (Liu et al., 2001).
```
20.3 SPECTROSCOPIC TECHNIQUES
Non-destructive techniques are highly required for testing in the food industry to
ensure the quality and safety of food and to increase productivity. Online monitor-
ing is now necessary in the expanding fermentation industry. It is of great impor-
tance that techniques available for online monitoring of industrial bioprocesses
have high throughput, short analysis time, multianalyte potential, and require no
sample pretreatment, to increase the efficiency of the process and reduce waste.
Spectroscopic techniques, in general, are ideal for fast and efficient food analy-
```
sis. They enable real-time monitoring at all stages of production (Woodcock et al.,
```
```
2008). The techniques used for online monitoring of bioprocesses usually include
```
near- and mid-infrared spectroscopy, while UV-visible, fluorescence, NMR, and
Raman spectroscopy are less explored.
FIGURE 20.1 Online monitoring of fermentation process by gas chromatography.
425Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
```
20.3.1 near- (nir) and mid -infrared (mir) speCtrosCopy
```
NIR and MIR spectroscopy have been successfully applied for the online moni-
toring of bioprocesses and fermentation with a high range of different analytes,
providing multianalyte determination within a few minutes, even in highly com-
plex liquids. Both are spectroscopic techniques that exploit the characteristic varia-
tions in vibrational/rotational frequencies of different molecules after absorption of
radiation within the near- and mid-infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum
```
(700 nm–15 μm). Different spectroscopic patterns correlate with matrix composi-
```
tion. The use of NIR/MIR technology is an alternative approach to online monitor-
ing of fermentation due to the development of more accurate and easy-to-handle
instruments, exhibiting several advantages compared to traditional analytical meth-
```
ods (GC and HPLC). NIR and MIR are non-invasive and non-destructive technolo-
```
gies based on optical measurements and spectroscopic principles. Both techniques
provide rapid analysis, in less than 2 min, require little or no sample preparation,
and provide the ability for simultaneous and multianalyte determination, as well as
real-time control in a process stream. Thus, NIR and MIR are among the most ideal
technologies for fast and efficient online monitoring of fermentation processes.
Several reports showed that MIR is more sensitive and provides more useful infor-
mation and better spectral resolution than NIR, due to much stronger absorbances in
the MIR spectra and because water has stronger influence on the NIR region. Thus,
MIR is gaining new applications in bioprocessing. In contrast, NIR absorption is
in general weaker than MIR absorption, enabling the direct measurement without
sample preparation or dilution of the sample.
Modern NIR instruments, as well as low-cost instruments based on filters, light
```
emitting diodes (LEDs), and Fourier transform are useful for routine analysis and
```
online applications. Moreover, advanced optical systems and probe technology in IR
equipment, along with superior software that enables statistical analysis of the data,
made IR spectroscopy more efficient in online monitoring. The development of optical
conduit/fiber probes made measurements in the IR spectra feasible even in aqueous
solutions, because water strongly absorbs IR radiation. Problems in signal instability
```
and background noise are overcome by the use of Fourier transform instruments (FT-
```
```
IR). FT-IR spectrophotometers also enable the determination of specific analytes in
```
```
complex liquids, such as the fermentation broths (Cervera et al., 2009; Roychoudhury
```
```
et al., 2006; Tamburini et al., 2014; Tosi et al., 2003). Moreover, the attenuated total
```
```
reflectance (ATR) technique in conjunction with FT-IR increased the applicability
```
of IR spectroscopy in solid or liquid state, even in aqueous solutions and biological
samples, without sample pretreatment. That is because ATR contains a novel sam-
ple accessory consisting of a crystal of high refractive index. As IR radiation passes
through the crystal, it undergoes multiple reflections on the internal surface in close
contact with the sample depending on the refractive index and the sample. An eva-
```
nescent wave is produced by the reflection, that penetrates into the sample (0.5–2 μm)
```
```
and is collected by the detector as it exits the crystal (Figure 20.2). The water con-
```
tribution, in case of aqueous solution, is eliminated by simply spectral subtraction.
```
The ATR crystal, though, can be replaced by fiber optics-based sensors (fiber optics
```
```
evanescence wave spectroscopy) (Etzion et al., 2004; Roychoudhury et al., 2006).
```
426 Advances in Vinegar Production
Online monitoring of bioprocesses depends on the ability to combine NIR/MIR
probes with the bioreactor. Special optical fibers have to be used in order to effi-
```
ciently transmit NIR or MIR radiation (Garrido-Vidal et al., 2004; González-Sáiz
```
```
et al., 2009). These fibers usually have restricted length due to limitations related
```
to poor transmission and strong absorbance. To transfer the IR beam to longer dis-
tances, optical conduits/wave guides with coated internal surfaces are attached to the
optical fibers, which focus the beam to the ATR crystal.
The online measurement and control can be performed in two major ways
```
(Figure 20.3) (Garrido-Vidal et al., 2004; González-Sáiz et al., 2009):
```
• In situ or inline using a sterilizable optical fiber probe immersed into the
fermentation reaction and directly combined with the NIR/MIR instrument.
• Ex situ or online using a reflectance probe attached to the glass wall of the
fermentation vessel.
```
• Ex situ using an optical fiber probe combined with a flow-cell (loop)
```
attached to the glass wall of the fermentation vessel.
The optical fibers used in these applications are made of materials such as heavy
metal fluorides, chalcogenide, and mixed silver halides in order to be effective for IR
radiation transmission. However, the selection of the suitable optical fibers depends
on the wavelengths used in the analysis. Employment of multiple optic probes to
different reactor vessels or various positions in the same reactor leads to an efficient
online monitoring of the fermentation process.
A typical NIR/MIR spectrum contains absorption information of all the constitu-
ents of the complex matrix of a fermentation broth. Multivariate statistical analysis
and chemometrics are required to obtain useful data relating to the fermentation
progress. NIR/MIR technologies provide sufficient accuracy for applications in
online bioprocess monitoring.
An NIR liquid analyzer was used for the real-time monitoring of vinegar fer-
mentation process in industrial vinegar production. It was connected online to the
fermentation vessel. The parameters analyzed for an efficient kinetic control of the
process were ethanol, acetic acid, biomass, ethyl acetate, and acetoin. Specifically,
the NIR analyzer was attached to a 10-L fermenter, including controllers for agita-
tion and temperature. Software was used to regulate the collection and the analysis
of the samples within selected intervals. Along with the NIR analyzer, a GC was
```
FIGURE 20.2 Schematic illustration of attenuated total reflectance (ATR) technique.
```
```
(D: detector).
```
427Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
connected to the gas outlet of the fermenter for online monitoring of oxygen, ethanol,
acetic acid, and ethyl acetate in the exhaust line. The analysis was performed using
```
two chromatographic columns and an electrical valve (Figure 20.4). The results
```
showed that NIR can be applied for online monitoring of five critical and funda-
mental parameters to optimize the industrial fermentation process for the production
```
of vinegar of good quality (Garrido-Vidal et al., 2004; González-Sáiz et al., 2009).
```
An automated NIR system has also been applied for industrial vinegar production
```
(CETOTEC). This system was combined with the industrial vinegar fermenter and
```
provided simultaneous and rapid online measurement of ethanol and acetic acid in
less than 1 min based on the different IR spectral patterns. The measurement range
was within 0–20% for ethanol and 0–25% for acetic acid. The total alcohol concen-
tration was also monitored continuously during fermentation by online measurement
of the conductivity of a gas sensor. The system can simplify routine analysis and
can provide full automation and optimal control of the fed-batch process for vinegar
```
production (CETOTEC).
```
20.4 CHEMICAL SENSORS
Chemical sensors are the most suitable for online monitoring of the fermentation pro-
cess. They are based on physical or chemical parameters. Their major functional prin-
ciple lies on the conversion of a measured magnitude to an optical or electrical signal.
```
FIGURE 20.3 In situ (A), ex situ using a reflectance probe (B), and ex situ using a by-pass
```
```
loop flow cell (C), online monitoring of vinegar fermentation using NIR or MIR spectroscopy.
```
428 Advances in Vinegar Production
The advantages of sensors include the ability of real-time monitoring, as well as
simultaneous detection of several parameters, such as biomass and product concen-
tration, simplicity, rapid analysis, low cost, little or no sample preparation, low con-
sumption of sample and reagents, and automation, while they are non-invasive, and
they do not require the removal of the sample. Few sensors, however, have been used
for fermentation process control due to lack of selectivity. The sensing technologies
```
should meet the following criteria to enable the fermentation process (Harms et al.,
```
```
2002; Tamburini et al., 2014):
```
• ensure asepsis of the fermentation process
• be sensitive
• be selective and not be affected by the bioprocess environment
• be rugged to condition variances
• provide fast, rapid and stable response
• provide a wide detection range to cover the whole fermentation process
• provide multiparametric analysis
• require no sample pretreatment, small sample volume and little mainte-
nance, and
• present operational stability in long-term processes without the need for
recalibration
For example, a portable colorimetric sensor array was constructed for real-time
monitoring of the vinegar fermentation process, as an alternative to GC–MS. This
```
sensor array was used for the detection of volatile organic compounds (VOCs)
```
FIGURE 20.4 Online monitoring of fermentation process by NIR analyzer and gas
chromatography.
429Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
during solid-state acetic acid fermentation. It consisted of a gas volatile system,
a gas detection system, a power system, and a control system. Each sensor array
contained 15 colorimetric dyes, nine metalloporphyrins, and six pH indicators,
printed on silica gel plates. The sensor was placed into a reaction chamber, and
the detection was accomplished through excitation, while the images of the sen-
sor array were captured by a CCD camera positioned at the top of the reaction
```
chamber (Guan et al., 2014) or a common scanner using disposable sensors (Chen
```
```
et al., 2013). The solid-state fermentation substrate was placed into a gas collecting
```
chamber, while a vacuum pump was used to allow the volatiles produced by the
```
fermentation process to enter the reaction chamber (Figure 20.5). The color change
```
of the colorimetric sensor was recorded by the CCD camera. Sampling intervals
could be controlled by a computer system, with a minimum interval set at 2 sec.
This means that the system could collect images every 2 sec, hence providing the
capability of real-time analysis. The color signal of the colorimetric array for each
```
dye, before and after substrate addition, was analyzed at red (R), green (G), and
```
```
blue (B) regions (RGB analysis), resulting in 45 color variables, representing the
```
color change profiles of vinegar samples. Color patterns and multivariate statisti-
cal analysis were then used for qualitative and quantitative determination of the
composition of the fermentation broth.
The sensor was applied for the discrimination of vinegar samples per day during
the whole process. The results showed that around 60% of the samples were cor-
rectly identified corresponding to their fermenting day and 92.3% of the samples
were correctly classified within an error range of 3 days, due to the inhomogeneity
of the solid-state fermentation and the continuity of the process. The advantages
of the colorimetric sensor array are the accuracy and the low cost, while there is
no need for sample pretreatment. Thus, this type of sensor can be useful for VOCs
determination. Compared to the electronic nose technology, a colorimetric sensor
array has better recognition ability, higher precision, wider dynamic range, and it is
not affected by environmental humidity. New materials, such as polymers, can, in
the future, provide a wider operation range.
An alcohol measuring system was also constructed for online measurement of
alcohol concentration during acetic acid fermentation. A special probe was directly
FIGURE 20.5 Colorimetric sensor array.
430 Advances in Vinegar Production
immersed into the broth with the help of a probe flange. The alcohol was measured
by diffusion through a permeable membrane. The change to the electric resistance
of a semiconductor of the sensor is proportional to the ethanol partial pressure and
thus to ethanol concentration. The results were compared with those of GC analysis
for validation of the sensor. The online monitoring of alcohol allows estimation of
the biological oxidation rate and the bacterial activity during the fermentation pro-
```
cess with good accuracy (Schlepütz and Büchs, 2013; García-García et al., 2007;
```
```
FRINGS, VOGELBUSCH).
```
An amperometric sensor was developed for acetic acid monitoring. A modified-
graphite electrode was used as the working electrode, which was inserted into a
flow-through amperometric cell, containing a platinum wire serving as the coun-
ter and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode. Three enzymes, acetate kinase, pyruvate
kinase, and lactate dehydrogenaseare, were immobilized on the three electrodes
```
into a poly(ethyleneglycole) diglycidyl ether (PEGDGE) film, containing also bril-
```
```
liant cresyl blue (BCB) as the electrochemical active compound. The flow cell was
```
then attached to a single channel flow injection system, and the electrodes were
connected to a three-electrode potentiometer. The samples were injected to the
flow cell, along with ATP, NADH, and phosphoenolpyruvate. Cyclic voltametric
measurements were subsequently performed. This sensor is based on the following
```
reactions: acetate firstly reacts with ATP producing ADP, a reaction catalyzed by
```
acetate kinase. Then, phosphoenolpyruvate reacts with ADP producing pyruvate
by pyruvate kinase. Pyruvate is subsequently reduced to lactate by NADH and
lactate dehydrogenase. The NADH is then reduced to NAD + at the modified graph-
ite electrode causing electric current decrease. This sensor was applied for the
quantification of acetate in vinegar samples with great accuracy and showed good
sensitivity, selectivity, and stability. Future improvements could focus on imple-
mentation of the proposed sensor to online monitoring of vinegar fermentation
```
(Mieliauskiene et al., 2006).
```
20.5 MONITORING OTHER PARAMETERS
OF VINEGAR FERMENTATION
Optimization of the fermentation process depends strongly on the accurate and
real-time monitoring of several chemical and physical parameters to increase
the productivity and the reproducibility of the process. Different chemical and
physical parameters are evaluated easily to ensure high yields and good quality
of the product. Key parameters are temperature, cell mass, pH, concentration of
```
dissolved oxygen (O 2), and produced carbon dioxide (CO 2). The required data
```
are obtained on a real-time basis by the online connection of specific probes or
```
sensors to the bioreactors (Figure 20.6) (González-Sáiz et al., 2009). Sterilizable
```
glass electrodes still remain the state-of-the-art, while temperature is controlled
by thermocouples, thermistors, or resistance temperature detectors. Standard
probes and electrodes, polarographic sensors, and the most commonly used
non-invasive optical fluorescence sensors are used for online measurement of pH,
```
dissolved O 2 , and CO 2 (de Ory et al., 2004; Harms et al., 2002; Ndoye et al., 2007;
```
```
Schäpper et al., 2009).
```
431Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
20.5.1 pH sensors
For pH determination, electrochemical and optical sensors based on the absorbance
or fluorescence of pH-sensitive dyes are preferred, with the disadvantage of narrow
working pH range. The selection of the sensor is based on the pH range of the fer-
mentation process. A potentiometric sensor with an H+ -selective glass electrode is
the most standard sensor for pH measurement. Novel polymers have been used for
the construction of optical sensors aiming to extend the dynamic range, but they still
have to be tested in fermentations. For example, photo-induced electron transfer in
```
N,N-bis(pyridylmethyl)naphthalene diimides have been exploited for the construc-
```
tion of a pH sensor with applications to commercial vinegars. The sensor was based
on the fluorescence enhancement of naphthalene diimide dyes by hindering the
```
photo-induced energy-electron transfer (PET) from the pyridine ring to the naphtha-
```
```
lene fluorophore due to protonation in acidic environment (pH 1.7–4.1). This sensor
```
was found to be sensitive, accurate, stable, reproducible, and with a rapid response.
The results were in great concordance with the common glass electrode-based pH
meters, indicating that the proposed pH sensor could be used for pH measurement in
```
strongly acidic conditions (Beutel and Henkel, 2011; Martínez-Quiroz et al., 2017).
```
20.5.2 dissolVed o2 sensors
The dissolved O2 in liquid phase is of greater importance than the gas O2 mea-
sured at the exhaust exit. Optical sensors are suitable for O 2 measurements at low
concentrations, while electrochemical sensors are used in higher O 2 concentrations.
However, electrochemical sensors consume O 2 which may influence the process and
the accuracy of the data. The most widely used sensor is based on the amperomet-
ric determination of dissolved O 2 using an electrochemical cell with a membrane
permeable to O2 and impermeable to water or other electrolytes. The diffusion of
O2 is proportional to the partial pressure of O 2 in the solution and thus to the O 2 con-
centration. The main disadvantage of this sensor is focused on the need for periodic
```
calibration of the electrode (Johnson et al., 1964).
```
FIGURE 20.6 Dissolved oxygen and temperature sensors for online monitoring of vinegar
fermentation.
432 Advances in Vinegar Production
Optical sensors are usually based on fluorescence quenching of a fluorophore,
such as Ru 2+and Pt-based molecules, by O 2 . The fluorophore is mainly attached to
a polymer tube that is combined to an optical filter at one end and a light source, a
LED or a laser, at the other end. The emitted fluorescence is collected and driven by
the optical fiber to the detector which can either be a photodiode or a photomultiplier.
These sensors provide long-term stability and higher sensitivity, they can be minia-
turized, while they do not consume O 2 and can be applied to gas and liquid samples
```
(Bambot et al., 1994; Beutel and Henkel, 2011). Fiber optics probes have been widely
```
```
used for in situ non-invasive online monitoring (Ocean Optics).
```
20.5.3 Co2 sensors
Sensitive electrochemical and optical sensors are also used for the determination of
the CO2 content. The common electrochemical sensor comprises of a pH electrode
and a reference electrode. A bicarbonate solution is in contact with the electrode by
a permeable membrane. The pH of the bicarbonate solution is measured and is in
```
equilibrium with the CO2 at the other side of the membrane (Figure 20.6). The con-
```
centration of CO 2 is related to the pH of the bicarbonate solution. Optical sensors are
based on pH-sensitive dyes, which can be absorbance- or fluorescence-based. Simple
absorbance-based dyes are phenol red, cresol red, and m-cresol purple, while fluo-
```
rescent dyes are hydroxypyrenetrisulfonic acid (HPTS), fluorescein, and seminaph-
```
thorhodafluor. The indicator’s solution is in close contact with one end of an optical
```
fiber, which is attached to a membrane made of polytetrafluoroetylene (PTFE). CO 2
```
causes protonation of the dye, the form of which has weaker fluorescence intensity.
Thus, fluorescent sensors are based on fluorescence quenching and are more sensi-
tive than colorimetric sensors. However, the narrow dynamic range is also a concern
```
here. The use of alternative indicative dyes may widen the analytical range (Oter and
```
```
Polat, 2015; Uttamlal and Walt, 1995).
```
20.5.4 Cell mass sensors
Finally, the online monitoring of cell mass is accomplished by optical fibers
combined with regular spectrophotometers or NIR instruments or by electrical
means. Polarizable membranes are used for electrical measurements, while light
absorbance is related to cell concentration. Biomass determination can also be
monitored by measuring other parameters such as O 2 uptake rate, CO 2 release
rate, and the reaction heat flow using proper sensors, or other parameters such as
different substrates and products. Online measurements of O 2 and CO 2 are con-
ducted in the fermenter’s exhaust gas, using a gauge for O 2 measuring its diffu-
sion and IR absorption for CO 2 . For the heat flow determination, the inlet and the
outlet temperature of the cooling water, the inlet and the outlet air temperature,
and the temperature of the broth in the fermenter using sterilizable Pt probes are
measured. Software analysis of the data obtained by the three aforementioned
sensors can indirectly be related to biomass concentration. The results from all
the three software sensors were in good agreement with the off-line measure-
```
ments (Golobič et al., 2000).
```
433Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
Finally, in situ microscopy has also been applied for online cell concentration
```
determination. Usually a CCD camera is used for real-time observations (Bittner
```
```
et al., 1998).
```
20.5.5 aCetiC aCid BaCteria identifiCation
Acetic acid bacteria are the microorganisms responsible for acetic fermentation and
vinegar production. They can oxidize ethanol to acetic acid. These bacteria mainly
belong to the genera Acetobacter and Gluconacetobacter. The cultivation-free tech-
niques used for identifying and monitoring acetic acid bacteria species are mainly
molecular techniques. After DNA isolation, the sample is subjected to various PCR-
```
based techniques. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is used for the amplification of
```
specific DNA sequences. The target DNA region that is selected for amplification
has to be present in all bacteria species analyzed and must contain conserved regions
to enable the design of universal primers, along with small variations to allow dis-
crimination among species. The proper target for bacteria identification is the 16S
RNA coding gene. The molecular techniques used for acetic acid bacteria identifi-
cation include real-time PCR, PCR followed by denaturing gradient electrophoresis
```
(DGGE), restriction fragment length rolymorphisms (RFLP) analysis, and sequenc-
```
```
ing after DNA amplification by PCR (Cocolin et al., 2013; Jara et al., 2013; Li et al.,
```
```
2016; Zhao and Yun, 2016; Zhu et al., 2018). In the PCR-DGGE method, the primers
```
selected produce more than one PCR product of different lengths. The electropho-
```
retic patterns are strongly dependent on bacterial genome (Xu et al., 2011). Moreover,
```
```
amplification by PCR using small primers (5bp) combined with gel electrophoresis
```
```
result in bacterial-specific PCR products allowing bacterial determination (Gullo
```
```
et al., 2016). Pyrosequencing is also used after DNA amplification for bacteria species
```
identification. After DNA isolation, specific primers are used for the amplification
of DNA barcodes, which means small conserved DNA sequences that are species-
```
specific. The amplified products are then subjected to pyrosequencing; during this
```
process only one nucleotide is incorporated by DNA polymerase. This nucleotide
is labeled, usually with a fluorophore, to enable detection. The nucleotides used are
```
dideoxynucleotides, meaning that they lack a free 3′-OH end (-OH is substituted by
```
```
-H) essential for the continuation of the polymerization by the DNA polymerase. The
```
amplicons are then detected mainly by capillary electrophoresis. Data are processed
```
by special software to obtain useful sequencing information (Peng et al., 2015).
```
A promising non-PCR based technique that can be applied to food microbiol-
```
ogy is fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). FISH uses fluorescently labeled
```
specific oligonucleotide probes that penetrate into the cells and are hybridized to the
corresponding genes. The hybridization reaction is monitored under a UV micro-
```
scope (Cocolin et al., 2013). A new method was indeed developed based on in situ
```
hybridization targeting the 16S RNA gene of acetic acid bacteria using a fluorescein-
labeled complementary probe. With this method, the fluorescence signal is measured
through flow cytometric analysis of the bacteria cells. The method enables an easy
```
microbial monitoring of vinegar during industrial vinegar production (Trček et al.,
```
```
2016). NMR spectroscopy was also used for the identification of bacteria species
```
during fermentation after extraction of polar compounds with cold Milli-Q water.
434 Advances in Vinegar Production
After statistical analysis, different metabolite profiles are obtained allowing species
```
discrimination (Li et al., 2018).
```
20.6 FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
In the future, new technologies that have already been tested in other fermentation
processes may also be applied for rapid, online monitoring of vinegar fermenta-
tions. For example, a novel sensor has been recently proposed for rapid monitoring
of industrial malolactic fermentation of wines, which monitored the physicochemi-
cal changes during the fermentation process. The sensor was based on ultrasound
technology that is attached to the stainless-steel tanks of the fermentation plant
```
(Figure 20.7) and can be applied to all fermentation processes. Ultrasound technol-
```
ogy is simple, non-invasive, rapid, accurate, inexpensive, and can provide online
monitoring and automation. By this technology, the ultrasound velocity diffusion
into the fermentation broth that can be related to the overall concentration in the
```
solution is measured (Figure 20.7). The results showed the feasibility of the sensor
```
```
for rapid monitoring of the fermentation progress (Çelik et al., 2018).
```
Raman spectroscopy has also been applied for food processing investigation. Its
principle is based on the interaction of the sample with a light beam. An inelastic
collision between an incident photon and a molecule of the sample occurs, causing
a change to the vibrational or the rotational energy of the molecule. The scattered
radiation is then shifted to a different wavelength. This shift is called a Raman shift.
Specific chemical groups generate specific Raman shifts, enabling discrimination
among different chemical compounds. Disadvantages lie with the weak signal, while
portable Raman systems do not provide as good spectral detection range and spectral
resolution as benchtop instruments. Fluorescence also interferes with Raman spec-
```
tra, eliminating its applications (Jin et al., 2016).
```
Generally, Raman spectroscopy has numerous advantages compared to other
spectroscopic techniques including its applicability to solid, liquid, and gas samples
```
FIGURE 20.7 Ultrasound sensor (A) attached to the fermenter, and (B) principle of signal
```
transmission through the fermenter broth.
435Rapid Detection Methods for Online Monitoring
directly without any preparation of the samples, especially in aqueous and complex
samples and the potential for automation and online measurements. A serious dis-
advantage is that Raman spectrometers are sensitive to temperature changes and
over time and need frequent calibration. For this reason, a new infra-red/Fourier
```
transform coupled to Raman spectroscopy (FT–RS) system with auto-calibration
```
was developed for online monitoring of wine fermentation. The Raman spectrom-
eter contained both a measurement and a reference optical path to obtain more
accurate results. The instrument also contained a 1,064 nm laser source and a liquid
nitrogen cooled Ge detector. For online measurements, the FT-IR was combined to
an optical fiber probe that was sealed in a filter tube to eliminate scattering effects
caused by impure samples during the fermentation progress and placed in the fer-
mentation tank. The results demonstrated the ability of this system for real-time
monitoring of chemical changes during fermentation, offering qualitative and quan-
titative analysis. Sugar, alcohol, and glycerol were determined with great accuracy
by this FT–RS system, and the results were in good agreement with other reports
```
(Wang et al., 2014).
```
In-line monitoring of glycose and ethanol was also conducted by a non-contact
Raman spectroscopy probe during yeast fermentation. The Raman probe enabled
non-invasive measurement through glass vessels or inspection glasses of the biore-
actors. The practical advantage of this probe is that it did not require sterilization
as it was not immersed into the fermentation broth. The probe was attached on an
adjustable slide next to the bioreactor to enable the optical alignment of the light
beam just behind the inner wall of the reactor through a 9 mm borosilicate glass. The
penetration length of the incident light was less than 2 mm, minimizing the scatter-
ing effects. A 785-nm laser was used for the excitation of the Raman probe, while
a system of mirrors and lenses was used for laser beam and signal light focusing.
Finally, the Raman signal of the foresaid Raman probe had a bigger wavelength than
the inside light due to Stokes shift and was driven through a quartz fiber to a Raman
spectrometer for detection by a CCD detector. Glycose and ethanol were monitored
and quantified at real time by their Raman spectra revealing different characteristic
peaks in a spectral range from 1,500 to 3,200 cm −1. The results, after multiple linear
regression analysis, were in good agreement with the results from HPLC analysis
```
(Schalk et al., 2017).
```
One of the most promising approaches for online monitoring of various fermen-
tation processes is the use of multisensory systems, such as electronic noses and
electronic tongues. These systems offer qualitative and quantitative analysis of mul-
ticomponent media. Both systems contain three major parts: a sample delivery sys-
tem, a detection system, and a data processing system. The sample system delivers
the sample directly into the detector. The detection system includes a sensor array
that consists of different chemical sensors that recognize simultaneously different
volatile compounds in a gas sample for e-noses or various compounds of different
nature in liquid samples for e-tongues and experiences a change usually in electrical
properties. In most sensor e-nose arrays, non-selective sensors are used that react to
all volatile compounds causing a change to the physical parameters measured pro-
viding a unique pattern or fingerprinting of the sample. A computing system, finally,
is used for data recording and processing. The advantages of this technology are the
436 Advances in Vinegar Production
sensitivity, the easiness to construct, and the short time of analysis. However, these
systems mainly suffer from contaminations or instability and require occasional
recalibration. Despite the disadvantages, they have become popular as non-invasive
techniques for real-time bioprocessing control. E-noses usually use chemical gas
sensors as the sensory systems that can be piezoelectric, electrochemical, optical,
```
calorimetric sensors, and biosensors or combined with mass spectrometry (MS),
```
```
ion mobility spectrometry (IMS), and MIR instruments. They mainly include
```
```
metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS), metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transis-
```
```
tors (MOSFET), organic conducting polymer (OCP), quartz crystal microbalance
```
```
(QCM), and surface acoustic wave (SAW) sensors. The sensor array of e-tongues
```
may consist of electrochemical, such as potentiometric, voltametric, amperometric,
impedimetric, and conductimetric, optical, mass, and biosensors. Finally, an innova-
tive “e-panel” combination of e-nose, e-tongue, and e-eye is an emerging and very
promising tool for online monitoring of bioprocesses, providing information for
```
gases, liquids, and colors (Jiang et al., 2015; Peris and Escuder-Gilabert, 2013).
```
20.7 CONCLUSIONS
The online monitoring of the vinegar fermentation process is crucial to ensure firstly
the aseptic conditions of the fermentation reaction and secondly the high efficiency
and reproducibility of the process, as well as the good quality of the final vinegar
product. A few efforts have been made for the development of online systems for
control of the progress of vinegar fermentation. These efforts include the application
mainly of near- and mid-infrared spectroscopy, as well as gas chromatography and
specialized chemical sensors. However, more online detection systems providing
rapid analysis, simplicity, and low-cost analysis should still be developed to facilitate
the vinegar fermentation process.

21
Fraud, Quality,
and Methods for
Characterization
and Authentication
of Vinegars
Rocío Ríos-Reina, María del Pilar Segura-Borrego,
Cristina Úbeda, María Lourdes Morales,
and Raquel María Callejón
21.1 INTRODUCTION
Nowadays there is a growing demand for high-quality food products, one such prod-
uct being vinegar. In the past, vinegar was considered a secondary product within the
family of fermented products and lacked a recognized quality standard. However, in
the last few years a radical change has taken place. Quality vinegar, which until
recently was only really appreciated in haute cuisine and gastronomy, has seen its
household demand increasing worldwide, as many consumers now acknowledge it
as a high-quality product. This has led to a huge diversity of vinegars appearing in
the market, with a wide variety of final sale prices according to their characteristics

21.2 Frauds ........................................................................................................... 443
21.3 Quality Parameters .......................................................................................444

21.5 Methods for Classifying and Authenticating Vinegars ................................446
