The carbon footprint of vinegar ranges between 1.94 and 2.54 kg CO 2 eq/L vin-
egar, for Sagrantino and Grechetto grapes, respectively. This difference is due to the
fact that the transport operations for Sagrantino grapes have lower impact, while the
impact of cultivation is quite similar for the two vine varieties. The ecological foot-
print of aged vinegar ranges from 9.83 to 13.23 g m 2 /L for Sagrantino and Grechetto
grapes, respectively, while the water footprint of aged vinegar varies between 1,332
and 1,892 L/L vinegar.
Regarding the indicators of the EPD 2013 method, contained in the SimaPro 8
software, the impact on Ozone Layer Depletion category of aged vinegar produced
from Sagrantino grapes is about 1.43 × 10 −7, while that of aged vinegar obtained
```
from Grechetto grapes is 1.8 × 10 −7 kg trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11) eq/L. The
```
impact on acidification category of aged vinegar produced from Sagrantino grapes
is about 0.0179, while that of aged vinegar obtained from Grechetto grapes is 0.0233
kg SO2 eq/L. The impact on eutrophication category of aged vinegar produced from
Sagrantino grapes is about 0.0064 kg PO 4 eq/L, while that of aged vinegar obtained
from Grechetto grapes is 0.0091 kg PO 4 eq/L. The impact on photochemical oxida-
tion of aged vinegar produced from Sagrantino grapes is −0.00019 kg C 2 H4 eq/L,
while that of aged vinegar obtained from Grechetto grapes is −0.00014 kg C 2 H4
eq/L. The results of the different impact evaluation methods confirm that vinegar
produced in the farm from Sagrantino grapes, using a decentralized production sys-
tem, has a lower environmental burden.
Figures 22.2 and 22.3 present the contribution to the impact indicators of the
different processes, which belong to the life cycle of aged vinegar produced from
Grechetto and Sagrantino grapes, respectively. In these figures only four impacts
are considered: carbon footprint, acidification, eutrophication, and water footprint,
```
according to Hoekstra et al. (2012).
```
As in most food industry products, the cultivation phase is the one that contributes
the most to the impacts of aged vinegar. Cultivation is also the phase with the highest
consumption of water, as indicated by the water footprint indicator, and also con-
tributes to the Eutrophication and Acidification impacts. The transport phase con-
tributes mostly to the following impacts: Acidification, Eutrophication, and Carbon
Footprint, while consumption of water during transport is very limited. The contri-
bution of transport to the total impact of vinegar is never higher than 3%. Despite
that, it can be seen that producing vinegar in the farm with a decentralized pro-
cess can reduce by about 1% of the total carbon footprint. The transformation phase
hardly ever contributes more than 50% to the total impact of aged vinegar. The only
exception is for the carbon footprint. In this case the GHG emissions released during
484 Advances in Vinegar Production
packaging production have an important contribution that is even higher than that of
the cultivation phase.
Important considerations must be reported on the following processes: nutrient
management, ageing, packaging, boiling, pressing, and transport. Nutrient manage-
ment accounts for more than 30% of the total impact on the carbon footprint. It has
also an important impact on the water footprint, due to the amount of water required
```
in the production of the fertilizer (mainly urea). The nutrient management process,
```
which consists mainly of fertilizer production and distribution, has also an important
impact on acidification and eutrophication. Ageing contribution to the total impact
varies from 3 to 9% due to the addition of must plus vinegar to the aged mixture, to
balance the losses that occur during 1 year of ageing in barrels. Packaging contri-
bution to the total impact ranges from 15 to 28%. Boiling and pressing contribute
respectively from 1 to 20% of the total impact. Wine cooling has a reduced impact,
because this operation is quite limited in time.

485Life Cycle Assessment in the Vinegar Sector
22.5 CONCLUSIONS
In this chapter, the impact of the food industry on the environment is briefly dis-
cussed. After examining what an LCA is and the main norms that regulate life cycle
analysis and impact certification, a case study is presented on the LCA analysis of
aged vinegar, based on a decentralized production chain in a small farm situated in
Umbria, Italy. The aged vinegar impact was calculated and expressed using differ-
```
ent indicators (carbon footprint, ecological footprint, water footprint, acidification,
```
```
eutrophication, ozone layer depletion, photochemical oxidation). The process system
```
was divided in the following sections: cultivation, pressing, boiling must, wine mak-
ing and acetification, aged vinegar production, packaging. The energy consumption
```
and materials consumption (fertilizers, herbicides, etc.) were measured at the dif-
```
ferent phases. Aged vinegar was produced in two ways: in the first case wine was
```
produced in an external winery (using Grechetto grapes), and in the second case the
```
FIGURE 22.3 Process contribution to the impact of aged vinegar produced from Sagrantino
```
grapes [(a) carbon footprint, (b) acidification, (c) eutrophication, (d) water footprint LCA,
```
```
according to Hoekstra et al. (2012)].
```
486 Advances in Vinegar Production
```
wine was produced in the farm (using Sagrantino grapes). The wine was then used to
```
produce an inoculum for the production of aged vinegar. The inoculum was mixed
```
with boiled must. The results show that: (1) the aged vinegar has a carbon foot-
```
print of 1.94 or 2.54 kg CO2 /L, when produced from Sagrantino grapes or Grechetto
```
grapes, respectively; (2) the ecological footprint of the aged vinegar is 9.83 or 13.23
```
```
gm 2 /kg when produced from Sagrantino grapes or Grechetto grapes, respectively;
```
```
(3) the water footprint of the aged vinegar is 1,332 or 1892 L/L, when produced from
```
Sagrantino grapes or Grechetto grapes, respectively. The most impacting processes
in aged vinegar life cycle are: nutrient management, ageing, packaging, boiling, and
pressing.
